glance.who: ICE, Border Patrol and CBP agents
glance.what: Immigration agents fired on people in 31 confirmed incidents since Jan. 2025, killing nine; one agent charged

what_changed:
TAP's list of shootings by ICE, Border Patrol and CBP agents during enforcement since January 20, 2025, one line each in date order, with one source per line. Incidents with their own TAP entry are linked, not retold. Agents are not named here.

- Jan. 20, 2025, Coventry, Vermont (Border Patrol): at an Interstate 91 stop, a CBP summary says driver Teresa Youngblut opened fire and a Border Patrol agent was killed; an agent returned fire, wounding Youngblut and fatally shooting passenger Ophelia Bauckholt, who the agent said was drawing a gun. Youngblut was indicted on federal firearm and assault charges (VTDigger), and in August 2025 a superseding indictment charged her with the killed agent's murder, and DOJ is seeking the death penalty (Justice Department, via Vermont Business Magazine).

- Feb. 11, 2025, Boca Chica, Cameron County, Texas (Border Patrol): an agent responding to suspected smuggling shot and hospitalized one person (KRGV).

- Mar. 15, 2025, South Padre Island, Texas (ICE HSI): U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez was fatally shot at a traffic stop; DHS's role surfaced only in 2026 records, and a grand jury declined to indict (CNN; own entry).

- July 1, 2025, Nogales, Arizona (CBP officers): a CBP officer shot a man in the arm and thigh at the DeConcini port of entry after, CBP says, he threw rocks at officers (13 News).

- July 31, 2025, Black Forest, Colorado (ICE): an officer fired three shots into a car ICE says nearly hit officers; no injuries were reported and the two occupants fled (KKTV).

- Aug. 16, 2025, San Bernardino, California (CBP): officers fired into Francisco Longoria's work truck after breaking its windows, narrowly missing his 18-year-old son. He was charged with assault; the government dismissed the case on Sept. 17, 2025, and the family sued the United States on July 24, 2026 (ABC7; federal complaint).

- Sept. 12, 2025, Franklin Park, Illinois (ICE): Silverio Villegas González was fatally shot at a traffic stop; bodycam undercut DHS's account (NBC News; own entry).

- Oct. 4, 2025, Chicago (Border Patrol): U.S. citizen Marimar Martinez was shot five times; her assault charges were dropped on Nov. 20, 2025 (CBS Chicago; own entry).

- Oct. 21, 2025, Los Angeles (ICE): Carlitos Ricardo Parias, a TikTok streamer who filmed raids, was shot in the elbow and a deputy U.S. marshal was hit in the hand after agents boxed in his car (NBC News). A judge dismissed his assault indictment with prejudice on Dec. 27, 2025, citing violations of his rights (AP).

- Oct. 29, 2025, Phoenix (ICE): an officer fired twice at an SUV pulling away from a stop on Interstate 17; the driver was hospitalized, and early reports did not say whether gunfire hit him (AZFamily).

- Oct. 30, 2025, Ontario, California (ICE): U.S. citizen Carlos Jimenez was shot in the back of the shoulder; his lawyers say he had stopped to warn agents about children at a bus stop, and DHS says he reversed at officers. He was charged with assault (Daily Gazette); the San Bernardino County Sentinel reports a diversion deal under which the charges are to be dismissed later in 2026.

- Dec. 11, 2025, Starr County, Texas (Border Patrol): Isaias Sanchez Barbosa, 31, of Mexico, was fatally shot during an arrest attempt near the Rio Grande; the agent says he fired in self-defense during a fight. A Starr County grand jury declined to indict the agent in June 2026 (KRGV; Texas Tribune).

- Dec. 21, 2025, St. Paul, Minnesota (ICE): an officer fired two rounds at Juan Carlos Rodriguez Romero's SUV, hitting no one, after DHS says he struck officers (CNN). Prosecutors moved to drop his assault charges for insufficient evidence in June 2026 (Minnesota Reformer).

- Dec. 24, 2025, Glen Burnie, Maryland (ICE): officers fired at a van ICE says rammed its vehicles; county police said the driver was hit by gunfire and that a man hurt in the crash was already in an ICE vehicle (WBAL-TV).

- Jan. 7, 2026, Minneapolis (ICE): U.S. citizen Renee Good was fatally shot in her SUV (CNN; own entry).

- Jan. 8, 2026, Portland, Oregon (Border Patrol): agents fired during a stop targeting Yorlenys Zambrano-Contreras; she and driver Luis Niño-Moncada were found with gunshot wounds, and he was charged with assaulting a federal officer (KPTV).

- Jan. 14, 2026, Minneapolis (ICE): Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis was shot in the leg; video undercut DHS's account, charges against him were dropped and the officer was charged (AP; own entry).

- Jan. 21, 2026, Willowbrook, Los Angeles County (DHS agent, agency not stated): an agent fired at a man DHS says rammed officers during a smuggling arrest; DHS said he was not hit (New York Times).

- Jan. 24, 2026, Minneapolis (Border Patrol and CBP): U.S. citizen Alex Pretti was fatally shot (AP; own entry).

- Jan. 27, 2026, Arivaca, Arizona (Border Patrol): agents shot Patrick Gary Schlegel after, the FBI says, he fired at agents and a helicopter (AP); he was later indicted on charges including attempted murder of a federal officer (KTAR).

- Feb. 10, 2026, Roxbury Township, New Jersey (ICE): an officer shot out the tires of a vehicle DHS says was driven at him; the New Jersey Attorney General's office is investigating (News 12).

- Feb. 22, 2026, Pittsburg, New Hampshire (Border Patrol): an agent shot a person near the Canadian border after, CBP's commissioner said, the person fired first (AP).

- Apr. 7, 2026, Patterson, California (ICE): officers shot Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez, who ICE says tried to run an officer over; bystander video shows his car reversing and pulling away (NBC News). He was indicted on assault charges, and his lawyer disputes ICE's account (KTVU).

- June 15, 2026, Stafford Township, New Jersey (ICE): per the criminal complaint, Eduardo Cruz Garcia's van struck an agent as he drove off from a stop; his lawyer said the agent fired three shots and that Cruz Garcia was struck in the back of the right arm. He was charged with assaulting a federal officer (Philadelphia Inquirer).

- June 16, 2026, Blaine, Washington (Border Patrol): an agent shot and injured a person in a residential area near the Canadian border; the FBI is investigating (Seattle Times).

- July 1, 2026, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (ICE): an officer fired at an SUV driving away from a stop and hit a parked car; ICE says the driver rammed its vehicle, and surveillance video shows the SUV appearing to clip it (CNN).

- July 7, 2026, Houston (ICE): Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, not the operation's target, was fatally shot (AP; own entry).

- July 10, 2026, Blythe, California (Border Patrol): agents shot and killed a man who CBP says stabbed an agent; the FBI and DHS inspector general are investigating (AZFamily).

- July 13, 2026, Biddeford, Maine (ICE): Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, not the operation's target, was fatally shot (Maine Morning Star; own entry).

- July 14, 2026 (policy): after the Houston and Maine killings, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ordered ICE to pause most vehicle stops for new training, sources told ABC News; the next day President Trump said he did not want the stops suspended and Mullin said they were "on the same page" (Texas Tribune).

- Sept. 20, 2026, Austin, Texas (ICE): Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a delivery driver, was shot in the back; he was charged with assaulting an officer, and on Sept. 30 a magistrate judge let the case proceed after prosecutors showed body-camera footage and denied him bond as a flight risk (AP).

- Sept. 30, 2026 (policy): an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations memo signed by executive associate director Marcos D. Charles bars officers from chasing vehicles that fail to pull over, requires every officer at a vehicle stop to wear and activate a body camera, and limits vehicle stops to officers who have completed specific training. The same day, testimony at Garcés Pérez's bond hearing showed the officer who shot him wore no body camera and the officer who had one turned it off during the pursuit (AP).

- Oct. 8, 2026, the Bronx, New York (ICE): an officer fired seven rounds into Oscar Belgal's car, hitting him in the neck while his 5-year-old son sat unhurt in the back; DHS says he rammed ICE vehicles, while the NYPD commissioner said he was parking when plainclothes officers approached with guns drawn (NBC New York). A judge barred his deportation and the Bronx district attorney opened an investigation (TheGrio); on Oct. 15 he appeared in immigration court with the bullet still lodged in his neck, his lawyers said (The National News Desk).
legal_status: One agent charged: the ICE officer in the Sosa-Celis shooting faces state assault and false-report charges and a federal false-statements indictment. Grand juries in Cameron County and Starr County, Texas, declined to indict the agents in the Ruben Ray Martinez and Sanchez Barbosa killings. Under investigation: the Belgal shooting (Bronx DA), Roxbury (New Jersey Attorney General), Blythe (FBI, DHS inspector general), Blaine (FBI), and the cases in the own entries. Charges against five people fired on were dropped or dismissed: Longoria, Marimar Martinez, Parias, Rodriguez Romero and Sosa-Celis. Also charged after being fired on, with no outcome found unless stated: Youngblut, Jimenez (diversion deal reported), Niño-Moncada, Schlegel, Mendoza Hernandez, Cruz Garcia and Garcés Pérez. Sued: Longoria's family sued the United States (C.D. Cal., July 24, 2026); other suits are in the own entries.

human_toll.summary: In 31 incidents TAP confirmed, immigration agents fired on drivers, passengers and people on foot from Vermont to California; nine people were killed, including U.S. citizens Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and others were wounded, some with bullets still lodged in them. Several of those killed were not the people agents were looking for, and a 5-year-old was in the back seat of the car fired on in the Bronx.

human_toll.caveat: These are TAP's own counts of incidents confirmed in official statements, court records or major and regional outlets, built from outside lists and checked one by one; they will miss shootings never reported, and they exclude off-duty incidents, a Jan. 27, 2025 incident in Fronton, Texas where shots were fired at agents from Mexico and no source says agents fired back, and a May 2025 Brownsville chase in which no source says an immigration agent fired. The Trace, a gun-violence newsroom, counts 32 incidents in which immigration agents shot at people (nine killed, 15 injured) as of Oct. 9, 2026, says its numbers are likely an undercount, and covers some cases TAP excludes, such as Washington, D.C. crime-surge patrols. DHS's stated account in most cases is that the person used a vehicle as a weapon or attacked officers, and that agents fired "defensive shots"; in the Vermont, Arizona and New Hampshire cases officials say the person shot fired first. Several of those accounts have been contradicted by video, witnesses or courts, and others have not been tested.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence that each listed incident happened as summarized: every line rests on an official statement, a court record or a major or regional outlet, and outside lists (The Trace, Wikipedia, the ACLU of Texas) were used only as pointers. Many lines rest on DHS or CBP's own account, which is attributed. MODERATE confidence on two details: the San Bernardino County Sentinel alone reports the Jimenez diversion deal, and Phoenix reports did not say whether gunfire hit the driver. No agents are named in this entry; people fired on are named only when they or their family went public or court filings or major outlets name them, and others are described. The Sept. 30 vehicle-stop memo rests on AP, which obtained it; ICE and DHS had no immediate comment.

section_summaries.human_toll: Nine people killed and many wounded, including three U.S. citizens killed; charges against five people agents fired on were later dropped or dismissed.

cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a broader pattern of DHS using its administrative subpoena power to pull personal data on immigrants from state and local systems built for other purposes, here a state-funded benefits program in a Democratic-led state, under a federal-fraud framing that reaches well beyond the federal-benefit question DHS says it is investigating.

what_changed: On May 12, 2025, the Los Angeles field office of ICE's Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) issued a Title 8 subpoena aimed at California's Cash Assistance Program for Immigrants (CAPI), a state-funded program providing **cash assistance to aged, blind, and disabled immigrants with lawful status who are ineligible for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) because of their immigration status**. The subpoena asked the Los Angeles County Department of Public Social Services, which administers CAPI in the county, for all program records from January 2021 to the present: applicants' names and dates of birth, copies of applications, immigration status, proof of SSI ineligibility, and affidavits supporting applications. DHS said the purpose was to determine whether ineligible people in the country illegally had received federal SSI from the Social Security Administration, and cited an April 15, 2025 presidential memorandum directing the Homeland Security Secretary to keep ineligible immigrants from receiving Social Security funds and to prioritize civil or criminal enforcement against states or localities. DHS's press release framed the action as investigating California for 'providing federal benefits to illegal aliens,' even though CAPI receives no federal funding and, per the county and state, is limited to non-citizens authorized by law to receive benefits. Secretary Kristi Noem said: "If you are an illegal immigrant, you should leave now. The gravy train is over. While this subpoena focuses only on Los Angeles County -- it is just the beginning." The New York Times described it as believed to be one of the first Trump administration requests for state personal data on immigrants outside the criminal justice system. After a May 28, 2025 inquiry from LA Public Press, a county spokesperson said LA County had not released applicants' personal information and had instead sent DHS information on the program's eligibility rules and asked for a meeting; the spokesperson did not say whether this was a formal refusal, and the county had not filed a legal challenge.
legal_status: No lawsuit, court ruling or inspector-general finding identified. The subpoena is an administrative Title 8 subpoena, not a court order; as of June 2025 LA County had not complied with its request for personal data or challenged it in court, and no DHS action in court to enforce it has been reported.

human_toll.summary: The subpoena sought identifying records, including immigration status, on everyone who applied to Los Angeles County's CAPI program since January 2021: older, blind or disabled immigrants with lawful status who rely on the state aid because they cannot get federal SSI. The county says it has not handed over their personal data. Local advocates said the demand created fear and mistrust among immigrants about sharing information with government programs, and the Migration Policy Institute noted such actions could deter eligible residents from applying for benefits.

glance.what: Cut DHS's civil rights office ~85% and its detention ombudsman 90%+ as ICE detention expanded

harm.who: DHS civil rights and detention oversight

what_changed:
On March 21, 2025, DHS ordered a work stoppage and issued Reduction-in-Force notices to nearly all staff at three offices: the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, the Immigration Detention Ombudsman -- which investigates complaints about conditions and treatment in ICE detention -- and the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman; these are DHS's own internal oversight mechanisms, specifically created to catch and address civil-rights violations and detention-condition abuses within the department's own operations, distinct from external oversight bodies like the Inspector General or Congress. According to the later lawsuit, CRCL then had about 150 full-time employees and the detention ombudsman's office about 110, most of them case managers assigned to detention facilities. A DHS spokesperson said the offices were closed because they "obstructed immigration enforcement by adding bureaucratic hurdles and undermining DHS's mission." The RIF notices prompted an April 24, 2025 lawsuit from Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, the Southern Border Communities Coalition, and the Urban Justice Center. DHS publicly announced on May 23, 2025 that it would not formally abolish the three offices, but the reduction in force itself went ahead; the court later noted that it "has already occurred."

In February 2026, Mother Jones reported that a February 2 letter from 22 Democratic members of Congress to Secretary Noem highlighted that staffing for the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman's office had been reduced by 85 and 91 percent, respectively. In the same article, Rebekah Tosado, a two-decade CRCL employee laid off in March 2025, said that to her knowledge CRCL had only two full-time staff members left, not counting its political-appointee acting head. A February 13, 2026 sworn declaration DHS filed in the lawsuit likewise counted two full-time federal employees at CRCL, while saying 25 to 30 contractors and several attorneys also work for the office and that its staffing is appropriate -- indicating the May 2025 reversal kept the offices nominally open without restoring their federal staffing. The staffing cuts leave ICE's rapidly expanding detention and enforcement operations -- documented in other TAP entries, including a separate AP review of ICE employee misconduct -- with substantially diminished internal capacity to receive, investigate, and act on civil-rights and detention-condition complaints. On March 27, 2026, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes denied the plaintiffs' motion for partial reconsideration of her July 2025 order denying their preliminary-injunction motion as moot; accepting the plaintiffs' clarification, she denied the injunction for lack of a showing of irreparable harm. In a May 12, 2026 court filing, DHS said the FY2026 appropriations law signed April 30, 2026 had completely defunded the Immigration Detention Ombudsman's office and that the office was being wound down, and argued the case was effectively moot; the plaintiffs responded that the zero funding was what DHS itself had requested and did not repeal the office's statutory duties. On July 1, 2026, Reyes heard the parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, took them under advisement, and directed the parties to settlement talks; after a July 21 meeting at DHS headquarters the parties asked for more time, and on July 31 the court stayed the case. After the parties' September 29 joint status report, the court on October 2 ordered another report on the progress of settlement discussions by November 30, 2026. No ruling on the merits, and no independent audit restoring functional staffing levels, has been identified.
legal_status: Sued: Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, Southern Border Communities Coalition and Urban Justice Center sued DHS and the Secretary of Homeland Security (official capacity) on April 24, 2025 (D.D.C. No. 1:25-cv-01270, Judge Ana C. Reyes), seeking restoration of the three offices. A preliminary injunction was denied in July 2025, and reconsideration was denied on March 27, 2026 for lack of a showing of irreparable harm. Cross-motions for summary judgment were argued July 1, 2026 and are under advisement; the case has been stayed since July 31, 2026 for settlement talks, with the next joint status report due November 30, 2026. No ruling on the merits.

human_toll.summary: DHS sent reduction-in-force notices to nearly all staff of its Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and every employee of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman's office, most of them case managers assigned to detention facilities, per the lawsuit. People in ICE detention and others who bring civil-rights complaints against DHS lost most of the internal staff meant to take and investigate those complaints. Of the implementation, training, monitoring and oversight needed for disability-law compliance, a laid-off CRCL employee said, "None of that can be happening now."

pull_quote: ICE contractors compile daily dossiers on flagged social-media posters -- including name, location, date of birth, workplace, Social Security number, vehicle registration, and criminal history -- under an $8 million surveillance contract, a Wall Street Journal investigation found.

glance.what: Sent hundreds of subpoenas to tech firms to unmask ICE critics; a judge blocked one warning notice

what_changed:
By October 2025, DHS was publicly calling the filming of ICE agents "doxing," beyond the term's traditional meaning (publishing someone's private identifying information to enable harassment), while White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller placed "organized doxing" on a "continuum" with violence and a Trump national security directive tied doxing to domestic terrorism. That framing accompanied a subpoena program already under way: DHS issued hundreds of administrative subpoenas to major tech companies -- including Google, Meta, Reddit, Discord, and X -- demanding names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other identifying data for accounts that criticized ICE, reported ICE agents' locations, or attended protests against immigration enforcement, including operators of anonymous Instagram accounts documenting ICE raids. In one specific instance reported by The New Republic, DHS subpoenaed Google for account data tied to a 67-year-old U.S. citizen after he sent an email criticizing a DHS prosecutor over an immigration deportation matter. DHS lawyers said in court filings that the subpoenas aim to "investigate threats to its own officers or impediments to their officers." The Electronic Frontier Foundation sued DHS and ICE in April 2026 after the agencies ignored a FOIA request seeking records of the subpoena program; separately, when specific subpoena targets challenged them in court, DHS withdrew some of those subpoenas before a judge could rule, though no comprehensive public accounting of the program's total scope has been provided by DHS. Separately, The New York Times reported that Reddit, Meta, and Google voluntarily complied with at least some of the subpoenas rather than contesting them, though at least one of the companies said it notifies users and gives them a 14-day window to challenge a subpoena in court before complying.

EFF's April 14, 2026 complaints to the California and New York Attorneys General allege Google engaged in deceptive trade practices -- Google disclosed Cornell Ph.D. candidate Amandla Thomas-Johnson's data to ICE on May 8, 2025 and notified him only the same day, breaking its own long-standing advance-notice policy with none of that policy's stated exceptions (gag order, threat, child safety, hijacked account) applying. Neither AG's office had publicly announced a formal investigation. EFF's August 2026 commentary on tech companies' private pushback documents Meta pushing back on September 11, 2025 ICE subpoenas targeting a Pennsylvania ICE-documentation account by telling ICE it lacked statutory authority, and ICE withdrawing those subpoenas in January 2026 after the account's operators challenged them in court with ACLU help; it also cites Reddit's July-December 2025 transparency report disclosing three DHS subpoenas covering 11 users, all withdrawn after Reddit's objection.

A Wall Street Journal investigation, reported in August 2026, found ICE runs a round-the-clock contractor operation scouring the public internet, from Facebook to Instagram to X, for criticism, paying private firms millions to flag posts as threats; contractors (working under an $8 million contract between ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, Amivero, and subcontractor Guidehouse) compile daily dossiers on flagged posters including name, location, date of birth, workplace, Social Security number, vehicle registration, and criminal history where available. ICE's surveillance-technology and consultant spending rose 57% year over year to $258 million in Trump's first full year back in office. DHS has since escalated beyond administrative subpoenas to grand jury subpoenas, which are harder for targets to fight, and has sent agents to question people in person over their posts; attorneys note most unmasked posters are never charged, leaving the tactic to function as intimidation even when it doesn't lead to prosecution. Per the same reporting, ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility describes the underlying monitoring as investigating at least 131 incidents of doxxing and threats toward agency personnel between January 2025 and March 2026. Of roughly 10 individuals identified as having formally challenged their subpoenas, judges upheld 4 grand jury subpoenas, DHS abandoned 3 cases, and 3 remained pending as of the WSJ's reporting -- no charges have been filed in any case where a subpoena was upheld; outcomes for challenged subpoenas were mixed, not uniform withdrawal, though the no-charges-filed pattern persists across every outcome. The WSJ also described what appears to be the same Reddit episode, in which Reddit objected on First Amendment grounds to DHS subpoenas targeting 11 accounts for "content critical of federal actions."

Members of Congress pressed the companies in two letters -- a February 25, 2026 House Homeland Security Committee Democrats' letter (Thompson/Correa/Thanedar) and a March 2, 2026 letter from Reps. Kelly and Jayapal plus 26 colleagues, both to major tech/telecom CEOs, neither of which any source reviewed shows as having received a public company response. A newer, September 1, 2026 letter from Sen. Wyden and Rep. Jayapal to Chief Justice Roberts and the GAO asks for an audit of DHS/DOJ nondisclosure demands on subpoena recipients, citing a documented case (DHS's Harvard subpoenas) where the agency asked the recipient to keep its subpoenas secret and then publicized the same enforcement action itself. Separately, EFF's own August 26, 2026 case list documents the program's target types extending beyond tech/social platforms: a March 2026 PayPal/Venmo subpoena for a Minnesota racial-justice organization, which PayPal/Venmo answered with data on March 20, 2026, and an April 12, 2026 summons to T-Mobile for Minnesota journalist Georgia Fort's records, which T-Mobile answered the same day, issued under 19 U.S.C. 1509, a customs law. According to The Guardian's reporting, DHS obtained six months of Fort's phone records, covering more than 10,000 calls and texts, without notice to her, and served Google a separate customs summons for her YouTube data after a federal magistrate judge had twice rejected prosecutors' warrant applications for that data; Google did not comply. EFF's list shows the same customs-law authority behind several of the social-media demands, including those to Meta, Reddit and X.

On September 15, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras granted a preliminary injunction barring DHS from taking any action against David Streever, a Rochester, New York man, based on a warning notice DHS had issued him over an email in which Streever called then-acting ICE Director Todd Lyons a "monstrous human being" and compared him to Nazi official Reinhard Heydrich. Federal agents later tried to track Streever down at his home, an airport and a hotel to confront him about the email and serve the warning notice; the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) sued DHS and ICE on his behalf. Contreras found the warning notice likely violated Streever's First Amendment rights, writing that "the threat of such an investigation or prosecution looms over him like the sword of Damocles, and he is forced to self-censor under that threat." The injunction also bars DHS from issuing similar warnings suggesting Streever cannot engage in non-threatening criticism of the government.
legal_status: Sued: EFF sued DHS and ICE on April 22, 2026 over unanswered FOIA requests for records of the subpoena program. FIRE sued DHS and ICE on David Streever's behalf in July 2026; on September 15, 2026, Judge Rudolph Contreras granted in part a preliminary injunction barring DHS and ICE from acting on the warning notice or issuing substantially similar threats, finding the notice likely violated the First Amendment, but declined to block the investigation, which the government says ICE closed; the case continues. By October 2025, federal judges had temporarily blocked DHS's subpoena to Meta for at least three immigration activists' Instagram account information. Several challenged subpoenas were withdrawn before any court ruled on them, including Doe v. DHS (N.D. Cal.), dismissed in February 2026 after DHS withdrew its subpoena, and the Pennsylvania MontCo Community Watch challenge. Georgia Fort, a defendant in the Cities Church prosecution, has asked the court to impound or return the phone logs DHS obtained; no ruling was found. EFF's April 14, 2026 complaints asked the California and New York attorneys general to investigate Google; no announced investigation was found in the sources reviewed. No court has ruled the subpoena program as a whole unlawful.

human_toll.summary: People who criticized ICE or documented its operations, mostly anonymous account operators, along with protest attendees, a retiree who emailed a DHS attorney, journalists who covered a Minnesota church protest and a racial-justice group, had identifying data sought from tech, payment and phone companies without a judge's approval, and some of it was handed over. Some were visited or questioned at home by agents, and one man was served a warning notice that a judge found likely forced him to self-censor. Attorneys say most unmasked posters are never charged.

title: DHS cut short humanitarian parole for hundreds of thousands, ending CHNV and CBP One parole and stalling Ukrainian renewals

officials.name: Donald Trump
officials.role: President; Executive Order 14165 directed DHS to end categorical parole programs including CHNV and to stop paroling people in through CBP One

officials.name: Benjamine Huffman
officials.role: then-Acting Secretary of Homeland Security; signed the January 2025 memo allowing review of parole and expedited removal for CHNV and CBP One parolees

officials.name: Andrew Davidson
officials.role: Acting Deputy Director of USCIS; signed the Feb. 14, 2025 memo pausing benefit requests from U4U, CHNV and family reunification parolees

officials.name: Kristi Noem
officials.role: then-Secretary of Homeland Security; signed the March 2025 notice terminating the CHNV programs and the parole granted under them

officials.name: Tricia McLaughlin
officials.role: DHS Assistant Secretary; defended the June 2025 CHNV termination notices

officials.name: Rodney Scott
officials.role: CBP Commissioner; issued the April 21, 2026 memo used to re-terminate CBP One parole after the court vacated the 2025 terminations

people.unnamed_affected: Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan and Venezuelan CHNV parolees; people paroled in after CBP One border appointments; Ukrainians in Uniting for Ukraine waiting on re-parole and work permits; family reunification parolees; the pseudonymous plaintiffs and organizational plaintiffs in the Boston suits; and a Massachusetts-born immigration lawyer, a U.S. citizen, who received a CBP One-style termination email.

status: CHNV parole ended June 2025 after the Supreme Court's stay; the First Circuit found it likely lawful. A judge ruled the CBP One terminations unlawful Mar. 31, 2026, but DHS re-terminated; she sanctioned DHS and on Oct. 16, 2026 set an Oct. 19 deadline for class lists.
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (Executive Order 14165 directs DHS to end categorical parole programs) through 2026-10-16 (Burroughs orders DHS to produce CBP One class lists by Oct. 19)
what_changed:
Backstory: Humanitarian parole lets DHS admit people temporarily, usually for two years with a work permit. The Biden administration used it at scale: the CHNV programs brought in about 532,000 Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans with U.S. sponsors (Federal Register); Uniting for Ukraine (U4U) paroled almost 240,000 Ukrainians (Ukraine Immigration Task Force); family reunification parole covered relatives waiting for green cards; and more than 936,000 people were allowed in from 2023 to January 2025 after booking border appointments through the CBP One app (NPR).

On January 20, 2025, President Trump's Executive Order 14165 directed DHS to end categorical parole programs contrary to his policies, naming CHNV, and to stop using CBP One to parole people in (Federal Register). Days later, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman signed a memo telling immigration authorities to review the parole of people admitted under CHNV and through CBP One and to consider expedited removal for them (NPR, Jan. 24, 2025). In a February 14 memo, Acting USCIS Deputy Director Andrew Davidson ordered an indefinite "administrative pause" on all pending benefit requests, including asylum, TPS and green card applications, filed by people admitted under U4U, CHNV and the family reunification programs, citing fraud and vetting concerns (CBS News).

On March 25, 2025, a Federal Register notice signed by Secretary Kristi Noem terminated the CHNV programs and ended, as of April 24, the parole of everyone under them whose parole had not already expired; DHS said it "generally intends to remove promptly" those without another lawful basis to stay (Federal Register). On April 3, DHS emailed some Ukrainians in U4U that their parole was terminated and "It is time for you to leave the United States"; the next day it said the message was "sent in error" and that U4U "has not been terminated" (States Newsroom). In early April, DHS began emailing people paroled in after CBP One appointments, up to 985,000 people by Politico's report (Immigration Policy Tracking Project), that their parole would end in seven days. CBP said the notices went to people "who do not have lawful status to remain"; at least one reached a U.S.-born immigration lawyer in Massachusetts (WIRED).

In mid-April, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston paused the CHNV termination in Svitlana Doe v. Noem, faulting the lack of any case-by-case justification (Clearinghouse); at an April 10 hearing she had said the secretary "has to have a reasoned decision" (AP). On May 28 she also blocked the suspension of benefit and re-parole processing for parolees (Clearinghouse). On May 30 the Supreme Court stayed her CHNV order without explanation, over the dissent of Justices Jackson and Sotomayor (ABC News). **On June 12, DHS began emailing CHNV parolees that their parole and work permits were revoked effective immediately**, urging them to self-deport through the CBP Home app for a $1,000 payment (CBS Miami; Mother Jones). On September 12, 2025, the First Circuit vacated Talwani's CHNV order, holding the early termination likely lawful (Justice Action Center; Clearinghouse).

U4U re-parole processing resumed in summer 2025 after a roughly four-month pause (Ukraine Immigration Task Force), but Reuters reported in November that immigration officials had processed only 1,900 renewal applications for Ukrainians and other nationalities and that almost 200,000 Ukrainians were at risk of losing legal status (Reuters, via LIGA.net). In December 2025 DHS moved to end family reunification parole for about 14,000 people (NPR); Talwani blocked that termination in January 2026, and the government's appeals were being briefed in the First Circuit as of October 2026 (Clearinghouse). In March 2026, House members wrote USCIS Director Joseph Edlow that Ukrainian re-parole filings from early and mid-2025 remained "functionally stalled" (Rep. Eugene Vindman); by May 2026, re-parole and work permits cost $2,350-$2,450 per person (Ukraine Immigration Task Force).

On March 31, 2026, U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs in Boston ruled in Sileiri Doe v. DHS that DHS had acted "not in accordance with law" when it ended the CBP One paroles without the process its statute and regulations require; she vacated the April 2025 terminations for a certified class and ordered parole restored (NPR; NBC News; CourtListener). On April 21, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott issued a memo saying those paroles' purposes had been served, and DHS told the court it would send class members new individualized termination notices (DHS status report on CourtListener; CLINIC; Reuters via WDEZ). On April 27, Burroughs declined to stop the new terminations, writing that her order "did not grant Plaintiffs a substantive entitlement to parole" (CourtListener). **On July 15 she announced an inherent-powers sanction against DHS for failing to comply with her order before re-terminating**, requiring notice to all class members and documentation of efforts to undo harm to their asylum and other immigration cases (Immigration Policy Tracking Project; CourtListener). She entered the sanctions order on September 28, and on October 16, 2026, ordered DHS to produce the lists of class members and of those with adverse consequences by October 19 (CourtListener). Effects on caregiving staff and the parallel TPS terminations are covered in separate entries.
legal_status: CHNV, U4U and other parole programs: sued (Svitlana Doe v. Noem, D. Mass., Judge Indira Talwani). Talwani paused the CHNV termination in April 2025; the Supreme Court stayed that order May 30, 2025, and the First Circuit vacated it Sept. 12, 2025, holding the termination likely lawful (rehearing denied Nov. 18, 2025). Talwani's May 28, 2025 injunction against the suspension of benefit and re-parole processing stands; the government dropped its appeal of it Nov. 4, 2025. Family reunification parole: termination preliminarily enjoined in January 2026; the government's appeals are pending in the First Circuit. CBP One: sued (Sileiri Doe v. DHS, D. Mass., Judge Allison Burroughs); terminations ruled unlawful and vacated March 31, 2026; the court declined to stay DHS's April 2026 re-terminations, then imposed an inherent-powers sanction for noncompliance (announced July 15, order entered Sept. 28, 2026); compliance deadlines continue.

human_toll.summary: People who entered legally with U.S. sponsors or border appointments, and had been told they could live and work here for two years, lost parole and work permits early or saw renewals stall, leaving them removable. CHNV parolees were told to leave immediately; CBP One parolees got seven-day emails; Ukrainians waiting on re-parole lost jobs and health insurance, Reuters reported, and some left the country.

human_toll.caveat: Counts come from DHS's own notice (CHNV), news reports and advocacy groups, and overlap: the 532,000 CHNV figure counts everyone ever paroled, many of whom had other status or whose parole had already ended, and CBP One counts range from nearly 900,000 to more than 936,000 depending on the source and period; the 985,000 email figure is Politico's, as relayed by a policy tracker. The Reuters U4U figures were read only in a Ukrainian outlet's summary. No official count of former parolees arrested or removed was found. DHS's stated rationale: the CHNV programs "do not serve a significant public benefit" and are inconsistent with the President's foreign policy goals (Federal Register); DHS Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said CHNV "was abused by the previous administration to admit hundreds of thousands of poorly vetted illegal aliens"; USCIS cited fraud such as "serial sponsors" for the benefits pause; and DHS called the CBP One ruling "blatant judicial activism," saying it "had full authority to revoke parole." The First Circuit agreed DHS likely could end CHNV parole categorically, and Burroughs held that courts cannot review DHS's choice to end parole categorically rather than case by case.

title: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' held 79 ICE detainees in 16-18 sq ft metal cages, DHS's own IG found

location.facility: Florida Soft-Sided Facility ('Alligator Alcatraz'), at the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport

officials.name: Ron DeSantis
officials.role: Governor of Florida; his administration built and opened the facility, which held detainees under Florida's 287(g) agreement with ICE

people.unnamed_affected: 79 immigration detainees held in the metal enclosures between July 17, 2025 and Jan. 18, 2026, and the wider detainee population exposed to the facility's water, hygiene and space conditions; none is named in the sourcing.

status: Facility shut down June 2026. DHS's inspector general reported on Sept. 14, 2026 that its cages did not meet humane-treatment standards; all 10 recommendations were closed because of the shutdown. No charges. Separate lawsuits over the facility are ongoing.
date_of_action: 2025-07-17 (earliest documented cage confinement) through 2026-09-14 (DHS Inspector General report released)
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a broader pattern in this database of state-run immigration detention facilities operating under federal 287(g) partnerships with contested lines of accountability -- when conditions draw scrutiny, the federal government has repeatedly pointed to state operational control while state officials point to federal statutory authority over immigration enforcement, leaving oversight gaps that this Inspector General report itself flags as ongoing at other facilities.
pull_quote: “The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the DHS Inspector General concluded.

glance.who: Gov. Ron DeSantis's Florida, with ICE (287(g))
glance.what: Held 79 ICE detainees in 16-18 sq ft metal cages, vs ICE's 37 sq ft minimum, per DHS's own IG

what_changed: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention facility (officially the Florida Soft-Sided Facility), built by Gov. Ron DeSantis's administration and opened in the Everglades in July 2025, held immigration detainees under a 287(g) agreement authorizing Florida officers to help enforce federal immigration law alongside ICE. A DHS Office of Inspector General report, released September 14, 2026 after an inspection in January, found the facility **confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures of roughly 16 to 18 square feet -- well below ICE's own minimum of 37 square feet for rooms designed to hold one person**. Records showed detainees held in these enclosures between July 17, 2025 and January 18, 2026, for an average of just under an hour and a maximum of about two hours; in at least one documented case a detainee was put in a cage as punishment, for 26 minutes after failing 'to comply with a lawful command.' Facility staff and posted signage described the enclosures as 'calming areas' where detainees could 'reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress and practice self-directed behavior,' and staff said detainees were not locked in, though inspectors observed locking mechanisms on the cages. The inspector general also found the facility gave detainees about 28 square feet of living space at maximum capacity, against a 75-square-foot requirement; detainees complained of inadequate clean drinking water and of being permitted to shower only three times weekly in bug-infested showers, against ICE's own daily-shower standard. The Inspector General concluded that 'the use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment.' DHS disputed federal responsibility for the conditions: in a response signed by DHS Under Secretary for Management Brian J. Cavanaugh and the acting ICE director, it said ICE held no contract with Florida to run the facility and that the 287(g) agreement did not give the federal government authority over its physical operations. The report itself noted ICE personnel were on-site, every detainee was given an ICE handbook calling it 'a facility of the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement,' and FEMA had provided Florida $608 million for its operation. The facility shut down in June 2026; the inspector general made 10 recommendations but closed them all, citing the shutdown, while warning that the issues 'remain consequential' because ICE is using other state-run facilities, one of them in Florida.
legal_status: No charges. DHS's Office of Inspector General found the metal enclosures 'highly unconventional' and not aligned 'with standards for humane treatment' (report released Sept. 14, 2026); its 10 recommendations were closed because the facility had shut down. Amnesty International's December 2025 report, which alleged the cage use amounted to torture, sparked a congressional probe, and a series of lawsuits over the facility are ongoing, per NBC News. DHS disputes that it had authority over the facility's day-to-day operations.

human_toll.summary: Immigration detainees held at the Everglades facility were confined, 79 of them in metal cages less than half ICE's minimum single-person room size, for up to about two hours at a time, in at least one case as punishment; detainees also reported dirty drinking water and showers only three times a week in bug-infested stalls, and the inspector general found about 28 square feet of living space each at maximum capacity.

human_toll.caveat: Figures come from the DHS inspector general's report, which relied on the facility's internal records, as reported by NBC News, The Washington Times and The Hill; outlets differ slightly on the cage size (NBC: 16 sq ft outdoor and 18 sq ft indoor; The Hill quotes the report as 'about 18 square feet'; The Washington Times: 4 feet 3 inches square). The inspector general said it could not 'independently confirm or refute' ICE officials' account of how the enclosures were used, or allegations such as deprivation of food or water in them; the count covers only recorded cage use, not the full detained population. ICE told the inspector general detainees were shackled only while being escorted to the enclosures, and staff said detainees sometimes 'asked to spend time' in them. DHS's position is that Florida, not the federal government, ran the facility day to day under its 287(g) authority. DeSantis's office said the cages were 'a confinement area for violent criminal aliens' that 'adheres to all federal standards for criminal confinement.'

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core findings -- the cage dimensions, the 79-detainee count and date range, the 'calming areas' staff justification, DHS's dispute of responsibility, and the IG's own conclusion -- corroborated directly by NBC News's reporting on the report itself, with additional facility-history and closure details corroborated across The Washington Times and The Hill. MODERATE confidence on the broader implications for other state-run facilities: the Washington Times reports the inspector general said the issues 'remain consequential' because ICE uses other state-run facilities, one in Florida, but the report's findings were not checked against that facility in sourcing reviewed for this entry. The responsibility question is contested: DHS says Florida ran the facility, while the report records ICE staff on-site, ICE handbooks and FEMA funding; this entry reports both. Re-verified 2026-10-18: NBC News re-fetched and still supports the core findings; no later inspector general, congressional or court action on the report found.

glance.what: Deported dozens of young asylum seekers a court settlement protected; a judge twice found DHS in contempt

harm.who: Asylum seekers who came as children

what_changed: Backstory: on Nov. 25, 2024, U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher in Maryland approved a settlement in J.O.P. v. DHS, a long-running class action over the asylum rights of people who came to the U.S. as unaccompanied children. Its Section III.I says ICE "will refrain from executing the Class Member's final removal order until USCIS issues a Final Determination" on an asylum application, and requires ICE to enter an alert in its records for every identified class member. On March 15, 2025, ICE removed a Venezuelan class member, called "Cristian" in court, to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act without a hearing. On April 23, 2025, Gallagher ruled the removal violated the settlement, ordered the government to facilitate his return, and ordered it "not to remove from the United States members of the certified 'Class.'" The 4th Circuit denied a stay pending appeal on May 19, 2025. On July 18, 2025, El Salvador released him to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange; the court later noted he never told his lawyers he wanted to return. More removals came to light as the government self-reported them in 2025. After a meet-and-confer ordered on Nov. 20, 2025, class counsel filed a third motion to enforce and for civil contempt on Jan. 22, 2026. On March 14, 2026, ICE removed E.L.A., who had arrived as a 16-year-old unaccompanied child and filed for asylum with USCIS on Feb. 14, 2025, to El Salvador on a removal order an immigration judge entered Feb. 25; USCIS had not put him on its lists of potential class members. At evidentiary hearings later that month, ICE officers involved in removals described either failing to notice class-member banners and case comments or "having proceeded in disregard of them." The government disclosed the removal on March 30 and conceded his class membership on May 22, 2026. On May 26, 2026, Gallagher extended the settlement's May 27, 2026 termination date to Nov. 18, 2026. The government reported that, as of June 26, 2026, 54 confirmed and 53 potential class members had been removed under final removal orders. On July 24, it appealed the extension. **On July 29, 2026, Gallagher found DHS, USCIS and ICE in civil contempt of her Nov. 25, 2024 and April 23, 2025 orders.** She held that removals "executed in ignorance or disregard of identification of their potential Class membership were and are in contempt," while declining to find contempt for removals of people ICE had never been told about, and rejected the government's good-faith defense. Under her separate authority to enforce and modify the settlement, not as a contempt sanction, she ordered ICE to check its records for class-member alerts before every removal, enter new alerts within two business days, issue monthly nationwide guidance, search for removed class members every two weeks and report to the court; the government can purge the contempt by showing it has stopped such removals. She imposed no sanctions, and denied a motion to return E.M.P., a class member ICE flew to Guatemala on Feb. 4, 2026 after he accepted voluntary departure. The opinion was made public on Aug. 6. E.L.A. flew back to the U.S. on Aug. 7, 2026, under a return the government agreed to on June 18, and was held in ICE detention in Louisiana. On Aug. 11 and 12, a USCIS official told ICE his asylum case "will be closed as soon as possible" over two biometrics appointments he missed in 2025 (his lawyers say he lost his attorney in late March 2025 to federal funding cuts for children's legal services); on Aug. 16, at an ICE officer's request, ICE removed the class-member banner from his file. USCIS had not closed the case as of a Sept. 21 government filing. On Sept. 1, 2026, ICE moved him from detention at about 2:21 a.m. and put him on a plane that took off for San Salvador at about 9:45 a.m., removing him a second time; the government told the court it was weighing steps to fix "the communication errors that led to ELA's erroneous removal." On Sept. 2, Gallagher ordered the government to say who decided to move him and put him on the plane. On Sept. 8, 2026, she awarded class counsel $160,823.09 in fees and $3,704.61 in costs over Cristian's removal, finding the government's overall position "has not been substantially justified" and calling its assertions that he was a Tren de Aragua member "unsubstantiated." From Sept. 14 she required daily status reports on E.L.A.'s return. On Sept. 23, the government's appeal of the extension was voluntarily dismissed. **On Sept. 25, 2026, Gallagher found the government in contempt a second time, of her Nov. 25, 2024, April 23, 2025 and July 29, 2026 orders, for removing E.L.A.** She ordered him returned, barred executing any removal order against him until USCIS issues a final determination on his asylum application or the settlement expires, ordered his property and documents returned, and required five business days' notice before any attempt to remove him; she did not bar detaining him on return. On Oct. 1, the government said he would be detained when he returns. On Oct. 6, it said it had exhausted reasonable efforts to find his property; class counsel reported the government confirmed its search had not included pinging his phones or reviewing security camera footage. On Oct. 8, 2026, in a separate ruling, Gallagher found DHS had violated the settlement's Section III.H in immigration court by opposing class members' requests to pause their cases, moving to restart paused cases and opposing motions to end proceedings without case-specific grounds, and ordered it to stop; the opinion was made public Oct. 14. On Oct. 9, the government asked her to drop the property part of the Sept. 25 order, saying the property is outside U.S. control, while ICE's removal office arranged E.L.A.'s return with his lawyer. A second motion to extend the settlement past Nov. 18, 2026 is pending; the government opposed it on Oct. 5.
legal_status: Ruled violations and civil contempt (no criminal contempt or sanctions): in J.O.P. v. DHS (D. Md., No. 8:19-cv-01944), Judge Stephanie Gallagher ruled on April 23, 2025 that removing "Cristian" violated the settlement; found DHS, USCIS and ICE in civil contempt on July 29, 2026 for removing class members in ignorance or disregard of their identification, with a purge condition but no sanctions, and separately ordered compliance steps under its authority to enforce and modify the settlement; and on Sept. 25, 2026 found them in contempt again over E.L.A.'s second removal and ordered his return. On Oct. 8, 2026 she ruled DHS violated the settlement's immigration-court provisions. On Sept. 8, 2026 she awarded about $164,500 in fees and costs under the Equal Access to Justice Act, ruling the government's position over Cristian not substantially justified. Pending: the government's Oct. 9 motion to amend the Sept. 25 property order, and class counsel's second motion to extend the settlement past Nov. 18, 2026. E.L.A. also filed a habeas petition in the Western District of Louisiana on Aug. 14, 2026, which had no government response ordered before his Sept. 1 removal.

human_toll.summary: Young asylum seekers who came to the U.S. as unaccompanied children were sent back to the countries they say they fled before USCIS decided their asylum claims, despite a court settlement barring it. One, "Cristian," was held in El Salvador's CECOT prison for months before being sent to Venezuela, the country he sought asylum from. Another, E.L.A., was removed to El Salvador twice; class counsel says the second time he was left there with no belongings, money or phone, wearing a detention jumpsuit.

human_toll.caveat: The counts are the government's own reports to the court; newer lists of removed potential class members are filed under seal, and class counsel and the National Immigration Project describe the June figures as "at least 107" people (confirmed plus potential). Because the settlement defines the class without listing its members and USCIS's lists missed some people (E.L.A. among them), the true number may be higher, and some potential members may turn out not to be in the class. The government has admitted that removing confirmed class members violated the court's order, but argued it acted in good faith and that some departures were voluntary; the court rejected the good-faith defense and declined to find contempt only where ICE had never been told a person was a possible class member. On E.L.A., the government says ICE understood his asylum case to be closed after USCIS said it would close it over missed biometrics appointments, called the second removal an "erroneous removal" caused by "communication errors," and disputes how his property claims were presented; a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek he requested voluntary departure at an ICE field office and was deported March 13, 2026 (court filings give March 14). glance.what: Swept LA-area Home Depots, car washes and workplaces from June 2025; ICE logged 14,394 area arrests in 2025

what_changed: Backstory: before the raids, an ICE official told the Washington Examiner in May 2025 that White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller "wants everybody arrested," asking "Why aren't you at Home Depot? Why aren't you at 7-Eleven?", and border czar Tom Homan had told reporters, "You're going to see more work site enforcement than you've ever seen in the history of this nation," according to Mother Jones; Miller's daily arrest target is covered in a separate entry. **On June 6, 2025, ICE and other federal agents raided the Ambiance Apparel warehouse in the Fashion District and a Home Depot, and followed with arrests at a Home Depot in Paramount; DHS said its Los Angeles operations led to 118 arrests that week.** That day agents pushed David Huerta, president of SEIU California, to the ground and arrested him outside a site where ICE was executing a search warrant; prosecutors said he had sat and paced in front of a gate, and he was charged with conspiracy to impede an officer and released on $50,000 bond. On June 7, Homan threatened to arrest anyone who impeded the operation, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Mayor Karen Bass, though he said neither had yet "crossed the line"; two White House officials told NBC News no such arrests were being planned. By June 9, Homan had acknowledged that agents were arresting people without criminal records. Lawyers from the Immigrant Defenders Law Center said people arrested were first held in the basement of a federal immigration building, and its president said "hundreds of people" were held "without food, water, or beds for 12-plus hours." Lawyers said one family with three children, the youngest three years old, was held 48 hours with no water on the first day; that at least one person was bused to Mexico almost at once without paperwork; and that agents and Guard troops largely blocked lawyers and families from detainees. On June 12, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem joined agents on a Huntington Park raid at a home where a pregnant mother and her four children were inside and the target was not, and said in Los Angeles that the aim was to "bring in criminals that have been out on our street far too long." ICE's own data, analyzed by the Los Angeles Times, showed 722 arrests in the region from June 1 to 10, with 69% having no criminal conviction and 58% never charged with a crime. On June 17, agents detained Francisco Urizar, a 64-year-old tortilla delivery driver, mid-delivery at a Pico Rivera grocery store; his co-workers called his daughter, a bystander's video showed him flanked by masked agents, and the next day she still did not know where he was being held. The same morning, the El Rancho school district said, about 10 agents on Salazar High School's grounds in Pico Rivera, where staff told them they had no permission to be, urinated near a preschool playground; DHS said the matter was "under investigation." DHS said 1,618 people were arrested in Los Angeles from June 6 to 22. Inside the downtown basement holding area known as B-18, an attorney said in late June, a client described a room holding as many as 70 other people with one open toilet, and being fed once a day at 3 a.m. On June 27, agents used explosives to blow out the windows of a Huntington Park home looking for a man CBP accused of ramming a CBP vehicle during a protest; he was not there, but his girlfriend and young children were. Border Patrol's Greg Bovino, who joined the raid and led the Los Angeles campaign, later called it a "very, very prudent, thoughtful application of tactics." On July 10, DHS executed criminal search warrants at Glass House Farms cannabis sites in Camarillo and Carpinteria and said it arrested 361 people, four of them with prior criminal records. Farmworker Jaime Alanis, 57, fell about 30 feet from a greenhouse roof after telling his wife he was hiding from agents and died on July 12; DHS said he was not being pursued. On July 11, in the Vasquez Perdomo case, a federal judge ordered a halt to indiscriminate stops in seven counties, and that month she also ordered daily lawyer access at B-18. On August 6, Border Patrol agents jumped out of a rented Penske truck at a Westlake Home Depot in what Bovino called "Operation Trojan Horse"; Penske said it had not authorized the use. In August 2025, after two months of being unable to enter, three members of Congress toured B-18 and found it nearly empty; Rep. Judy Chu said it had concrete floors and no beds, that some detainees reported one meal a day, and that she had heard of people held there for 12 days. Bovino described the campaign's pace to the AP as "turn and burn," and by late August the Los Angeles effort had topped 5,000 arrests; of four people Border Patrol agents arrested at a Montebello car wash on August 15, none had a criminal history. In October 2025, prosecutors reduced Huerta's felony charge to a misdemeanor. **On November 13, 2025, the judge issued a preliminary injunction finding that ICE had repeatedly closed B-18 to lawyers without warning, kept meeting-room doors open and blocked confidential attorney calls.** On November 24, House Oversight Democrats held a shadow field hearing in Los Angeles on wrongful detentions of U.S. citizens and other abuses. At the Cypress Park Home Depot, advocates said in December that agents had detained about 50 people there that year, and the Los Angeles Times reported that agents detained a U.S. citizen there whose child was in the car and drove off with the toddler; the store installed noise machines that advocates said drove day laborers away and that Home Depot called a parking safety measure. In December, DHS said it had made more than 10,000 arrests in Los Angeles since June. ICE data analyzed by LAist counted 14,394 arrests in the greater Los Angeles area in 2025, up from 4,681 in 2024, with 39% of those arrested having no criminal charges or convictions. Bovino was removed from his role as CBP's commander at large in January 2026, after the Minneapolis shootings, and in March was reported to be retiring. After more than 1,500 ICE arrests in the area in January 2026, arrests fell to 809 in February, according to an ABC7 analysis of ICE data. On June 6, 2026, families marked a year since the Ambiance Apparel raid; an organizing group said 11 of 14 detained family members it supports had been freed, and police arrested six people at protests downtown. **On July 27, 2026, prosecutors dropped the case against Huerta under a diversion agreement, and the court's dismissal became permanent on August 27, 2026.** In October 2026, weeks before the midterm elections, a new wave of immigration arrests hit the region: L.A. Taco counted at least 45 people arrested across Southern California in the week of October 5, LA Public Press reported, and on October 16 Los Angeles leaders and advocates said the raids appeared aimed at discouraging turnout; DHS said it would not discuss its operations.
legal_status: David Huerta was charged in June 2025 with conspiracy to impede an officer, a felony prosecutors reduced to a misdemeanor in October 2025; on July 27, 2026, prosecutors moved to dismiss under a diversion agreement, and Judge Stanley Blumenfeld Jr. dismissed the case, with the dismissal becoming with prejudice on August 27, 2026. The U.S. attorney's office said Huerta "has agreed to accept responsibility for his actions"; his lawyers said the case had no legal basis. Immigrant-rights groups and residents sued DHS in Vasquez Perdomo v. Noem over the roving stops and B-18 lawyer access; the court issued temporary restraining orders in July 2025, the Supreme Court stayed the stop order in September 2025, and the court issued a preliminary injunction on B-18 lawyer access on November 13, 2025 (covered in its own entry). DHS said the El Rancho school incident was "under investigation"; no result was found. No charges against Glass House Farms had been filed as of the AP's July 2025 report, and no inspector-general review of B-18 was found.

human_toll.summary: Thousands of people were arrested at workplaces, Home Depot lots, car washes and farms across the Los Angeles region, many with no criminal record. Detainees, their lawyers and lawmakers described days in a crowded basement with little food or water and no beds, and lawyers said they were blocked from clients. A farmworker died after falling from a greenhouse roof during a raid, families were separated, and at least one man was deported within hours.

DHS says it has not "verified the accuracy, methodology or analysis" of the project and that 61% of people ICE arrested nationwide had convictions or pending charges. Conditions at B-18 come from detainees, lawyers and members of Congress; the court's findings concerned lawyer access, not food or water. DHS says its operations are "highly targeted," that it was "removing murderers, pedophiles, and drug traffickers from Los Angeles," and McLaughlin said ICE "has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons"; Bovino says targets are chosen on intelligence, not profiling, and DHS says Alanis was not being pursued.

The El Rancho school account is the district's, backed by its surveillance footage; DHS has not reported findings. The man sought in the June 27 Huntington Park raid is not named because no charging record was found. what_changed:
Backstory and scope: this entry lists people DHS removed from the United States despite a court order barring the removal or a legal protection meant to stop it (an immigration-court grant of protection, DACA, Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, or a class settlement). Several larger cases are covered elsewhere and appear here in one line each. Kilmar Abrego Garcia's March 2025 removal to El Salvador's CECOT prison, despite a 2019 order barring his return there, is covered in the entry on his wrongful removal to CECOT. The March 15, 2025 Alien Enemies Act flights that kept going after Judge James Boasberg's order are covered in the entry on the 252 Venezuelans held in CECOT and the Boasberg contempt entry. Asylum seekers removed in breach of the J.O.P. class settlement, which a judge later found in contempt, are covered in the entry on the J.O.P. settlement removals. U.S. citizens, mostly children, deported with their parents are covered in the entry on U.S. citizens detained and deported.

The confirmed cases, in order of removal:

- **February 2025, Mexico then Guatemala: a Guatemalan man known in court as O.C.G.** An immigration judge had found he would likely be persecuted or tortured in Guatemala and granted him protection; he was put on a bus to Mexico and then sent to Guatemala, where he hid (TIME, ABC News). Judge Brian Murphy found his removal likely "lacked any semblance of due process" and in May ordered "all immediate steps" to return him; he was brought back in June 2025, the first return the administration carried out under a judge's order (ABC News).
- **March 14, 2025, Lebanon: Dr. Rasha Alawieh,** a Brown University transplant doctor with an H-1B visa, was sent back from Boston's Logan Airport after Judge Leo Sorokin ordered CBP to give the court 48 hours' notice before removing her; government lawyers said CBP got notice only after she had departed (CBS News, Ocean State Media). Sorokin later found the officers did not know of his order, so did not violate it, and dismissed her suit on October 31, 2025, leaving a five-year bar in place (Brown Daily Herald, Boston Globe). Her lawyers appealed in December 2025 (Ocean State Media); on October 13, 2026 the 1st Circuit upheld the dismissal, holding that the law bars review of her expedited removal order (Boston Globe).
- **March 23, 2025, Mexico: Evenezer Cortez Martínez,** a DACA recipient returning to Dallas-Fort Worth on approved advance parole from a trip to Mexico after his grandfather's death, was removed under a 2024 in absentia order he says he never knew of; CBP said in court papers his advance parole was "issued in error." He returned home to Kansas City on April 8, 2025 (NBC News).
- **May 7, 2025, El Salvador: Jordin Melgar-Salmeron** was put on a flight about 30 minutes after the 2nd Circuit stayed his removal; the government blamed "a confluence of administrative errors" (TIME, NBC News). On June 24, 2025 the court ordered the government to facilitate his return; on July 1 the government told the court it could not locate him (Bloomberg Law).
- **2025, abroad: three mothers covered by the Ms. L. family-separation settlement, with their children.** In one case the mother and her children had permission to stay through a grant of parole and were removed weeks after Judge Dana Sabraw paused deportations of families eligible under the settlement in June 2025. On February 5, 2026, Sabraw found the removals unlawful, involving "lies, deception, and coercion," and ordered the families returned at government expense (CBS News).
- **November 22, 2025, Honduras: Any Lucia Lopez Belloza,** a 19-year-old Babson College student detained at Logan Airport, was flown out a day after Judge Richard Stearns ordered her kept in the U.S. for 72 hours. The government apologized in court for an ICE officer's "mistake" but defended the removal under a 2016 order (WBUR). Stearns ordered her return on February 13, 2026 (AP); she declined the February 27 flight after the government said it would detain and deport her again (Reuters), and Stearns then dismissed her case for lack of jurisdiction (ABC News).
- **December 20, 2025, India: Francisco D'Costa,** in the U.S. since 2009, was put on a flight from Houston more than three hours after Judge Keith Ellison barred his removal; on January 9, 2026 the court found the removal unlawful and ordered the government to facilitate his return (IANS, court docket).
- **December 23, 2025, Mexico: Federico Reyes Vasquez,** a Provo-area, Utah resident of about 21 years, detained in Orem, was removed a day after Chief Judge Jill Parrish barred it; on December 31 she found a "direct violation" of her order and ordered him returned by late January at government expense (KSL, Salt Lake Tribune).
- **January 2026, Honduras: José Contreras Díaz,** a DACA recipient from Edinburg, Texas, was arrested at an immigration check-in and deported weeks before his son was born (Texas Tribune). After his lawyer wrote to ICE, he was flown back on April 29, re-detained on landing, and released on May 7, 2026 (Texas Tribune).
- **January 28, 2026, Guatemala: Domingo Tot Quip,** a Portland, Maine resident with no deportation order, was removed the day after a federal judge barred his removal; ICE admitted in an April filing it "inadvertently removed" him, having mistaken him for another man with the same first name and birthday. The government agreed to fly him back at its expense (Portland Press Herald), and a later lawsuit says ICE returned him to the U.S. in August (Newsweek).
- **February 2, 2026, Mexico: Emilio Pena Jimenez,** arrested at an Apple Valley, Minnesota Walmart during Operation Metro Surge, was bused from El Paso to Juárez although Judge Jeffrey Bryan had ordered him returned to Minnesota and then released; the government says he chose voluntary departure on January 28, which his lawyer says he signed under duress (Star Tribune). On March 2, 2026 Bryan ordered the government to facilitate his return at its cost and barred his re-detention (Bring Me The News).
- **February 19, 2026, Mexico: Maria de Jesús Estrada Juárez,** a Sacramento DACA recipient, was arrested at her green card interview and deported the next day under a 1998 order (AP, Mother Jones). On March 23 Judge Dena Coggins found her removal a "flagrant violation" of her DACA protections and ordered her return; she reunited with her daughter on March 30 (AP).
- **April 10, 2026, Honduras: José Eliezer Martinez-Andino,** a Raleigh resident with Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and deferred action, was removed after signing voluntary departure forms he says he signed out of fear (WUNC). Judge Beryl Howell ordered his return in June, writing that he was removed "in a manner that boggles the mind"; DHS flew him back on August 5 and ICE held him until his release on September 11, 2026 (WUNC).
- **May 20, 2026, Nigeria: Stanley Chigozie Nwabuwa** was removed despite Judge Nina Wang's April 14 order barring it; the government said it "greatly regret[s] this error," blaming a missed database comment. On June 1 Wang found ICE "unequivocally violated" her order but vacated it and denied his petition rather than order his return (court order, Colorado Politics).
- **May 26, 2026, Ghana then Togo: Etinosa Osahon,** a Nigerian man with 2012 protection under the Convention Against Torture after being tortured in Nigeria, was flown to Ghana, told his final destination was Nigeria, and is now in hiding in Togo. Judge Michelle Williams Court found he is likely to show ICE skipped the required steps for ending his protection, barred any transfer to Nigeria and ordered the government to report what it is doing to return him (Newsweek).
- **August 8, 2026, Mexico: Marco Uriel Rodriguez Hernandez,** moved out of the Aurora, Colorado detention center, was deported from Texas the morning after Chief Judge Daniel Domenico barred his removal. The government said it "greatly regret[s] the error," made by Texas officials unaware of the order; on August 25 Domenico ordered all available steps to facilitate his return (Colorado Politics).
legal_status: Courts ruled the removals unlawful or likely unlawful, or found their orders violated, in most of the cases listed. Return ordered or facilitated: O.C.G. (D. Mass.), Melgar-Salmeron (2nd Cir.), the three Ms. L. families (S.D. Cal.), Lopez Belloza (D. Mass., case later dismissed), D'Costa (S.D. Tex.), Reyes Vasquez (D. Utah), Pena Jimenez (D. Minn.), Estrada Juárez (E.D. Cal.), Martinez-Andino (D.D.C.) and Rodriguez Hernandez (D. Colo.). In Nwabuwa (D. Colo.) the judge found the order violated but declined to order a return, and on July 24 ruled she could not award fees as a sanction; in Osahon (C.D. Cal.) a temporary restraining order bars transfer to Nigeria. Alawieh's suit was dismissed after the judge found officers did not know of his order; the 1st Circuit affirmed on October 13, 2026 for lack of jurisdiction. TAP found no contempt finding against any official in the listed cases.

human_toll.summary: Fifteen people and three families were sent out of the country despite a court order or legal protection, many to countries they had left as children or where they feared harm. Some hid abroad; families, including U.S.-citizen children, were separated for months. Six of the fifteen are confirmed back in the U.S.; at least two were detained again on landing.

human_toll.caveat: The count is TAP's own: it covers only cases TAP could confirm in a court record or a major or regional outlet, and leaves out the Abrego Garcia, Alien Enemies Act, J.O.P. settlement and U.S.-citizen cases covered in other entries. It is not a full tally. Politico has reported, as quoted by the Immigration Policy Tracking Project, that judges found more than 170 people improperly deported, most from a single operation, plus nearly 30 individual cases; TAP has not verified that count. Three people with torture-convention protection who were sent to third countries (the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea and the Central African Republic) and later ordered returned are not counted, because the courts faulted the process, not a violated protection or order. DHS's position varies by case: it has called removals "administrative errors," "inadvertent" or one officer's "mistake" (Melgar-Salmeron, Tot Quip, Lopez Belloza, Nwabuwa, Rodriguez Hernandez); said court orders reached removal officers too late (Alawieh, Reyes Vasquez); said DACA "does not confer any form of legal status" (Contreras Díaz); said people left voluntarily (Pena Jimenez, one Ms. L. family); denied Martinez-Andino was kept from his lawyer; and pointed to prior removal orders or criminal records (Lopez Belloza, Reyes Vasquez, Osahon, and Melgar-Salmeron, whom DHS ties to MS-13) or, for Alawieh, her attendance at Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah's funeral. Several of those claims are disputed by courts or lawyers.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence that each listed person was removed after a court order barring it or while holding the stated protection: every case rests on a court order or docket, or on news reports quoting the court's ruling and government filings (TIME, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News, AP, Reuters, WBUR, Bloomberg Law, Texas Tribune, Salt Lake Tribune, KSL, Portland Press Herald, Star Tribune, Mother Jones, WUNC, Colorado Politics, Newsweek, IANS). Weaker sourcing is flagged here: D'Costa rests on the IANS wire account of the court's order plus the docket, which shows Judge Ellison's December 20, 2025 order barring removal; Rodriguez Hernandez and Osahon each rest on one outlet's account of court filings, and Tot Quip on the Portland Press Herald plus Newsweek's report of a later lawsuit; Nwabuwa rests on the court's own order; the report of Pena Jimenez's March 2 return order does not name him but matches his case in every detail (Walmart arrest January 24, February 2 departure, 26 years in the U.S.). Return status is current only as far as the latest report found: no return was found for Melgar-Salmeron, the Ms. L. families, D'Costa, Reyes Vasquez, Pena Jimenez, Nwabuwa, Osahon or Rodriguez Hernandez, and Tot Quip's August return rests on a later lawsuit as reported by Newsweek. Sources differ on O.C.G.'s protection (against return to Guatemala per TIME, against Mexico in ABC News's wording; TAP follows TIME) and on Melgar-Salmeron's removal date (May 7 per the government's court account reported by TIME and Bloomberg Law, May 8 in NBC's summary). People are named only when a court filing or major outlet names them; O.C.G. and the Ms. L. families are described as the court records describe them. DHS's accounts (errors, late notice, voluntary departure, no legal status) are reported in the caveat; whether the voluntary departures were voluntary is disputed and was rejected by the court in the Ms. L. case.
