title: DHS Opened Schools, Churches and Hospitals to Immigration Enforcement; Courts Have Shielded Only Some of the Congregations That Sued

officials.name: Benjamine Huffman
officials.role: Acting Secretary of Homeland Security (January 2025)

officials.name: Caleb Vitello
officials.role: Acting ICE Director (January 2025)

officials.name: Tom Homan
officials.role: White House border czar

people.unnamed_affected: Immigrants and mixed-status families who say they have stopped or delayed seeking medical care, worship or school out of fear of enforcement, including patients described by their doctors in the New York Times (among them an undocumented woman in San Francisco who, her emergency physician said, delayed care for severely untreated diabetes out of fear and died the day she arrived); congregations that report falling immigrant attendance; and people attending a martial arts class in the gymnasium of a Minneapolis church covered by a court injunction, whom an undercover federal agent recorded.

status: In effect nationwide since Jan. 20, 2025. Courts have blocked it only at some plaintiffs' houses of worship (a Maryland injunction the 4th Circuit upheld in Aug. 2026; a Massachusetts one, on appeal); other suits lost or await rulings, including an Oregon bid for a nationwide stay.
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (Acting Secretary Huffman's directive) through 2025-01-31 (ICE implementing memo)
what_changed: Since October 2011, written DHS policy had steered Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection agents away from arrests, searches, surveillance and questioning at "sensitive locations" such as schools, places of worship, hospitals, health clinics and doctors' offices; in October 2021 the Biden administration broadened these "protected areas" to include social service organizations, emergency response sites and places where children gather, and told agents to refrain from enforcement there "to the fullest extent possible," with agency approval needed first except in emergencies. On January 20, 2025, inauguration day, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued a directive rescinding that guidance for ICE and CBP. The replacement memo says bright-line rules are unnecessary and tells agents to use their discretion "with a healthy dose of common sense." Announcing it on January 21, a DHS spokesperson said: "Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America's schools and churches to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense." On January 31, then-Acting ICE Director Caleb Vitello issued ICE's implementing memo, "Common Sense Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas," leaving it to assistant field office directors and assistant special agents in charge to decide case by case whether, where and when to act in or near schools, hospitals, houses of worship and active public demonstrations. Since then, faith groups in court have described agents using church parking lots for surveillance, arrests and staging, and attempting to enter a New York church without a warrant; Minnesota school districts allege agents staged operations in school parking lots during the 2026 Twin Cities surge; and records from a federal conspiracy case showed DHS sent an undercover agent into an event in the basement gymnasium of a Minneapolis church in May 2026 and recorded participants, although a court order covered that church. Health care providers and researchers documented a chilling effect alongside the wider enforcement surge: doctors told the New York Times of patients forgoing care for injuries, chronic illnesses such as diabetes and high-risk pregnancies, and said Spanish-interpretation requests in one Atlanta emergency department fell more than 60 percent from January to February 2025, and a KFF/New York Times survey taken August to October 2025 found 48 percent of likely undocumented immigrant adults said they or a family member had avoided seeking medical care since January 2025 because of immigration concerns. In a survey of 691 health care workers by Physicians for Human Rights and Migrant Clinicians Network, **health workers reported children presenting at hospital emergency rooms unaccompanied, delayed diagnoses of life-threatening illnesses, and children as young as six presenting with anxiety due to fears of family separation**. Two Catholic dioceses, Nashville and San Bernardino, excused parishioners from attending Mass in 2025 over fear of enforcement.
legal_status: Sued in at least six federal cases; courts have blocked the policy only for some plaintiffs. Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of the Religious Society of Friends v. DHS (D. Md.): on Feb. 24, 2025, Judge Theodore Chuang enjoined warrantless enforcement at or near the plaintiff Quaker meetings', Sikh temple's and Cooperative Baptist Fellowship's houses of worship and required DHS to follow the 2021 guidance there, declining a nationwide order; on Feb. 3, 2026, he let the core Administrative Procedure Act claims proceed, ruling the 2025 policy a final agency action; on Aug. 18, 2026, the Fourth Circuit affirmed the injunction, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. New England Synod, Evangelical Lutheran Church in America v. DHS (D. Mass.): on Feb. 13, 2026, Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV enjoined warrantless enforcement, absent exigent circumstances, at the churches and religious facilities of the plaintiffs found to have standing; the government appealed to the First Circuit, and plaintiffs, who say they represent over 7,000 congregations, moved for summary judgment to make the order permanent and extend it. On Aug. 20, 2026, they alleged DHS violated the injunction by surveilling University Baptist Church in Minneapolis; Saylor ordered DHS to show cause why it should not be held in contempt and heard arguments Sept. 4, with no ruling reported; he also ordered DHS to report other possible violations, and in late September DHS acknowledged a July arrest in a California church parking lot, which the plaintiffs had raised, calling it a "hot pursuit." DHS argues the agents were not conducting immigration enforcement. Mennonite Church USA v. DHS (D.D.C.): Judge Dabney Friedrich denied a preliminary injunction on April 11, 2025, finding the 27 religious groups unlikely to show standing; their D.C. Circuit appeal is pending. Denver Public Schools v. Noem (D. Colo.): Judge Daniel D. Domenico denied emergency relief on March 7, 2025. Fridley Public Schools v. Mullin (D. Minn.): Judge Laura Provinzino denied a preliminary injunction on May 6, 2026. Pineros y Campesinos Unidos del Noroeste v. Mullin (D. Or.), filed April 28, 2025, also challenges the rescission; Judge Ann L. Aiken heard arguments April 22, 2026, on teachers' unions' motion to stay the policy nationwide and the government's motion to dismiss, and had not ruled as of late September 2026.

human_toll.summary: The policy change made schools, churches, clinics and hospitals places where immigrants can be arrested at an agent's discretion, and the people affected describe staying away. Surveys and clinicians report immigrants and their U.S.-citizen children skipping or delaying medical care, sometimes for serious and life-threatening conditions; congregations report falling immigrant attendance, which a federal appeals court accepted as evidence of a burden on religious exercise; and school districts report attendance drops.

human_toll.caveat: The survey figures measure fear of immigration enforcement generally since January 2025, not this policy alone: KFF and PHR tie the avoidance to the overall enforcement surge as well as the rescission, and no study isolates the policy's share or counts deaths or hospitalizations attributable to it. The health accounts are clinicians' reports, not verified case records. Federal judges in Washington, D.C., and Colorado found plaintiffs had not shown the policy itself, rather than the broader crackdown, caused the attendance drops they cited, and a Minnesota judge noted the 2021 guidance never barred enforcement outright and said what changed was "DHS' willingness — not its authority." DHS's stated rationale is that the change lets agents "catch criminal aliens" who would otherwise "hide in America's schools and churches," and in August 2026 it said ICE "does not target places of worship." Border czar Tom Homan has said agents "do" stay off sensitive locations but "there's no sanctuary for a national security threat or significant public safety threat," and challenged critics to "name one instance" of an arrest inside a church, elementary school or hospital.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the policy change itself: the DHS announcement, the Huffman and Vitello memos as summarized by the Immigration Policy Tracking Project, and the court rulings all agree on what changed and when. HIGH confidence on the litigation record, which comes from court reporting (Courthouse News, Maryland Matters, MPR News), the plaintiffs' counsel and case trackers. MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the health-care avoidance impact, which rests on the KFF/New York Times survey, the PHR/Migrant Clinicians Network survey of health workers and clinicians' accounts to the New York Times rather than a study isolating this policy from the broader enforcement surge. Contested: whether the policy itself, as opposed to enforcement generally, drives the avoidance; the Fourth Circuit and the Maryland and Massachusetts courts found it likely burdens the plaintiff congregations, while courts in D.C. and Colorado found that link unproven for the plaintiffs before them and a Minnesota court found the school plaintiffs unlikely to succeed. The surveillance of the Minneapolis church is alleged in the contempt motion and described in government filings; DHS disputes that it violated the injunction. Re-verified 2026-10-19: no court has reinstated the old policy nationwide, and no ruling on the contempt motion, in the D.C. Circuit appeal or on the Oregon stay motion has been reported.
pull_quote: Providers reported patients delaying or avoiding emergency-room visits -- including for gunshot wounds, diabetes complications, and high-risk pregnancies -- out of fear of encountering immigration enforcement.

section_summaries.what_changed: DHS scrapped limits on arrests at schools, churches and hospitals on Jan. 20, 2025, leaving it to agents' "common sense"; providers report immigrants skipping care.
section_summaries.human_toll: 48% of likely undocumented adults say they or family avoided medical care since Jan. 2025; clinicians report delayed diagnoses; churches report falling attendance.

title: ICE Ran 1.3 Million International Students Through a Crime Database and Terminated Thousands of Their SEVIS Records, Often Without Notice

officials.name: Andre Watson
officials.role: Senior DHS official who described the Student Criminal Alien Initiative in federal court and said it was done "at the instruction of leadership," per CNN

affected.name: Mansi Reddy Bushireddy
affected.description: Indian national and international student whose SEVIS record ICE terminated in April 2025 over a dismissed 2023 shoplifting charge; won summary judgment in her own lawsuit

people.unnamed_affected: Thousands of F-1 students and recent graduates on Optional Practical Training whose SEVIS records were terminated, most not publicly identified; plaintiffs in several suits proceeded under pseudonyms such as "Student Doe."

status: Ongoing. A Massachusetts federal judge let the colleges' challenge proceed in March 2026 and allowed limited discovery in September 2026; summary-judgment motions are due February 2027. ICE reactivated the terminated records by early May 2025; State has not reinstated revoked visas.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Student Criminal Alien Initiative begins) through 2026-03-20 (judge largely denies motion to dismiss)
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a broader pattern this database documents of the administration using existing data systems and databases in new, aggressive ways against noncitizens -- pairing pre-existing law-enforcement records with immigration-status decisions at a scale and speed that outpaces individualized due process, echoed in other entries involving ICE data practices and student-visa vetting.

glance.what: Ran 1.3M students through a crime database and cut thousands of SEVIS records, often without notice

narrative_override.headline: ICE cut thousands of students' SEVIS records after a mass crime-database check, often with no notice.

what_changed:
In mid-March 2025, DHS and the State Department began an effort referred to internally as the "Student Criminal Alien Initiative." Over multiple weeks, ICE employees ran the names of the 1.3 million international students then in the United States through the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database, which records arrests, charges and citations as well as convictions. About 6,400 names returned hits, among them students with no criminal history, only speeding tickets, or arrests that never led to charges. ICE sent that list to State, which revoked many if not all of the valid visas on it, and ICE then terminated the SEVIS (Student and Exchange Visitor Information System) records of thousands of the students -- **more than 4,736 by April 10, by the student-visa program's own count to Congress, without any individualized assessment and, in many cases, without notifying the students or their schools**, according to the colleges' lawsuit. A senior DHS official, Andre Watson, told a federal judge in Washington on April 29, 2025 that the initiative was done "at the instruction of leadership." Hundreds of students sued, and judges had granted temporary restraining orders in more than 35 of the suits by April 24, 2025, per Inside Higher Ed. That day the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and several students sued in federal court in Massachusetts to challenge the policy itself; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM) is a plaintiff on the amended complaint, and the individual students later dropped their claims. On April 25, 2025, a DOJ lawyer told a court that ICE would return the records to "active" while it developed a new termination framework. ICE issued a new SEVIS termination policy on April 26 that lists a State visa revocation as a ground, and by early May 2025 it had reactivated all the records terminated in the initiative, retroactively; State has not reinstated the revoked visas. On March 20, 2026, Judge Patti Saris largely denied the government's motion to dismiss, ruling the claims were not moot because the government had not shown the challenged conduct could not reasonably recur.

Update 2026-10-19: In a separate case in Washington, Judge Sparkle Sooknanan on March 18, 2026 granted summary judgment to Mansi Reddy Bushireddy, a student whose SEVIS record ICE terminated on April 4, 2025 over a 2023 shoplifting charge dismissed after she completed an awareness course and community service. The judge ruled the termination arbitrary and capricious and wrote that the government had acted "with a now all-too-familiar disregard for the law in hastily and callously terminating the F-1 status of international students across the country." A government witness in that case estimated DHS initiated about 5,500 SEVIS terminations from January to early May 2025, against about six in all of 2024. In the Massachusetts case, the government served the administrative record in June 2026, and on September 18, 2026 Judge Saris allowed the colleges limited discovery, including one deposition each of State and DHS; summary-judgment motions are due February 16, 2027.

Mass., No. 25-cv-11109) challenges State's visa revocations and DHS/ICE's SEVIS terminations under the Administrative Procedure Act. human_toll.summary: International students and recent graduates working on Optional Practical Training -- many with no criminal record, only traffic tickets, or charges that were dismissed -- had their SEVIS records terminated in spring 2025, often learning of it from their schools rather than the government. They were barred from classes and work and disenrolled, some lost jobs and income, and some left the country fearing detention; State's letters to visa holders warned of "fines, detention, and/or deportation" and pointed them to the CBP Home app to depart. Students also took on legal bills to sue, and the visas State revoked have not been reinstated.

what_changed.base: In mid-March 2025, DHS and the State Department began an effort referred to internally as the "Student Criminal Alien Initiative." Over multiple weeks, ICE employees ran the names of the 1.3 million international students then in the United States through the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database, which records arrests, charges and citations as well as convictions. About 6,400 names returned hits, among them students with no criminal history, only speeding tickets, or arrests that never led to charges. ICE sent that list to State, which revoked many if not all of the valid visas on it, and ICE then terminated the SEVIS (Student and Exchange Visitor Information System) records of thousands of the students -- **more than 4,736 by April 10, by the student-visa program's own count to Congress, without any individualized assessment and, in many cases, without notifying the students or their schools**, according to the colleges' lawsuit. A senior DHS official, Andre Watson, told a federal judge in Washington on April 29, 2025 that the initiative was done "at the instruction of leadership." Hundreds of students sued, and judges had granted temporary restraining orders in more than 35 of the suits by April 24, 2025, per Inside Higher Ed. That day the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and several students sued in federal court in Massachusetts to challenge the policy itself; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM) is a plaintiff on the amended complaint, and the individual students later dropped their claims. On April 25, 2025, a DOJ lawyer told a court that ICE would return the records to "active" while it developed a new termination framework. ICE issued a new SEVIS termination policy on April 26 that lists a State visa revocation as a ground, and by early May 2025 it had reactivated all the records terminated in the initiative, retroactively; State has not reinstated the revoked visas. On March 20, 2026, Judge Patti Saris largely denied the government's motion to dismiss, ruling the claims were not moot because the government had not shown the challenged conduct could not reasonably recur.

The judge ruled the termination arbitrary and capricious and wrote that the government had acted "with a now all-too-familiar disregard for the law in hastily and callously terminating the F-1 status of international students across the country." A government witness in that case estimated DHS initiated about 5,500 SEVIS terminations from January to early May 2025, against about six in all of 2024. In the Massachusetts case, the government served the administrative record in June 2026, and on September 18, 2026 Judge Saris allowed the colleges limited discovery, including one deposition each of State and DHS; summary-judgment motions are due February 16, 2027.

glance.what: Ended TPS for 13 countries; the Supreme Court let it stand and barred most court challenges

what_changed:
Backstory: Congress created Temporary Protected Status (TPS) in 1990. The Homeland Security Secretary can designate a country whose conditions prevent safe return and extend the designation in 6- to 18-month periods; holders get a work permit and protection from removal for as long as it lasts. When President Trump took office in January 2025, 17 countries had TPS designations (Congressional Research Service).

On January 28, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem canceled the 18-month extension her predecessor Alejandro Mayorkas had granted Venezuelans earlier that month, which ran to October 2, 2026 (NBC News); DHS's notice said it "vacates Mayorkas' notice immediately" (Federal Register, Feb. 3, 2025). Days later DHS terminated Venezuela's 2023 designation effective April 7, 2025, saying it was "contrary to the national interest" to let those Venezuelans stay (Federal Register, Feb. 5, 2025). In a notice published February 24 it cut Haiti's 2024 extension from 18 months to 12, moving its end from February 3, 2026 to August 3, 2025 (Federal Register). On March 31, U.S. District Judge Edward Chen in San Francisco paused the Venezuela moves in National TPS Alliance v. Noem, finding the plaintiffs likely to show they were "unauthorized by law, arbitrary and capricious, and motivated by unconstitutional animus" (AP). On May 19 the Supreme Court put Chen's order on hold without explanation, letting the government strip protection from **350,000 Venezuelans**, with only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson noting a dissent (AP).

Terminations followed country by country, each in a Federal Register notice saying the country no longer met the conditions for TPS: Afghanistan (published May 13, 2025, effective July 14), Cameroon (June 4; effective August 4), Nepal (June 6; effective August 5), Haiti (July 1; effective September 2), Honduras and Nicaragua (both July 8; effective September 8), Venezuela's 2021 designation (September 8; effective November 7), Syria (September 22; effective November 21), South Sudan (November 6; effective January 5, 2026), Burma (November 25; effective January 26, 2026), a new Haiti termination that replaced the July one (November 28; effective February 3, 2026), Ethiopia (December 15; effective February 13, 2026), Somalia (January 14, 2026; effective March 17, 2026) and Yemen (March 3, 2026; effective May 4, 2026) (Federal Register). CRS counts 13 of the 17 countries' designations terminated.

Courts slowed most of them. In July 2025 a federal appeals court briefly kept the Afghan protections in place on an appeal by the advocacy group CASA (NPR); the Afghan and Cameroonian terminations took effect later that summer (National Immigration Forum). On July 15, 2025, a federal judge in New York blocked the first Haiti termination, restoring the February 3, 2026 end date (National Immigration Forum). On July 31, 2025, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco kept TPS in place for about 60,000 people from Nepal, Honduras and Nicaragua, finding no "objective review of the country conditions" (AP); the Ninth Circuit stayed her order on August 20 (NPR). In August the Ninth Circuit upheld Chen's Venezuela order, writing that DHS lacked power to "vacate" an existing extension (JURIST), and on September 5 Chen set aside the Venezuela and Haiti actions (National Immigration Forum). On October 3, 2025, the Supreme Court again let the Venezuela termination proceed, over the three liberal justices' dissent (AP).

Judges then paused the Syria termination (November 19, 2025, New York) and South Sudan (December 30, Massachusetts) (CRS; National Immigration Forum). On December 31, 2025, Thompson ruled the Nepal, Honduras and Nicaragua terminations unlawful (National Immigration Forum). A Chicago judge paused Burma's in January 2026 (National Immigration Forum). On January 28, 2026, a Ninth Circuit panel held that Noem exceeded her authority in ending TPS for Venezuelans and, early, for Haitians (AP; Supreme Court docket). A Massachusetts judge paused Ethiopia's on January 30 (National Immigration Forum). On February 2, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington stayed the second Haiti termination for roughly 350,000 Haitians, finding it "substantially likely" Noem had preordained it out of "hostility to nonwhite immigrants" (NPR). On February 9 the Ninth Circuit stayed Thompson's ruling (National Immigration Forum). A Massachusetts judge paused Somalia's on March 13 (CRS; National Immigration Forum).

Markwayne Mullin succeeded Noem as Secretary in March 2026 (CNBC). On April 16 the House passed, 224-204, a bill (H.R. 1689) forced to a vote by a discharge petition that would require DHS to designate Haiti for TPS until April 2029; it stalled in the Senate (House Clerk; Michigan Advance; LeadingAge). On May 1 a New York judge paused Yemen's termination (CRS; National Immigration Forum). The Supreme Court took up the Haiti and Syria cases together, and on June 25, 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, ruled 6-3 that the TPS statute bars courts from hearing any non-constitutional challenge to a termination and that the Haitian plaintiffs' race-discrimination claim would likely fail (CRS). Justice Elena Kagan's dissent said the plaintiffs had shown racial motive was likely a factor (CRS). On July 1, Mullin said Haitians and Syrians who lost TPS must leave now through DHS's self-deportation program, which offers $2,600 and travel costs, or face forced removal (Bloomberg Law). The lower courts then lifted their stays: Yemen on July 20, Syria on July 27, Haiti in early August after the D.C. Circuit's mandate, Burma and South Sudan on August 7, Somalia on August 14 and Ethiopia on August 18 (National Immigration Forum; Jackson Lewis). **DHS began summoning Haitians in Ohio to check-ins where officers fitted them with ankle monitors, attorneys told The Washington Post** (Aug. 3, 2026). Deportation flights to Haiti resumed August 20; a USA Today tally reported October 21 put the number deported at 766 (The National News Desk).

Venezuelans whose work permits were issued by February 5, 2025 with an October 2, 2026 expiry kept work authorization to that date; the rest had already lost it (Latin Times). On October 5, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the Ninth Circuit's January ruling and sent the case back for reconsideration in light of Mullin v. Doe (Supreme Court docket). The designations for El Salvador (due September 9, 2026), Ukraine and Sudan (due October 19) reached their expiration dates without a published decision; on October 18 DHS said Ukrainian and Sudanese holders "retain protection" until decisions are announced "at the appropriate time" (CRS; CBS News). The CHNV humanitarian parole terminations and their effect on immigrant caregivers are covered in a separate entry.
legal_status: Sued in multiple federal courts. District judges in San Francisco, New York, Washington, Chicago and Massachusetts postponed or set aside terminations, and the Ninth Circuit ruled the Venezuela vacatur and early Haiti end unlawful (Jan. 28, 2026). The Supreme Court stayed the Venezuela rulings (May 19 and Oct. 3, 2025) and, in Mullin v. Doe (June 25, 2026), held non-constitutional challenges barred and the Haiti race claim likely to fail; the stays were then lifted. On Oct. 5, 2026 it vacated the Ninth Circuit's Venezuela and Haiti ruling and remanded. The Haiti equal-protection claim remains pending in D.C. district court.

human_toll.summary: People who had lived and worked legally under TPS, some for decades, lost their work permits and protection from removal and were told to leave. Venezuelans and Haitians were the largest groups. After the Supreme Court's 2026 ruling, federal officers fitted Haitians in Ohio with ankle monitors, attorneys said, and deportation flights resumed to Haiti, a country under the State Department's highest travel warning.

human_toll.caveat: Beneficiary counts are DHS figures given to CRS, as of June 25, 2026; CRS notes they include some people who have since obtained green cards, and holders revert to any other status they had or obtained, so not everyone counted lost all protection. The deportation count is a USA Today tally (El Pais counted 749) of all Haitians deported, not only former TPS holders; Haiti's migration office said the first flight carried both TPS holders and people who had served prison sentences (AP). No figure for arrests or removals of former TPS holders as a group was found. DHS's stated rationale: each notice says the Secretary reviewed country conditions, consulted other agencies and found the country no longer met TPS conditions, or that letting nationals stay was contrary to the national interest; DHS calls TPS "temporary" and says it had become "de facto amnesty" under earlier administrations. Several judges found the terminations preordained or racially motivated; the Supreme Court majority found the Haitian plaintiffs unlikely to prove a racial motive, and three justices disagreed.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the terminations and their dates, which come from DHS's own Federal Register notices and the Congressional Research Service. HIGH confidence on the Supreme Court actions (AP, CRS, the Court's docket). The dates on which each lower-court stay was entered and lifted rest mainly on the National Immigration Forum's fact sheet, an advocacy group's compilation, cross-checked against CRS, NPR, AP and Jackson Lewis where they overlap; Reuters, CBS and Guardian reports on the South Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia and Yemen rulings could not be fetched. Haiti's end date is reported differently: USCIS extended Haitian work permits through July 27, 2026, and the D.C. court said on August 4-5 that its stay was no longer in effect. Findings of racial animus by district judges are court findings at a preliminary or summary-judgment stage, not final; the Supreme Court majority disagreed for Haiti. The ankle-monitor account rests on attorneys quoted by The Washington Post; only its opening was readable. No public official count of former TPS holders arrested or removed was found.

glance.what: Reportedly told USCIS staff to pose as voters to search state voter records, on under 2 hours' training

what_changed: An anonymous, nearly 30-page whistleblower disclosure -- published September 14, 2026 by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Alex Padilla -- describes a DHS effort called the 'Unlawful Voter Initiative,' run through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and its Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate. To work around a lack of voter data from the states, USCIS staffers were pulled off their normal work in late August 2026, given under two hours of training, and then directed to run DHS-provided lists of individuals through state voter-registration lookup tools by posing as those individual voters. Staff were told to review 40 individuals per day (about 12 minutes each) and to create federal law-enforcement records (TECS records) on anyone flagged as an 'unlawful voter.' According to the disclosure, officers who raised concerns about the searches' legality were told to proceed and that they would not be held "personally liable." The disclosure, which includes screenshots and transcripts of the DHS training materials, warns that the practice likely violates state laws restricting who may access voter-lookup systems, and that inaccurate or incomplete DHS data could result in U.S. citizens being wrongly flagged and recorded as unlawful voters weeks before the November 2026 midterms. A DHS spokesperson said the department is "laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote" and "accessed publicly available data from states' voter rolls and cross referenced them with known aliens in our systems."
legal_status: Alleged by an anonymous whistleblower; no charges, lawsuit or ruling on the voter-lookup searches. pull_quote: “The vast majority of so-called criminal aliens are individuals charged with or convicted of traffic offenses, DUIs and immigration-related offenses,” said John Sandweg, former acting ICE director.

glance.what: Listed arrestees as 'worst of the worst' on a public site; DHS admitted hundreds of offenses were misstated

what_changed:
DHS created a public website in December 2025 branding a list of arrested immigrants -- roughly 25,000 people by mid-February 2026 -- as the "worst of the worst," which Secretary Noem, DHS, and the White House heavily promoted on social media to justify the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement operations. A CNN analysis found that while thousands of those listed were described as arrested for or convicted of serious charges such as sex crimes or homicide, hundreds more branded the "worst of the worst" were listed only for far less serious offenses, including single charges of traffic offenses, marijuana possession or illegal reentry. CNN also found that some of the cities with the most listed arrests were relatively small cities with large prisons or detention centers, a possible sign that many of those listed were already in custody rather than arrested in the community. John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under the Obama administration, said "the vast majority of so-called criminal aliens are individuals charged with or convicted of traffic offenses, DUIs and immigration-related offenses," adding of the serious-criminal population the administration describes: "That population is not out there."

After receiving CNN's questions, a DHS spokesperson admitted on February 17, 2026 that the charges against hundreds of listed immigrants had been described incorrectly, calling it "a glitch on the WOW website" that affected about 5% of entries and saying many of those listed for a single, less serious offense had additional crimes; on February 18 the spokesperson said the glitch had been "resolved." On February 20, DHS announced it had added another 5,000 people to the site, bringing the total to over 30,000. On March 4, ABC News reported that the site had listed Minnesota home renovator Telesforo Cerero-Palacios under "dangerous drugs" although a DHS record showed no criminal history; an ICE spokesperson pointed to an FBI number linked to multiple aliases, DHS appeared to remove him days after ABC began asking questions, and it did not answer whether he had been listed in error. Local outlet KTTC, which tracked the site's Minnesota listings, reported on March 16 that the count went from 486 in early February to 487 after the February 19 revision, rose to 505 by March 9, then dropped by 12 a week later; KTTC also found that roughly 44% of the Minnesota listings came from cities with federal or state prisons, and DHS responded that it "never claimed everyone on the website or every arrest in Operation Metro Surge was made at large in the community." DHS kept expanding the site, to more than 35,000 people by June 1, 2026 and more than 40,000 by July 28, 2026; no independent review of the accuracy of the added entries has been identified.
legal_status: None tied to the website: no lawsuit, court ruling or inspector general finding addresses its listings or the errors DHS admitted.

human_toll.summary: People arrested by ICE were posted on a public DHS website with their photo, country of origin, arrest city and alleged crimes under a "worst of the worst" banner. CNN found thousands listed for serious charges such as sex crimes or homicide, but hundreds more listed only for single, far less serious offenses such as a traffic charge, and DHS admitted the charges against hundreds of people had been described incorrectly. At least one man whose DHS record showed no criminal history, Telesforo Cerero-Palacios, was listed under "dangerous drugs"; he told ABC News his reputation was ruined and that he was afraid to leave home except to go to work.

KTTC's 44% covers Minnesota listings only. No independent audit has been identified of the more than 15,000 people added since mid-February, and no figure exists for how many listed people were harmed by a wrong listing. DHS called the errors "a glitch on the WOW website" that it had fixed, said many people listed for a single traffic or reentry offense "have additional crimes," and said "All of these individuals have been arrested by ICE and all of them committed crimes breaking our nation's laws." On the prison-town listings, DHS said it "never claimed everyone on the website or every arrest in Operation Metro Surge was made at large in the community." glance.what: Fired immigration judge Chloe Dillon two days after she reported an unlawful ICE detention, she says

what_changed: Chloe Dillon served as an immigration judge in San Francisco from September 2022 until August 2025, and her complaint says she 'received excellent reviews, resolved thousands of cases' in that time. In April 2025, San Francisco Assistant Chief Immigration Judge Loi McCleskey directed the court's judges to grant ICE's motions to move cases to other courts, denying them only in 'rare circumstances.' Dillon objected that the directive was contrary to law and could undercut immigrants' right to counsel, and her complaint says McCleskey 'warned her that "the White House" was paying attention to this and to be careful about pushing the issue further.' Dillon recalled the warning to MS NOW as 'The White House is watching this issue. Like, do you really want to push this?' and was never told who at the White House was watching. In one case where she denied ICE's venue motion, the case was transferred anyway, and in July and August 2025 she issued two orders denying ICE motions to re-calendar closed asylum cases of unaccompanied minors. On August 20, 2025, a young man who had come to court alone and without a lawyer appeared on her calendar at the 100 Montgomery Street courthouse; the ICE attorney moved orally to dismiss his case and said DHS would pursue expedited removal instead. Dillon gave him time to respond and to find counsel, and ICE detained him after he left the courtroom. Rereading his file, she concluded he was 'almost certainly a designated unaccompanied minor who could not be placed into expedited removal proceedings,' and that afternoon she emailed McCleskey about 'potential violations of statutory law and due process' and courthouse arrests disrupting the orderly administration of justice. **On August 22, 2025, about 48 hours later, Dillon was fired without notice or a hearing by an emailed letter signed by EOIR Acting Director Sirce Owen that cited only 'Article II of the Constitution.'** Dillon told MS NOW that no other San Francisco judges were fired that day. After her appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board stalled, she filed a federal lawsuit on September 10, 2026, against the Justice Department, Owen and Attorney General Todd Blanche (named in his official capacity as DOJ's current head), alleging retaliation under the Whistleblower Protection Act, violations of the First and Fifth Amendments, and that her removal was void because only the attorney general can remove an immigration judge under Article II. DOJ called the allegation 'patently false' and said it is 'restoring integrity to our immigration system.' Dillon is one of 14 San Francisco immigration judges fired since President Trump's return to office, according to NBC Bay Area, and one of more than 120 immigration judges removed during the administration's immigration crackdown, according to the union representing immigration judges.
legal_status: Sued: Dillon v. Blanche, No. 3:26-cv-10143 (N.D. Cal.), filed September 10, 2026, against the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche and EOIR Acting Director Sirce Owen in their official capacities, alleging retaliation in violation of the Whistleblower Protection Act, First and Fifth Amendment violations, violations of the Appointments Clause and Article II, and Administrative Procedure Act claims; it seeks reinstatement, back pay, damages and a declaration that the firing was unlawful. DOJ has not answered in court and no ruling has issued; an initial case management conference is set for December 10, 2026. Her earlier Merit Systems Protection Board appeal of the firing has not been decided. In a separate case over two February 2025 firings (Jackler v. DOJ), the MSPB ruled on March 20, 2026 that the firings were lawful under Article II and that it lacks jurisdiction over such appeals; the Federal Circuit granted initial en banc review on June 17, 2026, and no ruling has been reported.

human_toll.summary: Dillon lost her job and, she told NBC Bay Area, her family of four's health insurance. The young man she flagged, whom she believed was a designated unaccompanied minor entitled to have his asylum claim heard first by an asylum officer, was detained by ICE at the courthouse for expedited removal. Her firing is part of a turnover that has removed more than 120 immigration judges nationwide and most of San Francisco immigration court's bench, the judges immigrants with pending cases depend on for a fair hearing.

title: DOJ Reassigned the Senior Attorneys Running Its 60-Year-Old Program Accrediting Non-Lawyers to Help Indigent Immigrants, Freezing Its Core Functions
status: Ongoing. CBS reported April 23, 2026 that the program had approved no new applications since its attorneys were reassigned in March, with 40-60 arriving weekly. Nine senators asked DOJ in September 2026 to undo the cuts. No restoration reported.
date_of_action: 2026-03 (senior attorneys reassigned)
what_changed:
CBS News reported DOJ abruptly reassigned the handful of senior attorneys who operate the Recognition and Accreditation program -- a more than 60-year-old program, part of DOJ's Executive Office for Immigration Review, that accredits non-attorneys working for largely faith-based legal-aid organizations (such as Catholic Charities and Jewish Family Services) so they are authorized to assist immigrants with matters ranging from naturalization petitions to representation in immigration court. The program accredits more than 2,600 non-attorneys across more than 900 recognized programs, legal experts told CBS. The reassignment orders came from Jamee Comans, the acting Assistant Director for the Office of Policy, which administers the program, according to sources CBS cited. Most of the reassigned attorneys were told they would now work as entry-level law clerks in immigration courts -- a job typically reserved for people fresh out of law school -- leaving only two support staff with no legal authority to approve or renew accreditation applications. EOIR declined to comment on personnel matters; a government official told CBS the program "isn't ending or being abolished" and "will continue." Sources told CBS that around the time it sought comment, EOIR assigned two other employees to review pending applications, and that the program was being shifted to an already understaffed Public Resources Program. There was no public announcement of the changes.

Update 2026-10-19: CBS reported on April 23, 2026 that the program had **failed to approve a single new application since March**, while still receiving between 40 and 60 new applications per week, one source said; a DOJ spokesperson did not immediately respond to a new request for comment. That week more than 330 participating nonprofits wrote to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and EOIR Director Daren Margolin asking them to restore the program, noting processing times had already stretched to 6 to 8 months in 2025. Thirteen Illinois nonprofits made the same request in April, per WBEZ Chicago. In September 2026, nine senators led by Jacky Rosen wrote to Blanche urging DOJ to "undo the Department's harmful staffing cuts and reassignments"; KJZZ dated the letter September 2, and EOIR did not immediately respond to KJZZ.
confidence_note:
HIGH confidence -- the reassignment, its scope, Comans's role in ordering it, the two remaining support staff without approval authority, the zero new approvals and the 40-60 weekly applications all come from CBS News's March and April 2026 reporting, which rests on unnamed sources with direct knowledge; DOJ's on-record statement covers only that the program will continue. The ABA Journal's report restates CBS's. Re-verified August 2026: independent Illinois reporting (WBEZ Chicago, Chicago Sun-Times, April 30, 2026) corroborates the ongoing application freeze from local advocacy organizations' direct experience, consistent with CBS's national reporting. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- no reporting identified confirming the accreditation office has resumed processing applications or that staffing has been restored since the April 30, 2026 reporting reviewed above.

Update 2026-10-19: The WBEZ report rests on the advocacy groups' account of the reassignment; the zero-approvals figure is CBS's (April 23, 2026). The senators' September 2026 letter, per Sen. Rosen's office and KJZZ, repeats CBS's report of two remaining employees who cannot approve applications; no reporting of restored staffing was found.

More than 330 participating nonprofits (April 2026) and nine U.S. senators (September 2026) asked DOJ in letters to restore the program; no DOJ response to the senators has been reported.

what_changed.base: CBS News reported DOJ abruptly reassigned the handful of senior attorneys who operate the Recognition and Accreditation program -- a more than 60-year-old program, part of DOJ's Executive Office for Immigration Review, that accredits non-attorneys working for largely faith-based legal-aid organizations (such as Catholic Charities and Jewish Family Services) so they are authorized to assist immigrants with matters ranging from naturalization petitions to representation in immigration court. The program accredits more than 2,600 non-attorneys across more than 900 recognized programs, legal experts told CBS. The reassignment orders came from Jamee Comans, the acting Assistant Director for the Office of Policy, which administers the program, according to sources CBS cited. Most of the reassigned attorneys were told they would now work as entry-level law clerks in immigration courts -- a job typically reserved for people fresh out of law school -- leaving only two support staff with no legal authority to approve or renew accreditation applications. EOIR declined to comment on personnel matters; a government official told CBS the program "isn't ending or being abolished" and "will continue." Sources told CBS that around the time it sought comment, EOIR assigned two other employees to review pending applications, and that the program was being shifted to an already understaffed Public Resources Program. There was no public announcement of the changes.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-19: CBS reported on April 23, 2026 that the program had **failed to approve a single new application since March**, while still receiving between 40 and 60 new applications per week, one source said; a DOJ spokesperson did not immediately respond to a new request for comment. That week more than 330 participating nonprofits wrote to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and EOIR Director Daren Margolin asking them to restore the program, noting processing times had already stretched to 6 to 8 months in 2025. Thirteen Illinois nonprofits made the same request in April, per WBEZ Chicago. In September 2026, nine senators led by Jacky Rosen wrote to Blanche urging DOJ to "undo the Department's harmful staffing cuts and reassignments"; KJZZ dated the letter September 2, and EOIR did not immediately respond to KJZZ.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence -- the reassignment, its scope, Comans's role in ordering it, the two remaining support staff without approval authority, the zero new approvals and the 40-60 weekly applications all come from CBS News's March and April 2026 reporting, which rests on unnamed sources with direct knowledge; DOJ's on-record statement covers only that the program will continue. The ABA Journal's report restates CBS's. Re-verified August 2026: independent Illinois reporting (WBEZ Chicago, Chicago Sun-Times, April 30, 2026) corroborates the ongoing application freeze from local advocacy organizations' direct experience, consistent with CBS's national reporting. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- no reporting identified confirming the accreditation office has resumed processing applications or that staffing has been restored since the April 30, 2026 reporting reviewed above.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-19: The WBEZ report rests on the advocacy groups' account of the reassignment; the zero-approvals figure is CBS's (April 23, 2026). The senators' September 2026 letter, per Sen. Rosen's office and KJZZ, repeats CBS's report of two remaining employees who cannot approve applications; no reporting of restored staffing was found.

title: DOJ Fired More Than 100 Immigration Judges Starting in 2025, Even After Congress Funded Hiring More to Cut a Nearly 4-Million-Case Backlog
status: No reinstatements reported. UN experts said information indicates at least 113 immigration judges were terminated from January 2025 to July 2026. MSPB upheld two February 2025 firings under Article II (March 2026); the Federal Circuit granted en banc review in June 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02 onward: first immigration judge fired February 5, 2025; 17 judges fired July 11-14, 2025, days after the July 4 law funding more judges; further rounds in September, November and December 2025
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, the Justice Department's Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) fired immigration judges in successive rounds, most without a stated cause. On February 4, 2025, the day before the first firing, the corps of permanent immigration judges numbered 726 (683 immigration judges and 43 assistant chief immigration judges), according to data obtained by NPR. The first judge fired, Tania Nemer of the Cleveland Immigration Court, was dismissed in the middle of a hearing and escorted out of the building; she has since sued over her termination. On Friday, February 14, 2025, five assistant chief immigration judges and 13 incoming judges received termination notices, according to the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE), the union representing immigration judges. On July 4, 2025, the reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21) appropriated $3.33 billion to the Justice Department, with hiring immigration judges and support staff 'to address the backlog' as its first listed purpose, and capped the immigration judge corps at 800 effective November 2028; the backlog then stood at nearly 4 million cases. Days later, 15 immigration judges learned on Friday, July 11, that they would be placed on leave with termination effective July 22, and two more judges, in Chicago and Houston, learned on Monday, July 14, that they were being fired; IFPTE said the 17 worked in courts in California, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, New York, Ohio, Texas, Utah, and Virginia. The termination email NPR reviewed stated: 'Pursuant to Article II of the Constitution, the Attorney General has decided not to extend your term or convert it to a permanent appointment.' IFPTE president Matt Biggs said, 'It's outrageous and against the public interest that at a time when the Congress has authorized 800 immigration judges, we are firing large numbers of immigration judges without cause,' adding, 'you can't enforce immigration laws when you fire the enforcers.' On July 17, 2025, Ila Deiss, an immigration judge on the San Francisco court since 2017, was fired by email with no advance notice and no stated reason; she told NPR she had only excellent reviews and was on track to resolve about 1,000 cases that year (NPR could not independently verify her productivity statistics), and she was three months short of 25 years of federal service, when her pension would vest. The next day DOJ fired Carolyn Feinstein, a forensic accountant in Austin who had worked seven years for DOJ's U.S. Trustee Program policing bankruptcy fraud and whose husband developed the ICEBlock app for tracking immigration agents; DOJ said she had an interest in the company holding the app's intellectual property, and a DOJ spokeswoman said the app endangers ICE officers. DOJ cited the president's Article II power to dismiss both Deiss and Feinstein. NPR reported that more than 200 career DOJ civil servants had lost their jobs in 2025 by then, according to the group Justice Connection. On August 27, 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth approved sending up to 600 military and civilian Defense Department lawyers to serve as temporary immigration judges, in groups of 150 on details of up to 179 days, according to a memo reviewed by the AP. On August 28, 2025, DOJ published a final rule in the Federal Register allowing any attorney to be designated a temporary immigration judge; previously, eligibility was limited to former immigration judges, administrative law judges, and DOJ attorneys with at least 10 years of immigration-law experience. DOJ said the change was needed to address the backlog, which the rule said peaked at about 4.1 million cases in January 2025. In September 2025, nearly 20 more judges were fired, the largest monthly total since February, and NPR reported that EOIR had lost more than 125 judges to firings and voluntary resignations in nine months, with some cases delayed as far out as 2029. By year's end the firings reached tenured judges and court supervisors, including judges in New York and San Francisco in November and December; **NPR's independent tally counted nearly 100 immigration judges fired in 2025**. In November 2025 DOJ launched a public hiring campaign for 'deportation judges'; by February 2026 it had hired 17 permanent judges, most from ICE and other DHS backgrounds, and 52 temporary judges who are military lawyers. As of February 23, 2026, there were 520 permanent immigration judges and 33 assistant chief immigration judges, and 202 judges who had been working in early 2025 were gone; EOIR had also lost over 400 legal assistants, attorney advisers and legal administrative specialists, 14 courts were operating with two or fewer permanent judges, and the San Francisco court, which lost 16 judges in 2025, was set to close with its roughly 120,000 cases moving to Concord. On March 20, 2026, the Merit Systems Protection Board's two members ruled that DOJ lawfully fired two assistant chief immigration judges dismissed in February 2025, Megan Jackler and Brandon Jaroch, under Article II, reversing an administrative judge's August 2025 ruling that ordered their reinstatement; in June 2026 the Federal Circuit granted initial en banc review of their appeal. On July 16, 2026, two UN special rapporteurs said information indicated that at least 135 judges, including at least 113 immigration judges, 13 assistant chief immigration judges and nine appellate immigration judges, had been terminated since January 2025, and that 65 of 78 removed immigration judges with public data had asylum grant rates above the national or court average.
confidence_note: Strong. Judge counts come from NPR's own EOIR personnel data and independent firing tally (nearly 100 fired in 2025; 726 permanent judges in February 2025 versus 553 in February 2026) and from a July 2026 statement by two UN special rapporteurs (at least 113 immigration judges terminated since January 2025, framed as what 'information indicates'). The appropriation and 800-judge cap are from the enacted law's text, the temporary-judge rule from the Federal Register, and the 600-lawyer detail from the AP's review of Hegseth's memo. Deiss's performance and productivity claims are her own account, which NPR could not independently verify. Whether the firings were politically motivated is alleged by fired judges, the union and UN experts; DOJ says the judges were not managing caseloads and that the firings are lawful under Article II, which the MSPB accepted and the Federal Circuit is reviewing. Re-verified 2026-10-19: the Federal Circuit en banc case (Jackler v. DOJ) and Nemer's suit remain pending with no reported ruling; Government Executive reports Jackler and Jaroch were fired by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.

human_toll.summary: People facing deportation, including asylum seekers whose cases decide whether they are sent back to possible persecution or torture, have lost experienced judges: the permanent immigration judge corps shrank by about a quarter in a year, some cases were pushed out as far as 2029, and 14 courts were left with two or fewer permanent judges. UN experts warn that the removals, in which 65 of 78 removed judges with public data had above-average asylum grant rates, can deprive people of a meaningful opportunity to present their claims, with potentially irreversible consequences. NPR reported that the replacements include 'deportation judge' hires, mostly from ICE and other DHS backgrounds, and military lawyers serving as temporary judges. The losses came while Congress was spending $3.33 billion to hire more judges to cut a backlog of nearly 4 million cases.

title: Immigration Courts Stop Pausing Children's Cases, Ordering Abused and Abandoned Migrant Children Deported While Their Protection Petitions Are Pending
status: Ongoing -- Board precedents bar open-ended pauses for special immigrant juvenile cases; judges order children removed, some without lawyers; EOIR denies fast-tracking; a legal-aid group and six children sued in July 2026, no ruling yet; 51 lawmakers sought answers Oct. 16, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-01-29 (EOIR reinstates its 2017 juvenile-case guidelines) through 2026-09 (removal orders against children observed in Chelmsford and Harlingen courts)
what_changed:
In the past, immigration judges typically postponed or closed the deportation cases of migrant children who had been found by a state court to have been abused, neglected or abandoned by a parent, attorneys told the Boston Globe, while the children pursued special immigrant juvenile status -- a humanitarian path to a green card created by the Immigration Act of 1990 that can take years because of visa backlogs. Under the Trump administration, the Justice Department's immigration-court system has moved away from that practice in several steps. On Jan. 29, 2025, EOIR Acting Director Sirce Owen issued a policy memo (PM 25-10) rescinding a December 2023 directive on children's cases and reinstating a 2017 memo that, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project, removed certain child-friendly guidance and told judges to be vigilant about 'fraud and abuse.' On Nov. 14, 2025, the Board of Immigration Appeals, the Justice Department's highest immigration tribunal, issued a precedent decision, Matter of Cahuec Tzalam, written by Chief Appellate Immigration Judge Garry Malphrus, holding that an immigration judge erred in administratively closing a case for a respondent with a pending special immigrant juvenile petition, citing the lack of evidence of eligibility and the extended delay in visa availability. On March 11, 2026, in Matter of Pinzon Rozo, another precedent written by Malphrus, the Board took up an interlocutory appeal by the Department of Homeland Security 'to correct recurring problems in the handling of' continuance requests, and held that a judge erred in continuing a case to await a visa for a respondent with an approved special immigrant juvenile petition, where the visa 'will not be current for an uncertain and lengthy period of time'; the Board noted that such visas were then available only to applicants who filed before July 15, 2021, 'a nearly 4-year gap' from the respondent's May 2025 filing. The respondent in that case was 20 when he filed his petition. In a third precedent, Matter of Z-R-C-N-, decided March 18, 2026, a different Board panel denied a mother's and her daughters' motion to reopen, holding that the minor respondents' eligibility based on an approved petition was 'speculative considering the 4-year delay in visa availability.' On July 29, 2026, Jewish Family and Community Services of Pittsburgh, a legal-aid group that represents unaccompanied children, and six young immigrants sued DHS, the Justice Department, EOIR, ICE and USCIS in federal court in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, alleging that 'Immigration authorities, and immigration courts, throughout the United States are now refusing to afford children the due process to seek that protection'; one child described in the complaint, a 17-year-old from Guatemala whom the health department had found to be a trafficking victim, was ordered removed by a Philadelphia immigration court on July 16, Pittsburgh's Public Source reported. DHS said in a statement that 'All illegal aliens receive due process.' Bloomberg Law, reporting on an Aug. 5, 2026 Manhattan hearing, said two people familiar with the situation told it, on condition of anonymity, that EOIR supervisors were directing judges to limit continuances for unaccompanied children to 21 days, in internal guidance not formalized in any public policy or memo, compared with the three to six months former judges said was typical; according to Mobile Pathways data cited by Bloomberg Law, the continuance grant rate for unaccompanied children fell from nearly 80% at the start of the second Trump term to 46% in June 2026. The Boston Globe reported on Sept. 21, 2026 that an EOIR internal training document from early September that it reviewed coaches new judges to avoid rescheduling cases, stating that 'Some continuances are sought solely for the purpose of delay.' The Globe reported that **over the preceding month, its reporter observed Judge Luciana Dubuc, a former ICE attorney appointed this year, order the deportation of 17 children at the Chelmsford, Massachusetts immigration court, including 7-year-old twin boys from Colombia**, in hearings that usually lasted a few minutes; one, a 16-year-old whose special immigrant juvenile application was pending after a state court found he had been abused, neglected and abandoned by his mother, was ordered deported in early September after the judge said she could not delay his case. Lawyers also reported more deportation orders against children in Philadelphia and Chicago, the Globe said. CNN reported from the Harlingen, Texas immigration court on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026, where 25 migrant children, including a 3-year-old, appeared before a judge; a 13-year-old Honduran boy without a lawyer was ordered removed after telling the judge his family was in the U.S. and it was too dangerous to go back. The changes coincide with the lapse in July 2026 of the federally funded legal-aid contract for unaccompanied children, which the Globe said had provided more than 25,000 children with representation, a lawyer shortage the Globe said is likely to grow. The Justice Department told the Globe that the Biden administration had 'intentionally turned a blind eye to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied alien children in need of care' and that 'Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration.' EOIR told CNN and Bloomberg Law that it 'prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish,' and denied to CNN claims that cases are being fast-tracked.

Update 2026-10-19: On Oct. 16, 2026, Rep. Andrea Salinas and Sen. Ron Wyden led 51 members of Congress in a letter to the Justice Department, EOIR, ICE and USCIS that said courts 'are increasingly imposing accelerated timelines and restricted continuances due to directives from DOJ and EOIR.' The letter said a new judge on Chicago's juvenile docket ordered at least eight children eligible for special immigrant juvenile status removed in July and August 2026, a practice it said 'appears to draw on' Matter of Cahuec Tzalam, and it asked the agencies to answer 25 questions, including what continuance and scheduling directives EOIR has issued, by Oct. 30, 2026.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the Board of Immigration Appeals precedents, read directly from the three published decisions on the Justice Department's website, and on the courtroom scenes, which the Boston Globe and CNN reporters observed in person. MODERATE confidence on what the January 2025 policy memo changed, read from the Immigration Policy Tracking Project's summary; the memo itself, read directly, confirms its date, signer and the reinstatement of the 2017 guidelines. MODERATE confidence on the 21-day continuance guidance, which Bloomberg Law sourced to two unnamed people, and on the EOIR training document, which the Globe reviewed but did not publish. The nationwide removal-order and continuance-rate figures are Mobile Pathways' analysis of Justice Department data, not an official count; the Guardian article reporting them could not be read directly (bot-walled), so the figures here are checked against IBTimes UK's account of the same analysis, which is not independent corroboration. Named officials: Owen signed the January 2025 memo, and Malphrus is named as author in the two Board decisions he wrote. Owen was EOIR's Acting Director from January to September 2025 and has been again since July 2026, per her Justice Department staff profile; Daren Margolin was EOIR's director in between, from October 2025 until he resigned in July 2026, Bloomberg Law reported. Judge Dubuc, a public official ruling in open court, is named in the narrative only, as the Boston Globe named her from its reporter's observation of her hearings. No child is named because none of their families has made a name public. Re-verified 2026-10-19: the Board decisions, the January 2025 memo, and the Globe, CNN and Bloomberg Law accounts still say what this entry says; the July 2026 federal lawsuit (L.B.R.P. v. DHS) is read from its court docket and Pittsburgh's Public Source, which quotes the complaint; the Oct. 16, 2026 congressional letter is read from Rep. Salinas's release, which prints its full text, and its account of Chicago removal orders is the lawmakers' own, not independently checked here.

The Board's Pinzon Rozo precedent concerned a respondent who was 20 when he filed, and the Board said an approved petition has long not entitled a respondent to delay proceedings (Matter of Quintero, 1982); judges can still grant time for asylum applications, and the Globe saw the Chelmsford judge do so. The Justice Department frames the change as cutting a backlog in which, per Bloomberg Law citing DOJ data, the median unaccompanied child's case had been pending nearly 2,400 days as of July 2026; an EOIR spokesperson told Bloomberg Law that 'Unnecessary delay hurts both aliens with meritorious claims and the American public who wish to see aliens with non-meritorious claims removed as quickly as possible,' and, CNN reported, Trump officials argue the administration's changes are for the children's benefit, to keep them out of harm's way and ensure rigorous vetting. DHS general counsel James Percival, in a letter to the American Immigration Lawyers Association about asylum abuse, quoted by the Globe, wrote that 'We must stop the widespread abuse that is currently undermining our immigration system.'

legal_status: Sued: L.B.R.P. v. DHS, No. 2:26-cv-05346 (E.D. Pa.), filed July 29, 2026 by Jewish Family and Community Services of Pittsburgh and six young immigrants proceeding under initials against DHS, the Justice Department, EOIR, ICE, USCIS and their leaders, challenges the immigration courts' handling of children seeking special immigrant juvenile or trafficking-victim status and asks the court to vacate the policies and block the named children's removal. The docket lists a filing for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction on Sept. 21, 2026, a response in opposition on Oct. 14 and a reply on Oct. 19; no ruling has issued. The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled in three precedent decisions (Matter of Cahuec Tzalam, Nov. 14, 2025; Matter of Pinzon Rozo, March 11, 2026; Matter of Z-R-C-N-, March 18, 2026) that judges erred in closing or continuing, or should not reopen, cases to await special immigrant juvenile visas. Children ordered removed have 30 days to appeal. On Oct. 16, 2026, 51 members of Congress asked DOJ, EOIR, ICE and USCIS to reverse course; answers were requested by Oct. 30.

what_changed.base: In the past, immigration judges typically postponed or closed the deportation cases of migrant children who had been found by a state court to have been abused, neglected or abandoned by a parent, attorneys told the Boston Globe, while the children pursued special immigrant juvenile status -- a humanitarian path to a green card created by the Immigration Act of 1990 that can take years because of visa backlogs. Under the Trump administration, the Justice Department's immigration-court system has moved away from that practice in several steps. On Jan. 29, 2025, EOIR Acting Director Sirce Owen issued a policy memo (PM 25-10) rescinding a December 2023 directive on children's cases and reinstating a 2017 memo that, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project, removed certain child-friendly guidance and told judges to be vigilant about 'fraud and abuse.' On Nov. 14, 2025, the Board of Immigration Appeals, the Justice Department's highest immigration tribunal, issued a precedent decision, Matter of Cahuec Tzalam, written by Chief Appellate Immigration Judge Garry Malphrus, holding that an immigration judge erred in administratively closing a case for a respondent with a pending special immigrant juvenile petition, citing the lack of evidence of eligibility and the extended delay in visa availability. On March 11, 2026, in Matter of Pinzon Rozo, another precedent written by Malphrus, the Board took up an interlocutory appeal by the Department of Homeland Security 'to correct recurring problems in the handling of' continuance requests, and held that a judge erred in continuing a case to await a visa for a respondent with an approved special immigrant juvenile petition, where the visa 'will not be current for an uncertain and lengthy period of time'; the Board noted that such visas were then available only to applicants who filed before July 15, 2021, 'a nearly 4-year gap' from the respondent's May 2025 filing. The respondent in that case was 20 when he filed his petition. In a third precedent, Matter of Z-R-C-N-, decided March 18, 2026, a different Board panel denied a mother's and her daughters' motion to reopen, holding that the minor respondents' eligibility based on an approved petition was 'speculative considering the 4-year delay in visa availability.' On July 29, 2026, Jewish Family and Community Services of Pittsburgh, a legal-aid group that represents unaccompanied children, and six young immigrants sued DHS, the Justice Department, EOIR, ICE and USCIS in federal court in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, alleging that 'Immigration authorities, and immigration courts, throughout the United States are now refusing to afford children the due process to seek that protection'; one child described in the complaint, a 17-year-old from Guatemala whom the health department had found to be a trafficking victim, was ordered removed by a Philadelphia immigration court on July 16, Pittsburgh's Public Source reported. DHS said in a statement that 'All illegal aliens receive due process.' Bloomberg Law, reporting on an Aug. 5, 2026 Manhattan hearing, said two people familiar with the situation told it, on condition of anonymity, that EOIR supervisors were directing judges to limit continuances for unaccompanied children to 21 days, in internal guidance not formalized in any public policy or memo, compared with the three to six months former judges said was typical; according to Mobile Pathways data cited by Bloomberg Law, the continuance grant rate for unaccompanied children fell from nearly 80% at the start of the second Trump term to 46% in June 2026. The Boston Globe reported on Sept. 21, 2026 that an EOIR internal training document from early September that it reviewed coaches new judges to avoid rescheduling cases, stating that 'Some continuances are sought solely for the purpose of delay.' The Globe reported that **over the preceding month, its reporter observed Judge Luciana Dubuc, a former ICE attorney appointed this year, order the deportation of 17 children at the Chelmsford, Massachusetts immigration court, including 7-year-old twin boys from Colombia**, in hearings that usually lasted a few minutes; one, a 16-year-old whose special immigrant juvenile application was pending after a state court found he had been abused, neglected and abandoned by his mother, was ordered deported in early September after the judge said she could not delay his case. Lawyers also reported more deportation orders against children in Philadelphia and Chicago, the Globe said. CNN reported from the Harlingen, Texas immigration court on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026, where 25 migrant children, including a 3-year-old, appeared before a judge; a 13-year-old Honduran boy without a lawyer was ordered removed after telling the judge his family was in the U.S. and it was too dangerous to go back. The changes coincide with the lapse in July 2026 of the federally funded legal-aid contract for unaccompanied children, which the Globe said had provided more than 25,000 children with representation, a lawyer shortage the Globe said is likely to grow. The Justice Department told the Globe that the Biden administration had 'intentionally turned a blind eye to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied alien children in need of care' and that 'Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration.' EOIR told CNN and Bloomberg Law that it 'prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish,' and denied to CNN claims that cases are being fast-tracked.

narrative_override.headline: DHS called a U.S. citizen shot five times by Border Patrol a 'domestic terrorist'; bodycam contradicted it.

what_changed:
On October 4, 2025, **U.S. Border Patrol Agent Charles Exum shot U.S. citizen Marimar Martinez five times in Chicago's Brighton Park neighborhood during Operation Midway Blitz**, a large-scale immigration-enforcement surge. Martinez had been following the agents' SUV in her car, honking and shouting "la migra" to warn people about the agents, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. DHS's same-day press release branded Martinez and a co-defendant, Anthony Ian Santos Ruiz, "domestic terrorists," stated Martinez "was armed with a semi-automatic weapon and has a history of doxxing federal agents," and said agents "were ambushed by domestic terrorists that rammed federal agents with their vehicles." Martinez and Ruiz were federally charged over the alleged ramming. Between October 8 and 10, 2025, Exum drove the vehicle involved -- key physical evidence -- more than 1,000 miles back to his Border Patrol station in Maine rather than it being held for examination; his supervisor, who said in an email it was his idea, had scuff marks on the vehicle buffed out. Exum was separately quoted bragging in a text message, "I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys." On November 20, 2025, at prosecutors' request, a federal judge dismissed the indictment with prejudice, barring any refiling; a spokesman for U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros's office said prosecutors are "constantly evaluating new facts and information." In February 2026, a federal judge ordered the release of bodycam and other evidence, finding it would "counter the government's public narrative" of Martinez; the footage showed Exum appeared to turn his own vehicle's steering wheel toward Martinez immediately before the collision, after an agent in the vehicle said "it's time to get aggressive," directly contradicting the original ramming claim. DHS's October 2025 press release -- including the "domestic terrorist," armed, and ramming characterizations -- has not been corrected or retracted.

Update 2026-10-19: The evidence released in February 2026 included an email in which then-Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino, hours after the shooting, offered to extend Exum's retirement "in light of your excellent service in Chicago," and texts in which other agents called Exum "a legend among agents." Exum's own body camera was not turned on at the time of the shooting. Martinez's gun, which DHS cited, was in a holster snapped shut at the bottom of her purse, court records show; her attorneys say it was licensed, and agents never claimed she took it out. CBP said in February that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. In April 2026 the Illinois Accountability Commission, a state body created by Gov. JB Pritzker, concluded that Exum "shot an unarmed civilian without apparent justification" and that "evidence was deliberately tampered with and destroyed." On October 5, 2026, Martinez sued the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act, alleging Exum lied to the FBI and fired the last of his five shots through her rear passenger window; Chicago police have opened an investigation into the shooting. As of October 2026 the DHS release still labels Martinez a "domestic terrorist" on its website.
legal_status: Martinez and Ruiz were charged with assaulting federal officers in October 2025; Judge Georgia Alexakis dismissed the indictment with prejudice at prosecutors' request on November 20, 2025. Martinez filed an administrative Federal Tort Claims Act claim in February 2026 and sued the United States under the FTCA on October 5, 2026, alleging negligence, battery, assault, false arrest, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution and infliction of emotional distress; Exum is not a defendant, and no ruling has been reported. Exum has not been charged. Chicago police are investigating the shooting, and Martinez's attorney has said he believes federal prosecutors in Indiana opened a criminal investigation, which has not been publicly confirmed; DOJ declined to comment when the lawsuit was filed. CBP says significant use-of-force incidents go to its National Use of Force Review Board; no finding has been made public. The Illinois Accountability Commission, a state body created by Gov. JB Pritzker, concluded the shooting was "without apparent justification"; that is not a court finding.

human_toll.summary: Marimar Martinez, a U.S. citizen, was shot and wounded in her arm and both legs, arrested from the hospital, charged with assaulting federal officers and publicly labeled a "domestic terrorist" by DHS, a label still on its website after the charges against her and co-defendant Anthony Ian Santos Ruiz were dismissed with prejudice. Federal agents also fired tear gas and pepper balls at about 100 protesters who gathered in Brighton Park after the shooting.

human_toll.caveat: The wound and custody figures come from court records and Martinez's lawsuit as reported by the Sun-Times and AP. The account that the agents' SUV swerved into Martinez and that Exum fired from beside and behind her car rests on the released bodycam footage, which shows the steering turn but not the shots, and on a forensic reconstruction commissioned by her lawyers; no court has ruled on it. Exum testified that his life was at risk and that he takes "pride in my shooting skills"; DHS said agents "were ambushed" and showed "incredible restraint and prudence in their exercise of force"; CBP says Exum's leave is standard for significant use-of-force incidents, which it says are "thoroughly investigated." A chaotic encounter during a large operation may explain a split-second decision to fire, and prosecutors' dismissal was not a finding of agent misconduct. DHS has not retracted its accusations against Martinez and has referred questions to the Justice Department.
