title: FBI Told to Stop Investigating Confrontations Involving Immigration Agents, Shifting Oversight to ICE's Own Investigative Arm
status: Guidance reportedly distributed and in effect per internal emails reviewed by CBS News; DOJ and DHS publicly deny any change. Sens. Blumenthal and Schiff demanded rescission on Aug 11, 2026 (answers due Aug 25); no rescission or public response reported
date_of_action: 2026-07 (guidance distributed to FBI agents)
what_changed:
The New York Times reported, and CBS News independently confirmed via internal emails reviewed by its reporters, that FBI agents around the country were told in mid-July 2026 that the FBI would no longer investigate confrontations involving immigration agents -- including assault-on-a-federal-officer cases that can arise from violent encounters between ICE agents and members of the public. Under the change, responsibility for these investigations would shift to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), which is itself a component of ICE -- meaning cases involving potential misconduct by immigration agents would be investigated by an arm of the same agency employing those agents, rather than by the FBI as an independent investigative body. FBI and HSI personnel were advised the FBI would defer on all assault-on-federal-officer inquiries involving DHS agents to HSI, according to the emails CBS reviewed. The Justice Department and DHS both publicly denied that any policy change had occurred, despite the written guidance already having been distributed to FBI and ICE personnel.

The guidance came days after two fatal ICE shootings: an ICE agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston on July 7, 2026, and an ICE agent shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in his vehicle in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13. The New York Times reported that under the Trump administration the FBI's role in fatal ICE shootings has been limited to whether agents were assaulted before firing, but that those assault investigations can yield evidence for later civil rights cases, and that HSI has no jurisdiction to investigate civil rights violations. CBS News reported that one email said the change covers everything from minor assaults on DHS employees up to agent-involved shootings, that a local HSI official raised concerns about the training and resources needed for serious cases, and that the FBI would still provide help on request. On August 11, 2026, Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Adam Schiff wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel demanding the policy be rescinded and asking for answers and records by August 25.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the substance of the reported policy shift, since it originates from The New York Times and was independently corroborated by CBS News's review of actual internal emails (not merely anonymous characterization), with further pickup by The New Republic, Common Dreams, and CNBC (the Philadelphia Inquirer ran the NYT report itself). MODERATE confidence on the shift's final, official status, since DOJ and DHS have publicly denied it and no on-the-record government confirmation exists -- the tension between the documentary evidence and the official denial is itself a notable, sourced fact, not a gap in this entry's sourcing. No news report names who issued the directive; Sens. Blumenthal and Schiff wrote to Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel that they 'apparently' made the decision, so attributing it to Blanche rests on that letter and his role as head of the department that oversees the FBI. Re-verified 2026-10-19: the CBS News, New York Times (via the Philadelphia Inquirer), CNBC and Senate sources still say what this entry says; searches found no rescission, no public DOJ, DHS or FBI response to the senators, and no lawsuit or ruling on the guidance. Early reports, including the New York Times, CNBC and the senators' letter, spelled the Maine man's name "Joan Sebastian Guerrero"; later NPR and NBC News reporting gives Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, used here.

title: Pentagon's $1.3B Fort Bliss Migrant-Detention Camp Contract Went to a GOP Megadonor Whose Prior Company Pleaded Guilty to Hiring Undocumented Workers
status: ICE ended prime contractor Acquisition Logistics' contract in 2026; former subcontractor Amentum has run the camp since April under a noncompetitive award. A congressionally requested GAO report faulted the rushed award; its four recommendations remain open. No approving official named.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (contract announced)
what_changed:
In July 2025, the Department of Defense announced an Army contract to build a 5,000-bed migrant detention facility at Fort Bliss, Texas -- among the largest immigration-detention buildouts of the administration. Stars and Stripes, citing the Pentagon, reported a nearly $232 million firm-fixed-price award, while ProPublica reported that the government had allocated more than $1.2 billion for the project. The prime contractor is Virginia-based Acquisition Logistics, with subcontractors Disaster Management Group and Amentum. **Disaster Management Group, whose share of the work an industry insider estimated to ProPublica at 'hundreds of millions' of dollars, is owned by Nathan Albers, whom ProPublica described as a 'big-time Republican donor': he contributed more than $150,000 to Republican campaigns in the year before the award, spent election night 2024 at Mar-a-Lago, and co-chaired a charity fundraiser at the Trump National Golf Club with Eric Trump and his wife.** Albers previously co-owned TentLogix, a temporary-structures company that pleaded guilty in 2019 to a scheme to hire and conceal undocumented workers -- a 2016 audit had found 96 undocumented employees on its books, co-founder Gary Hendry (Albers's former brother-in-law) served time in prison, and the company forfeited more than $3 million before filing for bankruptcy in 2020. A Disaster Management spokesperson told ProPublica that Albers had been cleared in DHS's investigation of TentLogix and had parted ways with the company as a minority, non-operating owner once he learned of Hendry's conduct. Since 2020, Disaster Management Group has won more than $500 million in federal contracts, primarily for Afghan refugee housing, and only began federal lobbying in late 2024 -- spending $210,000 on immigration-related issues with no prior lobbying history -- shortly before securing the Fort Bliss subcontract. Neither the White House nor DOD identified which official approved or oversaw the award; the White House referred ProPublica's questions to DOD and DHS, neither of which provided comment.

Update 2026-10-06: A June 2026 GAO report, requested by the ranking members of four Senate and House committees, found that the Army awarded the contract in July 2025, valued at up to $1.3 billion, on an expedited schedule that Army and ICE officials said was directed by senior leadership. After two unsuccessful ICE attempts to award a contract for the camp, Army and ICE officials told GAO they jointly decided the Army should award it, with ICE providing operational support and leading contract oversight. The Army used a Defense Department small-business contracting vehicle that ICE contracting officials said had never been used for detention services, and a lowest-price-technically-acceptable evaluation, and selected a prime contractor with no prior detention experience. A Court of Federal Claims judge found in September 2025 that the Army violated federal procurement law by letting Acquisition Logistics keep working after a losing bidder's protest triggered an automatic stay, but upheld the Army's later override and dismissed the bidder's lawsuit. GAO named no individual official, said it had referred some concerns to the DOD Office of Inspector General, and made four recommendations that DHS and DOD accepted; the Guardian reported in September 2026 that all four remained open. The Army transferred contract administration to ICE in October 2025, and on March 12, 2026, ICE awarded a noncompetitive, undefinitized contract to a new vendor, which began operating the facility on April 18. ICE confirmed that vendor is Amentum, previously a subcontractor at the site. Public Citizen reported that it is unclear whether Disaster Management Group has any role under the new contract. Scripps News reported that Albers is listed as CEO of Disaster Management Group and had given $339,218 to Republican candidates ahead of the 2026 election.
confidence_note: Sourced primarily to ProPublica's own investigation, which reviewed campaign-finance records, court records from the 2019 TentLogix case, and lobbying disclosures, and sought comment from Disaster Management Group, the White House, DOD and DHS; Truthout republished that article, so it is not independent corroboration. The contract's value, the Army award and the rushed process are independently documented in GAO's June 2026 report, the prime contractor's identity by Scripps News, Public Citizen and the Guardian, and the move to Amentum by ICE's own statement and by the Guardian and Scripps News. No official denial of the underlying facts was identified, only Disaster Management's account of Albers's limited/exonerated role in TentLogix. DHS's statement that the contract was inherited from the Defense Department rests on NBC News; ICE's role in the award decision and oversight rests on GAO's report.

title: Immigration agents detained a U.S.-born Alabama construction worker three times; a judge stayed the raid practices he challenged

affected.description: U.S. citizen born in Florida, a concrete worker in Baldwin County, Alabama; detained by immigration officers in May 2025, June 2025 and May 2026, and the named plaintiff in the class action

harm.who: A U.S. citizen and Latino co-workers

what_changed: On May 21, 2025, armed officers, three of them masked, jumped the fence at a Lennar construction site in Foley, Alabama, ran past the No Trespassing sign and the non-Latino workers, and went straight for Leonardo Garcia Venegas's all-Latino concrete crew, according to the court's summary of his account. When officers tackled his brother, Garcia Venegas began filming; an officer grabbed him and a second tackled him as he shouted that he was a citizen. **Officers pulled his Alabama STAR ID, a REAL ID-compliant license, from his pocket, said it was fake, handcuffed him and held him for over an hour before confirming his citizenship and releasing him without charge.** On June 12, 2025, an officer walked into a nearly finished house in a D.R. Horton development in Fairhope where he was working alone, ordered him outside, called his REAL ID possibly fake, and marched him two blocks to an unmarked car lined up with other Latino workers, holding him about 20 to 30 minutes. On September 30, 2025, the Institute for Justice filed a proposed class action for him in federal court in Mobile against border czar Tom Homan, DHS, the Justice Department and regional heads of the agencies in the "Gulf of America Homeland Security Task Force," challenging three alleged practices: entering private construction sites without a warrant or consent, detaining workers who fit a demographic profile without individual suspicion, and holding them even after they show proof of citizenship or status. DHS said he "attempted to obstruct and prevent the lawful arrest of an illegal alien"; his lawyer said video showed him recording several yards away. In April 2026 ICE denied his separate damages claim without explanation, per ProPublica. On May 2, 2026, officers followed him home, pulled him from his brother's truck, handcuffed and shackled him and again did not credit his REAL ID before releasing him after about 15 minutes; DHS said he was "NOT detained" and that ICE made "a routine vehicle stop on a car registered to an illegal alien." On May 19, 2026, Chief U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Beaverstock ruled that Garcia Venegas has standing, finding the record showed the three practices existed; he heard evidence on May 27, where an HSI supervisor testified he knew of no such policies. **On September 21, 2026, Beaverstock found Garcia Venegas likely to succeed on his Fourth Amendment and DHS-regulation claims and temporarily stayed all three practices under the Administrative Procedure Act, rather than issue the broader preliminary injunction he sought; the same day he conditionally certified a class and refused to dismiss the APA claims.** On October 13, 2026, Garcia Venegas filed an amended class-action complaint adding Federal Tort Claims Act claims against the United States and naming three of the May 2025 officers as defendants.
legal_status: Sued: Garcia Venegas v. Homan, No. 1:25-cv-397 (S.D. Ala.), filed September 30, 2025. The court found he has standing on May 19, 2026. On September 21, 2026 the court found the three challenged practices likely violate the Fourth Amendment and DHS regulations and temporarily stayed them pending the case; the preliminary injunction was otherwise denied. A class was conditionally certified and the motion to dismiss the APA claims was denied. An amended complaint filed October 13, 2026 adds tort claims against the United States and claims against three officers individually; those claims are unresolved. Garcia Venegas was never charged with any crime. No appeal identified.

human_toll.summary: A U.S.-born construction worker was held three times in a year despite a REAL ID that Alabama issues only to citizens and lawful residents; he was tackled and handcuffed the first time and shackled the third. He took nearly two weeks off work after the first raid and told ProPublica the fear of being stopped again brings stress and depression. Other Latino workers in the same subdivisions were rounded up with him.

human_toll.caveat: The account of the two 2025 raids is Garcia Venegas's, as summarized by the court, backed by video of the May 2025 encounter; the length of the 2026 stop is ProPublica's. DHS's stated rationale: it said he "physically got in between agents and the subject they were attempting to arrest and refused to comply with numerous verbal commands," that "ICE does NOT arrest or deport U.S. citizens," and that the 2026 stop was a routine stop of a car registered to an undocumented immigrant. The government told the court it found no record of the June 2025 encounter, that the three policies do not exist, and that a construction site is like an open field officers may enter without a warrant. The judge found the video did not show him interfering and called the open-fields argument unconvincing, but these are preliminary findings, not a final judgment.

title: ICE Cut Training for Local Police Deputized to Make Immigration Arrests From Four Weeks In Person to 40 Hours Online as the 287(g) Program Grew Past 2,600 Agreements
status: In effect: officers under the revived 287(g) Task Force Model are deputized after a 40-hour online course. No reversal found, unlike ICE's own shortened academy, restored in 2026. DHS did not immediately respond to the Post. An ACLU of New Hampshire FOIA suit for the training materials is pending.
date_of_action: 2025 (Task Force Model revived with a 40-hour online course; ICE email describing the cuts sent February 2025) through 2026-10 (emails made public)
what_changed: As the Trump administration expanded the 287(g) program, under which ICE deputizes state and local police to carry out federal immigration enforcement, it cut the training those officers must complete. Historically, officers in both the Jail Enforcement Model and the Task Force Model attended a four-week, in-person course at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Charleston, South Carolina, according to the National Immigration Forum. In reviving the Task Force Model, which lets officers use immigration authority during routine duties such as traffic stops, the administration required only a 40-hour online course, while the jail model kept its four-week training. Lawfare reported that White House border czar Tom Homan announced in February 2025 that he intended to cut the training period to about one week. Emails that the watchdog group American Oversight obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, reported by The Washington Post on Oct. 6, 2026, show how the course was cut. In a February 2025 email to Todd Lyons, whom the Post describes as ICE's acting director at the time, and David Venturella, then an adviser and now the agency's head, an ICE official whose name was redacted wrote that ICE was first told to cut the four-week program to two weeks and then to one week, and that teaching on immigrant classifications and removal charges would be "truncated." **Instruction on real-world scenarios that officers might encounter in the field was eliminated altogether**, the Post reported. Ten topics remained in the 40-hour program, including use-of-force policy, liability and civil rights law, immigrant detention and "cross-cultural issues," with one test per training day. Venturella replied five hours later: "Thanks." **American Oversight's executive director, Chioma Chukwu, said some of the removed material "was seemingly designed to help the officers understand whether or not they have a lawful basis to act against someone in the first place."** Meanwhile the program grew from 135 active agreements in 16 states under the Biden administration to more than 2,600 agencies, most of them compensated for helping arrest people for civil immigration violations, according to the Post. DHS did not immediately respond to the Post's request for comment on the training changes; it had earlier said, "We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement work with us." Some agencies add their own in-person instruction: Florida deputies in Escambia and Santa Rosa counties were described in June 2025 as taking the 40-hour online course plus in-person modules.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the cut itself: ICE's own guidance, as described by the National Immigration Forum in September 2025, sets a 40-hour online course for Task Force Model officers, and the Washington Post's account of the ICE emails, obtained by American Oversight, is consistent with it. The email details rest on the Post's reporting of redacted records; the New Republic and others relay it rather than corroborate it independently. MODERATE confidence on effects: the link to wrongful arrests or civil rights violations is the assessment of critics and watchdogs, not a documented finding. Homan's stated intent is as reported by Lawfare. Re-verified 2026-10-19: the Post's account (via its Anchorage Daily News syndication), the National Immigration Forum explainer and the Lawfare report still say what this entry says; the ACLU of New Hampshire FOIA case docket shows it still pending. Current 287(g) counts come from a third-party tracker of ICE's published lists, since ICE's own 287(g) page could not be fetched.

The harm is projected by critics, not counted: no tally of wrongful arrests tied to the shorter training was found. The 8,501 trained-officer figure is ICE's from September 2025, as reported by the National Immigration Forum; no newer figure was found. section_summaries.what_changed: ICE cut training for local police deputized under 287(g) task forces from four weeks in person to a 40-hour online course, dropping field scenarios as the program grew past 2,600 agreements.
section_summaries.confidence_note: The 40-hour rule is in ICE guidance and the Post's account of ICE emails. Harm to the public is critics' assessment, not a documented finding.
section_summaries.human_toll: Thousands of 287(g) task force officers make civil immigration arrests after 40 online hours. Critics warn of wrongful arrests; no count of resulting harm found.

title: ICE and Border Patrol face-scanned people in street stops, incl. a teen with no ID; DHS's IG opened an audit

what_changed:
DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari opened an audit titled "DHS' Security of Biometric Data and Personally Identifiable Information (PII)" on February 4, 2026, a week after Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine asked his office to examine whether DHS's immigration surveillance tools have led to violations of federal law and of rules that protect privacy and guard against unlawful searches. Its stated objective is "to determine how DHS and its components collect or obtain PII and biometric data related to immigration enforcement efforts and the extent to which that data is managed, shared, and secured in accordance with law, regulation, and Departmental policy." Cuffari's letter did not name the programs under review; an IG spokesperson told CyberScoop the audit would "begin with OBIM, ICE and could include other components of the Department," OBIM being the Office of Biometric Identity Management, which runs DHS's biometric databases. The senators' January 29 letter had raised DHS's contracts with Palantir and Clearview AI, its access to Flock license-plate data, social media monitoring through Penlink, a phone-hacking contract with Paragon, its face-scanning mobile app and its use of government biometric databases, and Cuffari wrote that the audit "will address a number of the questions" they asked. **The face-scanning app, Mobile Fortify, lets ICE officers point a phone at a person and run their face against a bank of 200 million images drawn from DHS, State Department, FBI and state records, 404 Media reported from ICE user manuals.** Social media videos reviewed by 404 Media showed ICE and CBP officers scanning faces in street stops, including one in the Chicago area in which a Border Patrol agent stopped two teenagers on bikes and, when one boy said he was born in the U.S. but had no ID on him, called to another officer, "can you do facial?" The second officer held a phone over the boy's face, then asked him to confirm his name. Rep. Bennie Thompson, ranking member of the House Homeland Security Committee, said ICE officials had told them an apparent Mobile Fortify match is a "definitive" determination of status that can override evidence of citizenship, including a birth certificate, and a DHS document published by 404 Media says ICE does not let people decline the scan and keeps the photos, including those of U.S. citizens, for 15 years.

Added 2026-10-19: Illinois and the City of Chicago sued the Trump administration in federal court in Chicago on January 12, 2026, alleging, among other claims, that ICE and Border Patrol agents in the Chicago area engaged in "widespread, suspicionless collection of biometric identifiers" with mobile facial-recognition and fingerprint tools, chiefly Mobile Fortify; that DHS has used the app more than 100,000 times nationwide since launching it around June 2025; and that the practice exceeds DHS's statutory authority and violates Illinois's constitutional privacy protections. The complaint also says DHS rescinded Directive 026-11, its 2023 department-wide rules on facial recognition that included bias testing and opt-out rights for U.S. citizens in non-law-enforcement uses, on or before February 14, 2025. On April 1, 2026, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law sued DHS and ICE under the Freedom of Information Act for records on Mobile Fortify and a companion app, Mobile Identify, saying the agencies had missed legal deadlines and produced no records.
legal_status: Under audit: the DHS Inspector General's audit of how DHS collects, shares and secures biometric data and PII for immigration enforcement, announced February 4, 2026, is open with no published findings. Sued: Illinois and the City of Chicago allege in a January 12, 2026 federal lawsuit that agents' Mobile Fortify scans in the Chicago area are suspicionless and exceed DHS's statutory authority; U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis is set to rule November 17, 2026 on DHS's motion to dismiss the suit. Sued: Democracy Defenders Fund and the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law filed a Freedom of Information Act suit against DHS and ICE on April 1, 2026 seeking Mobile Fortify and Mobile Identify records. No court or IG finding on the lawfulness of the scans has been found.

human_toll.summary: People stopped on the street by ICE and Border Patrol, U.S. citizens among them, have had their faces scanned against federal databases without a chance to decline, and DHS keeps the images for 15 years. A teenager who said he was U.S.-born was scanned when he had no ID, and Illinois alleges a Chicago man was handcuffed and scanned before agents confirmed his citizenship. Rep. Bennie Thompson says ICE officials treat a match as definitive even over a birth certificate, which leaves citizens open to detention on a false match.

human_toll.caveat: The 200-million-image figure comes from ICE manuals 404 Media viewed, and the 100,000-use figure is an allegation in Illinois and Chicago's lawsuit that no court has tested; DHS has published no count of scans, false matches or people detained after a match, and the IG has released no findings. The street-stop videos show individual encounters, not how often citizens are scanned. DHS says its expanded surveillance measures are justified to boost efficiency and safeguard national security, per the American Immigration Council, and Secretary Kristi Noem said in late October 2025 that "no American citizens have been arrested or detained" in the administration's deportation campaign. Facial recognition is a widely used law-enforcement tool, DHS has authority to verify immigration status, and an IG audit is a review, not a finding of wrongdoing.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the audit's existence, title and stated objective, from the IG's own February 5, 2026 letter to Sens. Warner and Kaine, reported by 404 Media and CyberScoop, and on Mobile Fortify's 200-million-image reach and street use, from 404 Media's reporting on ICE manuals and social media videos, Common Dreams and Biometric Update. The audit's precise scope is not public: the IG's letter names no programs, and the technologies listed here come from the senators' request, which the IG said the audit would address in part. The American Immigration Council describes the teenager video as internal footage of ICE officers; 404 Media's own report describes a social media video of a Border Patrol stop in which one boy was scanned, and this entry follows 404 Media. The lawsuit's claims, including the 100,000-use figure and the Gutierrez detention, are allegations no court has ruled on; Jesus Gutierrez is named in a court filing (Illinois and Chicago's complaint, as reported by Biometric Update). TAP matched the Illinois and Chicago suit that the Chicago Sun-Times reports is pending before Judge Ellis to the January 12 complaint by its parties and court. Re-verified 2026-08-18: no material change -- audit remains open with no published findings. Re-verified 2026-09-08: the audit remains open with no published findings or legality conclusions. Update 2026-10-19: the IG letter and core reports were re-read, and searches found no published audit report or findings; the Illinois and Chicago lawsuit and an April 2026 FOIA suit over Mobile Fortify were added.

section_summaries.what_changed: DHS's IG opened an audit of how DHS collects and shares biometric data for enforcement after senators flagged tools like ICE's Mobile Fortify, which scans faces in street stops against 200M images.
section_summaries.human_toll: People face-scanned in street stops, including a teen who said he was U.S.-born, can't decline; DHS keeps photos 15 years; Illinois alleges 100,000+ uses. DHS has published no false-match count.
section_summaries.confidence_note: The audit and Mobile Fortify's reach are well documented; the audit's exact scope and findings are not public, and the lawsuit's 100,000-use figure is an untested allegation.

legal_status: DHS said the Houston shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo is under investigation by its Office of the Inspector General; his family and Texas members of Congress have called for an independent investigation. In the Biddeford shooting of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, ICE said DHS's Office of Inspector General was notified, and the Maine attorney general's office and DHS's inspector general have both investigated; neither has announced a result. The Travis County district attorney said his office sought an independent investigation of the Austin shooting, with access to video and an interview with the ICE agent who fired. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez is charged with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer; a magistrate judge found probable cause and denied bond; a federal judge in San Antonio vacated the Sept. 30 hearing on his habeas petition against deportation and paused the case until his criminal detention is resolved, and his lawyers voluntarily dismissed the petition on Oct. 1. No charge against any officer who fired in these shootings has been reported. GAO's body-camera report is an audit with recommendations, not a legal ruling.
title: Months After Promising Body Cameras for All Immigration Agents, DHS Still Hasn't Confirmed Full Deployment -- Agents in Two Fatal Shootings Had None
status: Ongoing -- both 2026 rollout targets (end of August, then end of September) passed; DHS said Oct. 14 it has cameras for all ICE officers but training is still ongoing. A GAO report found most offices lack usage guidance; DHS rejected GAO's call for automatic camera activation.
date_of_action: 2026-02 (body camera pledge made) through 2026-10 (GAO report released; DHS rejected automatic camera activation for ICE)
what_changed: After immigration agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens (Alex Pretti, a VA nurse, and Renee Good) in Minneapolis in January 2026, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem pledged to rapidly expand body camera deployment to immigration agents nationwide. Congress allocated $20 million in FY2026 DHS funding for body camera procurement, deployment, and operations, with plans to purchase more than 5,000 body-worn cameras; as of February 2026, ICE had roughly 3,000 body cameras for approximately 13,000 officers, with another 6,000 in the deployment pipeline. In July 2026, White House border czar Tom Homan said “hundreds” of cameras had been sent to Minnesota after the Good and Pretti shootings, but “there wasn't enough cameras to outfit every ICE agent,” and that officer training was “delayed by the shutdown.” Nearly six months after the pledge, **none of the officers involved in two subsequent fatal ICE shootings -- of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero -- were wearing body cameras**, according to NPR reporting; the Salgado Araujo shooting took place in Houston on July 7, 2026, and DHS said the ICE officers involved had not been issued body-worn cameras, despite the DHS funding allocation. Update 2026-08-17: on August 7-8, 2026, ICE Acting Director David J. Venturella said the agency expects to complete nationwide body-camera deployment to every field officer by the end of August 2026 -- a significant acceleration from the ~3,000-of-13,000 partial deployment this entry documents as of February 2026, following the additional fatal shootings without cameras already covered above. Independent confirmation that the rollout was actually completed by the announced deadline was not available as of this update, since the deadline itself had not yet arrived. Separately, ICE's body-camera policy has drawn scrutiny for provisions that let agency leadership withhold or indefinitely delay release of footage following serious injuries or deaths in custody; Venturella defended the restrictions as protecting investigations and privacy and consistent with other federal law enforcement agencies' policies, while reporting noted this means the expanded camera coverage will not automatically translate into public access to the footage. Update 2026-08-30: on August 8-9, 2026, ICE publicly disputed the Associated Press's framing of the footage-release policy, with Venturella issuing a statement saying the AP conflated the narrower expedited-release provision that applies specifically to serious-injury/death-in-custody cases with a claim that ICE would broadly withhold routine footage; ICE maintains the underlying policy -- expedited release when appropriate, withholding when release could compromise investigations or privacy -- is unchanged from what this entry already documents. As of August 30, 2026, the day before the announced end-of-August completion deadline, no independent reporting confirming (or disputing) that the full nationwide rollout was actually completed was found in sourcing reviewed -- consistent with this entry's existing caveat that the target had not yet been independently verified. Update 2026-09-01: a same-week (Aug 7-8, 2026) PBS/AP account, published within hours of the NBC/Venturella 'end of August' report already documented above, instead described the rollout target as 'the end of September,' with more than half of field officers already equipped and the rest to follow by then -- a discrepancy this entry documents rather than resolves, since sourcing reviewed does not establish which deadline is the agency's operative one. The PBS/AP reporting also added funding and design detail beyond what this entry previously documented: ICE spent $30.9 million in July 2026 to purchase equipment from Axon, on top of the $20 million FY2026 congressional appropriation already documented above; and the deployment plan's actual coverage standard requires only 'at least one member of every arrest team' to wear a camera, not every individual field officer, a materially narrower standard than the 'every officer' framing in DHS and ICE public statements. The same reporting detailed the footage-release policy more specifically than previously documented: the ICE Director may withhold or indefinitely delay release following 'specific and compelling circumstances,' on a review committee's recommendation, if release is not determined to be in the agency's 'best interests' -- a broader, more discretionary standard than this entry's prior 'expedited release when appropriate' framing suggested. As of September 1, 2026, no reporting confirming rollout completion under either the August 31 or end-of-September deadline was found. Update 2026-10-07: the end-of-August target passed without full deployment. At a September 1, 2026 press conference, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “We’re getting close. By the end of September, I’m pretty sure we will be there,” describing the goal as “everybody that’s in the field — that doesn’t mean every ICE agent.” ICE told NPR the same day that it had acquired enough devices to equip all its officers and agents, but that “Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing”; ICE did not tell NPR how many officers already had cameras, and NPR reported it was still unclear how many cameras the agency owns. Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told NPR he understood training had been completed across all ICE areas of responsibility, which ICE's own statements did not say. The end-of-September target then also passed: Spectrum News reported on October 1, 2026 that not all ICE field agents had been trained to use body cameras, with a DHS spokesperson repeating that training “remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon.” Whichever date was originally operative, both have now passed without confirmed full deployment. Meanwhile, on September 20, 2026, an ICE officer shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old DoorDash driver, while he was making deliveries in Austin, Texas; two DHS officials told NBC News the officer had been issued a body camera but was not wearing it, and that a second officer's camera captured partial footage that does not include the moment of the shooting. Update 2026-10-16: a Government Accountability Office report publicly released October 14, 2026 (GAO-26-108157), requested by Democratic members of Congress and covering February 2025 to September 2026, found that CBP and ICE had not updated their body-camera program plans since 2022 and 2024 respectively, had not implemented results-oriented performance goals, and that most CBP and ICE offices had not developed operational guidance on when to use the cameras, which GAO said “increases the risk that CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy.” GAO found ICE had deployed approximately 4,800 cameras as of April 2026; DHS told GAO that all ICE offices had received cameras as of August 5. Some ICE and CBP officers told GAO they did not know whether to activate cameras during vehicle searches or when transporting detainees, and at one ICE office staff were so unsure that they had not begun using the cameras even after being trained. GAO made seven recommendations; DHS agreed with six but rejected automated activation for ICE, under which a camera starts recording when an officer draws a weapon or turns on emergency lights, as CBP's cameras already do. DHS argued automatic activation could result in “the unauthorized recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims”; GAO answered that DHS's response “did not include information on environments where automated activation could be effective,” and warned that “Without reliable control activities, ICE risks gaps in documentation and video evidence that can make reviews of incidents more challenging.” In an October 14 statement, DHS said it had purchased devices for all ICE officers but that the required training was still ongoing and expected to be finished “soon.” Update 2026-10-19: an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations memo signed by executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Sept. 30, 2026 requires all officers at the scene of a vehicle stop to wear and activate their body cameras, bans chasing vehicles that fail to pull over, and limits vehicle stops to officers who have completed specific training, according to the Associated Press, which noted that the officers in the Austin shooting would not have complied with it: testimony at Garcés Pérez's Sept. 30 bond hearing showed the officer who shot him was not wearing a body camera, and the officer who had one, driving a separate car, turned it off during the pursuit.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across NPR (the original detailed report), CNN, US News, and Fox News/AOL coverage of the original Noem pledge, with consistent figures on funding and deployment pace across outlets. Update 2026-08-17: the end-of-August completion target and Venturella's statement are corroborated across NBC News, CNN, the Washington Post/AP, and CNBC. This is the agency's own announced target, not an independently verified completion -- worth rechecking directly once the deadline has passed rather than assuming it was met. Update 2026-08-30: the ICE/AP dispute over footage-release-policy framing is corroborated across Federal News Network, the Epoch Times, and multiple radio-syndicate wire pickups of the same AP story; no outlet reviewed disputes ICE's underlying description of the policy itself, only whether the AP's characterization of it was accurate. Still worth a direct recheck once the announced deadline is further in the rearview and post-deadline reporting exists. Re-verified 2026-09-01, real correction: the $30.9M Axon-purchase figure, the 'best interests'/review-committee footage-release standard, and the 'one camera per arrest team' coverage detail are HIGH confidence, corroborated directly via PBS NewsHour's Aug. 7, 2026 account of the same AP wire story already partially documented in this entry, plus independent pickups (CNN, Boston Globe, WBUR, ABC News, Washington Times) found in a broader search. The August-vs-September deadline discrepancy is presented as an unresolved conflict between two same-week reports rather than resolved to one date, consistent with this tracker's practice for unreconciled figures. Re-verified 2026-10-07, real correction: the passing of both the August and September targets, Mullin's September 1 statements and ICE's "training remains ongoing" statement are corroborated across CNN, NPR and Spectrum News. The Austin camera-not-worn detail rests on two unnamed DHS officials speaking to NBC News and was repeated by Newsweek and Spectrum News. The "separate" Houston shooting earlier counted as a third fatal incident was the Salgado Araujo shooting itself (Houston, July 7, 2026, per ABC News and the Texas Tribune), so the count is corrected from three to two. Update 2026-10-16: the GAO findings, its seven recommendations and DHS's rejection of automated activation are HIGH confidence, read on GAO's own report page (GAO-26-108157, published Sept. 15 and publicly released Oct. 14, 2026) and in AP's and States Newsroom's Oct. 14 accounts. The full report text was not read directly; DHS's quoted objection, the vehicle-search and detainee-transport confusion and DHS's Aug. 5 offices figure rest on AP's reading of it, and GAO's reply to DHS on States Newsroom's. Re-verified 2026-10-19: NPR, CNN, ABC News, NBC News, Spectrum News, AP and States Newsroom accounts re-read and hold; the US News and PBS pages did not load this time. The people named here are named in major reporting, Garcés Pérez's charge and bond ruling in court reporting (Fox San Antonio), his deportation petition in CNN's, and the petition's vacated hearing and Oct. 1 voluntary dismissal on the federal court docket (Garces Perez v. Thompson, W.D. Tex.). NPR's July report spells the Maine man's name “Joan”; NPR's September report and NBC News give Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, used here. Update 2026-10-19: the Sept. 30 vehicle-stop memo rests on AP, which obtained it; ICE and DHS had no immediate comment.

what_changed.base: After immigration agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens (Alex Pretti, a VA nurse, and Renee Good) in Minneapolis in January 2026, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem pledged to rapidly expand body camera deployment to immigration agents nationwide. Congress allocated $20 million in FY2026 DHS funding for body camera procurement, deployment, and operations, with plans to purchase more than 5,000 body-worn cameras; as of February 2026, ICE had roughly 3,000 body cameras for approximately 13,000 officers, with another 6,000 in the deployment pipeline. In July 2026, White House border czar Tom Homan said “hundreds” of cameras had been sent to Minnesota after the Good and Pretti shootings, but “there wasn't enough cameras to outfit every ICE agent,” and that officer training was “delayed by the shutdown.” Nearly six months after the pledge, **none of the officers involved in two subsequent fatal ICE shootings -- of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero -- were wearing body cameras**, according to NPR reporting; the Salgado Araujo shooting took place in Houston on July 7, 2026, and DHS said the ICE officers involved had not been issued body-worn cameras, despite the DHS funding allocation.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-17: on August 7-8, 2026, ICE Acting Director David J. Venturella said the agency expects to complete nationwide body-camera deployment to every field officer by the end of August 2026 -- a significant acceleration from the ~3,000-of-13,000 partial deployment this entry documents as of February 2026, following the additional fatal shootings without cameras already covered above. Independent confirmation that the rollout was actually completed by the announced deadline was not available as of this update, since the deadline itself had not yet arrived. Separately, ICE's body-camera policy has drawn scrutiny for provisions that let agency leadership withhold or indefinitely delay release of footage following serious injuries or deaths in custody; Venturella defended the restrictions as protecting investigations and privacy and consistent with other federal law enforcement agencies' policies, while reporting noted this means the expanded camera coverage will not automatically translate into public access to the footage.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-30: on August 8-9, 2026, ICE publicly disputed the Associated Press's framing of the footage-release policy, with Venturella issuing a statement saying the AP conflated the narrower expedited-release provision that applies specifically to serious-injury/death-in-custody cases with a claim that ICE would broadly withhold routine footage; ICE maintains the underlying policy -- expedited release when appropriate, withholding when release could compromise investigations or privacy -- is unchanged from what this entry already documents. As of August 30, 2026, the day before the announced end-of-August completion deadline, no independent reporting confirming (or disputing) that the full nationwide rollout was actually completed was found in sourcing reviewed -- consistent with this entry's existing caveat that the target had not yet been independently verified.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-01: a same-week (Aug 7-8, 2026) PBS/AP account, published within hours of the NBC/Venturella 'end of August' report already documented above, instead described the rollout target as 'the end of September,' with more than half of field officers already equipped and the rest to follow by then -- a discrepancy this entry documents rather than resolves, since sourcing reviewed does not establish which deadline is the agency's operative one. The PBS/AP reporting also added funding and design detail beyond what this entry previously documented: ICE spent $30.9 million in July 2026 to purchase equipment from Axon, on top of the $20 million FY2026 congressional appropriation already documented above; and the deployment plan's actual coverage standard requires only 'at least one member of every arrest team' to wear a camera, not every individual field officer, a materially narrower standard than the 'every officer' framing in DHS and ICE public statements. The same reporting detailed the footage-release policy more specifically than previously documented: the ICE Director may withhold or indefinitely delay release following 'specific and compelling circumstances,' on a review committee's recommendation, if release is not determined to be in the agency's 'best interests' -- a broader, more discretionary standard than this entry's prior 'expedited release when appropriate' framing suggested. As of September 1, 2026, no reporting confirming rollout completion under either the August 31 or end-of-September deadline was found.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-07: the end-of-August target passed without full deployment. At a September 1, 2026 press conference, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “We’re getting close. By the end of September, I’m pretty sure we will be there,” describing the goal as “everybody that’s in the field — that doesn’t mean every ICE agent.” ICE told NPR the same day that it had acquired enough devices to equip all its officers and agents, but that “Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing”; ICE did not tell NPR how many officers already had cameras, and NPR reported it was still unclear how many cameras the agency owns. Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told NPR he understood training had been completed across all ICE areas of responsibility, which ICE's own statements did not say. The end-of-September target then also passed: Spectrum News reported on October 1, 2026 that not all ICE field agents had been trained to use body cameras, with a DHS spokesperson repeating that training “remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon.” Whichever date was originally operative, both have now passed without confirmed full deployment. Meanwhile, on September 20, 2026, an ICE officer shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old DoorDash driver, while he was making deliveries in Austin, Texas; two DHS officials told NBC News the officer had been issued a body camera but was not wearing it, and that a second officer's camera captured partial footage that does not include the moment of the shooting.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-16: a Government Accountability Office report publicly released October 14, 2026 (GAO-26-108157), requested by Democratic members of Congress and covering February 2025 to September 2026, found that CBP and ICE had not updated their body-camera program plans since 2022 and 2024 respectively, had not implemented results-oriented performance goals, and that most CBP and ICE offices had not developed operational guidance on when to use the cameras, which GAO said “increases the risk that CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy.” GAO found ICE had deployed approximately 4,800 cameras as of April 2026; DHS told GAO that all ICE offices had received cameras as of August 5. Some ICE and CBP officers told GAO they did not know whether to activate cameras during vehicle searches or when transporting detainees, and at one ICE office staff were so unsure that they had not begun using the cameras even after being trained. GAO made seven recommendations; DHS agreed with six but rejected automated activation for ICE, under which a camera starts recording when an officer draws a weapon or turns on emergency lights, as CBP's cameras already do. DHS argued automatic activation could result in “the unauthorized recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims”; GAO answered that DHS's response “did not include information on environments where automated activation could be effective,” and warned that “Without reliable control activities, ICE risks gaps in documentation and video evidence that can make reviews of incidents more challenging.” In an October 14 statement, DHS said it had purchased devices for all ICE officers but that the required training was still ongoing and expected to be finished “soon.”

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-19: an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations memo signed by executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Sept. 30, 2026 requires all officers at the scene of a vehicle stop to wear and activate their body cameras, bans chasing vehicles that fail to pull over, and limits vehicle stops to officers who have completed specific training, according to the Associated Press, which noted that the officers in the Austin shooting would not have complied with it: testimony at Garcés Pérez's Sept. 30 bond hearing showed the officer who shot him was not wearing a body camera, and the officer who had one, driving a separate car, turned it off during the pursuit.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across NPR (the original detailed report), CNN, US News, and Fox News/AOL coverage of the original Noem pledge, with consistent figures on funding and deployment pace across outlets.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-17: the end-of-August completion target and Venturella's statement are corroborated across NBC News, CNN, the Washington Post/AP, and CNBC. This is the agency's own announced target, not an independently verified completion -- worth rechecking directly once the deadline has passed rather than assuming it was met.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-30: the ICE/AP dispute over footage-release-policy framing is corroborated across Federal News Network, the Epoch Times, and multiple radio-syndicate wire pickups of the same AP story; no outlet reviewed disputes ICE's underlying description of the policy itself, only whether the AP's characterization of it was accurate. Still worth a direct recheck once the announced deadline is further in the rearview and post-deadline reporting exists. Re-verified 2026-09-01, real correction: the $30.9M Axon-purchase figure, the 'best interests'/review-committee footage-release standard, and the 'one camera per arrest team' coverage detail are HIGH confidence, corroborated directly via PBS NewsHour's Aug. 7, 2026 account of the same AP wire story already partially documented in this entry, plus independent pickups (CNN, Boston Globe, WBUR, ABC News, Washington Times) found in a broader search. The August-vs-September deadline discrepancy is presented as an unresolved conflict between two same-week reports rather than resolved to one date, consistent with this tracker's practice for unreconciled figures. Re-verified 2026-10-07, real correction: the passing of both the August and September targets, Mullin's September 1 statements and ICE's "training remains ongoing" statement are corroborated across CNN, NPR and Spectrum News. The Austin camera-not-worn detail rests on two unnamed DHS officials speaking to NBC News and was repeated by Newsweek and Spectrum News. The "separate" Houston shooting earlier counted as a third fatal incident was the Salgado Araujo shooting itself (Houston, July 7, 2026, per ABC News and the Texas Tribune), so the count is corrected from three to two.

updates.text: Update 2026-10-16: the GAO findings, its seven recommendations and DHS's rejection of automated activation are HIGH confidence, read on GAO's own report page (GAO-26-108157, published Sept. 15 and publicly released Oct. 14, 2026) and in AP's and States Newsroom's Oct. 14 accounts. glance.what: Made warrantless arrests barred by a decree ICE had called 'terminated'; a judge ordered dozens freed

what_changed:
Backstory: the Castañon Nava consent decree settled a class action over an earlier Chicago-area ICE operation. In it, ICE agreed to follow the federal statute that allows a warrantless immigration arrest only when an officer has reason to believe the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, and to issue a nationwide "Broadcast Statement of Policy" telling officers so. The decree covers ICE's Chicago Area of Responsibility (Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky and Kansas).

On June 11, 2025, while the plaintiffs' motions to enforce and extend the decree were pending, ICE Principal Legal Advisor Charles Wall emailed all ICE employees under the subject line "Termination of the Castanon-Nava Settlement Agreement": "it remains terminated. Accordingly, I hereby rescind" the decree's statement of policy. Operation Midway Blitz began in the Chicago area on September 8, 2025. On September 26 and 30 the plaintiffs, represented by the National Immigrant Justice Center and the ACLU of Illinois, told the court of more than 25 further violations tied to the operation. Among the arrests cited in the wider warrantless-arrest litigation, per the Sun-Times, was a Guatemalan family taken at Millennium Park on September 28, 2025: agents in Border Patrol uniforms loaded Alfa Nohemi Chavez Alvarez, Jaime Misael Ramirez Ambrosio and their two young children into a Border Patrol vehicle while, the mother told the Tribune, the couple demanded to see a warrant.

**On October 7, 2025, U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Cummings found that ICE had arrested 22 of 26 class members without a warrant in violation of the decree and the statute**, in arrests made after January 2025 and raised in the plaintiffs' earlier motion to enforce. He found that Wall's email meant "all obligations under the Agreement, including those for training and reporting, stopped," extended the decree by 118 days to February 2, 2026, ordered the Broadcast reissued to all ICE officers nationwide, and ordered ICE to hand over records of every warrantless arrest in the district from June 11 to October 7, 2025. In an October 29 filing, ICE reported about 3,000 arrests from June 11 to October 7, 2025, about 615 of them people "not subject to mandatory detention" and without final removal orders. On November 13 the court ordered 13 people the government agreed were arrested in violation of the decree released without bond or conditions, and ordered those of the 615 still detained and not rated a "high public safety risk" released on a $1,500 bond into ICE's Alternatives to Detention program. The court noted that only 13 of the 46 agreed violations were still in detention, and that an estimated 60% of those arrested in the operation had been removed from the country. DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin called Cummings an "ACTIVIST JUDGE" who was "putting the lives of Americans directly at risk." Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino told Fox News: "If he releases those 650, we're going to apprehend 1,650 on the streets of Chicago." The Seventh Circuit administratively stayed both orders on November 20, 2025, and in December granted the government's stay motion in part and denied it in part.

**On February 13, 2026, after the decree's set end date, Cummings ruled that it remains in force** while the plaintiffs' motions to enforce are pending (written order February 17). He ordered people freed under the decree released without the bonds and check-ins ICE had imposed, and ordered the Broadcast sent again to agents nationwide. In its February 20 certification, DHS told agents the Broadcast applied only to five Midwestern states and that all other ICE offices should follow a January 28, 2026 memo on warrantless arrests from Todd Lyons, the senior official performing the duties of ICE director. Cummings called that language "inconsistent with this Court's orders" and, per Capitol News Illinois, asked government lawyers in court: "Is it your practice to violate orders of a federal court?" Reviewing 53 arrests one by one, he ordered 36 more people released by March 5, 2026; their lawyers said at least 11 of the first 32 had already left the country. On April 3 the parties agreed to limit the Broadcast requirement to the Chicago area for the rest of the decree.

On April 29, 2026, the court granted further releases, including for Delfino Flores-Blanco, and barred DHS from relying on six I-200 arrest warrants it produced only that day. **On May 5, 2026, the Seventh Circuit (2-1) affirmed the 118-day extension**, citing the "unilateral proclamation by a DHS senior official" that DHS would stop complying, and affirmed release of people individually found to have been arrested in violation of the decree. It reversed the release of "potential" class members not yet individually reviewed, and of anyone arrested on an I-200 warrant, defective or not. When DHS asserted in late May that the decree had expired on April 3, Cummings called that "a non-starter." On June 1 he ruled on the October 14, 2025 arrest of Eriksen Ventura Romero, a Venezuelan man waiting in a parked car outside a West Town health center while his pregnant partner saw a doctor. He found that about eight CBP agents pinned the car in, broke the window and, after he became distraught and tried to pull away, tased him four times, and that body-camera footage did not confirm the arrest report's claim that he "attempted to flee on foot." On June 16 the court approved an agreed wind-down: reporting ends with arrests through May 31, 2026, and the plaintiffs have 60 days after the final records production to file their last challenges. Enforcement rulings continued through the summer: on August 26, Cummings found that the arrest report for Carlos Chillogalli-Puzhi, arrested at an ICE check-in, was "riddled with indisputably inaccurate yet material information," and inferred that the field warrant it cited "does not exist." On October 9, 2026, he ordered eight more people freed, citing a California ruling that "no likelihood of escape analysis could have been conducted" where agents asked nothing beyond immigration status. Motions to enforce filed September 25 and October 9, 2026, were pending.
legal_status: Ruled in violation of a court-approved consent decree: Judge Cummings found ICE arrested 22 of 26 class members unlawfully (October 7, 2025), and in a long series of individual rulings since then has ordered dozens more released without bond or conditions. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the decree's extension and the individual releases on May 5, 2026, and reversed the release of class members not yet individually reviewed. No contempt finding found. Motions to enforce filed September 25 and October 9, 2026, are pending.

human_toll.summary: Court rulings found dozens of people arrested in the Chicago area since mid-2025 were held without the flight-risk finding the decree requires, and hundreds more arrests were challenged; many were removed or left the country before the court could rule. Those the court did rule on include workers, parents and people arrested at ICE check-ins. One man waiting in his parked car was pulled out and tased.

human_toll.caveat: The violation counts come from court orders and the government's own filings; they cover only people whose records were produced and reviewed, mostly those still in the U.S., so they understate the total. The 60% removal figure is the court's estimate, and the 16-of-607 figure is CBS Chicago's reading of a government list. Capitol News Illinois counted 32 releases in court on February 27, 2026, and four more in the written order. DHS's position: it says the operation targeted "the worst of the worst," called the release order a risk to public safety, argued in court that detainees were subject to mandatory detention and that the decree had expired, and told the court its field I-200 warrants were valid. The Seventh Circuit agreed that people arrested on I-200 warrants cannot be freed under the decree's release remedy. The court also denied some individual claims, for example where the arrest record showed a man put his car in reverse to escape agents, per Capitol News Illinois.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence: the findings, figures and dates come from the district court's orders and the Seventh Circuit's opinion, read in full on CourtListener, plus CBS Chicago, CNN, Capitol News Illinois, Block Club Chicago and the Sun-Times. The individuals named here are named in court orders or court filings and in news reports. The children of the Millennium Park family are minors and are not named. No contempt finding was located. Charles Wall is named in the court's October 7, 2025 opinion as the author of the June 11, 2025 email; the Seventh Circuit calls him "a senior DHS official." The Bovino quote is from his Fox News interview as reported by CBS Chicago. Lyons is named as the author of the January 28, 2026 memo in DHS's certification, quoted in the court's February 23, 2026 order. The Millennium Park family's link to this case rests on the Sun-Times report that their arrest was cited in the warrantless-arrest litigation; no court ruling on their arrest under the decree was found. Individual teachers and parents arrested during Midway Blitz who won release through separate habeas cases are not counted here.

what_changed: Backstory: Chaofeng Ge, a 32-year-old Chinese national who lived in Flushing, Queens, was arrested by Border Patrol near Tecate, California, on November 22, 2023, and released with a notice to appear. On January 23, 2025, Lower Paxton Township, Pennsylvania, police arrested him in a gift-card fraud case, and ICE lodged a detainer with the Dauphin County Prison. On July 31, 2025, a Dauphin County court convicted him of accessing a device issued to another without authorization and sentenced him to six to 12 months with credit for time served; the same day, ICE's Philadelphia field office arrested him and sent him to the Moshannon Valley Processing Center in Philipsburg, Pennsylvania, an immigration detention center run by GEO Group. On August 1, a nurse screened him with a Mandarin interpreter, recorded that he denied any past mental health conditions or thoughts of suicide, and placed him in general population; the same day a medical provider signed off on his transfer summary, which documented a past suicide attempt, a diagnosis of unspecified affective disorder and antidepressant use, but did not evaluate him or refer him to behavioral health, according to ICE's later mortality review. **At about 5:20 a.m. on August 5, 2025, two detention officers found Ge hanging in a shower stall in his housing unit, bound at the hands and feet; he was pronounced dead by the Clearfield County coroner at 6:03 a.m.** ICE's August 6 announcement said the cause of death was under investigation and described him as found hanging by his neck, without mentioning bindings; Pennsylvania State Police determined the death a suicide and found a handwritten note, ABC News reported. The coroner's autopsy ruled the manner of death suicide and the cause hanging and, Scripps News reported, states that "he was found with his hands and feet tied behind his back"; Newsweek, which saw the report, said it described linens around his wrists and ankles in a "hog-tied" position and no obvious defense wounds, and Scripps News reported that the medical examiner cited "a few references to patients binding their hands and feet prior to suicide by hanging." On September 9, 2025, his brother Yanfeng Ge asked ICE for records on his detention and death; ICE received the request on September 15 and had not answered by the October 14 deadline. **On November 12, 2025, Yanfeng Ge sued ICE and DHS under the Freedom of Information Act in federal court in Manhattan**, alleging that no one at the facility could speak Mandarin and that staff "refused to even try to communicate with him, much less offer him the mental health care that he so urgently needed." **ICE Health Service Corps' mortality review, dated November 17, 2025, found that Moshannon "did not provide Mr. GE medical care within the safe limits of practice":** medical staff did not act on his transfer summary, custody staff who found him delayed life-saving measures and had no cut-down tool at hand, CPR was ineffective, and officers had not done timely, thorough rounds or checked the showers on each round. It reported that the facility had changed its intake and cut-down tool procedures and replaced the shower hooks with hooks rated for three pounds. Yanfeng Ge dismissed the Manhattan case without prejudice on February 17, 2026. In March, Documented reported that the family's lawyers were preparing a wrongful-death lawsuit; on March 17 he refiled the records case in federal court in Brooklyn, and the government answered on May 18. In a September 30, 2026 joint status report, the government said ICE had made a third production of about 390 pages on September 29, that production was substantially complete, and that more than 1,000 hours of possibly responsive video remained, with the parties to confer on limiting it.
legal_status: Sued: Yanfeng Ge sued ICE and DHS under the Freedom of Information Act in the Southern District of New York on November 12, 2025 (No. 25-cv-9430), voluntarily dismissed that case without prejudice on February 17, 2026, and refiled in the Eastern District of New York on March 17, 2026 (No. 26-cv-1583, Magistrate Judge James R. Cho). The government answered on May 18, 2026, and the case is in court-supervised records production. The coroner ruled the death a suicide, a manner-of-death ruling, not a criminal finding; Pennsylvania State Police reportedly suspect no foul play. No criminal charge, wrongful-death suit or inspector general investigation was found; in March 2026 the family's lawyers were reported to be preparing a wrongful-death suit.

human_toll.summary: Chaofeng Ge, 32, died five days after ICE detained him, after a provider signed off on records of a past suicide attempt without referring him for a mental health evaluation, according to ICE's own review. His brother, his only family in the U.S., has spent more than a year seeking records of how he died.

human_toll.caveat: The account rests on ICE's own mortality review, the coroner's autopsy as quoted by Scripps News and Newsweek, and the family's court filings. The coroner ruled the death a suicide and the medical examiner found precedent for people binding themselves before hanging; Pennsylvania State Police reportedly suspect no foul play, and the family's lawyers say the bindings raise questions, including whether he was assisted, that the records have not answered. ICE says Ge denied any mental health history at intake with a Mandarin interpreter; the family says no one at the facility spoke Mandarin, and GEO Group says it provides "translation services." The family's lawyer also disputed ICE's account of how long Ge was at Moshannon. DHS says "all in-custody deaths are tragic, taken seriously, and are thoroughly investigated by law enforcement," that suicides in its custody are rare, and that the records request would be answered "through the proper channels."

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the death, the suicide ruling and the bindings: ICE's own mortality review says officers found him "bound at the hands and feet," and the autopsy's description of his hands and feet tied behind his back was reported by Scripps News and Newsweek from the report itself. HIGH confidence on the lawsuit, from the CourtListener dockets and filings. The family's allegations about language access and mental health care are allegations in a complaint; ICE's review independently found that medical staff did not act on his documented suicide history. Earlier ICE public statements did not mention the bindings. The brother's name appears as "Yangeng" in one outlet; the court filings say Yanfeng. The newest news coverage found is Documented's March 2026 report; searches found nothing newer than the September 30, 2026 status report.

title: ICE dropped its limits on courthouse arrests and seized people at their immigration hearings; courts have since struck the policy down

location.place: Nationwide (immigration courts and state and local courthouses)

officials.name: Caleb Vitello
officials.role: Acting ICE Director; signed the Jan. 21, 2025 interim courthouse guidance

officials.name: Todd Lyons
officials.role: Acting ICE Director; signed the May 27, 2025 final courthouse guidance

officials.name: Sirce Owen
officials.role: Acting EOIR Director; issued the Jan. 28, 2025 memo cancelling immigration-court enforcement limits

people.unnamed_affected: People arrested as they left immigration court hearings, many of them asylum seekers or parolees who had entered within two years, and defendants, witnesses and others arrested at state and local courthouses; a Boston defendant detained on the first day of his jury trial; court watchers, including a 71-year-old volunteer handcuffed and held for eight hours in San Diego.

status: ICE's 2025 courthouse-arrest policies are vacated nationwide (N.D. Cal., June 23, 2026; government appeal pending) and for immigration courts by a Manhattan judge (Sept. 30). On Oct. 15, 2026 that judge set Dec. 18 for a sanctions motion over the government's misstatement.
date_of_action: 2025-01-21 (ICE rescinds its 2021 courthouse-arrest limits) through 2026-10-15 (Manhattan court sets sanctions schedule)
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the push to raise ICE arrest numbers by targeting people already in contact with the government, here people obeying orders to appear in court, paired with case dismissals that route them into expedited removal. It runs alongside the rescission of protected-area limits for schools, churches and hospitals (see the entry on DHS opening schools, churches and hospitals to enforcement), and one state-courthouse arrest attempt led to the entry on Judge Hannah Dugan's prosecution.

pull_quote: "The courthouse is meant to be a refuge for the pursuit of justice, not a hunting ground for ICE," said plaintiffs' lawyer Jordan Wells after a federal judge struck down the policy nationwide.

glance.what: ICE dropped courthouse-arrest limits and arrested people at their immigration hearings; courts struck it down

what_changed: Backstory: an April 27, 2021 ICE and CBP memo allowed civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses, immigration courts included, only in narrow cases such as a national security threat, an imminent risk of death or violence, hot pursuit of a public-safety threat, or an imminent risk that evidence in a criminal case would be destroyed; a December 2023 immigration court (EOIR) memo likewise limited enforcement in or near its courtrooms and waiting areas. On January 21, 2025, Acting ICE Director Caleb Vitello rescinded the 2021 memo with interim guidance letting officers make courthouse arrests when they have "credible information" that the person will be there, while telling them to "generally avoid" courthouses wholly dedicated to "non-criminal proceedings (e.g., family court, small claims court)." On January 28, Acting EOIR Director Sirce Owen cancelled the 2023 immigration court memo, calling its other grounds "unpersuasive, inconsistent with current Executive Branch policy, pretextual, or unsubstantiated on any systematic basis." Arrests at state and local courthouses followed. In Boston, an ICE officer detained a defendant on March 27, 2025, the first day of his jury trial, and did not return him; on March 31 a Boston Municipal Court judge dismissed the state charge and found the officer in contempt, a finding a federal judge later dismissed as moot after the state court system did not oppose dismissal. In April, an ICE attempt to arrest a defendant at a Milwaukee County courthouse led to the federal prosecution of Judge Hannah Dugan, accused of steering him out a non-public exit (see the Cabinet-Level entry on her prosecution). **From late May 2025, ICE turned immigration courts themselves into arrest sites.** According to the New York Times, a May 20 internal memo told ICE trial attorneys to help deportation officers make arrests by moving to dismiss immigration cases; government lawyers then asked judges to drop cases, and officers waiting in hallways arrested people as they left so they could be placed in expedited removal, a fast-track process with no hearing before a judge. The Washington Post reported officers in Arizona, Virginia and more than 20 other states had been instructed to arrest people right after a deportation order or a dismissal. DHS confirmed it was dismissing cases of people in the country less than two years and arresting them at court. On May 27, Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons replaced the January guidance with a final memo that dropped its limit to places where local law did not bar such arrests. An EOIR email told judges that motions to dismiss "may be made orally and decided from the bench." Court watchers who began escorting people to hearings in Sacramento, San Diego and Denver reported being shoved, photographed and, in San Diego, a 71-year-old volunteer handcuffed and held for eight hours; then-New York City Comptroller Brad Lander was arrested in June 2025 at 26 Federal Plaza, Manhattan's largest immigration court, while escorting someone through a crowd of ICE agents. Lawsuits followed: a class action in Washington, D.C. (Immigrant Advocates Response Collaborative v. DOJ, July 16, 2025); African Communities Together and The Door in Manhattan (African Communities Together v. Lyons, Aug. 1); and a Northern California class action that became Pablo Sequen v. Albarran (Sept. 18). On Aug. 1, Judge Jia Cobb in Washington barred expedited removal of people who entered on humanitarian parole, a ruling CBS News said could curtail the arrests. On Sept. 12, Judge P. Kevin Castel in Manhattan paused EOIR's quick-dismissal policy for Manhattan and the Bronx but declined to pause ICE's arrest policy, accepting the government's position that the May 2025 memo justified the arrests. State courts pushed back: Cook County's chief judge barred civil arrests of people attending court without a judicial warrant (Oct. 14, 2025), and on Nov. 17 a federal judge dismissed a Justice Department suit against New York's Protect Our Courts Act, which bars such arrests at state courthouses without a judge-signed warrant. In Massachusetts, WBUR counted 386 ICE courthouse arrests at 46 courts from January through mid-October 2025, against 131 a year earlier. On Dec. 24, 2025, Judge P. Casey Pitts stayed ICE's 2025 courthouse-arrest policies for immigration courts in ICE's San Francisco area. **On March 24, 2026, Justice Department lawyers told Judge Castel the May 2025 memo "does not and has never applied" to immigration courts, saying ICE had told them otherwise; DHS replied, "We will continue to arrest illegal aliens at immigration courts following their proceedings."** Castel reversed himself on May 18, barring most arrests at three Manhattan immigration courts except in narrow circumstances; a man was arrested in one of those buildings the next day, and AP reported it was not clear whether the arrest fell under an exception. On June 23, Pitts vacated the ICE and EOIR courthouse-arrest policies nationwide as "arbitrary and capricious," reinstating the 2021 ICE and 2023 EOIR limits; DHS General Counsel James Percival called the ruling "naked judicial activism in service of an anti-American, open borders agenda." The government appealed to the Ninth Circuit on July 2, and Pitts denied its request to pause the ruling on July 10. On Sept. 30, Castel granted the Manhattan groups summary judgment, vacating the 2025 guidance as applied to immigration courts; on Oct. 15 he allowed discovery into possible sanctions over the government's misstatement and set Dec. 18, 2026 for the groups' sanctions motion.
legal_status: Ruled unlawful. Pablo Sequen v. Albarran (N.D. Cal. No. 5:25-cv-06487): Judge P. Casey Pitts stayed ICE's 2025 courthouse-arrest policies for ICE's San Francisco area on Dec. 24, 2025, then on June 23, 2026 vacated ICE Policies 11072.3 and 11072.4, EOIR's memo 25-06 and ICE's hold-room waiver as arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act; the government appealed (Ninth Circuit No. 26-4310) and Pitts denied a stay pending appeal on July 10, 2026; on Aug. 26, 2026 the Ninth Circuit referred its stay motion to the merits panel without ruling, and the plaintiffs' answering brief is due Nov. 16, 2026. African Communities Together v. Lyons (S.D.N.Y. No. 1:25-cv-6366): Judge P. Kevin Castel declined to pause the arrest policy on Sept. 12, 2025, reversed that on May 18, 2026 after the government's March 24 correction, and on Sept. 30, 2026 ruled the policy arbitrary and capricious and vacated the 2025 guidance as applied to immigration courts; the groups may file a sanctions motion on Dec. 18, 2026. Immigrant Advocates Response Collaborative v. DOJ (D.D.C. No. 1:25-cv-02279): sued July 16, 2025; no ruling on the courthouse-arrest claims was found. State courthouses: the Justice Department's suit against New York's Protect Our Courts Act was dismissed on Nov. 17, 2025; its suit against Illinois's courthouse-arrest ban survived a motion to dismiss on Aug. 19, 2026 and is pending. A Boston judge's March 2025 contempt finding against an ICE officer was dismissed as moot in federal court.

human_toll.summary: People who showed up for mandatory immigration hearings, many of them recently arrived asylum seekers or parolees and, as the government conceded in court, not only people in high-priority groups, were arrested in courthouse hallways, often right after government lawyers had their cases dismissed; many were moved toward fast-track deportation and detained in short-term holding cells or facilities hundreds of miles away. Defendants, victims and witnesses at state courts faced arrests that prosecutors say derailed cases and scared people away. Attorneys tie a sharp rise in missed hearings, and deportation orders issued in absentia, to fear of arrest at court.
