human_toll.caveat: No nationwide count of courthouse arrests was found; NPR described "hundreds" at immigration courts. The Massachusetts tally is WBUR's analysis of ICE data compiled by the Deportation Data Project, and WBUR says it is "almost certainly an undercount." The in-absentia figure is NPR's analysis of EOIR data; tying the rise to courthouse arrests is attorneys' explanation, and lawyers also cite missed notices and other fears. The motion-to-dismiss figures come from the American Immigration Council's FOIA data as summarized by the Immigration Policy Tracking Project. DHS's stated rationale: it is "commonsense to take illegal aliens into custody following the completion of their removal proceedings" and "Nothing prohibits arresting a lawbreaker where you find them"; it says people with a valid fear claim stay in immigration court, and the Justice Department argued courthouse arrests are safer because people are screened for weapons.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the policy changes, their dates and signers, which come from the court orders that reviewed them (Judge Pitts's Dec. 24, 2025 order cites each memo) and the Immigration Policy Tracking Project's summaries of the documents. HIGH confidence on the litigation record, taken from the CourtListener dockets for Pablo Sequen v. Albarran and African Communities Together v. Lyons, the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse summary, and Courthouse News, Documented, NPR, WBUR, KTVU and Scripps/CNN reporting. The May 20, 2025 internal memo is described as the New York Times reported it, not read directly. The Boston contempt account rests on AP reporting and a Trellis summary of the federal dismissal, which gives no dismissal date. The government's March 2026 correction is its own admission to the court; whether sanctions follow is undecided. The Ninth Circuit referred the government's stay request to its merits panel on Aug. 26, 2026; no ruling on it was found as of the latest appeal filings reviewed (Sept. 21, 2026). The court watchers' accounts are their own, reported by Mother Jones; DHS called them "rioters" who obstructed officers.

section_summaries.what_changed: ICE scrapped its 2021 courthouse-arrest limits in 2025 and arrested people leaving immigration hearings; two federal judges have since struck the policy down.
section_summaries.human_toll: People obeying court dates were arrested in hallways and fast-tracked for deportation; Massachusetts courthouse arrests nearly tripled and missed hearings soared.

title: ICE Dropped Its Protections for Immigrant Crime Victims With Pending U Visa, T Visa and VAWA Petitions; a Court Paused the Policy in May 2026
status: Stayed in part: on May 20, 2026 a federal judge in Los Angeles paused ICE's January 2025 guidance and two related practices for three nationwide classes of U visa, T visa and VAWA petitioners. The government's Ninth Circuit appeal is in briefing (opening brief due Nov. 17, 2026); no ruling.
date_of_action: 2025-01-30 (ICE Directive 11005.4 issued) through 2026-05-20 (stayed in part by a federal court; appeal pending)
what_changed: Federal law gives immigrants who survive domestic violence, human trafficking and other serious crimes a path to legal status through a self-petition under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), the U visa for crime victims who help police and the T visa for trafficking victims. For years ICE guidance (a 2011 policy statement and a 2021 directive titled "Using a Victim-Centered Approach with Noncitizen Crime Victims") generally kept officers from arresting, detaining or deporting people with pending petitions. On January 30, 2025, ICE issued Directive 11005.4, interim guidance from then-Acting ICE Director Caleb Vitello, that rescinded both. It told officers they are "not required to affirmatively seek to identify indicia or evidence suggesting an alien is a victim of a crime or consider such evidence as a positive discretionary factor," and that "ICE will no longer routinely request expedited adjudications from USCIS," doing so only case by case when "in ICE's best interests." According to class counsel's later summary, the guidance directed ICE instead to "achieve the total and efficient enforcement of immigration laws against all inadmissible and removable" noncitizens. A lawsuit filed October 14, 2025 by the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, Public Counsel and other groups (Immigration Center for Women and Children v. Noem, now v. Mullin) alleged that ICE went on to arrest, detain and deport U and T visa petitioners who held deferred action without notice (the "De Facto Revocation Policy") and to deport petitioners without the review of their eligibility the law requires (the "Blind Removal Policy"). The named plaintiffs include Lupe A., a domestic-violence survivor with deferred action and a pending U visa who, the case page says, was arrested outside her Los Angeles home in April 2025 and deported to Mexico the next day; Carmen F., who had called police on an abusive husband and was detained with her son at an ICE check-in, deported, and met at the airport by the abuser, who forced her to live with him again; and Yessenia Ruano, a trafficking survivor and Milwaukee teacher's aide who left for El Salvador with her U.S.-citizen twin daughters after ICE denied her a stay of removal. On May 20, 2026, U.S. District Judge André Birotte Jr. certified three nationwide classes of U visa, T visa and VAWA petitioners and stayed the 2025 guidance and both practices for them under the Administrative Procedure Act, finding that the policies likely violate the APA, immigration law and the Fifth Amendment's right to due process. The order says the guidance "dramatically changed ICE's enforcement posture … to a policy of enforcement despite their pending applications." **The court ordered the government to let three plaintiffs who were deported or forced to leave, Lupe A., Carmen F. and Ruano, return to the U.S.** DHS said it "complies with all court orders, even as radical NGOs shop for the most favorable forum and activist judges seek to thwart our operations." The government appealed to the Ninth Circuit in June 2026, and on July 27 the district court refused to put its order on hold while the Solicitor General decided whether to pursue the appeal; the government's opening brief is due Nov. 17, 2026. Two return disputes are also pending in the district court. On June 25, 2026, Carmen F. and Ruano asked the court to enforce or clarify its order after, they said, the government refused to let Carmen F.'s nine-year-old son and Ruano's husband, both derivatives on their petitions, return with them because the order does not name them; the same day, the plaintiffs asked the court to bar the government from blocking the return of a fourth plaintiff, Daniel H., a U visa petitioner deported to Guatemala in December 2025 while the plaintiffs' request to pause the policy was pending. Both requests were fully briefed by July 7, with no ruling on the docket as of mid-October 2026. In October 2026, ProPublica reported that the rollback, alongside the inauguration-day end of limits on arrests at "sensitive locations" such as domestic violence shelters, left immigrant abuse victims exposed after calls to police: reviewing hundreds of habeas petitions filed since January 2025, it "found dozens of petitioners who were arrested on suspicion of domestic violence and turned over to ICE, even though they were never charged or their charges were dropped," and it interviewed a half-dozen alleged victims held at the North Lake detention center in Michigan. Kent County, Michigan's jail turned more immigrants over to ICE in the first half of 2026 than during the whole Biden administration, ProPublica found. A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, said ICE targets the "worst of the worst," and DHS said "we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that's how we save lives."
confidence_note: HIGH on the policy itself: the directive's text is quoted by the Immigration Policy Tracking Project and by class counsel's practice advisory, which agree on its terms. HIGH on the May 20, 2026 order's scope (three nationwide classes, a stay of the guidance and two practices, the return of three plaintiffs), read in the order itself; its findings are preliminary (likely unlawful), not a final judgment. The plaintiffs' individual stories are their allegations. MODERATE on how widely survivors were harmed: ProPublica's habeas review documents dozens of cases but no national total. The appeal (No. 26-3961) was still in briefing, with the government's opening brief due Nov. 17, 2026, a motion to dismiss heard in October 2026 had no ruling in the docket's public text, and the plaintiffs' June 2026 requests to return Carmen F.'s son, Ruano's husband and a fourth plaintiff, Daniel H., were undecided, as of mid-October 2026. Lupe A., Carmen F. and Daniel H. are named in a court filing under the pseudonyms the filings use; Yessenia Ruano is named in a court filing and has spoken to WPR. No minor is named.

human_toll.summary: **Immigrant survivors of domestic violence, trafficking and other crimes were detained and deported despite pending petitions for protection, some with deferred action**: the court ordered three plaintiffs who were deported or forced to leave allowed back, and ProPublica found dozens of uncharged or cleared domestic-violence arrestees turned over to ICE. By the plaintiffs' estimate, cited in the court's order, about 600,000 people were awaiting decisions on these petitions in 2025; a local prosecutor and advocates report victims now afraid to come forward.

human_toll.caveat: No government count exists of how many survivors with pending petitions ICE arrested, detained or deported under the 2025 guidance; ProPublica says there is "no comprehensive way to track" it. The 600,000 figure is the plaintiffs' estimate of everyone awaiting a decision, not the number harmed, and the 6,000 figure is one legal group's own client count. ProPublica's cases mix two causes: the guidance and the wider growth of local police cooperation with ICE (287(g) agreements rose from fewer than 150 to more than 2,600). Some detainees ProPublica describes said they were victims but were arrested as alleged abusers. No estimate of health effects was found. The government's stated rationale: the guidance implements the executive order calling for the "total and efficient enforcement" of immigration law against all removable noncitizens; a White House spokesperson said ICE targets the "worst of the worst," and DHS said "we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that's how we save lives."

glance.what: Ran enforcement under a 3,000-arrests-a-day target as arrests of people with no conviction rose 770%

what_changed:
A New York Times Magazine investigation published April 14, 2026, drawing on interviews with more than 80 former and current DHS employees plus Justice Department officials, reported that Stephen Miller, Trump's homeland security adviser, had set a target of 3,000 arrests a day and one million deportations a year. The Times reported that on May 21, 2025, Miller and Noem called the heads of DHS field offices to Washington for a meeting about increasing arrests and deportations; a former ICE senior executive recounted Miller telling acting ICE director Todd Lyons, "there is no list. Everyone is fair game." (A White House spokesperson said Miller was highlighting the need to implement the president's agenda, not chastising Lyons.) Many of those interviewed supported increased enforcement but criticized the administration's execution, aspects of which they characterized as chaotic, dangerous and ineffective. One Homeland Security Investigations agent told the Times, "There was an incredible amount of pressure for numbers"; a senior ICE officer said, "There were never official quotas, just pressure to produce and a questioning of our tactics if we didn't arrest." **Citing ICE data, the Times reported that arrests of people with no conviction of any kind had risen 770% under Trump, against a 37% rise in arrests of people with violent convictions.** The same 770% figure had been published on April 7, 2026 by the UC Berkeley-based Deportation Data Project, from ICE records released through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit; a DHS spokesperson called that analysis "cherry picked" and said DHS and ICE had not verified its accuracy. NPR later reported that Lyons, acting director from March 2025 to May 2026, faced intense pressure to meet a 3,000-person daily arrest quota imposed by the White House, and that the quota was never met.

Separately, a Wall Street Journal investigation (February 12, 2026) reported that Noem and adviser Corey Lewandowski had fired or demoted roughly 80% of the career ICE field leadership in place when they started, and that Noem sidelined rivals and dissenters and carried out confrontational operations over the objections of longtime immigration officials.

Trump fired Noem on March 5, 2026, and former Sen. Markwayne Mullin was sworn in as Secretary on March 24, 2026; Lyons stepped down in May 2026. The arrest pace rose again under Mullin. The Associated Press reported that ICE arrested about 10,000 people in the five days ending June 30, 2026, roughly 2,000 a day, against an average of 1,283 a day in December 2025, the previous high. ABC News reported August 4, 2026, citing sources familiar with the data, that ICE arrested 51,000 people in July. DHS's own September 2, 2026 press release then put June 2026 arrests at 43,900, July at 50,208 and August at 50,925, three straight monthly records; DHS's official July count is about 800 below ABC's figure. The Deportation Data Project found that the share of ICE arrests leading to book-ins that involved people with criminal convictions fell to an all-time low of 27% in July 2026. On October 2, 2026, Noticias Telemundo, NBC News's sister network, reported that an administration official had confirmed to NBC News that ICE arrested more than 48,000 people in September and held 69,000 in custody, and that the arrests followed an order to ICE field offices nationwide to detain 2,000 people a day.
legal_status: No ruling or inspector-general finding on the daily arrest targets found as of October 19, 2026. Plaintiffs in Vasquez Perdomo v. Noem, a suit over Los Angeles immigration stops, cited Miller's 3,000-a-day goal; in a July 30, 2025 Ninth Circuit filing the Justice Department said no such goal had been set as policy.

human_toll.summary: The push to meet daily arrest targets fell increasingly on people with no criminal record. Per ICE data reported by the Times, arrests of people with no conviction of any kind rose 770% under Trump while arrests of people with violent convictions rose 37%, and only about 5 percent of people booked into ICE custody in the prior year had been convicted of a violent crime. Arrests then set monthly records under Mullin in June, July and August 2026, and the Deportation Data Project found that the share of ICE arrests leading to book-ins that involved people with criminal convictions hit an all-time low of 27% in July 2026.

human_toll.caveat: The June-August 2026 counts are DHS's own; the September count comes from one unnamed administration official and ABC's July figure from unnamed sources. The 770% and 27% figures are the Deportation Data Project's analyses of ICE arrest data (the 770% figure, also cited by the Times, from records released under FOIA). DHS told NBC News the project "cherry picked" data, that "70% of ICE arrests are criminal illegal aliens" (a figure DHS has said counts people convicted or charged), and that everyone here illegally "committed a crime when they came into this country illegally" (a first unlawful entry is a misdemeanor). DHS acting assistant secretary for public affairs Lauren Bis told the Times officers are arresting "the worst of the worst" and that HSI has no quotas. In a July 30, 2025 Ninth Circuit filing, the Justice Department said of the 3,000-a-day figure, "No such goal has been set as a matter of policy, and no such directive has been issued to or by" DHS or ICE. The Deportation Data Project notes that because the number of noncitizens with convictions is limited, the convicted share typically falls whenever arrests rise. Arrest counts do not show how many people were lawfully present, later released, or deported.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core findings: the Times' sourcing base of more than 80 current and former DHS employees, whose descriptions of specific incidents it says it corroborated with colleagues, contemporaneous notes and court documents, and a 770% figure drawn from ICE's own records (the same figure the Deportation Data Project derived from ICE data released under FOIA, which DHS disputes). The Times attributes the 3,000-a-day target to Stephen Miller and reports Miller and Noem called field-office heads to Washington to press for more arrests; NPR separately reported that Lyons faced intense pressure to meet a 3,000-a-day quota imposed by the White House. Interviewees describe pressure for numbers rather than a written quota; DHS denies HSI has quotas, and the Justice Department told the Ninth Circuit in July 2025 that no 3,000-a-day goal had been set as policy. The officials listed are those these sources tie to setting, pressing or announcing the arrest push; the reporting otherwise describes an institutional pattern, not one official's directive. HIGH confidence that record arrests continued after Noem's removal: DHS's own September 2, 2026 release reports 43,900 arrests in June, 50,208 in July and 50,925 in August 2026; ABC News's earlier 51,000 figure for July came from unnamed sources and differs from DHS's count by about 800. MODERATE confidence on the September figure and the reported 2,000-a-day order, which rest on one administration official and Telemundo's reporting; the Associated Press separately put late-June arrests at roughly 2,000 a day.

section_summaries.human_toll: Per ICE data, no-conviction arrests rose 770% vs 37% for violent convictions; arrests then hit records of 43,900 to 50,925 a month in June-August 2026.
section_summaries.confidence_note: High confidence: 80+ sources and ICE data; DHS disputes the 770% analysis and DOJ told a court no 3,000-a-day goal was set as policy. Record arrests continued under Mullin.

title: ICE Quietly Stopped Listing Detainees With Final Deportation Orders in Its Public Locator, Leaving Lawyers and Families Unable to Find Them
status: Ongoing: ICE has not confirmed, explained or reversed the change. On Sept. 30, 30+ advocacy groups petitioned a UN working group and 45+ House Democrats asked ICE to restore the listings, seeking answers by Oct. 14. No court ruling on the policy itself found.
what_changed: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement stopped listing detainees who are subject to final deportation orders in its public Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15, 2026, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity. ICE did not announce the change. AP reported it on Sept. 21, after several lawyers confirmed that their clients had vanished from the system and the American Immigration Lawyers Association had warned its members on Sept. 18. A detainee drops out of the locator once their removal order becomes final, even without being moved, the American Immigration Council wrote. Border Report and the American Immigration Council, citing Washington Post reporting, said ICE staff have also been told not to give these detainees' locations to lawyers and relatives who call to ask. **Lawyers told AP the change leaves families unable to tell whether a relative has been moved or already deported, and can keep attorneys from reaching clients in time to bring last-minute legal challenges before removal.** People with final orders can still seek to reopen their cases or file habeas petitions, and some have protection from deportation to their home countries and face removal to third countries where they have no ties. The Amica Center for Immigrant Rights told AP that every one of its clients with a final order, 17 in all, had disappeared from the locator, and an ACLU attorney said eight Somali men held at the U.S. military base at Guantanamo Bay were among those removed from it. The officials told AP the practice does not cover the Adelanto, California detention facility or temporary holding sites in Minneapolis, New York City and suburban Chicago, where judges in separate litigation have ordered ICE to list detainees promptly. In a statement to AP, ICE neither confirmed nor denied the change, saying detainees with final removal orders were being prioritized for deportation even as the agency faces a "historic number of injunctions" against individual removals. ICE launched the locator in 2010; before it, relatives and lawyers had to call ICE regional offices or individual facilities to find detained people. On Sept. 30, 2026, a coalition of more than 30 advocacy groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights First and Refugees International, petitioned the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law. **The petition described a mother and her 7-year-old daughter who lost access to their lawyers while facing deportation to Venezuela; ICE disclosed where they were only about 18 hours after a judge ordered it to, and then released them.** The same day, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar wrote to ICE Acting Director David Venturella asking ICE to restore the listings and to answer questions about the policy by Oct. 14. DHS denied that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees "have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers" and that "the appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple."
confidence_note: HIGH confidence that the listings were removed: AP's report rests on three current and former ICE officials plus several lawyers whose clients disappeared from the system, and the American Immigration Council and Global Detention Project describe the same Sept. 15 change. ICE has neither confirmed nor denied it, and DHS disputes that it amounts to disappearing people. MODERATE confidence on effects: the harm to legal access is the assessment of lawyers and advocates, the instruction to refuse phone requests rests on Washington Post reporting as cited by Border Report and the American Immigration Council, and the petition's case examples are the petitioners' accounts. Re-verified 2026-10-14: AP's reporting and the Sept. 30 House letter (which asked ICE to respond by Oct. 14) still say what this entry says; no ICE reply, reversal, UN action or lawsuit challenging the policy was found. No official is on record as ordering the change; the House letter was addressed to ICE Acting Director David Venturella as the agency's head, so no official is listed as responsible. Re-verified 2026-10-18: AP's Sept. 21 and Sept. 30 reports, the American Immigration Council, the Global Detention Project, Border Report and the Rivas release still say what this entry says; no ICE reply, reversal, UN action or lawsuit challenging the policy was found.

The three are different scopes and should not be added together. No count of deportations carried out before a lawyer could intervene, and no estimate of health or mental-health harm, was found; the petition's individual accounts of distress are the petitioners' own. title: ICE Detention Deaths: 2025 Was the Deadliest Year in Two Decades; TAP Lists 71 Deaths in ICE and CBP Custody or Soon After Release Since January 2025
status: Ongoing -- deaths continue: Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found dead in his cell at ICE's Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo on October 17, 2026 (Texas Tribune), the 71st death on TAP's list since January 2025; AP counted at least 58 ICE deaths as of September 18.
date_of_action: 2025-01-23 (first death on TAP's list) through 2026-10-17 (latest death on the list)
what_changed: The Guardian reported that **31 people died in ICE custody in 2025, the agency's deadliest year in more than two decades**, as the Trump administration detained a record number of people: 68,440 were held in mid-December 2025, nearly 75% of them with no criminal convictions. Documented causes included seizure, heart failure, stroke, respiratory failure, tuberculosis, and suicide; families and lawyers alleged some deaths resulted from medical neglect after detainees repeatedly sought and failed to receive care. A KFF health-policy tracker using a slightly different count found 33 deaths in 2025 (versus 11 in 2024 and fewer than 10 in earlier years) and 46 from January 2025 through March 18, 2026; of those 46, it counted 32 among people with existing medical conditions whose health appeared to worsen, 9 that ICE reported as suicides, and 5 from other causes such as a fatal traffic collision during arrest. The Project On Government Oversight found a 36.25% decline in ICE detention-facility inspection reports published in 2025 compared with 2024, even as detention populations surged; 2025 inspection reports that were published found staff not properly monitoring people at risk of suicide, failures to report patients with suspected active tuberculosis, and too few toilets. A later POGO analysis found the number of documented detention-standard violations fell by nearly 70% between fiscal years 2022 and 2025 while deaths rose -- a decline POGO frames as weakened inspections rather than improved conditions. NPR reported that some Public Health Service officers deployed to detention centers described 'moral distress' over life-threatening delays in getting medicine and care to detainees, chaotic screenings, and overcrowded yet understaffed conditions; one nurse described delays in anti-epileptic medication and insulin leading to seizures and dangerously high blood sugars. Separately, Members of Congress represented by Democracy Forward Foundation and American Oversight sued after DHS blocked lawmakers' unannounced oversight visits to ICE facilities (Neguse v. ICE). After the court stayed DHS's seven-day notice policy in December 2025, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem reinstated the requirement in a January 8, 2026 memo; the plaintiffs say it came to light only after Members of Congress were denied entry to a Minnesota ICE facility despite presenting a valid court order, days after a federal agent fatally shot a U.S. citizen there. Judge Jia Cobb granted a temporary restraining order against the new policy on February 2, 2026 and stayed it on March 2. DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin denied that detention conditions were declining, stating it is 'a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody.' Update 2026-10-19: TAP's own list of deaths in ICE and CBP custody, and shortly after release from it, since January 2025 comes to 71, checked against ICE's detainee death reports and posted list, CBP's death notices and news reports: 59 people died in ICE custody (32 in 2025, 27 in 2026 through October 17), 4 died after ICE released or deported them, which ICE does not count, and 8 died in CBP or Border Patrol custody or just after release (7 in custody, 1 after release). Unless marked, each ICE line comes from ICE's own detainee death report and each CBP line from CBP's own notice. Update 2026-10-03: The Associated Press reported that Carlos Josue Marchena Marchena, a 36-year-old Costa Rican man with type 1 diabetes, was found unresponsive on September 18, 2026 at Winn Correctional Center in Winnfield, Louisiana, and was later pronounced dead at a hospital; his official cause of death was pending further medical examination. **His sister, his girlfriend and a detainee in the adjacent cell told AP he had complained of missed insulin shots, missed meals and too little water as he was moved between facilities; his family said his condition worsened after he reached Winn, where he died less than a week later.** By AP's own count he was at least the 58th person to die in ICE custody since January 2025, and the third ICE detainee to die at Winn in less than six months. AP also reported that medical examiners and coroners have ruled diabetes a contributing factor in at least six ICE detainee deaths during Trump's second term. The DHS Office of Inspector General's June 2026 report on an unannounced March 2025 inspection found Winn did not fully comply with detention standards for medical care, food service, use of force and other areas: medical staff did not always update medical records or document interpretation of lab test results, perishable food was not stored at required temperatures, and facility staff refused to provide the OIG with copies of all facility video recordings. ICE concurred with all nine of the report's recommendations. ICE said in a statement that Marchena 'received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.' Update 2026-10-18: DHS appealed Judge Cobb's March 2 stay; on May 8, 2026 the D.C. Circuit denied the government's emergency motion to put the stay on hold pending appeal, and on July 27 the district court paused its own proceedings while the appeal goes forward. A JAMA study reported by ABC News found the ICE detention death rate fell from 127.7 per 100,000 person-years in fiscal year 2004 to 13.0 in fiscal 2023, then climbed to 47.5 in fiscal 2025 and 88.9 in partial fiscal 2026; the researchers said the increases came alongside disrupted or terminated oversight mechanisms, rapid detention expansion with reports of overcrowding, and potentially delayed medical care. POGO's August 2026 analysis also found the share of facilities given ICE's top 'Superior' inspection rating nearly tripled from fiscal 2024 to July 2026.
confidence_note: Very strong, multi-source corroboration across distinct methodologies: The Guardian's original investigative count (re-syndicated via RSN, AOL), KFF's independent health-policy tracker, POGO's inspection and violation-rate investigations, a peer-reviewed JAMA study, and NPR's interviews with Public Health Service officers all converge on the same pattern (record deaths, reduced oversight, understaffed and overcrowded conditions) via different data sources and methods. The congressional-oversight court fight (Noem's January 8 memo, the Minnesota denial of entry) rests on a plaintiff's press release (Rep. Torres), CBS Colorado's report on the February 2 order and the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case summary; it is included as context connecting reduced oversight to the mortality trend, not as this entry's central claim. Contested: DHS says detainees receive comprehensive medical care and that death rates are low; the inspection data's own decline is part of what critics dispute. Update 2026-10-03: the Winn death rests on AP's reporting (read via syndicated copies) and ICE's own statement; Marchena is named because his family went public with AP; the family's and fellow detainee's accounts of missed insulin and food are allegations ICE disputes, and the official cause of death was still pending. The Winn inspection findings come from the DHS inspector general's report itself. Update 2026-10-18: corrected two figures to what their sources say: the Guardian's 'nearly 75% with no criminal convictions' describes the whole December 2025 detention population, not those who died, and KFF's cause-of-death breakdown (32, 9, 5) covers its 46 deaths through March 18, 2026 and does not double-count. The ~70% violations figure is now sourced to POGO's August 2026 analysis. Re-verified 2026-10-18: Guardian/RSN, KFF, POGO, NPR, ABC, CBS Colorado, the Torres release, AP via WSOC-TV and Detention Watch Network still say what the entry says; the Neguse v. ICE appeal status comes from the Clearinghouse summary (current to July 30, 2026). U.S. News, AP's own page, ICE's death notice and the OIG PDF could not be re-fetched this pass; the Winn OIG findings rest on the report as read on 2026-10-03 and on AP's summary of it. Update 2026-10-19: the per-death list rests on ICE's own detainee death reports (read in full for each ICE-listed death) and its posted list of deaths, CBP's own death notices, and, for deaths ICE has not yet reported or does not count, AP, CBS News Baltimore, The Texas Tribune, The Guardian, Telemundo/NBC News and The New York Times. Names come from ICE's own death notices or from reporting in which families went public; CBP's notices do not name the dead, so those seven are described. Ages and dates follow ICE's reports where outside lists differ. The list may be incomplete: ICE stopped reporting deaths after release in 2026 and posts its reports weeks to months late.

human_toll.summary: People held in ICE custody died in the largest numbers in two decades, and TAP lists 71 deaths in ICE and CBP custody or soon after release from January 2025 to October 17, 2026, 59 in ICE custody and 7 in CBP custody, from seizures, heart failure, strokes, tuberculosis, suicide and chronic illness such as diabetes; two were shot by an outside gunman at a Dallas ICE office. The other five died soon after ICE or Border Patrol released or deported them, and two of those deaths were ruled homicides by medical examiners. Families and lawyers allege some died after repeatedly seeking care. The deaths came as published inspections, cited violations and congressional access to facilities all fell.

human_toll.caveat: Death counts come from journalists' and researchers' tallies built on ICE's own death notices and reports, so they differ by method and date: The Guardian counted 31 deaths in 2025 (POGO, citing The Guardian, gives 32) and KFF 33; cumulative counts since January 2025 run from KFF's 46 (March 18, 2026) to Detention Watch Network's at least 56 (September 23, 2026) and AP's at least 58 (September 18, 2026). The AP figure is shown as the most recent, not as a reconciled total. The counts miss deaths shortly after release, which ICE said in June 2026 it will stop reporting, and official causes of death are often pending or differ from independent findings. The 'nearly 75% with no convictions' figure describes everyone held in December 2025, not those who died; KFF counted 6 of 46 deaths among people with no reported criminality or pending criminal charges. DHS's position: spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin said it is 'a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody' and that death rates in custody are '0.00007%' (DHS later told ABC News '0.009% of the detained population'), without providing the underlying data; border czar Tom Homan said 'Our deaths in custody are lower than everybody's' and that many detainees have poor medical histories. ICE said Marchena had misdemeanor convictions and a deportation order and received proper medical care. TAP's list of 71 is TAP's own count, built from ICE's detainee death reports and posted list, CBP's death notices and news reports, and is not a figure any agency publishes. ICE's own list, last updated September 23, 2026, names 57 deaths from January 23, 2025 to August 23, 2026; it includes Silverio Villegas Gonzalez, shot during an ICE traffic stop in Franklin Park, Illinois in September 2025, who is covered with agent shootings rather than on TAP's list, and leaves out the three later ICE-custody deaths (Marchena, Curo-Churata and Andrade-Covarrubias, known from ICE statements and news reports) and the deaths after release. AP's count (at least 58 ICE deaths as of September 18, 2026) is AP's own. Not counted on TAP's list: two men who died while fleeing ICE stops rather than in custody (Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, struck by a tractor-trailer in St. Augustine, Florida in July 2026, and Mario David Coronado Juarez, who crashed fleeing an attempted traffic stop in Grand Rapids, Michigan in September 2026; DHS says agents were not pursuing him when he crashed). ICE counts Jose Castro Rivera, struck by a vehicle while running from an ICE stop, as a custody death, so he is on the list. Medical examiners' homicide rulings (Lunas Campos, Shah Alam, Michel) are findings on the manner of death, meaning a death caused by others' acts or failures; they are not criminal findings, and TAP found no criminal charge in any death on the list. ICE's position: its detention standards 'require facilities to provide comprehensive medical, dental and mental health care,' and it says many detainees may not have had recent or reliable medical treatment before custody; it said Marchena and Curo-Churata received proper medical care. DHS said ICE 'had NOTHING to do with' Michel's death and that ICE is no longer responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths after someone leaves its custody. CBP said Shah Alam's death "had NOTHING to do with Border Patrol."

legal_status: Members of Congress sued DHS and ICE over limits on unannounced oversight visits (Neguse v. ICE, D.D.C.). The court stayed the seven-day notice policy on December 17, 2025, granted a temporary restraining order against Noem's January 8, 2026 replacement policy on February 2, and stayed that policy on March 2; DHS appealed, the D.C. Circuit denied a stay pending appeal on May 8, and the appeal is pending. The DHS inspector general's June 2026 report found Winn Correctional Center did not fully comply with detention standards for medical care, food service and use of force; ICE concurred with all nine recommendations. Medical examiners ruled the deaths of Geraldo Lunas Campos, Nurul Amin Shah Alam and Daphy Michel homicides, a manner-of-death finding, not a criminal one. Families and lawyers have alleged medical neglect in several deaths; TAP found no criminal charges in any death on its list.

what_changed.base: The Guardian reported that **31 people died in ICE custody in 2025, the agency's deadliest year in more than two decades**, as the Trump administration detained a record number of people: 68,440 were held in mid-December 2025, nearly 75% of them with no criminal convictions. Documented causes included seizure, heart failure, stroke, respiratory failure, tuberculosis, and suicide; families and lawyers alleged some deaths resulted from medical neglect after detainees repeatedly sought and failed to receive care. A KFF health-policy tracker using a slightly different count found 33 deaths in 2025 (versus 11 in 2024 and fewer than 10 in earlier years) and 46 from January 2025 through March 18, 2026; of those 46, it counted 32 among people with existing medical conditions whose health appeared to worsen, 9 that ICE reported as suicides, and 5 from other causes such as a fatal traffic collision during arrest. The Project On Government Oversight found a 36.25% decline in ICE detention-facility inspection reports published in 2025 compared with 2024, even as detention populations surged; 2025 inspection reports that were published found staff not properly monitoring people at risk of suicide, failures to report patients with suspected active tuberculosis, and too few toilets. A later POGO analysis found the number of documented detention-standard violations fell by nearly 70% between fiscal years 2022 and 2025 while deaths rose -- a decline POGO frames as weakened inspections rather than improved conditions. NPR reported that some Public Health Service officers deployed to detention centers described 'moral distress' over life-threatening delays in getting medicine and care to detainees, chaotic screenings, and overcrowded yet understaffed conditions; one nurse described delays in anti-epileptic medication and insulin leading to seizures and dangerously high blood sugars. Separately, Members of Congress represented by Democracy Forward Foundation and American Oversight sued after DHS blocked lawmakers' unannounced oversight visits to ICE facilities (Neguse v. ICE). After the court stayed DHS's seven-day notice policy in December 2025, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem reinstated the requirement in a January 8, 2026 memo; the plaintiffs say it came to light only after Members of Congress were denied entry to a Minnesota ICE facility despite presenting a valid court order, days after a federal agent fatally shot a U.S. citizen there. Judge Jia Cobb granted a temporary restraining order against the new policy on February 2, 2026 and stayed it on March 2. DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin denied that detention conditions were declining, stating it is 'a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-03: The Associated Press reported that Carlos Josue Marchena Marchena, a 36-year-old Costa Rican man with type 1 diabetes, was found unresponsive on September 18, 2026 at Winn Correctional Center in Winnfield, Louisiana, and was later pronounced dead at a hospital; his official cause of death was pending further medical examination. **His sister, his girlfriend and a detainee in the adjacent cell told AP he had complained of missed insulin shots, missed meals and too little water as he was moved between facilities; his family said his condition worsened after he reached Winn, where he died less than a week later.** By AP's own count he was at least the 58th person to die in ICE custody since January 2025, and the third ICE detainee to die at Winn in less than six months. AP also reported that medical examiners and coroners have ruled diabetes a contributing factor in at least six ICE detainee deaths during Trump's second term. The DHS Office of Inspector General's June 2026 report on an unannounced March 2025 inspection found Winn did not fully comply with detention standards for medical care, food service, use of force and other areas: medical staff did not always update medical records or document interpretation of lab test results, perishable food was not stored at required temperatures, and facility staff refused to provide the OIG with copies of all facility video recordings. ICE concurred with all nine of the report's recommendations. ICE said in a statement that Marchena 'received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-18: DHS appealed Judge Cobb's March 2 stay; on May 8, 2026 the D.C. Circuit denied the government's emergency motion to put the stay on hold pending appeal, and on July 27 the district court paused its own proceedings while the appeal goes forward. A JAMA study reported by ABC News found the ICE detention death rate fell from 127.7 per 100,000 person-years in fiscal year 2004 to 13.0 in fiscal 2023, then climbed to 47.5 in fiscal 2025 and 88.9 in partial fiscal 2026; the researchers said the increases came alongside disrupted or terminated oversight mechanisms, rapid detention expansion with reports of overcrowding, and potentially delayed medical care. POGO's August 2026 analysis also found the share of facilities given ICE's top 'Superior' inspection rating nearly tripled from fiscal 2024 to July 2026.

confidence_note.base: Very strong, multi-source corroboration across distinct methodologies: The Guardian's original investigative count (re-syndicated via RSN, AOL), KFF's independent health-policy tracker, POGO's inspection and violation-rate investigations, a peer-reviewed JAMA study, and NPR's interviews with Public Health Service officers all converge on the same pattern (record deaths, reduced oversight, understaffed and overcrowded conditions) via different data sources and methods. The congressional-oversight court fight (Noem's January 8 memo, the Minnesota denial of entry) rests on a plaintiff's press release (Rep. Torres), CBS Colorado's report on the February 2 order and the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case summary; it is included as context connecting reduced oversight to the mortality trend, not as this entry's central claim. Contested: DHS says detainees receive comprehensive medical care and that death rates are low; the inspection data's own decline is part of what critics dispute.

what_changed: The "detainee" index of the FBI's Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) -- the sub-index where DHS-collected profiles are stored -- grew by roughly 995,000 profiles in 2025 alone, reaching 3,345,692 by December 2025, per FBI records analyzed by Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology and reported by WIRED. Subtracting the roughly 75,000 people whose DNA CBP sent to the FBI in 2025, Georgetown estimates ICE alone may have added as many as roughly 920,000 profiles, which by Georgetown's estimate makes DHS the single largest source of new genetic profiles in the national criminal DNA system; ICE has refused to release its own totals. The vast majority of people in ICE custody have no criminal conviction; DNA is taken from nearly everyone in immigration custody under a 2020 policy change, then retained indefinitely and made searchable by law enforcement nationwide against unsolved-crime evidence. Georgetown's data show such detainee profiles rose from about 0.2% of the CODIS "Offender" index that police search against crime-scene evidence before the 2020 rule to more than 17% by December 2025, and it projects that at 2025 rates DHS may have added more than one-third of the FBI's criminal DNA database by 2030. **DHS documents describe routine collection as starting at age 14, but CBP records identify 492 children under 14 whose DNA CBP sent to the FBI between January 2025 and January 2026, including thirty-three 7-year-olds, thirty-two 6-year-olds, twenty-one 5-year-olds, and a 4-year-old processed in El Paso on January 7, 2026**. By 2025, federal prosecutors were charging people in immigration custody who refused to provide a DNA sample. WIRED identified two such prosecutions: Hugo Moreno-Mendez, arrested by ICE at a March 13, 2025 probation check-in in Waco, Texas, was found guilty by a magistrate judge on August 18, 2025 and sentenced to time served; Ronald Genao-Diaz, who refused CBP officers at the airport in Carolina, Puerto Rico, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to time served and a fine. A 2021 ICE training presentation had stated the agency was unaware of a single refusal case ever accepted for prosecution. Georgetown and two immigrant-rights groups are also pursuing the records in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit -- Georgetown Law Center on Privacy & Technology, et al. v. CBP, et al., No. 1:25-cv-01732 (D.D.C.), filed June 2, 2025 by the Center on Privacy and Technology, the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, and Americans for Immigrant Justice after ICE and CBP failed to make a determination on the groups' August 1, 2024 FOIA requests for records on DNA collection policy and practice; Georgetown's research draws on ICE training materials and CBP records it has since obtained. At a July 2025 congressional hearing, DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari told Rep. Ayanna Pressley his office had "just got done writing" a report related to the collection of DNA from children; when Georgetown requested it under FOIA, the inspector general's office identified no completed report, no draft and no other records showing it had examined the program. In late March 2025, an attorney in ICE's Office of the Principal Legal Advisor wrote that the "primary purpose" of the government's DNA-collection authority is to build "a national DNA database for solving crimes," not to establish family relationships. During a May 26, 2026 oversight visit to the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, Reps. Joaquin Castro, Greg Stanton, and Nanette Barragán learned that ICE was collecting DNA from detained parents and children; the lawmakers told WIRED officials gave conflicting explanations of why the samples were taken, where they were sent, and how long they would be kept. In a letter made public June 13, 2026, they pressed DHS Secretary Mullin and ICE's leadership for ICE's DNA-collection policies, sharing and retention practices, and any privacy or civil-rights assessments. In July 2026 correspondence, DHS told them ICE may collect DNA from children as young as 14 and confirmed that samples collected under the program are sent to the FBI for entry into CODIS; ICE said it was unaware of any privacy or civil-rights assessment of the practice. DHS has not explained why CBP records show submissions for 492 children under 14. In May 2026, four U.S. citizens arrested at protests outside the Broadview, Illinois ICE facility during Operation Midway Blitz sued, alleging agents took their DNA in violation of the Fourth and First Amendments; two were never charged and the other two had their charges dropped.
legal_status: Sued (records): Georgetown Law Center on Privacy & Technology, et al. v. CBP, et al., No. 1:25-cv-01732 (D.D.C.), a FOIA suit filed June 2, 2025 after ICE and CBP failed to answer the groups' August 2024 requests on DNA collection; the agencies filed their answer to the complaint on August 20, 2025, and as of September 2026 records production is ongoing with periodic status reports. Sued (the program): in Briggs v. Mullin, No. 1:26-cv-05238 (N.D. Ill.), filed May 6, 2026, four U.S. citizens arrested at Broadview, Illinois protests allege DHS's DNA collection violates the Fourth and First Amendments and seek destruction of their samples and expungement of their profiles; the government moved to dismiss on October 5, 2026, with the plaintiffs' opposition due November 10, and no ruling has been reported. George Retes Jr. is separately suing over his detention after a California cannabis-farm raid, during which he says agents took a cheek swab. Charged: in 2025, prosecutors charged at least two people in immigration custody with refusing a DNA sample; Hugo Moreno-Mendez was found guilty by a magistrate judge on August 18, 2025 and sentenced to time served, and Ronald Genao-Diaz pleaded guilty and was sentenced to time served and a fine. No court has ruled DHS's DNA collection unlawful, and in answer to Georgetown's FOIA request the DHS inspector general's office identified no report or draft reviewing it.

human_toll.summary: Nearly everyone held in civil immigration custody, most with no criminal conviction, now has a DNA profile entered into the FBI's criminal DNA database, where police nationwide can search it against crime-scene evidence, while the physical sample is kept in a federal lab indefinitely. ICE swabbed parents and children at the Dilley family detention center, and CBP records show DNA sent to the FBI for 492 children younger than DHS's own age-14 floor, some as young as 4. Flores settlement lawyers say families are confused about why their DNA is taken and often never learn the results, and people who refused a swab have been prosecuted.

human_toll.caveat: The counts come from FBI and CBP records obtained and analyzed by Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology and reported by WIRED, which independently reviewed the CBP records. The ICE-only figure is an estimate: the FBI does not disclose which agency submitted each profile, and ICE has refused to release its own numbers. The 492 under-14 count covers CBP submissions only, so it does not show how many children ICE swabbed at Dilley or elsewhere. DHS defends the collection as a border-security and identification measure, saying CBP takes samples from people arrested on federal charges and from detained noncitizens who are subject to fingerprinting and not otherwise exempt; Congress authorized DNA collection from people detained under federal authority in 2005, and a 2020 Justice Department rule ended DHS's exemption. Asked about children, DHS pointed to a separate DNA program used to verify family relationships, which is distinct from CODIS collection, and it has not explained the 492 CBP submissions. On the protesters' suit, DHS said federal law requires DNA collection from people arrested for federal crimes. Against that, the trigger for most collection is civil immigration custody, not a criminal charge, and an ICE attorney wrote in 2025 that the authority's "primary purpose" is a national database for solving crimes.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the documented figures -- the CODIS detainee index's growth of roughly 995,000 profiles in 2025 to 3,345,692 (FBI records) and the 492 children under 14 in CBP records -- from Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology research, independently reviewed and reported by WIRED; The New Republic and Biometric Update relay the same Georgetown/WIRED findings rather than independently corroborating them. what_changed:
Shortly after 7 a.m. on Monday, July 13, 2026, plainclothes ICE officers tried to stop a white car driven by Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 25, at the corner of Pool and Hill streets in Biddeford, Maine. Business security video of the aftermath shows the car turning in a slow circle in the intersection as officers followed, an SUV bumping it to a stop, and agents pulling the driver out; photos showed four bullet holes in the driver's side of the windshield. **An ICE officer shot and killed Durán Guerrero, who was not the target of the operation.** ICE said agents were "conducting targeted surveillance on the last known address of an illegal alien with a final order of removal" and that "the vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon." Sen. Angus King said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin first told him the driver had "weaponized" the vehicle and was the target, then said hours later he was not the target. The Maine Attorney General's Office opened an investigation, said the officer was with ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations and would be placed on administrative leave, and the FBI responded to the scene. None of the officers wore body cameras, DHS confirmed.

On July 14 ICE directed agents to halt most vehicle stops; border czar Tom Homan called it a "short pause." Within hours of reports of the pause, President Trump posted that ICE "CANNOT give up" the traffic stop, and White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on July 16, "Vehicle stops are continuing." That day his partner spoke publicly, and the family's lawyer said Durán Guerrero was on his way to work and had a work permit; DHS said he "illegally entered the United States" across the southern border in 2023 and was granted a work permit in 2025 (backstory). On July 17 NPR reported that the officer's ex-wife identified him as David Brouillette; ICE would not confirm or deny it. On July 28 investigators from the Maine Attorney General's Office and DHS's inspector general interviewed her, she told the Boston Globe.

At a Democratic congressional hearing in Biddeford on Aug. 17, Rep. Chellie Pingree said ICE's apparent target, Durán Guerrero's housemate and the car's owner, also had no final removal order. DHS stood by its account and said it had never named either man as the target. On Aug. 24 Vice President JD Vance told critics to "have a little bit of perspective"; the family's lawyer said no federal agency had contacted the family and that he is preparing a lawsuit against the federal government. At a Democratic forum in Washington on Sept. 22 another family lawyer said a bullet had pierced the 3-year-old daughter's empty car seat and called for the officer to be prosecuted. As of Oct. 2 the attorney general's office had no public update.
legal_status: Under investigation: the Maine Attorney General's Office is investigating the shooting as a use of deadly force and for any criminal activity, and the DHS Office of Inspector General announced its own investigation. No one has been charged. The FBI responded to the scene, but a DOJ official told CBS it is not conducting a civil-rights review, per the Portland Press Herald. The family's lawyers say they are preparing a civil suit against the federal government; none had been filed as of early October 2026.

human_toll.summary: Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian father on his way to work, was shot and killed while driving; he was not the person ICE was looking for. He left a partner and a 3-year-old daughter, whose car seat was struck by a bullet while she was not in the car, per the family's lawyer.

what_changed: On June 10 and 11, 2026, agents from ICE's Homeland Security Investigations and the HHS Office of Inspector General showed up in person at the Washington, D.C.-area offices of three nonprofit legal aid organizations that represent unaccompanied migrant children -- the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, Kids in Need of Defense (KIND), and Ayuda -- **seeking client files, financial records, and information about the children the organizations serve. The agents presented no warrant, no subpoena, and cited no legal authority for the requests**. Amica said neither agency had previously asked for these records through formal administrative or legal channels. At Ayuda, two agents asked to see billing and invoice information and left after the executive director asked them to put the request in writing; Amica and KIND turned the agents away, and none of the three handed over any records. KIND called it "a coordinated operation targeting federal subcontractors who provide legal services to unaccompanied children." Amica executive director Michael Lukens called the visits "a blatant abuse of power to try to intimidate child advocates," and KIND president Wendy Young said the pattern reflects "an overarching approach which is to harass and intimidate those organizations that are set up to provide services to this very vulnerable population." The June 11 visits came the same day DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced a crackdown on so-called "supersponsors" of unaccompanied children, and at a time when, KIND said, HHS's Office of Refugee Resettlement was withholding back payments for completed legal work until the groups handed over information never requested before. DHS did not confirm the visits, and HHS's inspector general's office said only that it generally doesn't confirm or deny ongoing investigations; no warrant, OIG report or agency statement has explained what specific misconduct, if any, HSI or HHS OIG believed they were investigating.
legal_status: No warrant, subpoena or charge against any of the three organizations or their staff has been reported. HHS's inspector general's office said it generally doesn't confirm or deny the existence of ongoing investigations, so whether any investigation exists is not public. The organizations alleged the visits were intimidation; no lawsuit over the visits has been reported. Separately, legal service providers sued in 2025 after the administration cut funding for legal representation of unaccompanied children, and a judge ordered the funding restored.

human_toll.summary: No one was arrested and no records were handed over. The harm alleged falls on three nonprofits that represent unaccompanied migrant children and on the children themselves: Ayuda's executive director said unannounced visits by federal agents send "a chilling message to immigrant families who may already be afraid to seek help," and KIND's president said the visits could chill legal service providers already financially strained under the administration, including KIND, which says it is owed more than $20 million for completed work.

narrative_override.headline: Noem defended masked ICE agents; the FBI then warned of criminals impersonating them.

what_changed: Since early 2025, ICE agents have routinely worn masks and used unmarked vehicles during immigration enforcement operations nationwide. Kristi Noem, DHS Secretary until March 2026, publicly defended the practice, saying it protects agents' personal safety and their ability to continue investigative work; acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said on Face the Nation that while he is "not a proponent of masks," he would allow them if agents chose them to protect themselves and their families. The Guardian reported June 28, 2025 on a spate of arrests of people accused of impersonating immigration officers, from California to North Carolina, including a North Carolina man accused of posing as an ICE officer to sexually assault a woman -- documenting the impersonation-crime pattern months before the FBI's own October 2025 bulletin, first reported in early November, made it a matter of formal federal warning. Critics -- including New York Attorney General Letitia James, who led a coalition of 20 other attorneys general urging Congress on July 15, 2025 to act, and the Democratic lawmakers who introduced the federal VISIBLE Act in July 2025 to require agents to display identification and limit mask use -- warned the practice made it impossible for the public to distinguish real agents from impersonators. **In October 2025, the FBI issued a bulletin -- an advisory prepared by its Office of Partner Engagement and New York field office, first reported by Wired on November 4 -- warning that criminals were posing as ICE officers to carry out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults across several states, and urging law enforcement to identify themselves and help the public verify agents' identities.** Wired's Nov. 4 report also quoted Noem, at what it called a recent press briefing, saying agents "wear masks at times to protect their identities from dangerous situations," and "we leave that up to them to discern what's necessary." House Homeland Security Committee Democrats then demanded a briefing from DHS and the FBI (letter of Nov. 12-13, 2025), tying the crimes to ICE's masked, unidentified agents; DHS said its agents verbally identify themselves. In September 2025, California enacted SB 627, the 'No Secret Police Act,' banning extreme masking by law enforcement including federal agents statewide, effective January 1, 2026, along with SB 805, the 'No Vigilantes Act,' requiring officers to visibly display identification. The Justice Department sued California over both laws on November 17, 2025. In February 2026 a federal district judge preliminarily enjoined the mask ban as applied to federal officers, finding that it unlawfully discriminated against the federal government, and on April 22, 2026 a Ninth Circuit panel barred California, pending appeal, from enforcing SB 805's requirement that non-uniformed federal officers visibly display identification, finding the administration likely to succeed on its Supremacy Clause claim. Philadelphia's City Council passed a similar ordinance, part of its 'ICE Out' package, on April 23, 2026; adopted May 8 without Mayor Cherelle Parker's signature, it barred law enforcement, including federal agents, from concealing their identity or using unmarked vehicles within the city. Rather than adopting mandatory identification measures in response to the FBI's own warning, the Justice Department sued Philadelphia on June 18, 2026, calling the ordinance unconstitutional; Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said DOJ "will not sit by while Philadelphia flagrantly violates our Constitution." DOJ also sued Virginia, New York and New Jersey over similar laws. In a September 2026 filing in the New Jersey case, DOJ said federal agents "have and will continue to wear masks and refrain from providing identification" in ways the state objects to. On June 30, 2026, a federal judge preliminarily enjoined Virginia's new mask ban hours before it took effect. On July 2, 2026, days before Philadelphia's ordinance was to take effect, Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Chad Kenney preliminarily enjoined it on Supremacy Clause grounds, holding that no state has the power to impede or burden federal agents carrying out federal law. In early August 2026, a federal judge in New York preliminarily enjoined that state's ban on masked federal immigration agents and its identification requirement. On August 24, 2026, DOJ expanded its lawsuit against Philadelphia to challenge a second 'ICE Out' ordinance, one barring city agencies from honoring ICE immigration detainers. On October 14, 2026, the Ninth Circuit panel unanimously held that California's identification law violates the Supremacy Clause as applied to federal officers and ordered the district court to issue a preliminary injunction; California's attorney general's office said it was reviewing the opinion.
legal_status: DOJ sued California (Nov. 17, 2025), Philadelphia (June 18, 2026; complaint amended Aug. 24, 2026), Virginia, New York and New Jersey over state and local laws requiring officers, including federal immigration agents, to unmask or display identification. Courts have preliminarily enjoined California's mask ban (Feb. 2026), Virginia's mask ban (June 30, 2026), Philadelphia's ordinance (July 2, 2026) and New York's mask and identification law (Aug. 2026); the Ninth Circuit enjoined California's identification law pending appeal (April 22, 2026) and on Oct. 14, 2026 ruled it void as applied to federal officers and ordered a preliminary injunction. The New Jersey suit, filed in April 2026, was still pending in mid-September 2026. No court has ruled the masking practice itself unlawful. Separately, several people have been arrested and charged with impersonating immigration officers, per local police and press accounts.

human_toll.summary: People targeted by impostors claiming to be ICE officers -- in the cases the FBI bulletin describes, restaurant workers tied up during a robbery, a woman driven to an apartment complex before she escaped, a woman punched in a stairwell by a man claiming to be an immigration officer, and a woman threatened with deportation if she did not have sex with a man posing as one -- along with immigrants and bystanders who cannot tell a real, masked agent in an unmarked car from a criminal posing as one.

human_toll.caveat: The count is the FBI's own: Wired confirmed four of the five cases in public reporting, and House Democrats said there are "surely many others that have gone unreported," so it is a floor, not a tally; no public figure counts impersonation crimes nationwide. The bulletin ties the crimes to ICE's "enhanced public profile" and does not itself say masking caused them; that link is drawn by House Democrats, state attorneys general and outside experts. DHS says masks and unmarked vehicles protect agents and their families from doxxing and retaliation: Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin cited an "830% increase in assaults" on ICE agents and said officers verbally identify themselves and wear vests marked ICE/ERO or Homeland Security, and DHS said anyone caught impersonating an immigration agent will be prosecuted. In Virginia, a federal judge found evidence that enforcing the state's mask law "would expose federal employees to real risk of physical harm"; in California, a different judge found the presence of masked, unidentifiable law enforcement "more likely to heighten the sense of insecurity for all." DOJ's Supremacy Clause argument holds that states and cities cannot dictate how federal agents perform official duties, whatever the policy's wisdom.

The New Jersey suit (filed April 2026) is sourced to New Jersey Monitor; no ruling had been reported as of its Sept. 16, 2026 report. Whether the masking practice is the direct cause of the impersonation wave, or one contributing factor among others, is a matter of interpretation the FBI's bulletin raises but does not settle, and DHS has not conceded a causal link. The people charged in individual impersonation cases are described rather than named: they are private defendants, not officials or agents, and the entry relies on press accounts, not court filings, for their cases. The sources show one: an October 2025 memo from the FBI's New York field office, first reported by Wired in early November (the Los Angeles Times on Nov. 7 and The Hill on Nov. 13 each describe a single bulletin). House Homeland Security Committee Democrats answered it with a letter dated Nov. 12-13 demanding a briefing from DHS and the FBI. title: ICE Accidentally Exposed a Live Manhunt's Sensitive Data to a Stranger via an Unencrypted Group Text
status: Reported August 2025; no ICE or DHS public response, corrective action, inspector general review or lawsuit about the exposure has been found as of October 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-08-14 (reported by 404 Media; the civilian said they had been added weeks earlier)
what_changed: 404 Media reported that members of a law-enforcement group text called 'Mass Text,' including ICE and other agencies, inadvertently added a random person to the chat, which was being used in an active search for a convicted attempted murderer seemingly marked for deportation. The chat had six members; 404 Media verified one as an ICE official and identified another as likely from the U.S. Marshals Service. The person is not a law-enforcement official or connected to the investigation, and said they had been added weeks earlier and at first thought the messages were spam. **The chat exposed an unredacted ICE 'Field Operations Worksheet' containing detailed information about the target, and showed ICE pulling data from a DMV and automated license-plate readers (LPRs)**. The messages were ordinary MMS texts, not end-to-end encrypted like messages sent over Signal or WhatsApp; 404 Media noted the breach's 'startling similarities' to Signal Gate, in which a senior administration official added The Atlantic's editor-in-chief to a group chat. 404 Media called the episode 'a significant data breach and operational security failure for ICE,' and a DHS official who was not in the chat told it, speaking anonymously, 'This breach strikes me as indicative of the current carelessness of officers.' No agency statement confirming a fix to the group-messaging or access-control practices that allowed the mistaken addition was identified in sourcing reviewed.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence that the incident occurred as described -- 404 Media's reporting is based on screenshots it obtained and verified directly from the mistakenly added person, and the story was repeated without contradiction by The Daily Beast, Techdirt, Alternet, Futurism and others, all relying on 404 Media's reporting rather than their own sourcing. The Marshals Service's role rests on 404 Media's identification of one chat member as likely from that agency. No ICE or DHS on-record response confirming or disputing the account was identified in sourcing reviewed, so this entry reflects the reporting outlet's account rather than an agency-confirmed narrative; the one DHS voice quoted is an anonymous official. Neither the target nor the person added to the chat has been publicly named, and no location has been reported. There is no public figure for how often ICE coordinates operations over unencrypted group texts. Re-verified 2026-10-19: 404 Media's opening and Alternet's and Futurism's write-ups still say what this entry says (the rest of the 404 Media article is paywalled and Techdirt blocked fetching), and no later ICE response, oversight action or lawsuit was found.

pull_quote: “The Court is not aware of another occasion in the history of the United States in which a federal court has had to threaten contempt—again and again and again—to force the United States government to comply with court orders.” — Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz, February 26, 2026

glance.what: ICE violated 210 court orders in 143 Minnesota habeas cases in early 2026, a chief judge's review found

what_changed:
During Operation Metro Surge, the immigration enforcement operation that ran from December 2025 until February 12, 2026, federal judges in Minnesota were flooded with habeas corpus petitions from people challenging their detention: Patrick Schiltz, then Chief Judge of the District of Minnesota, later told FOX 9 the court had 12 such cases in all of 2024, 130 in 2025 and 1,111 in the first three months of 2026. Judges repeatedly ordered detainees released or given bond hearings, and ICE repeatedly failed to comply.

In one case, Schiltz on January 14, 2026 ordered ICE to give a detained man a bond hearing within seven days or release him; neither happened. On January 26 he ordered Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons to appear in person and show cause why he should not be held in contempt, writing that this was "one of dozens of court orders with which respondents have failed to comply in recent weeks" and that the practical consequence had almost always been significant hardship: **a detention was extended, a person who should have stayed in Minnesota was flown to Texas, or a person flown to Texas was released there and told to figure out a way to get home.** ICE released the man, and on January 28 Schiltz canceled the hearing but attached an appendix identifying 96 court orders issued since January 1 that ICE had violated in 74 cases, warning that the list was hurriedly compiled and that "ICE has likely violated more court orders in January 2026 than some federal agencies have violated in their entire existence."

In a February 9 email to Schiltz, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen accused the court of wildly overstating ICE's noncompliance, based on a review of the first 12 listed cases. Days later, U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino held a Justice Department attorney in civil contempt, with $500 daily fines, after the government released Rigoberto Soto Jimenez in Texas without his identification documents despite her order to release him in Minnesota with his property; the government quickly returned the documents, and two days later she lifted the contempt finding without imposing any fines. The Justice Department appealed the contempt order to the Eighth Circuit, which declined to dismiss the appeal. The judges rechecked every case on Schiltz's list, and in a February 26 supplemental order Schiltz found that ICE had violated 97 orders in 66 of the originally listed cases, plus 113 more orders in 77 additional cases, most of them violated after January 28: 210 violated orders in 143 cases in all. He wrote that the administration had sent 3,000 ICE agents to Minnesota "to detain people without making any provision for handling the hundreds of lawsuits that were sure to follow," and that the court was "not aware of another occasion in the history of the United States in which a federal court has had to threaten contempt -- again and again and again -- to force the United States government to comply with court orders," and that it would move to criminal contempt if necessary: "One way or another, ICE will comply with this Court's orders." The same day, Judge Jeffrey Bryan ordered Rosen and an ICE representative to a contempt hearing over property not returned to released detainees; at that March 3 hearing Bryan said he had not "ruled out the consequence of imprisonment," then took the matter under advisement without acting.

In a September 2026 interview with The New York Times, Schiltz, by then a senior judge after stepping down as chief judge in June, said the government's conduct during the surge had created "a grave threat to the rule of law," while saying most of the failures appeared to be due to incompetence rather than conscious defiance. The Times put ICE's violations at nearly 100 orders, the size of the January tally; the 210 figure is the February total. A Justice Department spokesperson said the administration "will continue to fully comply with court orders" and had generally satisfied the substance of the orders, and a DHS spokesperson said the department operates in line with the Constitution and federal law.
legal_status: Federal judges in the District of Minnesota found, in Chief Judge Schiltz's January 28 and February 26, 2026 orders, that ICE violated 210 court orders in 143 habeas cases; DOJ disputes the characterization. Judge Provinzino held a DOJ attorney in civil contempt in February 2026; she lifted it two days later after the documents were returned, with no fines imposed. DOJ's appeal is pending in the Eighth Circuit, which declined to dismiss it in April; oral argument is set for October 21, 2026. Judge Bryan's March 3, 2026 contempt hearing on unreturned property ended under advisement, with no ruling found. No ICE official has been held in contempt. DOJ's September 30, 2026 misconduct complaint against Schiltz and other Minnesota judges is pending before the Eighth Circuit's chief judge.

human_toll.summary: People detained during Operation Metro Surge who won release or bond-hearing orders were held past court deadlines, flown to Texas when they should have stayed in Minnesota, or released in Texas and told to find their own way home; others were released without their identification documents, phones, cash or passports. The district's immigration habeas caseload went from 12 cases in all of 2024 to 1,111 in the first three months of 2026.
