glance.what: ICE cut training and vetting in a hiring surge and limited oversight visits as officers shot two men (2025-26)

what_changed:
**An Associated Press review found at least two dozen ICE employees and contractors have been charged with crimes since 2020, involving patterns of physical and sexual abuse, corruption, and other misuse of authority.** Specific documented cases include a former top official at a Texas ICE contract facility sentenced to probation in February 2026 after admitting he grabbed a handcuffed detainee by the neck and slammed him into a wall; an ICE contractor who pleaded guilty in December 2025 to sexually abusing a detainee over a five-month period at a Louisiana facility; and two Minnesota ICE employees who faced federal sexual-misconduct charges involving underage girls, including an ICE investigator who pleaded guilty to sending images and videos of himself having sex with a 17-year-old. While AP found most documented cases predated Congress's recent $75 billion appropriation to expand ICE hiring and detention capacity, the review reports that legal experts warn such misconduct could accelerate given the volume of new hires and their empowerment to use aggressive tactics. The Trump administration has argued ICE agents have 'absolute immunity' for on-duty actions and has weakened independent oversight mechanisms.

Concrete evidence of the hiring-surge vetting risk legal experts warned about was already documented as early as October 22, 2025 -- NBC News reporting, citing a current and two former DHS officials and former ICE Baltimore field office director Darius Reeves, found ICE had shortened academy training from 13 weeks to eight, and later to six, waived age limits, and sent recruits to training before completing standard background checks, fingerprinting, and drug testing, in pursuit of the administration's target of expanding ICE to 10,000 agents by year's end. Since the hiring surge began in summer 2025, ICE dismissed over 200 recruits during training -- most for failing physical-fitness or written exams (nearly half of recent arrivals failed the written exam) -- but fewer than 10 were dismissed specifically after training staff discovered pending criminal charges, failed drug tests, or safety concerns, including one recruit charged with strong-arm robbery and domestic-violence-related battery. A current DHS official told NBC News: 'There is absolutely concern that some people are slipping through the cracks.' DHS told NBC the figures were 'not accurate' and said most new hires were experienced law enforcement officers.

A direct, concrete instance of the administration weakening independent oversight mechanisms: in December 2025, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb blocked DHS Secretary Noem's policy requiring members of Congress to give seven days' advance notice before inspecting ICE facilities, finding it likely violated a 2019 appropriations law permitting unannounced congressional inspections. After an ICE officer fatally shot a U.S. citizen in Minneapolis, Noem issued a new memorandum on January 8, 2026 reinstating the same notice requirement; on January 10, 2026, Reps. Ilhan Omar, Angie Craig and Kelly Morrison were denied an oversight visit to ICE detainees at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building at Fort Snelling. Noem's stated justification was that the facility was funded through the 'One Big Beautiful Bill' Act rather than DHS's own appropriations bill, exempting it from the law Judge Cobb had cited. The twelve House Democrats who had brought the original July 2025 suit (Reps. Neguse, Espaillat, Raskin, Garcia, Correa, Crow, Escobar, Goldman, Gomez, Ruiz, Thompson, and Torres) sought emergency relief; on January 19, 2026, Judge Cobb denied that request on procedural grounds, writing 'the court emphasizes that it denies plaintiffs' motion only because it is not the proper avenue to challenge defendants' January 8, 2026, memorandum and the policy stated therein, rather than based on any kind of finding that the policy is lawful.' After the lawmakers amended their complaint, Cobb temporarily blocked the January 8 policy on February 2, 2026, and on March 2, 2026 stayed it for the rest of the case, finding significant evidence it had been issued and enforced with the annually appropriated funds the law restricts. The administration appealed; on May 8, 2026, a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel unanimously refused to pause Cobb's ruling during the appeal, saying only that the administration had not met the stringent requirements for a stay; Judge Neomi Rao, concurring, wrote that the record did not show unannounced visits caused harms beyond administrative inconvenience, but that the administration was very likely to win its appeal because the lawmakers lack standing. The appeal itself remained pending, with the main briefs filed in June and July 2026. Limits on access continued in practice: on September 10, 2026, Rep. Escobar, one of the suit's plaintiffs, made an oversight visit to Camp East Montana, the ICE tent camp at Fort Bliss in El Paso that can hold up to 5,000 people and is the country's largest immigration detention facility, after DHS reported two detainee disturbances there on September 1 and 7. She told the Guardian she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants, and that she had requested surveillance footage of the incidents but had not received it. A DHS spokesperson disputed her account, saying 'any member of Congress can still request to speak with any illegal alien in ICE custody' and that ICE will facilitate a meeting if both sides agree, and denied that there had been an official request for data and footage; lawmakers have said ICE limits such visits by requiring them to submit, in advance, the names and personal information of detainees they want to speak with. At least three people detained at the camp have died in ICE custody, including a 55-year-old man whose January 2026 death was ruled a homicide after security guards beat him, according to the Guardian.

Subsequent reporting has substantiated the accelerating-risk mechanism experts warned about: internal ICE academy syllabi obtained by CBS News showed the deportation-officer academy course cut from 72 days (July 2025) to 42 days (February 2026); a CNN analysis found deportation officers, previously required to complete about 20 weeks (roughly 100 days) of training, now get less academy training than almost any other federal law enforcement role; and former ICE instructor Ryan Schwank told a forum held by congressional Democrats that 240 hours of a 584-hour program had been cut, including firearms and constitutional-law classes, which DHS denied. An internal ICE email reviewed by Reuters warned that the 'high volume of new hires' and stalled background checks could create uncertainty when misconduct allegations arise, and a former official told Reuters background checks were not being completed before recruits reached the academy, with two recruits flagged as suspected MS-13 members and at least five trainees fired over active arrest warrants; DHS denied any vetting problem. Separately, on February 25, 2026, a Cameron County, Texas, grand jury declined to indict the HSI agent who fatally shot U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez in March 2025 -- identified as HSI Special Agent Jack Stevens in a South Padre Island police report obtained by Newsweek and in state records released to KSAT -- amid disputed DHS claims and conflicting agency statements, prompting a formal House Oversight Democrats investigation demand -- a fatal shooting that has produced no criminal charge. In May 2026, two DHS officials said ICE would scrap the 42-day course and return to 72 days of academy instruction for classes starting July 1, 2026 (The Washington Post, republished by the Boston Globe); DHS's statement to the Post did not confirm the change, but a spokesperson confirmed to NOTUS the same day that ICE would end the shortened course, which NOTUS reported would return to 72 days; in June 2026 an internal ICE memo, which DHS confirmed, extended the core course from 42 days to roughly 71 days starting in July and required officers trained under the 42-day course to take an additional follow-on program (CBS News). That is still shorter than the roughly five-month (about 20-21-week) total training deportation officers previously received, which included about five weeks of Spanish-language instruction cut in 2025 (PolitiFact, citing ICE's careers page and AP; CNN: '20 weeks, or roughly 100 days'); no source reviewed says the Spanish-language portion was restored. Beyond these training changes, a Sept. 30, 2026 ICE memo banned vehicle chases and required body cameras at vehicle stops (AP); no broader vetting reform has been identified.

Newsweek's report on House Oversight Democrats' March 2026 letter demanding a DHS Inspector General probe into Martinez's death and the concealment of its circumstances situates the case within a broader count: 23 people shot by DHS personnel over the preceding 14 months, with Martinez one of three U.S. citizen fatalities in that period -- the other two, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both in Minneapolis in January 2026, are documented in TAP's separate entries rather than this one. That broader count is cited here as scale context, not as evidence that the same weakened-oversight mechanism documented above caused all three deaths; no source ties Good's or Pretti's cases to this entry's specific claims about ICE training cuts, vetting failures, or the Martinez grand jury outcome. No further public accountability finding, and no update to the House Oversight investigation's status, has been identified. Joshua Orta, a passenger-witness who disputed DHS's account of the Martinez shooting -- saying the vehicle was moving slowly and agents fired without warning -- died in a car accident on February 21, 2026, hours after a friend texted him a news story reporting that ICE was responsible for Martinez's death -- news his family believes may have contributed to the crash (Texas Tribune, May 4, 2026). Noted here as context on the case's human toll, not as further evidence of misconduct or oversight-weakening in itself.

A second named-victim shooting occurred September 20, 2026, when an ICE officer shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, a Venezuelan man working as a DoorDash driver in Austin. His lawyer says he entered the U.S. in 2024 through the CBP One app to seek asylum and received a removal order after missing a hearing whose notice went to the wrong address; a senior administration official told NBC News he had no criminal history beyond being in the country illegally, and DHS said he had a final order of removal and that the shooting followed a 'dangerous attempt to evade arrest.' Garcés Pérez says an officer refused his request to pull over and be detained, and that an ICE SUV then struck his car before he was shot. The officer, a recent hire who had previously worked for another federal law enforcement agency and completed ICE training in August 2025, was not wearing a body camera, CNN reported, citing sources. Garcés Pérez was taken from the hospital to an ICE detention center in Pearsall with a bullet lodged near his spine; a federal judge ordered him to appear at a Sept. 30 hearing in San Antonio on his petition against deportation, which his attorney said bars his removal in the meantime. Federal prosecutors then charged him with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, alleging he struck an officer with his side mirror while fleeing the initial stop; the defense called the charge retaliation. On September 30, U.S. Magistrate Judge Dustin Howell found probable cause and denied bond as a flight risk, keeping him in federal custody (AP; WOAI). The day before, the judge in the deportation case had vacated the Sept. 30 hearing and paused that case until his criminal detention is resolved; on Oct. 1 his lawyers voluntarily dismissed the petition (federal court docket). His attorney said the bullet was removed in surgery on Oct. 1 (Telemundo). The ICE officer who did wear a body camera, driving a separate car, turned it off during the pursuit (AP). The shooting drew protests in Austin. Separately, a GAO report publicly released October 14, 2026 found that most ICE and CBP offices had not developed specific operational guidance on how personnel should use body-worn cameras; DHS agreed with six of GAO's seven recommendations but did not agree to implement controls that would automatically activate ICE officers' cameras (see the separate entry on DHS's body-camera rollout).
legal_status: Neguse v. ICE: twelve House Democrats sued over DHS's seven-day notice rule for congressional visits; the district court stayed the January 8, 2026 policy on March 2, 2026, and the D.C. Circuit denied DHS a stay pending appeal on May 8, 2026; the appeal is pending. A Cameron County, Texas, grand jury declined to indict the HSI agent who shot Ruben Ray Martinez; House Oversight Democrats asked the DHS Inspector General to investigate, with no result public. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez is charged with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, which his defense calls retaliation; a magistrate judge found probable cause and denied bond; a federal judge in San Antonio vacated the Sept. 30 hearing on his habeas petition against deportation and paused the case until his criminal detention is resolved, and his lawyers voluntarily dismissed the petition on Oct. 1. No charge against the officer who shot him has been reported. The AP-reviewed misconduct cases were individually charged; some ended in guilty pleas or sentences.

human_toll.summary: Detainees and others abused by ICE employees and contractors charged with crimes since 2020, including physical and sexual abuse of people in custody; a U.S. citizen, Ruben Ray Martinez, killed by an HSI agent with no charge filed; an asylum seeker, Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, shot, with a bullet lodged near his spine until surgery 11 days later, then jailed on an assault charge; and detainees whose conditions members of Congress were limited in inspecting.

what_changed: Backstory: at his March 18, 2026 confirmation hearing, DHS Secretary nominee Markwayne Mullin told senators, "We will not enter a home or a place of business without a judicial warrant, unless we're pursuing the individual that runs into a place of business or a house." On Friday, August 14, 2026, armed ICE officers came to the Sacramento office of Morris Law Group, an immigration law firm, according to the firm. Its head, attorney Raissa Morris, told KCRA 3 that the officers arrived in unmarked cars, some without license plates, and said they had "a list from Washington, D.C." showing her office as her clients' mailing address. **Staff told them they could not come through without a search warrant; the officers said they wanted to "walk through and make sure you guys don't have any beds for clients we're looking for."** Morris said one officer threatened to come back: "I don't want to come back at 3 a.m. and break in and look for these people if we want to." The officers left without searching the office; one had come into the front lobby, according to the firm and The Sacramento Bee. Morris, who was not present, said her staff called her during the visit. In a statement reported by KCRA 3 on August 17, DHS said officers "approached an unmarked door during a targeted enforcement operation," thinking it was the address of people they planned to arrest, and "upon finding out it was a law firm; they departed." Sen. Adam Schiff called the conduct "unacceptable" on X, per News247Plus, and in a written statement reported by The Sacramento Bee said "ICE agents chose to threaten violence against a law firm because of whom they represent." On August 27 Schiff and Sen. Alex Padilla wrote to Mullin and David Venturella, the senior official performing the duties of ICE director, asking for an investigation of the officer's conduct and the alleged threat, and for answers by September 11 on the purpose of the operation, why no judicial warrant was obtained, where the "list" came from and how law firms are chosen as targets. The senators called DHS's statement "troubling and unsatisfactory," noting that a Google search identifies the address as a law firm and that "Morris Law Group" is written on the front of the building next to the building number. ICE told California Assemblymember Maggy Krell on September 2 that her records request about the visit was "not sufficiently specific" and, after she narrowed it, "administratively closed" it, her lawsuit alleges; on September 22 she sued DHS and ICE under the Freedom of Information Act in federal court (Eastern District of California). Padilla's office said DHS had not responded to the senators' letter.
legal_status: Krell v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, No. 2:26-cv-03349 (E.D. Cal.): a Freedom of Information Act suit filed Sept 22, 2026 by Assemblymember Maggy Krell seeking ICE's records on the Aug 14 operation; the docket shows only the complaint and summons. No charges or formal investigation found. Sens. Schiff and Padilla asked DHS and ICE to investigate the alleged threat and the attempted warrantless entry; no reply or opened investigation has been made public. The threat and the officers' statements are alleged by the firm and have not been tested by any court or agency.

human_toll.summary: No one was arrested or hurt, and the officers did not get past the lobby. The firm's staff faced armed officers in their lobby and, by the firm's account, a threat of a 3 a.m. break-in. The firm says the visit was meant to scare immigration lawyers away from taking cases, and a neighbor said watching it made her afraid.

The client figure comes from news reports (News247Plus; Hoodline, citing The Sacramento Bee), not from a firm document. DHS says this was a targeted enforcement operation, that the officers went to an unmarked door they believed was the address of people they planned to arrest, and that they left once they learned it was a law firm. DHS has not publicly addressed the alleged threat or the request to search for beds.

The threat to return and break in, the "list from Washington, D.C." and the request to tour the office for beds rest on the firm's account alone and are alleged. what_changed: ICE agents attempted to pull over a van on Shanley Avenue in Newark, New Jersey on the morning of February 25, 2026; when the driver fled, agents pursued, and the chase ended in a multi-vehicle crash near Clinton Avenue, on roads still being cleared after a major snowstorm. **Three children -- two 15-year-olds and a 12-year-old, siblings riding to school in a rideshare car -- were taken to University Hospital after complaining of pain; the fleeing driver was also injured and hospitalized.** DHS said the crash happened during a "targeted operation" to arrest Christian Oswaldo Guevara-Guerra, whom it said had been charged with receiving stolen property and ordered removed in 2017, and that he rammed federal vehicles and struck civilian cars before being taken into ICE custody; Newark's public safety director likewise said the fleeing driver struck the rideshare car. Newark police were not involved in the pursuit and responded only to the resulting crash. Newark Mayor Ras Baraka said ICE should "adhere to local laws regarding vehicle pursuits," noting that state law bars chases unless the suspect poses an imminent threat, called the pursuit "illegal," and said the city would ask the governor and attorney general to act. Baraka also signed an executive order barring immigration enforcement operations in Newark city buildings without a judicial warrant and directing city employees to report suspected unauthorized federal enforcement activity.

Mayor Baraka alleged the pursuit was "illegal" under New Jersey's limits on police chases and said the city would use the police report to "ask the governor and attorney general to take action"; no source reviewed confirms the New Jersey Attorney General opened an investigation. pull_quote: July 2026 was the first month of the second Trump administration in which people with only civil immigration violations -- rather than pending criminal charges or convictions -- made up more than half of those arrested by ICE, CBS News reported.

glance.who: DHS under Kristi Noem and Markwayne Mullin
glance.what: Billed ICE as targeting 'criminal aliens' while its own data showed most detainees had no serious record

harm.who: People detained with no criminal record

what_changed: Beginning within Trump's first two weeks back in office, reporting repeatedly found that ICE's actual enforcement and detention activity did not match the administration's public framing that enforcement prioritized 'criminal aliens' and 'the worst of the worst.' On January 31, 2025, HuffPost compiled early reporting showing the gap: NBC News, citing an unnamed government source, reported that 48% of the 1,179 people immigration agents arrested on the first Sunday after the inauguration had no criminal history apart from possible unauthorized border crossing; Colombian officials said none of the 200 people deported to Colombia on two flights were criminals, and the Washington Post reported that those flights carried more than 20 children and two pregnant women. HuffPost tied the pattern to Trump's reversal of the prior, narrower enforcement priorities and to a quota of 75 arrests per day for ICE field offices. **On June 16, 2025, CNN reported that internal ICE data it had obtained showed fewer than 1 in 10 of the roughly 185,000 immigrants booked into ICE custody from October 2024 through May 2025 had been convicted of serious crimes like murder, assault, robbery or rape, with more than 75% having no criminal conviction other than an immigration or traffic-related offense.** That period covers the last months of the Biden administration and the first months of Trump's. The week before, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem had said on Fox News, "In L.A., what we have been going after is the worst of the worst," and DHS Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin told CNN that ICE targets "the worst of the worst--including gang members, murderers, and rapists." On June 30, 2025, a CBS News analysis of ICE data released to the Deportation Data Project found that after White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller announced a target of 3,000 arrests a day in late May, new ICE detentions of people facing only civil immigration charges rose more than 250% from the first week of May to the first week of June, and that only about 8% of everyone detained since January 20 had a violent-crime conviction. This pattern predates and is distinct from a separate entry documenting a specific December 2025 DHS 'worst of the worst' public website found to contain factual errors overstating individual arrestees' offense severity. The pattern continued into FY2026. In November 2025 the Cato Institute reported that leaked nonpublic ICE data showed nearly three in four (73%) people booked into ICE custody so far that fiscal year had no criminal conviction, nearly half had neither convictions nor pending charges, and only 5% had a violent one. In January 2026, immigration researcher Austin Kocher's analysis of ICE's published detention statistics found that people without criminal convictions accounted for 92% of the 11,296-person growth in the ICE-arrested detained population between September 21, 2025 and January 7, 2026: 72% had no criminal charges or convictions and 20% had at most pending charges, while 8% had convictions. Kristi Noem, who publicly defended the 'criminal aliens' framing throughout 2025, was fired as DHS Secretary in March 2026. The Senate confirmed Markwayne Mullin as her successor 54-45 on March 23, 2026, and he was sworn in the next day. The pattern continued and deepened into July 2026: CBS News reported that July was the first month of the second Trump administration in which people with only civil immigration violations -- no criminal convictions or pending charges -- made up more than half of ICE arrestees, and that people with violent-crime convictions made up about 4% of those taken into custody that month. The Associated Press, in a report carried by PBS NewsHour, counted a monthly arrest total of 49,571, the highest of the second Trump administration, up 15% from June and up 70% from February 2026 (DHS's own September 2, 2026 release later put July at 50,208 and August at 50,925, under a "WORST OF THE WORST" heading listing individual arrests). In August 2026, at a conference of state governors, Mullin used the same framing while urging more local cooperation with ICE: "let's work to get the worst of the worst off the streets and then you won't see me in your cities and states like you do as much," CBS News reported.
legal_status: None tied to this pattern: no lawsuit, court ruling or inspector general finding addresses the gap between DHS's "worst of the worst" framing and its own arrest and detention data. Republican members of Congress asked ICE in a 2025 letter to say how many convicted criminals it had deported.

human_toll.summary: Most of the people ICE arrested and held since January 2025 had no serious criminal record. Many had no conviction at all beyond an immigration or traffic offense, and the share rose as arrest targets climbed: by July 2026 people with only civil immigration violations were more than half of ICE arrests, at a record of more than 800 people without criminal records arrested a day.

DHS says unlawful presence alone makes someone a target: "ICE enforces the law as written. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S.-- full stop," a spokesperson told CBS News in 2026, adding that many people counted as non-criminals "are actually terrorists, human rights abusers, gangsters and more; they just don't have a rap sheet in the U.S." In 2025 McLaughlin said 75% of ICE arrests in Trump's first 100 days were of people with convictions or pending charges, and border czar Tom Homan called arrests of people found alongside targets "collateral arrests." The point at issue is the specific public framing of enforcement as aimed at 'the worst of the worst,' which implies convictions for serious crimes; the pattern held, by a wider margin, through FY2026 and July 2026. The July 2026 no-conviction-majority finding and the 49,571 monthly arrest figure are confirmed against the published text of CBS News and of the Associated Press report carried by PBS NewsHour. what_changed: A little after 7 a.m. on Saturday, October 10, 2026, ICE officers tried to stop a white pickup truck near Clay Road and Texas 6 in northwest Harris County, outside Houston. Two men got out and ran in different directions. Surveillance footage from a nearby business, described by the Houston Chronicle and AP, shows an unmarked Jeep Cherokee jumping a median, entering a parking lot and driving toward one of them, **Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican construction worker who has lived in the Houston area for 34 years**; another truck blocks the view of the collision, and he is then seen on the ground. The ICE officer who drove called 911 for an ambulance, the Harris County Sheriff's Office said. Parra Hernandez's leg was broken in three places, according to FIEL Houston; he was taken to a Katy-area hospital and placed in ICE custody there. In a statement the same day, ICE said its officers had been trying to arrest a different man, a Mexican national it said had a criminal record and a final removal order, and that Parra Hernandez "ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck." Two people already detained during an unrelated enforcement operation were inside the ICE vehicle at the time, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare later said. Between October 13 and 15, Teare said the footage shows the vehicle "jumped a median, drove into a parking lot and drove directly at and then over Mr. Parra," that his office is weighing charges including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, and that ICE and DHS have not cooperated. He said agents declined to let investigators examine the vehicle and drove it away before a search warrant could be obtained, which he said may have erased its crash data, calling it intentional or grossly negligent destruction of evidence. ICE called the allegations that the strike was intentional "reckless" and "false" but did not address the evidence claims, Texas Scorecard and NBC News reported. On October 13 a senior DHS official told NBC News that several officers at the scene wore body cameras and that ICE was reviewing the video in an internal investigation; on October 15 the official said the officer who drove had been placed on administrative leave and that no decision had been made on sharing the video with the DA. That day Teare said his office had interviewed one of the detainees from the ICE vehicle at the Port Isabel detention center near the border, after ICE told his office it planned to deport the man, and that the case could go to a grand jury as soon as the following week. On October 15 and 16, FIEL and the family said the man pictured in ICE's wanted bulletin for its target is a different man who died in 2017 while fleeing immigration agents near the border; his daughter gave FIEL his Mexican death certificate, which was passed to the DA, and the New York Times reported that the dead man had used aliases, including the name DHS gave, and had the same charges ICE listed. A DA spokesperson told AP that ICE's named target was not in the truck. Rep. Sylvia Garcia said pursuing a man who died years ago "raises serious questions" about whether agents verify whom they are seeking. One of the detained men who were in the ICE vehicle, a potential witness, was still being held in federal custody as of October 16, according to his sister and the family's lawyer, who said he suffered soft-tissue injuries when he was thrown around the back of the vehicle, handcuffed and unbelted, during the pursuit. As of October 19, Parra Hernandez had been moved to another hospital for rehabilitation after several surgeries and remained in ICE custody under guard, Univision reported.
legal_status: Under investigation by the Harris County District Attorney's Office; Teare says "the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon" and said on October 15 that the case could go to a grand jury as soon as the following week; no charges announced. His office has interviewed Parra Hernandez and one of the two detainees who were in the ICE vehicle, and has subpoenaed his medical and emergency-medical records, per NBC News. Teare has alleged that ICE destroyed potential evidence by driving the vehicle away; ICE's statement did not address that allegation, per Texas Scorecard, and ICE did not answer NBC's questions about it. A senior DHS official told NBC News that ICE is reviewing body-camera video in an internal investigation and has placed the driving officer on administrative leave; a federal investigation is active, per Univision. No lawsuit identified.

human_toll.summary: Miguel Parra Hernandez, a construction worker ICE says was not the person it was trying to arrest, suffered a leg broken in three places plus hip and ankle injuries, has had surgery and faces more, and has been held in ICE custody in the hospital under round-the-clock guard. His family and lawyer say he is depressed. A detained man who was handcuffed in the ICE vehicle suffered soft-tissue injuries during the pursuit, his lawyer says, and is still held.

title: ICE Kept No Miscarriage Count After Oct. 3, 2025, as It Detained More Pregnant Women
status: Unresolved: DHS confirmed to The Guardian it has no ICE miscarriage data for October 2025 through June 2026, then told other outlets ICE tracks miscarriages monthly. The 2021 directive limiting detention of pregnant people remains formally in place.
date_of_action: 2025-10-03 to 2026-06 (miscarriage records end Oct. 3, 2025; DHS confirmed no data through June 2026; reported Sept. 15, 2026)
what_changed:
Records that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released to The Guardian, after the outlet sued under the Freedom of Information Act together with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, show that **at least 18 women miscarried in ICE custody from January through September 2025**, a count experts told The Guardian is very likely an undercount, but ICE provided no miscarriage data after Oct. 3, 2025. In internal documents, ICE attributed the gap to a change in its medical accounting system: it ended its arrangement with the Veterans Affairs Financial Services Center, which had handled ICE's medical billing, and Acentra Health, a private Virginia-based company, was contracted to replace it starting in October 2025. ICE's medical claims processing has since been delayed for months; Acentra did not say whether it tracks miscarriages for ICE and pointed to government shutdowns for the delays. Immigration attorneys and former DHS officials told The Guardian it was odd that ICE tracked miscarriages only through its billing provider. Asked about the gap, a DHS spokesperson first told The Guardian the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports, then confirmed it has no miscarriage data from October 2025 through June 2026; The Guardian reported that DHS had never before acknowledged the gap, including when senators asked for the data. After The Guardian's Sept. 15, 2026 report, DHS spokespeople told Reason and NPR's Here & Now that ICE tracks and reports miscarriage data monthly under ICE Directive 11032.4; the statement to Here & Now called the report "FALSE."

The same records, which run from October 2024 through mid-January 2026, show ICE holding more pregnant people in detention in fall and winter 2025 than at any time over the previous year: at least 87 pregnant women and adolescents in October 2025 and 101 in November. Directive 11032.4, issued in 2021 and still in place according to DHS, says ICE should not detain pregnant, postpartum or nursing people for civil immigration violations unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist, and requires ICE to monitor the health of any it does detain. In more than a dozen cases The Guardian reviewed, attorneys said ICE gave no clear explanation of how those criteria were met. In a September 2025 letter to then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, 29 Democratic senators wrote that ICE had stopped the semiannual reports to Congress on pregnant, postpartum and nursing women in detention that it had provided until that year, and asked DHS to resume them. DHS's delayed response, signed by Noem on Feb. 23, 2026 and released by Sen. Patty Murray on March 18, 2026, reported 121 pregnant, postpartum and nursing women in detention as of Feb. 16, 2026, 363 removals of pregnant, postpartum or nursing women between Jan. 1, 2025 and Feb. 16, 2026, and 16 miscarriages from Jan. 1 through Sept. 23, 2025, the date DHS received the letter.

Women interviewed by The Guardian, and testimonies shared by their attorneys, describe difficulty getting routine and emergency care. **One woman said she began bleeding heavily about a month after her arrest, was taken to an emergency room a day after her urgent written request for care, and was told there, shackled to a hospital bed, that she was no longer pregnant; she said the detention center has offered no follow-up care despite the ER doctor's instruction.** Another, held at the Dilley facility in Texas in a high-risk pregnancy, stated in a legal declaration that the facility had not approved or scheduled the specialist consultation its own physician said she needed. Deborah Ottenheimer, an obstetrician-gynecologist with Physicians for Human Rights, told The Guardian that detained women "are not getting the prenatal visits that they're supposed to get" and that the care they receive after a miscarriage is "minimal to none." DHS says pregnant detainees receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support and "accommodations aligned with community standards of care," and told MS NOW and NPR's Here & Now that pregnancy in ICE detention is "exceedingly rare," which it put at 0.15% of people in custody as of June 30 in its statement to Here & Now.
confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence. The miscarriage count, the Oct. 3, 2025 cutoff, the monthly pregnant-detainee counts and the billing-contract explanation come from ICE's own records and internal documents, obtained through a FOIA lawsuit and reported by The Guardian (read in full); a DHS spokesperson confirmed the October 2025-June 2026 gap to The Guardian, but DHS later denied the gap to Reason and called the report false to NPR's Here & Now. Frame the gap as ICE's documented admission, contested by DHS's later statements. The 121, 363 and 16 figures are DHS's own numbers, from its Feb. 23, 2026 response released by Sen. Murray's office; the end of semiannual reporting to Congress is the senators' statement in their September 2025 letter. Individual women's accounts are their own statements and attorney filings, not independently verified. MS NOW and Reason relayed The Guardian's findings and are not independent confirmation of the data. No source reviewed names the official who ended ICE's billing arrangement with the VA Financial Services Center or decided how miscarriages would be tracked afterward, so no official is listed; DHS's response to the senators was signed by Secretary Kristi Noem. The women whose accounts appear here are not named in this entry. Re-verified 2026-10-18: Sen. Murray's release, DHS's enclosure and signed cover letter, the senators' letter, Reason, MS NOW, NPR's Here & Now and The Guardian (read via browser; it blocks direct fetches) still say what this entry says; no later ruling, report or DHS data release found.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The missing miscarriage count is one of several losses of visibility into conditions in ICE detention that this database tracks. what_changed:
Backstory: Jonathan Ross, an ICE deportation officer in the Twin Cities area, had testified at an earlier federal trial that he was a firearms instructor and Special Response Team member who had made hundreds of vehicle stops, and that a driver fleeing an arrest had dragged him with a car.

**On the morning of January 7, 2026, during DHS's Operation Metro Surge, Ross shot and killed Renee Nicole Macklin Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother of three, in her SUV on a residential street in south Minneapolis.** Good's SUV had been stopped for a few minutes across the street, obstructing traffic, while her partner, Becca Good, stood outside filming the agents, CNN reported. Ross filmed on his own phone as he walked around the car; Good told him, "That's fine, dude. I'm not mad at you." After another officer told her to "get out of the f**king car," Good reversed, turned the wheel to the right and moved forward; Ross cried out "whoa" and fired three shots, first into the windshield and then at close range through the open driver's window. Bystander video shows Ross was standing out of the vehicle's path when he opened fire, CNN reported, and video analyses by The New York Times and The Washington Post found Good appeared to be turning away from him. Agents turned away a bystander who said he was a physician and asked to check her pulse. Efforts to revive Good stopped at around 10:30 a.m., about an hour after she was shot.

About two hours after the shooting, DHS called it an "act of domestic terrorism," saying the officer "fired defensive shots" at a vehicle trying to "run over" agents. Secretary Kristi Noem accused Good of "[weaponizing] her vehicle," and President Trump said she "violently, willfully, and viciously ran over" the agent. Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey called the self-defense account "bullshit." That same afternoon, according to Minnesota's Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA), the FBI and the BCA had agreed to a joint investigation, but the FBI then told the BCA the case would "be led solely by the FBI" and that it would lose access to "case materials, scene evidence or investigative interviews"; the state later alleged that HSI agents kept BCA investigators out of interviews with the officers at the scene. BCA Superintendent Drew Evans's texts to an FBI official asking for access went unanswered for at least two days, records obtained by WIRED show. A few hours after the shooting, Border Patrol agents, with commander Greg Bovino on scene, clashed with teachers and residents outside Roosevelt High School, less than 3 miles away, after a car chase; DHS said a teacher assaulted an agent, and Minneapolis Public Schools closed all schools until the following Monday.

The next day, Vice President JD Vance told reporters Good's death was "a tragedy of her own making" and said the agent "is protected by absolute immunity." After the Minnesota Star Tribune first named Ross, DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin told WIRED the department was "not going to expose the name of this officer. He acted according to his training." Within days, video that appears to come from Ross's phone leaked to a conservative outlet; it ends with a voice saying "f**king b*tch" as the SUV moves off. On January 9, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty and Attorney General Keith Ellison announced their own investigation, without access to Good's car, the agent's gun or the shell casings. WIRED later reported that an FBI agent's testimony at Ross's earlier trial contradicted Ross's sworn claim that the driver in that case asked for a lawyer, and described FBI training to avoid positions where a vehicle could hit an agent. How the Justice Department handled the case, including its refusal to open a civil-rights investigation and its push to investigate Good's widow, is covered in a separate entry.

In February, Good's brothers testified at a Democratic-led congressional forum on DHS use of force. On March 24, Minnesota, the Hennepin County Attorney and the BCA sued DHS and the Justice Department for access to the evidence in the Good, Alex Pretti and Julio Sosa-Celis shootings. On April 9, in the separate federal case of the driver convicted of assaulting Ross in 2025, Judge Jeffrey Bryan ordered DHS, ICE and the Justice Department to give the court unredacted evidence from Good's killing for a magistrate judge to review. Federal officials turned over evidence including Good's vehicle and the gun used to shoot her, along with body-camera footage and officer statements from the shootings, under an agreement negotiated over three weeks from late June, then stopped sharing within days of Moriarty's July press conference.

**On October 1, 2026, Good's family filed two lawsuits in federal court in Minnesota:** a wrongful-death claim against the United States, and a civil-rights conspiracy suit against Ross, Stephen Miller, Noem, DHS adviser Corey Lewandowski, Tom Homan, Todd Lyons, Bovino and 10 unnamed agents, alleging the shots were "the predictable and intended product" of the surge. The White House said it would "vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits." In court filings on October 13, Minnesota investigators said they are still blocked from the cellphone of the agent who shot Good and from her clothing, and the state is still fighting for the evidence in federal court in Washington, D.C.
legal_status: No criminal charges have been filed against Ross; Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty's review is ongoing, with no charging decision announced. Minnesota, the Hennepin County Attorney and the BCA sued DHS and the Justice Department on March 24, 2026 for access to the evidence; that suit is pending. On October 1, 2026, Good's family sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota: a Federal Tort Claims Act wrongful-death suit against the United States, and a suit under Bivens and the Ku Klux Klan Act (42 U.S.C. 1985(3) and 1986) against Ross, Miller, Noem, Lewandowski, Homan, Lyons, Bovino and 10 John Doe agents (Ganger v. Ross, No. 0:26-cv-04231). The claims are allegations; no ruling has been made, and the White House calls the suits "baseless."

human_toll.summary: Renee Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother of three, was shot and killed in her car. Her partner watched from a few feet away, and her 6-year-old son lost his mother on the morning she took him to school. Nine months later her family says no one has been held to account.

glance.what: An ICE officer shot and killed a Houston man who was not the operation's target; DHS claims self-defense

what_changed: Early on Tuesday, July 7, 2026, ICE officers in unmarked SUVs followed and stopped a white work van on Canal Street in Houston's East End, and an ICE officer shot and killed its driver, **Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican construction business owner who had lived in the U.S. for about 35 years and, by ICE's later account, was not the person the operation was looking for.** He was driving his brother and two workers to a job site. ICE said hours later that he "rammed an ICE law enforcement vehicle, refused to follow multiple verbal commands, and weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over an ICE law enforcement officer," and that the officer fired "in self-defense"; he was shot in the abdomen and died at Ben Taub Hospital. None of the ICE officers wore body cameras and there was no dash-camera footage, per The Texas Tribune, and no video of the moment of the shooting has surfaced, per CNN; DHS blamed the government shutdowns for the delay in issuing cameras (see the body-camera entry). The three passengers -- his brother Victor Hugo Salgado Araujo and workers Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego and Daniel Tirado Pantoja -- were detained at the scene and held at the Montgomery ICE Processing Center in Conroe. On July 9 a spokesperson for Rep. Sylvia Garcia said acting ICE Director David Venturella had told her neither Salgado Araujo nor his brother was the intended target, and a DHS official told ABC News that officers stopped the van because the driver "resembled the target." On July 10 a lawyer for two of the passengers said "at no point was there ever an ICE agent directly in front of the vehicle" and that "the shots came from the sides"; the brother's lawyer later said he "didn't know it was ICE until his brother was shot." The Harris County Medical Examiner listed the death as a homicide, a manner-of-death ruling that is not a criminal finding. The FBI investigated a potential assault on a federal officer and DHS's inspector general opened a review, while Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said his office had far less access than in other police shootings. On July 13 Teare said he would investigate the case "like we do all criminal investigations" and called the lack of federal cooperation unprecedented. On July 16 U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz said ICE had been looking for two Guatemalan men driving a similar van, that Salgado Araujo made a U-turn over a median to evade a first stop, and that when agents surrounded the van, one was "partially inside the van or immediately next to it" as he tried to reverse and then drive forward; AP noted that his account mentioned no collision with an ICE vehicle. An FBI search warrant released in mid-July described a substance in the van as possible methamphetamine; on July 24 the district attorney's office said lab testing found it was not a narcotic or illicit drug. Rojas Pliego filed a habeas petition on July 20, U.S. District Judge Keith Ellison ordered that he not be removed from the district while it was pending, and on July 27 the judge ruled his mandatory detention unconstitutional as applied to him and ordered his release; the government appealed. On August 6 Harris County commissioners approved $2.5 million over three years for the district attorney's investigation. Tirado Pantoja had been released on a separate federal court order by late August, and Victor Hugo Salgado Araujo was released on August 30 after nearly two months in detention, the last of the three witnesses. Grand jury proceedings began in September, and at least three people, including Tirado Pantoja, had testified by September 23. On September 28 The Texas Tribune reported the name of the agent it said fired, citing an unnamed official and ICE records; the agent has not been charged and DHS defends the shooting as self-defense. On October 14 AP, reporting on Teare's separate probe of an ICE vehicle striking a man in Houston, said ICE and DHS had not cooperated with that investigation and recalled that DHS had ignored his July request for information in this case.
legal_status: Under investigation: the Harris County District Attorney's office is presenting the case to a grand jury (no charges); the FBI investigated a potential assault on a federal officer, and DHS's Office of Inspector General is reviewing the shooting. A passenger-witness's habeas petition was granted (Rojas Pliego v. Mullin, S.D. Tex. No. 4:26-cv-05719, July 27, 2026), holding his mandatory detention unconstitutional as applied to him; the government's appeal is pending in the Fifth Circuit (No. 26-20426), with its opening brief due October 26, 2026. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide, which is not a criminal finding.

human_toll.summary: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a husband and father of three U.S.-citizen sons with no criminal record, per his family, was killed on his way to work. The three men in his van, none the operation's target, were taken into ICE custody; though they were the only eyewitnesses, they were held for weeks to nearly two months before courts or ICE released them.

glance.what: An ICE officer shot a father dead at a traffic stop; the 'dragged' officer called his injuries "nothing major"

what_changed:
Silverio Villegas González, a 38-year-old line cook from Michoacán, Mexico, who had lived in the U.S. for about 18 years, was raising two sons, aged 6 and 3. On the morning of September 12, 2025, four days into Operation Midway Blitz, he had just dropped them at school and day care in Franklin Park, Illinois, when two ICE officers, who the New York Times reported had been following him, pulled an unmarked Jeep in front of his car. Nail-salon security video shows the officers leaning in through his open windows; he reversed and drove forward, and an auto shop's camera picked up the sound of at least two gunshots. **One officer shot him in the neck; his car crashed into a parked delivery truck, and he was pronounced dead at Loyola University Medical Center less than an hour later.** The officers gave first aid at the scene. Neither wore a body camera, and no video shows the shooting itself.

The same day, DHS said he "drove his car at law enforcement officers," dragging one "a significant distance," and that the officer, "fearing for his own life," fired; Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said the officer "followed his training, used appropriate force, and properly enforced the law." DHS described him as an undocumented immigrant "with a history of reckless driving"; NBC News found he had never been criminally charged and had pleaded guilty to four traffic violations. Franklin Park police handed the case to the FBI. Late that month, Franklin Park police body-camera footage obtained through public-records requests showed the officers saying the injured officer was "dragged a little bit" and that officer calling his injuries "nothing major." On September 29 Gov. JB Pritzker said the video left "more questions than answers," and Democratic members of Congress, including both Illinois senators, wrote to DHS calling its account "inconsistent" with surveillance footage and asking 18 questions. The Cook County medical examiner ruled the death a homicide, a manner-of-death finding rather than a criminal one, and found a bullet struck the back of his neck at close range.

On April 30, 2026, the Illinois Accountability Commission's final report concluded that "federal agents shot and killed Villegas González without apparent justification," and that day Franklin Park police asked the Illinois State Police Public Integrity Task Force to investigate, telling it the department had no evidence logs, use-of-force reports or scene photos. The state police confirmed the probe in May 2026; its finished case goes to Cook County State's Attorney Eileen O'Neill Burke. In July, DHS told the Chicago Sun-Times that federal prosecutors had declined to charge the officer, without a public explanation. Mexico, which had sent the U.S. a diplomatic note seeking an investigation, had no official response by July, and later called for investigations into the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals linked to immigration enforcement, including his. On October 8, 2026, his brother, José Villegas González, filed a Federal Tort Claims Act wrongful-death claim for the estate, represented by the MacArthur Justice Center, calling the shooting "unlawful and wholly preventable" and alleging the two officers created a dangerous confrontation when they could have stepped away from the car.
legal_status: No one has been charged. DHS told the Chicago Sun-Times in July 2026 that federal prosecutors declined to charge the ICE officer who fired; no reason has been given publicly. The FBI responded to the scene but will not confirm or deny an investigation; the family's lawyers believe it closed its case in mid-October 2025. The Illinois State Police Public Integrity Task Force opened an investigation in May 2026 that was still open as of October 8, 2026; when complete it goes to the Cook County State's Attorney for a charging review. On May 21, 2026, a Cook County judge rejected a bid for a special prosecutor over Midway Blitz abuses, citing the state's attorney's commitment to the state police case. On October 8, 2026, the estate filed an administrative wrongful-death claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act, the required step before suing; the government has six months to settle or deny it before a lawsuit can be filed. The officer's conduct has not been ruled on by any court.

human_toll.summary: Silverio Villegas González, 38, was shot in the neck and died within the hour, leaving two young sons who lost their primary parent. DHS says one ICE officer was hurt. No charges have followed, and his family says it still has not been told the officers' names.

date_of_action: 2026-01-14 (ICE officer shoots Sosa-Celis) through 2026-10-13 (Minnesota court filings say it is still seeking the federal evidence)
what_changed:
On the evening of January 14, 2026, during Operation Metro Surge and one week after an ICE officer killed Renee Good, ICE officers chased a car driven by Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, a Venezuelan man, to the north Minneapolis duplex he shared with Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis; an FBI affidavit later said the officers had mistaken Aljorna for another Latino man, the Minnesota Reformer reported. ICE officer Christian Castro chased Aljorna on foot, and a brief scuffle followed at the front steps. Once both men had run inside, Castro fired through the closed front door, the Hennepin County Attorney later charged; the bullet struck Sosa-Celis in the leg "before making its final impact in the wall of a child's room." Officers then used tear gas on the home and took both men and their partners into custody. A downstairs neighbor, Gabriel Alejandro Hernandez Ledezma, was also detained and flown within hours to an ICE facility in Texas; his court petition alleged this was done to keep him from becoming an eyewitness, and a judge later ordered his release.

That night DHS said the officer had been "ambushed by three individuals" who attacked him "with a snow shovel and broom handle" and that he "fired defensive shots to defend his life." On January 15, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem called it "an attempted murder of federal law enforcement" and accused Gov. Tim Walz and Mayor Jacob Frey of encouraging assaults on officers. Federal prosecutors charged Sosa-Celis and Aljorna with assaulting an officer. At a January 21 hearing, the officer's account differed from that of the two men and three eyewitnesses, and the available video did not back his story of a broom and shovel attack, the Associated Press reported. The FBI refused to share evidence with state investigators, give them the officer's name or make him available for an interview, court filings showed.

On February 12, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen moved to dismiss the case, saying "newly discovered evidence" was "materially inconsistent with the allegations," and on February 13 Judge Paul Magnuson dismissed the charges with prejudice. The same day, then-acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said video showed that "sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements"; both unnamed officers were put on administrative leave, and ICE and the Justice Department opened a joint investigation. In March, Minnesota and Hennepin County sued the administration for the evidence in this shooting and in the Good and Pretti killings. On April 6, Minneapolis released city camera video showing Sosa-Celis throw his shovel into the snow and retreat, and a scuffle of roughly 10 to 12 seconds (outlets' counts differ), not the three-minute fight Castro had described.

On May 18, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, joined by Attorney General Keith Ellison's office, charged Castro with four felony counts of second-degree assault and one misdemeanor count of falsely reporting a crime; the county's announcement said he "was not hit with any shovels, brooms, or weapons of any kind" and was alone in the yard when he fired. Agents from the DHS inspector general's office and Texas Rangers arrested Castro in Cameron County, Texas, on May 29; a DHS spokesperson called the arrest "unlawful" and a "political stunt" and said the case belonged in federal hands. Gov. Greg Abbott declined to sign Minnesota's extradition warrant, citing Minnesota fraud investigations; Minnesota sued, and on August 26 U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. said he could not order Castro held or the warrant signed. Castro was released from jail in Brownsville on August 27 after 90 days.

ProPublica reported that Justice Department leaders in Washington had quashed plans for civil-rights charges, and that late on September 1 the prosecutor handling the case, Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans, told victims' lawyers to prepare for Castro to be charged "only with False Statements," writing that "This is being directed by the Main Justice and the US Attorney." CBS News later reported that Evans was fired, citing unnamed sources. On September 2 a federal grand jury indicted Castro on six counts of making false statements to the FBI, the first Justice Department prosecution of a federal officer over the surge. He turned himself in in Texas and was released on a $75,000 bond with a GPS monitor. The Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension arrested him in Minneapolis on September 16; on September 17 a Hennepin County judge set bail at $400,000, or $200,000 with conditions, Castro signed an extradition waiver, and Ellison dropped the suit against Texas. On September 18 Castro pleaded not guilty to the federal charges in St. Paul. In court filings on October 13, Minnesota said federal authorities had stopped sharing evidence in the Good and Pretti investigations in September, and that it was also still seeking evidence in this shooting.
legal_status: Christian Castro is charged in Hennepin County with four felony counts of second-degree assault and one misdemeanor count of falsely reporting a crime (filed May 18, 2026), and is indicted in federal court in Minnesota on six counts of making false statements to the FBI (September 2, 2026). He pleaded not guilty to the federal charges on September 18, and his lawyer said he plans to plead not guilty to the state charges; both cases are pending and he is presumed innocent. Castro is expected to try to move the state case to federal court and claim Supremacy Clause immunity; no such ruling was found. No civil-rights charge has been filed; before the indictment a DOJ official said the department "has not yet reached a conclusion," and NBC News's source said a civil-rights investigation was ongoing. The federal assault charges against Sosa-Celis and Aljorna were dismissed with prejudice on February 13, 2026. Minnesota's suit against Gov. Abbott over the extradition was dismissed by the state in September after a federal judge declined to intervene. Minnesota's suit for the federal evidence in this and the Good and Pretti shootings is pending.

human_toll.summary: Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, 24, a Venezuelan man whom state prosecutors say was legally in the U.S., was shot in the leg through his own front door while four adults and two children were inside, prosecutors allege. He and Aljorna were then charged with assaulting an officer, jailed for weeks, facing years in federal prison if convicted, before the charges collapsed, and their partners were sent to an immigration detention camp in El Paso. A downstairs neighbor was flown to Texas and held until a judge ordered him freed.

human_toll.caveat: The account of the shooting comes from state charging papers, the city's camera video and court testimony; Castro has not been tried and is presumed innocent. DHS's stated rationale was that the officer fired "defensive shots" because he "was being ambushed by three individuals"; DHS called the two men "violent criminal illegal aliens" and said the man stopped had entered illegally in 2022, while their lawyers said neither had a violent criminal record and Moriarty said both were legally in the U.S. ICE itself later said the two officers' sworn accounts appeared untruthful. DHS calls the state prosecution "unlawful and nothing more than a political stunt," saying only federal authorities have jurisdiction. No public figure was found for the severity of Sosa-Celis's injury or the length of each person's detention.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the shooting, the collapse of the federal case and the charges against Castro: the Hennepin County charges are described in an official statement by the Minnesota Attorney General, the dismissal and ICE's admission come from the U.S. Attorney's motion and Lyons's statement as reported by the Associated Press, and the arrest, extradition fight, indictment and court appearances are reported by AP, CNN, NBC News, NPR, Fox News and the Minnesota Reformer. Castro is named in a court filing (the Hennepin County criminal complaint and the federal indictment) and in an official statement by the Minnesota Attorney General; ICE and the FBI did not name him, and state investigators identified him after hearing FBI agents name him at the scene, Moriarty said. The second ICE officer whose sworn account ICE called untruthful has not been named and is not named here. MODERATE confidence on the reasons DOJ dropped civil-rights charges, which rest on a prosecutor's email reviewed by ProPublica and on two unnamed sources who told MPR News the U.S. Attorney's office chose not to seek a civil-rights indictment; DOJ says no conclusion has been reached, and a person familiar told CNN no formal decision had been made. Evans's firing rests on unnamed sources: CBS News (relayed by the Minnesota Reformer) and a person who told CNN he was fired and is under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury probe. Details differ slightly across outlets: the scuffle on the city video is put at 10, 11 or 12 seconds; CNN calls Aljorna Sosa-Celis's cousin while other outlets call him his roommate; NBC reported Castro pleaded not guilty at his first federal appearance in Texas, while CNN and Fox report the plea in St. Paul on Sept. 18. NBC's source put the indictment on Wednesday, Sept. 2, while The New York Times put it on Sept. 3; it was unsealed Sept. 4. The ProPublica email date is inferred from the article's "late on Tuesday" and its report that Castro had been released the week before.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a pattern during the Minneapolis surge of DHS leaders blaming the person shot within hours, before any investigation (see also the entry on DHS accounts accusing people of assaulting agents), as when an ICE officer killed Renee Good a week earlier and when federal officers killed Alex Pretti ten days later. This case differs in that video led prosecutors to drop the charges against the men, ICE conceded its officers' sworn accounts appeared untruthful, and the state charged the officer. The Justice Department's handling of the Good shooting, with which Moriarty compared its overruling of the prosecutor who sought civil-rights charges here, is covered in the separate entry on DOJ's Renee Good investigation. title: ICE Cut Its New-Officer Academy to 42 Days to Rush a 10,000-Officer Hiring Surge, and FLETC Pushed Back Other Agencies' Training to Make Room
status: Reversed in part: ICE said in May 2026 it would end the 42-day course, and classes from July 2026 get about 71-72 academy days, still short of the roughly five months recruits once got. No source says whether other agencies' postponed FLETC classes were made up.
date_of_action: 2025-08 (FLETC reschedules other agencies' training for the ICE surge; ICE shortens its academy) through 2026-07 (longer academy course resumes)
what_changed:
After the One Big Beautiful Bill Act funded a surge of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers, the administration shortened ICE's new-officer academy and cleared space for it at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers (FLETC), the main federal police academy in Glynco, Georgia. **On August 27, 2025, acting FLETC Director Paul Baker and his deputy, Ariana Roddini, told staff that to onboard 10,000 ICE ERO personnel and 1,000 Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) personnel by December 31, 2025, 'training programs for agencies not directly involved in these efforts, originally scheduled between Sept. 9 and Dec. 31, 2025 will be rescheduled to later dates in Fiscal Year 2026.'** More than 75 federal law-enforcement agencies train at FLETC, from Border Patrol and the Transportation Security Administration to the National Park Service, military police and inspectors general offices; Defense One reported the freeze affected military police, inspectors general offices 'and dozens of other agencies.' Baker and Roddini said they were looking at whether other FLETC sites could take critical programs, and DHS said it was still 'actively supporting training programs for many agencies during the surge' and would restart rescheduled training as early as possible in fiscal 2026 (Government Executive). The ICE hires were exempt from the governmentwide hiring freeze.

ICE's own academy was cut at the same time. Deportation officers previously had about 20 weeks of training (CNN: '20 weeks, or roughly 100 days'); ICE's careers page described five weeks of language training and 16 weeks of law-enforcement training, and ICE's training chief, Caleb Vitello, told AP in August 2025 the agency had cut the Spanish requirement, shortening training by five weeks (PolitiFact). Reported lengths for the shortened course varied: The Atlantic reported 47 days, citing three officials; DHS called that false and said training ran eight weeks, and acting ICE Director Todd Lyons confirmed an eight-week, six-day-a-week schedule, or 48 days (PolitiFact); NBC News and Government Executive later reported about six weeks, which DHS and ICE did not confirm to PolitiFact. Internal syllabi that two whistleblowers disclosed to Congress, obtained by CBS News, showed the deportation-officer course falling from 72 days in July 2025 to 42 days in February 2026. Lyons told Congress ICE 'reduced the timeline' for recruits who were already certified federal officers.

On February 23, 2026, former ICE training attorney and instructor Ryan Schwank, who resigned February 13, told a forum held by congressional Democrats that the academy program was 'deficient, defective, and broken' (CBS News; AP), and that ICE had cut 240 hours of classes from a 584-hour program, including classes on the Constitution, firearms and the use of force (his written statement; The Washington Post, via the Boston Globe, reported 580 hours). DHS said 'no subject matter has been cut' and that recruits get 56 days of training plus an average of 28 days on the job.

On May 6, 2026, an ICE spokesperson confirmed to NOTUS that ICE would end the 42-day course and return to 72 days at Glynco, part of a broader shift under White House border czar Tom Homan; two DHS officials told The Washington Post the change came because the hiring surge was complete, having more than doubled ICE's immigration officers to 22,000, while DHS's own statement to the Post did not confirm it. On June 3, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a House hearing: 'All training starting July 1st will be back up to the regular standards' (AP). An internal ICE memo the following week, which DHS confirmed, set the core course at roughly 71 days from July and required officers trained under the 42-day course to take a follow-on program (CBS News). Even restored, the course is shorter than the roughly 20 weeks deportation officers used to get, and no source reviewed says the Spanish-language training was brought back.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on FLETC's rescheduling of other agencies' training, which rests on FLETC leaders' own message to staff and DHS's statement as reported by Government Executive (Defense One ran the same story); the 'more than 75' figure is how many agencies train at FLETC, not a count of agencies whose classes were moved. HIGH confidence on the 72-to-42-day academy cut, which rests on internal syllabi obtained by CBS News and matches CNN's analysis and the ICE spokesperson's statement to NOTUS. Earlier figures (47 days, 48 days, about six weeks) came from anonymous officials and DHS statements and were never reconciled; PolitiFact rated Sen. Mark Warner's 47-day claim Mostly True. The 240-of-584-hour figure is Schwank's account in his written statement (the Post reported 580 hours), which DHS denies. The restored length is 72 days per ICE's spokesperson and DHS officials, and roughly 71 days per the internal memo CBS obtained. Contested: DHS says it streamlined training without cutting content and that on-the-job training makes up the difference. Re-verified 2026-09-22: the September 9-December 31, 2025 rescheduling window comes from FLETC leaders' own message; no source reviewed confirms whether the postponed classes were held in fiscal 2026.

what_changed: Backstory: Winn Correctional Center in Winnfield, Louisiana opened in 1990 and was taken over by ICE from the state in 2019; it is one of ICE's largest detention centers, holding more than 1,500 men, and ICE lists 70% of them as having "No ICE threat level." It is managed by the Winn Parish Sheriff's Office and ICE contractor LaSalle Corrections. In March 2025 the DHS Office of Inspector General made an unannounced inspection of the facility. **On April 11, 2026, Alejandro Cabrera Clemente, 49, a Mexican national who had recently lived in Tennessee and was taken into ICE custody there in January, was found unresponsive during a security check and was pronounced dead at Winn Parish Medical Center.** A coroner's report obtained by AP says he woke up coughing and wheezing about two and a half hours earlier but said he was OK and went back to sleep; the coroner ruled he died of natural causes due to cardiovascular disease. ICE's own death report said detainees alerted nursing staff, who found him "with left-sided facial droop," and that he had been treated for high blood pressure and other problems during his detention. ABC News counted him as the 47th person to die in ICE detention in the second Trump administration. On June 3, 2026 the inspector general published its report on the March 2025 inspection (OIG-26-08). It found Winn did not fully comply with detention standards for medical care, environmental health and safety, food service, use of force and other areas: medical staff failed to keep updated treatment documents and laboratory testing records, which could "negatively impact detainee health care and safety"; kitchen vents leaked; food was stored above required temperatures; one officer used a prohibited chokehold and another "stabbed the detainee's right thumb with a pen" when a detainee would not take his hand off a door. ICE agreed with all nine recommendations; a DHS spokesperson called the findings "minor infractions." **On June 4, 2026, Mamuka Artmeladze, 43, from Georgia, was found unresponsive at 10:37 p.m. and was pronounced dead at the same hospital at about 11:22 p.m.; ICE said his cause of death was pending an autopsy.** He had been held at Winn for nearly four months after ICE arrested him in February near Fackler, Alabama, in an operation targeting commercial vehicle drivers, and AP reported he had no criminal record. He was the second Winn death since April 11 and, by ABC's count, the 50th ICE detention death of the term. On June 18, Senators Alex Padilla and Richard Durbin wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and ICE Acting Director-Designate David Venturella demanding a pause on expansion or contract changes at facilities with recent deaths or failed inspections, and asking by June 30 for all records on the Artmeladze and Cabrera deaths, including communications with LaSalle Corrections. An August 25 letter from Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. and other House Democrats also cited the two Winn deaths and the inspector general's medical-recordkeeping findings. **On September 18, 2026, Carlos Josue Marchena Marchena, 36, a Costa Rican man with type 1 diabetes, was found unresponsive at Winn and later pronounced dead at a hospital; AP called him the third detainee to die there in less than six months.** His sister, his girlfriend and a detainee in the next cell told AP he complained of missed insulin shots, missed meals and too little water as he was moved between facilities, and that his condition worsened after he reached Winn, where he died less than a week later; the fellow detainee said he was vomiting and pale the day before. ICE said Marchena "received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals"; a LaSalle Corrections spokesperson, Scott Sutterfield, said the death was under review. The official cause of death was pending further medical examination as of AP's September 22 report.
legal_status: No charges, lawsuits or court rulings found. The DHS inspector general's June 2026 report (OIG-26-08) found Winn did not fully comply with detention standards for medical care, use of force, food service and other areas; ICE concurred with all nine recommendations, and five were open as of October 19, 2026. Senators Padilla and Durbin demanded death records from DHS on June 18; no public DHS response was found. The family's and fellow detainee's account of missed insulin is alleged; ICE denies it.

human_toll.summary: Three men held by ICE died after being found unresponsive at Winn between April and September 2026: a 49-year-old Mexican man, a 43-year-old Georgian man with no criminal record, and a 36-year-old Costa Rican man with type 1 diabetes whose family says he missed insulin shots and meals. title: Treasury Watchdog Finds ICE Didn't Meet Data-Safeguarding Standards Before Signing Taxpayer Data-Sharing Deal; Judge Found About 42,695 Unlawful Disclosures, and Appeals Court Upheld Block
status: Courts have barred further IRS address disclosures to ICE since November 2025 (upheld by the D.C. Circuit September 8, 2026) and ICE's use of the data since February 2026 (on appeal in the First Circuit). A judge found about 42,695 of the 47,289 addresses shared were disclosed unlawfully.
date_of_action: 2025-04 (ICE-IRS memorandum of understanding signed) through 2026-10 (First Circuit heard the appeal of the block on ICE's use of the data)
what_changed:
In April 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem signed a memorandum of understanding allowing ICE to submit names and addresses of immigrants it identified as in the U.S. illegally to the IRS for cross-verification against confidential tax records, supporting the administration's mass-deportation operation; the acting IRS commissioner left the agency after it was signed. In summer 2025 ICE requested 1.28 million taxpayer records, and the IRS shared last known addresses for 47,289 people. In November 2025 U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly blocked further disclosures, and in February 2026 she found **the IRS had violated taxpayer-confidentiality law "approximately 42,695 times"** by disclosing addresses through TIN Matching without confirming that ICE had supplied the taxpayer's address. In June 2026, the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) released a partially redacted report finding that ICE did not meet safeguarding standards before the MOU was signed: findings from a November 2023 IRS safeguard review of ICE remained open, ICE had submitted no corrective action plan, and the IRS was "unable to accurately and consistently match ICE records" because ICE's data lacked uniform formatting. On September 8, 2026, a unanimous D.C. Circuit panel upheld the block, finding the IRS's data-exchange procedure "indisputably contravenes the requirements" of the tax code's confidentiality section.

Update 2026-10-19: In a separate Massachusetts lawsuit, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani had preliminarily enjoined ICE and DHS on February 5, 2026 from using tax return information the IRS disclosed under the agreement. On September 30, 2026 she denied the government's motions to dismiss that case except for one claim, and on October 7, 2026 the First Circuit heard the government's appeal of her injunction.
confidence_note:
HIGH confidence on the TIGTA report's core findings and the February 2026 ruling's figure of about 42,695 unlawful disclosures (of 47,289 addresses shared), corroborated across FedScoop, CPA Practice Advisor, and Courthouse News; Fox News's coverage of an IRS court declaration confirms the roughly 47,000 addresses shared. MODERATE confidence on the full scope of data-quality errors given the report's partial redaction.
