title: Rollback of Longstanding Military-Family Protections Leads to 50+ Detentions of Spouses and Parents of Active-Duty Troops
status: Ongoing: more than 60 congressional Democrats opened an investigation by letter to DHS, the Defense Department and the VA on Aug. 9, 2026. The Pentagon said it would reply to the letter's authors; no policy reversal was found as of Oct. 18, 2026.
date_of_action: Ongoing since early 2025 (start of Trump's second term); publicly reported by the Associated Press in August 2026
what_changed: An Associated Press investigation published Aug. 5, 2026 found the Trump administration has rolled back longstanding, bipartisan-consensus protections that historically shielded immediate family members of active-duty U.S. service members from immigration enforcement. As a result, **more than 50 spouses and parents of active-duty troops have been detained by immigration authorities since the start of Trump's second term, with at least six deported and one self-deported**; at least eight remained in custody. The AP found troops' relatives repeatedly detained by ICE while applying for military parole-in-place or seeking to adjust their status, including at USCIS appointments, and held for months. A new policy implemented in April 2025 states that "military service alone does not exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws," and the average wait for military parole-in-place has more than doubled to 12 months, per USCIS data. A former ICE deputy chief counsel and military-immigration lawyers told the AP this departs from past practice under both parties, including Trump's first term. Some service members have been forced to take leave from their duties -- including delaying deployments -- to care for children after a spouse was detained. A handful of cases drew public backlash and led Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to intervene to secure releases. In response to the AP's findings, more than 60 members of the U.S. House and Senate sent a letter on the evening of August 9, 2026 to the Department of Homeland Security, the Defense Department, and the Department of Veterans Affairs announcing an investigation into whether DHS and the Pentagon are coordinating to deport service members and their families, and urging the administration to restore the earlier protections.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the detention figures and examples come from the AP's own investigation (Aug. 5, 2026), which named its method (federal habeas records, media coverage, verification with families and attorneys) and was carried by PBS NewsHour and other outlets; DHS's statement responding to it is quoted in the same report. The congressional letter's existence, its Aug. 9, 2026 date and its 60-plus signers are reported by the AP, which was provided the letter. The PBS NewsHour and Washington Post copies are AP syndications, not independent reporting. Named affected people are relatives who, with their service-member family members, spoke to the AP or were named in its reporting. Re-verified 2026-10-18: AP reports re-read; no policy reversal, lawsuit or administration response to the congressional letter was found.

what_changed: Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minneapolis Democrat who came to the United States as a child refugee from Somalia and became a citizen in 2000, has been a target of President Trump for years; he has repeatedly claimed, without releasing proof, that she married her brother in an immigration scam, which she calls "disgusting lies." The Bulwark reported that the brother-marriage claim traces back to a single anonymous post on a Somali-American web forum. In May 2026, Vice President JD Vance said the Justice Department was investigating Omar for immigration fraud. In September, at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told commentator Benny Johnson that DHS was investigating: "We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States," adding, "There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with." Asked by Johnson when Omar would be deported, he replied, "Something's going to happen," but offered no documentary evidence. White House border czar Tom Homan also said on Fox News that "things are going on" regarding Omar and, asked whether that meant there was an open investigation, said, "I'm confirming that ICE is — yeah, like I said months ago, that is something that's been reported and needs to be looked at." **Early on Monday, October 12, 2026, Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home,** 22 days before the November 3 election in which she is seeking reelection, with voting already underway in Minnesota. A neighbor said agents woke her at about 4:30 a.m., and CNN saw investigators removing boxes. The Justice Department said HSI "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an "ongoing federal criminal investigation," and gave no details. Per multiple people familiar with the investigation who spoke to CNN, federal magistrate judge Matthew Sharbaugh of the D.C. federal court approved the warrant only after a days-long back-and-forth in which DOJ had argued for broad access to the records in her home; he required prosecutors to set up a process for screening the records to protect her legislative work under the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause. Per officials who spoke to NPR anonymously, it is a multiyear probe that includes whistleblower complaints and concerns immigration fraud allegations; Fox News and MinnPost reported it is tied to immigration paperwork her father filled out when the family arrived. Per NPR's sources, senior DOJ leadership, including Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, approved the search; a source told CNN it was approved after thorough deliberation given the election's proximity. DOJ has long avoided overt investigative steps involving candidates in roughly the 60 days before an election; the policy is not legally binding, and a source told CNBC that DOJ did not consider the search a violation because it was not meant to be public. Some former federal prosecutors told the Minnesota Star Tribune the search appeared to break long-standing norms. A counsel for the American Immigration Lawyers Association told MinnPost that fraud in an entry application is usually a civil matter, and questioned what guilt would attach to Omar, who was a child when her father filled out the forms. Omar called it "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," and House Democratic leaders promised "full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice." Trump called Omar "a terrible person" but said the search "has nothing to do with me." On October 13, D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro told Fox News that her office was separately examining Omar's financial disclosures: a filing covering 2024 reported assets of $6 million to $30 million, which Omar later revised to $18,000 to $95,000 and blamed on an accounting error, and a House watchdog had voted in September to recommend dismissing misconduct allegations over it. "It doesn't matter what the House does," Pirro said. The Washington Post wrote that her public acknowledgment appears at odds with long-standing Justice Department practice, and Trump posted that day, "America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!" People familiar with the immigration probe told the Post that it grew out of a renewed look at Omar's immigration history that HSI began earlier this year, after the agency had declined a similar probe years earlier. It centers on whether Omar or her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, intentionally misstated her birth date so she could derive citizenship through him as a minor when he naturalized in 2000, and on whether he misstated his past military service. Per one person familiar with it, the warrant listed potential charges of conspiracy, immigration fraud and false statements; the Post reported that DOJ could pursue those charges or a criminal or civil denaturalization case, and the Wall Street Journal reported that the investigation is "aimed at building a case to strip her of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her." On October 14, NBC News reported, citing two people familiar with the investigation, that agents had seized Omar's phone in the search and that roughly a dozen subpoenas had gone out the Friday before it, including to family members. The subpoenas are tied to a federal grand jury in Minnesota; Omar herself was not subpoenaed, and agents want to talk to her sister. HSI, the U.S. attorney in Minneapolis and the Justice Department are running the investigation. Al Jazeera, citing the Washington Post, reported that agents also took her passport. On October 16, Omar's lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, sent prosecutors a letter calling the probe "vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated" and the search "neither justified nor lawful." They wrote that the House Office of General Counsel was not notified until after the search was publicly reported, despite notice procedures the judge had mandated, that no one from the U.S. attorney's office or DOJ was present to advise Omar of her Speech or Debate privileges, and they demanded the return of her property and the preservation of agents' recordings of the search. A Justice Department spokesperson called the letter "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and said, "Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do." Omar has not been charged.
legal_status: No charges. HSI executed a search warrant a D.C. federal magistrate judge approved, reportedly with screening required for material protected by the Speech or Debate Clause. Omar is under investigation over alleged immigration fraud, false statements and conspiracy, the potential charges the warrant reportedly listed, and DOJ could reportedly pursue a criminal or civil denaturalization case. A federal grand jury in Minnesota has reportedly issued about a dozen subpoenas. On October 16 her lawyers alleged in a letter to DOJ that the search did not follow the judge's procedures and was unlawful and demanded her property back; DOJ says it complied with all court orders. title: DHS Secretary Mullin wouldn't rule out ICE at 2026 polling places, citing threats or warrants; now sued

officials.name: Markwayne Mullin
officials.role: Secretary of Homeland Security (nominee at his March 2026 confirmation hearing); declined to rule out ICE at polling places and said agents could be there for a threat or to serve a warrant

people.unnamed_affected: Voters at 2026 polling places nationwide, particularly voters of color and immigrant communities whom the plaintiffs say fear federal interference when they vote; no individual voter is named.

status: Sued; no ruling. Three D.C. federal suits (LULAC and Denver, Sept. 10; NAACP-led groups, Sept. 18; Democratic Party committees, Sept. 23) challenge Mullin's threat-or-warrant exceptions. The judge is weighing consolidation; no emergency motion filed. DHS says ICE isn't targeting polls.
date_of_action: 2026-03 (Mullin declines to rule out ICE at polling places)
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The Bannon characterization ('test run') is a third-party statement rather than established fact, and shouldn't be treated as sourced evidence about Mullin's intent. A more supportable reading: an administration that has used immigration enforcement in an expanding set of public venues (courthouses, churches, schools, airports during funding lapses) in ways courts have repeatedly found legally questionable, and that has declined to draw a bright line excluding polling places. Whether this reflects a deliberate incremental-expansion strategy or ad hoc enforcement overreach is genuinely uncertain.

glance.what: DHS Secretary Mullin wouldn't rule out ICE at 2026 polling places, citing threats or warrants; now sued

what_changed: Ahead of the November 3, 2026 midterms, Markwayne Mullin, as nominee and then as Secretary of Homeland Security, repeatedly declined to rule out immigration agents at polling places. At his March 2026 confirmation hearing he said agents could be sent for a "specific threat" and questioned the concern itself: "I don't understand what the concern about enforcing immigration at polling places is anyways. Because, honestly, if you're not a citizen, you shouldn't be voting anyways." Democracy Docket reported that his comments were at odds with federal law, which bars stationing law enforcement officers or troops at polling places, and with earlier statements from DHS and ICE officials: a senior DHS "election integrity" official, Heather Honey, had told state authorities that ICE and other armed federal agents would not be dispatched to polling places, and acting ICE chief Todd Lyons had told senators immigration officials would have "no reason" to be at voting locations, though he did not definitively rule it out. Before his confirmation, state election chiefs asked Mullin to confirm in writing that ICE agents would not be sent to the polls under his leadership; Democracy Docket found no indication that he did. Steve Bannon, Trump's former chief strategist, called a separate ICE deployment to major airports during a DHS funding lapse a "test run" for using federal officers to interfere in the November elections; that is Bannon's characterization, not a statement by Mullin or DHS. On CNN's "State of the Union" on June 14, 2026, asked whether he would rule out sending ICE agents, Mullin said, "No, what I said was that we would only be there if a threat has arised," said ICE agents are trained as special response teams that could be mobilized quickly if a threat arose at a polling station, and added that local law enforcement "would be part of that conversation, so we wouldn't show up on our own." In a CNN "State of the Union" interview reported by Fox News, he also defended DHS's review of voter information under Trump's March 31 executive order directing DHS, with the Social Security Administration, to compile state citizenship lists for election officials. In late July, Raw Story reported a DHS official's emailed statement: "ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action." Raw Story wrote that "The details of what would constitute such a threat were left vague," and reported that the Democratic National Committee, in a records suit, had pointed to media reports of ICE agents at voting sites during primaries in Texas and California and entering a polling place in New York state to question a poll worker. Votebeat separately reported that in May, ICE agents came to question a driver stopped near a polling place until local law enforcement told them to leave; county officials said voters weren't questioned. At a news conference in New York on September 1, 2026, Mullin widened the stated exceptions: "ICE isn't there to patrol the polling places," he said, but "The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we're serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down," and "If we're serving a warrant we will be where we need to be." A senior DHS official told NBC News that ICE officers had received no guidance to do anything beyond their regular duties on Election Day. Three federal suits in Washington, D.C., followed. On September 10, the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause, UnidosUS and the city of Denver, represented by Democracy Forward, sued DHS, ICE, Mullin and ICE leader David Venturella, asking the court to declare unlawful any plan to put armed agents at polling places under the federal law barring "any troops or armed men" at "any place where a general or special election is held." On September 18, the NAACP and eight other civil rights, immigrant and labor groups sued DHS, ICE, DOJ, the FBI, Mullin, Venturella, Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and Thomas Homan under Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act; the complaint says Mullin "has repeatedly declined to rule out deploying DHS agents in the vicinity of voting locations," and asks the court to bar the defendants "from deploying agents in a manner that unlawfully intimidates voters or anyone urging or aiding voters." A DOJ spokesperson called any suggestion that DOJ would send federal law enforcement to polling locations "fearmongering," and a DHS spokesperson said ICE was not planning operations targeting polling locations. On September 23, the DSCC, the DCCC, the Democratic Governors Association, Sen. Charles Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries sued DHS, ICE, the FBI, Mullin, Venturella and Patel, citing Mullin's September 1 remarks and alleging that a "Polling Place Policy" violates 18 U.S.C. §592 and Section 11(b), and asking the court to "Declare the Polling Place Policy unlawful" and bar the defendants from "operating or carrying weapons in the vicinity of open polling places." Judge Loren L. AliKhan is weighing consolidating the three cases and ordered a joint status report, which the parties filed October 16. In the NAACP case, plaintiffs moved for discovery on October 5; the government opposed on October 13 and plaintiffs replied October 16. In mid-October Democracy Docket reported that no plaintiff had sought a temporary restraining order, making a definitive ruling before November 3 unlikely.
legal_status: Sued; no ruling. Three pending suits in the U.S. District Court for D.C. name Mullin: League of United Latin American Citizens v. DHS (No. 26-cv-3157, filed Sept. 10), invoking the federal ban on armed men at polling places; NAACP v. DHS (No. 1:26-cv-03263, filed Sept. 18), alleging Section 11(b) Voting Rights Act intimidation; and DSCC v. ICE (No. 1:26-cv-03330, filed Sept. 23), alleging the defendants' "Polling Place Policy" violates 18 U.S.C. §592 and Section 11(b). These are allegations. Judge Loren L. AliKhan is considering consolidation; a discovery motion in the NAACP case is fully briefed. No motion for a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction is on the NAACP docket. 18 U.S.C. §592 is a criminal statute; no one has been charged, and TAP's sources document no ICE deployment to a polling place.

human_toll.summary: No voter is documented as stopped, questioned or turned away by ICE at a polling place. The harm alleged is a chilling one: the plaintiffs say DHS leaders' statements have put voters of color and immigrant voters in fear of federal interference when they go to vote, and the DSCC suit says the policy "chills voting everywhere." Wisconsin election officials are training, and Michigan's attorney general's office has prepared legal filings, in case armed federal agents appear, and a national poll found many Americans expect ICE at the polls.

DHS's stated position: ICE "is not planning operations targeting polling locations," conducts "intelligence-driven targeted enforcement," and gave officers no extra Election Day guidance, per a senior DHS official; Mullin says "ICE isn't there to patrol the polling places" and that local law enforcement would be part of any response. DOJ calls suggestions that it would send law enforcement to polls "fearmongering." Against that, DHS has not defined the "threat" exception, Mullin added a warrant exception in September, and state election chiefs' request for a written commitment has gone unanswered as far as reporting shows.

title: DHS kept two deportation flights to El Salvador going despite a judge's turnaround order; he found probable cause of contempt

officials.name: Kristi Noem
officials.role: Secretary of Homeland Security at the time (fired in March 2026, per CNN); the administration has said she was responsible for the transfer decision

cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Nonpartisan reporting (Just Security, Brennan Center) documents a broader pattern of repeated noncompliance with court orders across multiple agencies and cases in this administration, suggesting this reflects a deliberate compliance posture rather than an isolated failure. In Minnesota alone, the federal court listed 96 court orders ICE violated in January 2026 (210 in 143 cases by late February), though the chief judge there attributed most of those failures to incompetence rather than deliberate defiance. The Brennan Center characterized the administration's approach as 'legalistic noncompliance' -- using legal language and appeal processes to mask substantive defiance while claiming to respect the courts. This entry is best understood as one documented instance of that pattern, not an outlier. Kilmar Abrego Garcia's March 2025 deportation to CECOT, despite a 2019 immigration-court order barring his removal to El Salvador, is a related instance: the administration called it an error, then resisted court orders to facilitate his return; the prosecution that followed his lawsuit is covered in the entry on his vindictive-prosecution case. What happened to the men in CECOT, and Boasberg's later due-process ruling, are covered in the entry on the 252 Venezuelans held in CECOT. The proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act and the litigation over whether it was lawful are covered in the entry on the Alien Enemies Act removals. Other people deported despite a court order or legal protection are listed in the entry on removals despite court orders or protections.

glance.what: Kept two deportation flights going despite a turnaround order; a judge found probable cause of contempt

harm.who: Federal courts' power to enforce orders

what_changed: On March 15, 2025, Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg issued a temporary restraining order barring the administration from transferring Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act, a wartime authority used to deport noncitizens with little-to-no due process, and verbally ordered the two planes carrying the men turned around. **DHS officials, under Noem's authority, failed to turn around the two flights**, which carried more than 200 men the administration alleged were Tren de Aragua members; the men were imprisoned at El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison. The Justice Department acknowledged that its official Drew Ensign "promptly conveyed" Boasberg's orders to DHS and Justice Department leadership, but argued the oral instructions were defective and the written order lacked the explanation needed to be enforced. On April 16, 2025, Boasberg found "probable cause exists to find the government in criminal contempt," writing that the government's actions "demonstrate a willful disregard for its Order" during the three weeks it was in effect, even though the Supreme Court later vacated the order. He set out to identify whose "specific act or omission" caused the noncompliance, and later said a declaration from Noem did "not provide enough information for the Court to determine whether her decision was a willful violation of the Court's Order"; the administration has identified Noem as the official responsible for the transfer decision. After the full D.C. Circuit let him restart the proceedings in November 2025, he ordered Ensign to testify under oath; on Dec. 12, 2025 a D.C. Circuit panel administratively stayed his Dec. 8, 2025 contempt-proceedings order. On April 14, 2026, Judges Neomi Rao and Justin Walker, over Judge Michelle Childs's dissent, ordered him to end the inquiry, calling it "a clear abuse of discretion"; Childs wrote that "contempt of court is a public offense, and the fate of our democratic republic will depend on whether we treat it as such." The full court vacated that ruling on June 22, 2026, kept the stay in place, and heard argument on Sept. 29, 2026, where AP reported it "often appeared to be deeply skeptical of the government's case" and judges suggested Boasberg "should be able to identify other possible targets for a contempt investigation before referring the matter to a prosecutor." The men were released to Venezuela in a prisoner swap in July 2025.
legal_status: Judge Boasberg found probable cause of criminal contempt against the government on April 16, 2025; the court has not identified any individual as responsible, and no one has been referred or charged. A divided D.C. Circuit panel granted mandamus on April 14, 2026 directing him to end the contempt proceedings; the full D.C. Circuit vacated that order on June 22, 2026, kept the Dec. 12, 2025 administrative stay of his inquiry in effect, and heard en banc argument on Sept. 29, 2026. No en banc decision has been entered. The Justice Department denies violating the order.

human_toll.summary: The Venezuelan men on the two flights were removed under the Alien Enemies Act while a court order barred it, and were held at El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison until a prisoner swap in July 2025. Their ACLU lawyers say they "were subjected to horrific physical and psychological abuse, and deprived of food, water, and medical care." The episode also tests whether federal courts can enforce their own orders against the executive branch.

The abuse account comes from the ACLU's court filing, not from a court finding. The administration says it "complied with the law" and did not violate the order "as it was best construed"; the Justice Department argues the oral turnaround instruction was defective, the written order could not be enforced, the inquiry is "unlawful, unnecessary and futile" because a prosecutor, not a judge, investigates crimes (DOJ attorney Brett Shumate at the en banc argument), and the Supreme Court's later vacatur shows the order should never have issued. The April 2026 panel majority (since vacated) called the inquiry an intrusion into national-security decision-making. Boasberg's view is that the order bound the government while it was in effect, whatever its later fate. Per the White House, 137 of the 238 Venezuelans sent to CECOT on March 15 were removed under the Alien Enemies Act and the rest under ordinary immigration law (see the entry on the Alien Enemies Act removals).

what_changed: The Coast Guard, the only military branch inside the Department of Homeland Security, began flying detained immigrants for DHS days after the January 2025 inauguration: on Jan. 25, 2025, it announced flights between California and Texas to "assist with the national transport of aliens to designated locations in Texas and California, where the Department of Defense will transport the aliens internationally." Under Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem the work grew. From late June 2025, Coast Guard C-27J Spartan aircraft, which until recently flew mainly search-and-rescue, made at least 263 flights by late August that Rolling Stone's analysis of public flight data found were likely for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, moving shackled detainees between ICE hubs in Alexandria, Louisiana, and Harlingen, Texas, the "Alligator Alcatraz" camp in Florida, and midsize cities. **According to ICE Flight Monitor, as reported by NBC News in February 2026, more than 750 Coast Guard flights were redirected under Noem from regular missions such as maritime patrols and search-and-rescue to fly detained immigrants to deportation hubs, and Coast Guard flights carrying immigrants rose from 14 in June 2025 to 149 in November.** The Coast Guard itself told Military.com it flew 886 sorties carrying 9,805 people on C-130 and C-27 aircraft, over what Military.com described as two fiscal years. NBC also reported, citing multiple U.S. officials, that new guidance to Coast Guard Air Station Sacramento made transporting detained immigrants within the U.S. on its C-27s its first priority, ranking search-and-rescue below counternarcotics and training; DHS called that "ridiculous" and said "No such guidance was ordered." The most serious reported incident is contested. On Feb. 4, 2025, Seaman Bryan K. Lee, 23, went missing from the cutter Waesche about 300 nautical miles south of Mexico. According to two U.S. officials and a Coast Guard official who spoke to NBC News, hours into the search Noem learned that a Coast Guard C-130 scheduled to fly detained migrants from California to Texas was among the aircraft searching, and verbally instructed the acting commandant, Adm. Kevin Lunday, to pull it off the search so it would not miss the flight, part of DHS's so-called Alien Expulsion Operations. Lunday notified the National Command Center, which ordered the C-130 to San Diego; the regional command found two C-27s to fly the detainees, freeing the C-130 to return to the search after about an hour. The search ran nearly 190 hours over more than 19,000 square nautical miles, and Lee was never found; NBC said it is not clear the directive had any impact on the search. DHS said "the C-130 never left the search" and that there is no documentation it was diverted, and Lunday, now Commandant, called the allegation "categorically false. That never happened."

human_toll.summary: The people flown were ICE detainees, moved in shackles between detention centers and deportation staging hubs, transfers that advocates say cut people off from family and lawyers. The other cost the reporting describes falls on the Coast Guard's own missions: aircraft and crews that fly search-and-rescue and maritime patrol were tasked with detainee transport, which a Coast Guard official told NBC "puts so much stress on the wing," and a former official said morale at headquarters "is terrible." Whether any rescue suffered is disputed: no source shows the search for Seaman Lee was harmed, and the Coast Guard says no search-and-rescue mission was delayed or reassigned.

what_changed: A Washington Post investigation found **DHS used administrative subpoenas -- which, unlike grand jury or judicial subpoenas, require no judge's sign-off -- to seek personal data on government critics and people engaged in constitutionally protected speech**, including at least one case in which DHS sought to identify a person who had emailed a DHS attorney criticizing the agency's handling of an asylum seeker's case. That person, a 67-year-old Philadelphia-area retiree identified in court filings as Jon Doe, sent the email on October 30, 2025; about four hours later DHS issued an administrative subpoena to Google for information about him and his Gmail account, and about two and a half weeks later two DHS agents and a local police officer came to his home to question him about the email. Google did not hand over the data. Court filings show the demand was an "Immigration Enforcement Subpoena" in a Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) case. Represented by the ACLU, Doe moved in federal court in the Northern District of California on February 2, 2026 to quash the subpoena as retaliation for protected speech; on February 5, DHS told Google it wanted the subpoena retracted and told Doe's lawyers the investigation was closed, without explaining why he had been investigated, and Doe dismissed his motion on February 10. His lawyers told the court it was "the fifth such action in recent months" they knew of in that court, each involving DHS subpoenas against people who had "communicated opposition to or concern about DHS's immigration enforcement operations," and that withdrawing them "forestalls a court ruling" on their legality. The Post and the ACLU also reported earlier DHS subpoenas seeking to unmask Instagram users who posted about ICE raids in Los Angeles and the people behind an Instagram and Facebook account that tracked ICE raids in Pennsylvania; DHS abandoned both after the ACLU challenged them. The same unsigned-administrative-subpoena mechanism was also used by May 2025 against a different target: landlords, pressured to turn over tenant records for immigration enforcement, tracked as a companion entry in this database. On March 2, 2026, Reps. Robin Kelly and Pramila Jayapal and 26 other House Democrats wrote to ten tech and telecom CEOs asking how they handle DHS administrative subpoenas; no Republicans signed the letter. Following the Post's reporting, a bipartisan group of three Democratic and three Republican lawmakers, led by Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Adriano Espaillat, introduced the Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act (S. 4594, May 20, 2026, with Sen. Cynthia Lummis; H.R. 8966, May 21, 2026, with Reps. Thomas Massie, Robin Kelly and Eric Burlison), which would require government officials to certify under penalty of perjury that they are not using subpoenas to monitor or retaliate against people exercising free-speech or other constitutionally protected activity, and would separately limit the government's ability to obtain phone records without a judge's order.
legal_status: Doe moved to quash the subpoena in federal court (N.D. Cal. No. 5:26-mc-80026-SVK) on February 2, 2026, arguing it exceeded DHS's authority under 8 U.S.C. 1225(d) and the Electronic Communications Privacy Act and was retaliation for First Amendment-protected speech. HSI withdrew the subpoena on February 5 and Doe voluntarily dismissed without prejudice on February 10, so no court ruled on its lawfulness. The Los Angeles and Pennsylvania subpoenas were also withdrawn after ACLU challenges, without a ruling on their lawfulness. No charges have been reported against Doe or the account holders. The Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act (S. 4594 / H.R. 8966) has been referred to the Senate and House Judiciary Committees, with no further action.

human_toll.summary: A Philadelphia-area retiree who emailed a DHS attorney urging decency toward an Afghan asylum seeker had DHS demand his Google account data within hours and was questioned at home by two DHS agents and a police officer; the Post reported he has become "less trusting, more paranoid." Anonymous users who posted about ICE raids in Los Angeles and Pennsylvania faced subpoenas seeking to unmask them.

DHS is not required to disclose how many administrative subpoenas it issues, so the yearly figure is an outside estimate, and people who never got a company's notice, or didn't challenge one, are not counted anywhere. DHS has not said why it investigated Doe. Its stated position: Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis called the congressional inquiry "partisan" and said DHS "conducts all operations in strict accordance with the U.S. Constitution, the Fourth Amendment, and federal law." Asked about the subpoenas, Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said "HSI has broad administrative subpoena authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1225(d) and 19 U.S.C. § 1509(a)(1) to issue subpoenas," but would not say why DHS sought the data or why it withdrew them. DHS disputes the critics' framing, and because each subpoena was withdrawn, no court has tested the retaliation claims. No affected person is named; Jon Doe is a court pseudonym. what_changed:
A Wall Street Journal investigation published February 12, 2026, described infighting, dysfunction and self-promotion at the top of DHS under Secretary Kristi Noem and her close adviser Corey Lewandowski, a special government employee who, the Journal reported, directed personnel and contracting. **The Journal reported that the pair had fired or demoted roughly 80% of the career ICE field leadership that was in place when they started, and, in Reason's summary of the Journal's reporting, career immigration-enforcement staff were let go or demoted for questioning or objecting to Noem's decisions.** According to the Journal, citing two dozen current and former administration officials, Noem carried out confrontational enforcement operations over the objections of longtime immigration officials who warned that such flashy displays would discredit the department's mission. For months she and Lewandowski demanded that ICE capture its arrests on video for social media; then, more than a week after federal agents shot and killed Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, they berated acting ICE Director Todd Lyons over videos of officers tangling with protesters and demanded a plan for targeted enforcement -- an approach ICE officials said Lyons had advocated all along. The Journal also reported that the pair elevated Border Patrol official Greg Bovino, who led the combative Chicago and Minneapolis operations, with his unit reporting directly to Noem over the objections of CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott, and that around Christmas they reassigned Scott's chief of staff and pressured his deputy to resign. In one episode the Journal detailed, Lewandowski sought a law-enforcement badge and a federally issued gun: Tom Feeley, a former top ICE official in New York whom the administration was preparing to make ICE director, declined to issue them and was passed over for the job, and a top ICE lawyer, Ken Padilla, declined to sign off on a legal justification and days later was placed on administrative leave; he was later demoted and moved to FEMA. DHS denied that Lewandowski sought a federal gun, said he did not talk to Feeley, and said Padilla's leave was for unrelated reasons. Axios reported that multiple reports described a culture of fear inside DHS as Noem and Lewandowski fired, reassigned and demoted people throughout its 23 sub-agencies. The Journal also reported, and DHS denied, that Noem kept track of her own and border czar Tom Homan's television appearances to make sure she was on TV more than him; Homan, the Journal said, rarely speaks to her.

Separately, Noem put all DHS spending over $100,000 under her personal approval, a process the Journal reported held up contracts across the department and gave Noem and Lewandowski a bigger role in spending decisions than is typical for a secretary; Reason, summarizing the Journal, said the centralization led to delays, higher prices and potential conflicts of interest. The Journal reported that Florida officials struggled for months to secure money for building the "Alligator Alcatraz" detention camp, and that a bulk-steel contract for the border wall sat awaiting Noem's approval from December until February 10 while the price of steel rose more than $100 million, according to some people familiar with it. DHS said Noem had awarded more than $12 billion in border-wall contracts and that the approval process helped root out waste, fraud and abuse.

On March 5, 2026, after weeks of internal turmoil and two contentious congressional hearings, Trump announced on Truth Social that Sen. Markwayne Mullin would replace Noem effective March 31 and moved her to a newly created envoy role. On March 18, 2026, the top Democrats on the House Oversight, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Homeland Security committees (Reps. Robert Garcia, Rick Larsen and Bennie Thompson) asked the DHS Inspector General to investigate Lewandowski's influence over DHS contracting. On March 26, CNN reported, citing two people familiar with it, that Inspector General Joseph Cuffari had opened a sprawling investigation into how DHS contracts were solicited and handled, including Noem's and Lewandowski's involvement; the IG's office said it does not confirm or deny the existence of investigations. On April 1, The New York Times reported that the inquiry was scrutinizing Lewandowski's interactions with companies seeking DHS business, among them Palantir, which reportedly complained to administration officials about its dealings with him. NBC News had reported on March 23 that the IG was investigating the award of a $220 million advertising contract without full and open competition, and separately reported allegations that Lewandowski sought payments from contractor GEO Group in exchange for favorable contract decisions, which he denies. In July 2026 the Journal reported that investigators had found evidence Lewandowski may have been involved in improperly awarding contracts and were weighing a criminal referral to the Justice Department that was not imminent; a representative for Lewandowski denied he issued contracts and said he had not been contacted by investigators. No referral, charges, or findings have been publicly reported; the inquiry remains open.
legal_status: Under investigation (reported): CNN reported on March 26, 2026, citing two sources, that the DHS Inspector General is investigating how DHS contracts were solicited and handled, including Noem's and Lewandowski's involvement; the OIG neither confirms nor denies investigations. In July 2026 the Journal reported investigators were weighing a criminal referral of Lewandowski to the Justice Department, not expected soon; he denies wrongdoing. No referral, charges or IG findings reported. Earlier, the White House Counsel's Office opened an inquiry into Lewandowski's use of his special-government-employee role, and no action was taken, per the Journal. No lawsuit, ruling or IG finding on the ICE personnel actions has been identified.

human_toll.summary: Most of ICE's career field leadership -- roughly 80% of those in place when Noem and Lewandowski arrived -- was fired or demoted, per the Journal. Individual officials were also pushed aside, per the Journal: an ICE lawyer who declined to back Lewandowski's badge-and-gun request was later moved to FEMA, and the CBP commissioner, who had objected to their decisions, lost his chief of staff and deputy. The Journal also reported that Noem ran confrontational enforcement operations over the objections of longtime immigration officials. The spending approval process held up contracts and grants across DHS, including detention and border-wall money.

glance.what: Publicly accused 279 people of assaulting agents; none of the 181 U.S. citizens among them convicted at trial

what_changed: A Wall Street Journal investigation reviewed more than 100,000 posts made over roughly a year by accounts linked to DHS, ICE, CBP, and senior administration officials during Kristi Noem's tenure as Secretary -- the Journal's graphic of government posts includes two from her own X account -- as part of the administration's social-media campaign defending aggressive immigration enforcement. **The Journal identified 279 people publicly accused by name or identifying detail of assaulting federal immigration or Border Patrol agents. Of those 279, 181 -- about 65% -- were U.S. citizens, not the undocumented immigrants the enforcement campaign is officially aimed at.** The Journal, publishing its findings in March 2026, tracked each identified case through the legal system: close to half of the 181 citizens accused were never charged with assault, and none of them had been convicted at trial. Fifteen people named in government posts had pleaded guilty before trial, ten of them to lesser offenses than the government first charged. The Journal's team separately reviewed more than 200 videos tied to the assault allegations, using both agency body-camera footage and bystander recordings, and found many of the videos cast doubt on the government's own claims that agents had been assaulted. One case the Journal tracked was that of Sydney Lori Reid, a 44-year-old U.S. citizen arrested July 22, 2025, after recording agents at the D.C. jail; videos showed an agent grabbing her and pinning her to a wall, but ICE alleged she had assaulted agents, and a week later ICE's X account posted her name and mug shot with the line 'Assault an officer or agent get arrested. It's not rocket science.' Three grand juries declined to indict her on a felony assault charge, and she was acquitted at trial of the misdemeanor charge prosecutors brought instead, per Robert Reich's summary of the Journal's reporting. The Journal also found, per Reich, that officials had accused 32 U.S. citizens of intentionally using their vehicles as weapons; one pleaded guilty to an assault charge, three had their cases dismissed, and the rest were never charged. Independent DOJ referral data, published by POGO and the Investigative Reporting Workshop on February 24, 2026, before the Journal's investigation, corroborates the charging-failure pattern from a second, official-statistics angle: a record 274 DHS referrals to federal prosecutors in FY2025 with Section 111 (assaulting, resisting or impeding a federal officer) as the lead charge (126 from ICE alone, up from 28 in FY2024), with at least two dozen already dismissed, resulting in acquittal, or rejected by grand juries. By then, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller had posted on X that failed cases in Los Angeles were the result of 'mass judge and jury nullification, deep in blue territory, of slam-dunk assault cases against federal law enforcement.' The National Lawyers Guild called Section 111 "the Government's Offense of Choice" to silence dissent toward immigration operations. The same POGO/IRW report noted that within hours of the Minneapolis shooting of Renee Good, Noem said Good engaged in 'an act of domestic terrorism' by allegedly trying to hit an agent with her SUV, though video appeared to show her turning the car away. Noem also said Alex Pretti 'committed an act of domestic terrorism,' a claim video contradicted; she later said 'We were being relayed information from on the ground from CBP agents and officers that were there,' and at a March 2026 Senate hearing declined to say she had been wrong. A separate New York Times review published July 18, 2026, of more than 550 people charged with assault over encounters with immigration agents found that of 459 resolved cases, 246 ended in guilty pleas, only four trials ended in convictions, and 213 ended in jury acquittals, charges thrown out by judges, or cases withdrawn by prosecutors. On October 6, 2026, ProPublica, which had counted more than 170 U.S. citizens held by immigration agents in the administration's first nine months, published an expanded tally of 506 citizens detained between January 2025 and September 2026, a count it calls an undercount. Of the more than 300 Americans it tracked as detained for allegedly assaulting or obstructing agents, fewer than half were charged in federal court, and in nearly half of the 137 instances in which citizens were charged with federal crimes, the charges were dropped or dismissed. At least 63 Americans were detained while recording agents; ProPublica reported that top DHS officials, including Noem, had claimed that filming ICE agents was interfering with arrests. DHS told ProPublica its enforcement operations are 'highly targeted.'
legal_status: No lawsuit, court ruling or inspector-general finding on DHS's practice of publicly accusing people of assault on social media has been reported in the sources reviewed, and no official has been charged over it. In the underlying cases, the Journal found close to half of the 181 accused citizens were never charged with assault and none had been convicted at trial; 15 people named in government posts pleaded guilty before trial, 10 to lesser offenses. Sydney Lori Reid was charged with felony assault of a federal officer, three grand juries declined to indict her, and she was acquitted at trial of a misdemeanor assault charge. A New York Times review of more than 550 assault prosecutions found 213 of 459 resolved cases ended in jury acquittals, dismissals or withdrawn charges.

human_toll.summary: Hundreds of people, most of them U.S. citizens, were publicly accused by government accounts of assaulting immigration agents, often with names, mug shots and identifying details posted, before any court had ruled; most were never convicted. Per the Journal, they had to explain the accusations to family, friends and employers, and in a few cases their home and workplace addresses were leaked online, drawing death threats. Even those exonerated paid for bail, lawyers and days off work, and Reid said she has become more hesitant about political speech.

glance.what: DHS moved to bar Harvard from enrolling international students; a judge blocked it within a day

what_changed:
On April 16, 2025, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem demanded that Harvard University provide information about "the criminality and misconduct of foreign students on its campus," warning that refusal would result in termination of its Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) certification, per DHS. The request asked for disciplinary records on international students' "illegal," "dangerous," or "violent" activity over five years and for audio and video of these students at protests. Harvard produced records on April 30 and May 14 and says it turned over everything the law requires; DHS called the response insufficient. On May 22, 2025, Noem ordered DHS to terminate Harvard's SEVP certification -- which is required to enroll international students on F-1, J-1, and M-1 visas and is administered by ICE -- citing the records dispute, a "hostile environment" for Jewish students, and "racist" DEI policies. **Without SEVP status, Harvard's more than 7,000 visa-holding students would have had to transfer to another university or lose their ability to stay in the United States legally.** Harvard sued DHS and other agencies the next day, May 23, alleging First Amendment retaliation, Administrative Procedure Act violations, and denial of due process; U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs granted a temporary restraining order within hours. On May 28, DHS served a second, slower-track notice of intent to withdraw the certification, giving Harvard 30 days to respond. On June 4, President Trump signed a proclamation barring entry to international students coming to study at Harvard; Burroughs blocked it as well. On June 20, 2025, she granted a preliminary injunction barring the government from giving the May 22 revocation any effect until the case is decided. DHS then announced administrative subpoenas on July 9, 2025 (the Crimson reported three were served July 8), demanding records, communications, and other documents relevant to immigration-law enforcement since January 1, 2020; Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said, "We tried to do things the easy way with Harvard. Now, through their refusal to cooperate, we have to do things the hard way." On July 29, Harvard said it would comply with a related DHS notice of inspection and subpoena for the I-9 employment forms of thousands of staff, while for now withholding records for jobs open only to students over privacy concerns, as it also fought a separate freeze of billions in federal research funding. On August 6, 2025, government lawyers filed a stipulation that DHS will not enforce the May 22 letter, saying it would "simplify this case and narrow the issues in dispute"; the separate withdrawal process was ongoing at the time. On March 31, 2026, Burroughs stayed the case pending the government's First Circuit appeal of the proclamation injunction. The proclamation expired in December 2025 without being reissued.

Update 2026-10-19: At First Circuit oral argument on October 6, 2026, a Justice Department lawyer said Trump would likely reissue the Harvard proclamation if the court order were lifted, and the judges asked both sides why the court should still rule now that it had expired. No ruling has issued.
legal_status: Harvard sued DHS, ICE, Noem and other agencies and officials in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (No. 1:25-cv-11472) on May 23, 2025, alleging First Amendment retaliation, Administrative Procedure Act violations and denial of procedural due process. Judge Allison D. Burroughs granted a temporary restraining order the same day and a preliminary injunction on June 20, 2025 against the May 22 revocation; on June 23 she separately enjoined the June 4 presidential proclamation. The June 20 injunction left DHS free to pursue withdrawal through the regulatory procedures, "including as executed by issuance of the May 28, 2025 Notice of Intent to Withdraw." On August 6, 2025, the government stipulated that DHS will not enforce the May 22 letter. The government appealed the proclamation injunction to the First Circuit (No. 25-1627), which heard argument on October 6, 2026 and raised whether the appeal is moot; the CourtListener docket shows no appeal of the SEVP injunction. On March 31, 2026, Burroughs stayed the case pending that appeal and denied the government's motion to dismiss as moot, without prejudice. No final judgment.

human_toll.summary: Harvard's international students -- more than 7,000 on visas, about a quarter of the student body per Harvard's lawsuit -- learned days before graduation that they would have to transfer or lose their ability to stay in the U.S. legally. Court orders kept the revocation from taking effect, but the Harvard Crimson reported that international students still met obstacles at consulates, embassies and airports, and at least two were denied papers despite the court's order.

DHS's stated rationale is that Harvard "repeatedly refused" requests for information it says SEVP certification requires, and Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said Harvard "has allowed foreign students to abuse their visa privileges and advocate for violence and terrorism on campus"; the May 22 letter also cited antisemitism and DEI policies. Harvard says it produced every record the law requires it to keep; its lawyer told the appeals court, "Their complaint to us is that we didn't give them documents that we are not required to keep."

The retaliation characterization is Harvard's allegation: DHS disputes it, saying Harvard refused lawful records requests. A court blocked the revocation at the preliminary stage, but there is no final judgment, and the First Circuit appeal concerns the separate proclamation injunction, not the SEVP injunction, and is undecided.

officials.name: Tricia McLaughlin
officials.role: then-Homeland Security spokeswoman; told AP it is "false to say that subpoenas from ICE can simply be ignored" and that noncompliance "may result in serious legal penalties"

status: No lawsuit or court ruling on the landlord subpoenas has been reported. DHS has not said how widely they were issued, and no reporting on their use after July 2025 was found.
date_of_action: 2025-05 (earliest reported subpoena, dated May 1; reported by AP July 2025)
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a broader pattern, also documented in the DHS subpoena-abuse entry, of DHS leaning on the ambiguous enforceability of administrative subpoenas to extract compliance through uncertainty and pressure rather than judicial process, applied here to landlords, third parties holding records on tenants who may never learn the records were sought.

pull_quote: "The danger here is overcompliance. Just because a landlord gets a subpoena, doesn't mean it's a legitimate request." -- Stacy Seicshnaydre, Tulane University law professor, to AP

glance.what: Sent landlords unsigned administrative subpoenas for tenant records, claiming penalties for noncompliance

narrative_override.headline: DHS sent landlords subpoenas for tenant records that no judge signed, and said ignoring them could bring legal penalties.

what_changed: By May 2025, DHS was sending landlords and property managers two-page 'information enforcement subpoenas' demanding tenants' leases, rental applications, forwarding addresses, identification cards and information on other people who lived with them, the Associated Press reported in July 2025 (a report NBC News, Fortune and WBUR republished). The subpoena AP reviewed, shared by Atlanta-area real estate attorney Eric Teusink, is dated May 1, comes from USCIS's Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate and is signed by a USCIS officer, not a judge, yet it threatens that a judge may hold a landlord in contempt of court for failure to comply. A Boston attorney told AP a landlord client had received a voicemail from an ICE official requesting information about a tenant, and a Los Angeles property management CEO said tenants had heard rumors about ICE subpoenas. AP said it is unclear how widely the subpoenas were issued. The National Immigration Law Center says an immigration subpoena 'is not enforceable on its own, unless a court orders you to comply with it,' and Cardozo law professor Lindsay Nash told AP that ICE would first have to file a lawsuit in federal court and get a judge to sign off on enforcement. Some legal experts and property managers told AP that landlords who comply might risk violating the Fair Housing Act, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color or national origin, and critics said the tenants whose records are sought may never know immigration authorities have them. **DHS spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin, without confirming the subpoenas were being issued, said 'it is false to say that subpoenas from ICE can simply be ignored' and that failure to comply 'may result in serious legal penalties,' adding: 'The media needs to stop spreading these lies.'**
legal_status: No lawsuit, charge or court ruling over the landlord subpoenas has been reported. Legal experts quoted by AP say the subpoenas can be enforced only if ICE sues in federal court and a judge orders compliance; no such enforcement action has been reported. Fair Housing Act liability for landlords who comply is a risk alleged by legal experts and property managers, untested in court.

human_toll.summary: Tenants, and other people who lived with them, had their leases, rental applications, identification cards, forwarding addresses and roommate details demanded from their landlords, records that AP noted can include work history, marital status and family relationships; critics said tenants may never learn their records were handed to immigration authorities. Landlords faced subpoenas that threatened contempt of court and a DHS warning of legal penalties, which experts told AP pressures them toward overcompliance.
human_toll.caveat: There is no public count of subpoenas sent, landlords who complied or tenants whose records were disclosed: AP reviewed one subpoena, shared by an Atlanta-area attorney who said several of his clients had received them, and said it is unclear how widely they were issued, and the Boston and Los Angeles accounts are a voicemail and tenant rumors, not confirmed subpoenas. Whether any disclosed records led to arrests or removals is not reported. DHS's stated position is that ICE is authorized to obtain records through specific administrative subpoena authorities and that noncompliance may bring serious legal penalties; DHS said it would not comment on "law enforcement's tactics surrounding ongoing investigations", and the one AP reviewed came from USCIS's fraud directorate, so whether these were fraud inquiries or a tool to locate tenants for removal is not established. Law professor Lindsay Nash told AP that ICE subpoenas predate Trump's first term, though they rose under him and landlords rarely received them before.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence that DHS sent landlords subpoenas for tenant records signed by a USCIS officer rather than a judge, and that DHS publicly said noncompliance may bring serious legal penalties: AP reviewed one subpoena and quoted DHS on the record. title: HHS/ORR Ends Confidentiality Wall Protecting Unaccompanied Migrant Children and Their Sponsors, Sharing Data With ICE and Cutting Legal Aid
status: Ongoing -- ICE data-sharing active; Mother Jones reports ICE sends hundreds of interior children to ORR, some who lived with a parent; Acacia legal-aid contract lapsed July 31, 2026; HHS created an in-house legal division for the children Sept. 29; N. v. HHS appeal argued Sept. 15, no ruling yet
date_of_action: 2025-02-15 (fingerprinting reimposed) through 2026-07-31 (legal-aid contract lapses)
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, ORR reimposed strict fingerprint-based background-check requirements for every adult in a household sponsoring an unaccompanied migrant child -- a policy first introduced in 2018 and later rolled back after it was found to cause mass detention overcrowding and discourage otherwise-qualified sponsors, many of whom are themselves undocumented, from coming forward for fear of their own deportation. In March 2025, the administration went further, issuing an interim final rule, effective March 25, 2025, that struck a provision of ORR's April 2024 Foundational Rule (45 CFR 410.1201(b)) that had kept sponsors' immigration status information from being shared with immigration enforcement specifically so status alone would not deter family reunification; ORR began providing ICE with sponsor and household immigration-status data on request, and no longer barred denying a child's release based on a sponsor's immigration status. Separately, on March 21, 2025, HHS's Office of Refugee Resettlement terminated its contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, worth more than $200 million a year, which funds legal representation for unaccompanied children in immigration court -- U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin (N.D. Cal.) issued a temporary restraining order on April 1, 2025 blocking the termination, and on April 29, 2025 granted a preliminary injunction ordering the funding restored; NBC News reported in mid-April 2025, citing a filing by the plaintiffs' attorneys, that the administration had not complied with the restraining order. Reuters reported on July 28, 2026, citing internal government data it reviewed exclusively, that ORR had shared more than 460,000 'leads' with ICE about unaccompanied children, sponsors, and other household members since January 2025, that more than 12,000 people had been arrested following ORR tips during Trump's second term, and that **the additional vetting requirements had driven the average time a child spends in ORR custody from about 30 days in fiscal year 2024 to 194 days by June 2026, according to ORR figures.** Added 2026-08-17: At a June 11, 2026 news conference, Acting ORR Director Angie Salazar defended the data-sharing change, saying some children released to unvetted sponsors under the prior policy 'were sexually assaulted, others deceased, and some committing heinous crimes,' and framing the change as closing a child-welfare gap rather than an enforcement expansion: 'when the government lacks reliable contact information or an effective means of tracking children, that is a child welfare failure.' Former Biden-era ORR deputy director Jen Smyers countered that 'the claim that children were released to unvetted sponsors is factually inaccurate.' Added 2026-08-30: Separately from the Acacia Center for Justice legal-aid contract case, a second lawsuit -- N. v. HHS (also captioned Diego N. v. HHS), 1:26-cv-00577 (D.D.C., Judge Carl J. Nichols), filed February 23, 2026 -- directly challenges the re-vetting practice at this entry's core: four unaccompanied minors alleged they were 'suddenly uprooted' from living with previously-approved sponsors and held in federal custody without individualized justification after ORR began forcing sponsors to reapply, raising Fifth Amendment due-process and Administrative Procedure Act claims. The court denied plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion on April 30, 2026, finding them unlikely to succeed on the merits; defendants filed a motion to dismiss May 4, 2026, arguing the case was moot after ORR released three of the four named plaintiffs to a parent; plaintiffs filed an interlocutory appeal to the D.C. Circuit May 8, 2026; and the case was stayed pending settlement negotiations as of May 15, 2026. Update 2026-09-01: the district court's May 15 stay order required the parties to file a joint status report within 90 days; in that report, filed Aug. 6, 2026, the parties said settlement talks had ended without a resolution and asked the court to keep the case stayed pending the plaintiffs' D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 26-5157), which was fully briefed, with the plaintiffs' reply brief filed July 31, 2026, and set for argument on Sept. 15, 2026. Separately, the plaintiffs' own complaint alleges that, 'upon information and belief' and as of January 2026, more than 300 children had been separated from previously-approved sponsors and re-referred to ORR under the challenged re-vetting policy -- a scale figure beyond the four named plaintiffs, but sourced only to the plaintiffs' own pleading (not independently corroborated by a government count or a second source) and not independently adjudicated. Update 2026-09-26: ORR's contract with the Acacia Center for Justice lapsed on July 31, 2026, ending funding for a network of nearly 100 legal service providers that Acacia said had served more than 20,000 unaccompanied children; Acacia said HHS had withheld more than $65 million, with payments stopping around November 2025, and PBS NewsHour, reporting the same day, said Acacia claims the administration stopped making the payments late the previous year. On Aug. 6, 2026, Judge Martinez-Olguin ordered HHS to pay the withheld funds, and CBS News reported the next day that payments were being processed. ORR announced on Aug. 6, 2026 that it intended to award a single-source cooperative agreement of up to $150 million to Burke Law Group, a Houston law firm, to represent children in its care; the firm withdrew from consideration on Aug. 11, and ORR published a withdrawal of the notice on Aug. 17. NPR reported on Aug. 12, 2026 that ORR had awarded a no-bid $158 million contract, running Aug. 7, 2026 to Feb. 6, 2027, to Our Rescue, formerly Operation Underground Railroad, and that ORR had been using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to represent children in its care since Aug. 5. The D.C. Circuit (Judges Millett, Pillard and Childs) heard argument in the N. v. HHS appeal on Sept. 15, 2026. Update 2026-10-03: The Guardian reported on Sept. 19, 2026, citing several unnamed sources briefed on the initiatives, that White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller is directing an effort across at least five cabinet-level departments -- HHS, the Department of Homeland Security (including ICE and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services), and the Justice Department, which houses the immigration courts, with the State Department and the Pentagon in more subsidiary roles -- to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children. Sources told the Guardian that ICE officers are present at new in-person appointments in the sponsorship process, that prospective sponsors have been detained shortly before or after a child's scheduled release, that ORR appears to be working with USCIS to rush children's asylum interviews, and that ICE now has access to children's confidential ORR files; sources also said ORR was pushed to adopt tactics meant to increase deportations of children and their family members; these are allegations from unnamed sources, not official findings. The Guardian reported that more than 1,800 children were stuck in ORR custody. Citing an analysis of Justice Department immigration-court data by the advocacy group Mobile Pathways, it reported that **immigration judges have ordered almost 200,000 children removed from the U.S. since January 2025, about 70% of them under the age of 13**, with monthly removal orders for children rising from 7,366 in January 2025 to a peak of 16,750 in July 2026 before easing to 14,744 in August; that count covers all children in immigration court, whether they arrived alone or with family, not only unaccompanied children in ORR care. The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort but said it was not new; spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the agencies were 'working to locate and rescue these children' and reunite them with their families in their home countries, and an HHS spokesperson said 'ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process.' HHS also told the Guardian it had considered detailing military lawyers to represent children in its care but was no longer pursuing that option. Update 2026-10-06: On Oct. 1, 2026, ORR released a memo that identifies six types of fraud in the Biden-era unaccompanied children program -- false or fraudulent identity documents, manipulated photographs, misrepresented or unverifiable addresses, fingerprint-related fraud, failure to disclose household members, and children misrepresenting their age. HHS's announcement says the report concludes that intentional document fraud by some sponsors put children at risk and in some instances released them into dangerous or harmful situations. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the prior administration 'weakened safeguards and prioritized speed over scrutiny' and that HHS is 'restoring rigorous oversight, verifying who takes custody of these children.' These are HHS's own findings, not an independent review. Update 2026-10-11: Mother Jones reported in October 2026 that federal agents have picked up hundreds of immigrant children in the interior of the country and sent them to ORR, which it called 'a vast departure from prior administrations, when interior referrals to the agency were rare.' According to sources familiar with the cases, anywhere from 500 to more than 700 of these children had previously crossed the border alone and spent time in ORR custody, but were living with their sponsors when ICE returned them to the agency -- the 're-referrals' the N. v. HHS lawsuit challenges. Mother Jones also described a second group: children who were never unaccompanied but whom ICE labeled 'unaccompanied' and sent to ORR, such as an 11-year-old Venezuelan boy taken into custody with his father, who had brought him to the U.S. and lived with him, and placed in foster care after the father's arrest. ORR does not systematically track how many such children there are, and DHS did not answer the magazine's questions about them, but a source with knowledge of federal immigration data said they now make up a 'huge chunk' of ORR's caseload. Citing a source familiar with the data, Mother Jones reported that ORR received just 3,500 referrals from July 2025 through May 2026 and that interior referrals were about 20 percent of the total in that period; Jonathan White, who managed ORR's unaccompanied children program in 2017, said interior referrals were between 3 and 5 percent of the total under the Obama administration and the first Trump administration, and many attorneys the magazine interviewed believe they now make up about half of all new ORR cases. Mother Jones compared the practice to the 2018 zero-tolerance family separations at the border. A DHS spokesperson said 'ICE does not separate families,' and an ORR spokesperson said its vetting changes are meant to ensure children are not placed with criminals and that ORR is being 'careful, not slow, because children's lives are at stake.' Update 2026-10-13: On Sept. 29, 2026, HHS published a Federal Register notice, signed by Secretary Kennedy, that creates an Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division in its Office of the General Counsel. Its attorneys are to 'provide direct legal advice and counsel' to unaccompanied children and 'represent individual UAC as counsel in immigration proceedings, including by entering appearances on behalf of UAC before immigration courts,' and the notice says the division works 'independently of' ORR and the Administration for Children and Families. HHS told the AP the division would give the department 'an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support,' but did not say whether it would keep contracting with nongovernmental groups or when the division would be fully operational, and it did not tell Mother Jones when the lawyers would begin work. Under the plan, the children's lawyers, the immigration judges (Justice Department) and the attorneys seeking the children's deportation (DHS) would all be federal employees. Acacia executive director Shaina Aber told the AP that placing children's representation 'inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,' and Kids in Need of Defense president Wendy Young called the new team 'part of a pattern of attacks' on children's representation. Mother Jones wrote that the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act and other federal regulations require that unaccompanied children be assigned independent lawyers; the statute's counsel provision directs HHS to ensure children have counsel 'to the greatest extent practicable' and does not itself use the word 'independent.' Advocates told the AP that children have lately been going to their court hearings without lawyers. Acacia's leaders have said HHS withheld the earlier payments because the network's attorneys refused to hand over sensitive case data on the children, such as medical records and the kinds of legal relief they were seeking; ORR did not respond to States Newsroom's request for comment for that article. The AP reported that the Our Rescue contract has a potential value of up to $244 million; NOTUS, citing the federal contracting database, reported that just over $158 million had been allocated toward it, the figure NPR reported as the contract's value. Mother Jones reported that the Our Rescue award was put on hold after Acacia filed a bid protest, and the AP that the transition has led to short-term arrangements, including a temporary contract with the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants; immigration advocates said in recent court filings, according to Mother Jones, that USCRI was not representing children in court and that its lawyers often sat silently as judges considered the children's cases. Update 2026-10-19: Law360 reported on Sept. 24, 2026 that the Government Accountability Office, in a Sept. 18 decision, denied Acacia's protest of the terms of a new ORR solicitation for children's legal services, finding that ORR had justified requiring invoices to be submitted at the completion of a representation or an identified phase of it, which ORR said ties payments to services actually delivered. Law360 also reported that at a Sept. 8, 2026 evidentiary hearing on whether the administration had violated Judge Martinez-Olguin's order to maintain funding for the children's legal services, ORR acquisitions chief Richard B. Debany acknowledged the government could not quickly secure a long-term replacement after the Acacia contract expired, said he could not specify how many children were unrepresented, and testified that competing bidders' GAO protests had slowed a replacement.

human_toll.summary: A 2024 Biden-era rule barring ORR from sharing sponsors' immigration-status information with enforcement agencies was struck in March 2025 and sponsor vetting was tightened, resulting in a large, quantified increase in enforcement actions against sponsors and household members and, from the added vetting, in the time children spend in federal custody. ORR's legal-aid contract for unaccompanied children, terminated in March 2025 and then ordered restored by a court, lapsed in July 2026 after HHS withheld payments; HHS has since created its own division of federal lawyers to represent the children, which advocates say lacks independence, and advocates say children have lately been going to court hearings without lawyers. A lawsuit also alleges that the related sponsor re-vetting policy has uprooted children from homes with previously-approved sponsors, and Mother Jones reported in October 2026, citing unnamed sources, that ICE has returned 500 to more than 700 such children to ORR and has also sent ORR children of arrested parents as 'unaccompanied', with interior referrals rising to about 20% of ORR's total from July 2025 through May 2026. The Guardian reported in September 2026 that these changes are part of a wider White House-directed push to remove migrant children, as monthly immigration-court removal orders against children more than doubled between January 2025 and mid-2026.
