The 194-day custody figure is ORR's own statistic as reported by Reuters. The 300+ separated-children figure comes only from the plaintiffs' own complaint ('upon information and belief'), is not corroborated by a government count or an independent named source, and has not been adjudicated; Mother Jones' later 500-to-700+ re-referral count is consistent with it but rests on unnamed sources, and the magazine also interviewed attorneys from the National Center for Youth Law, which represents the plaintiffs; the court denied the plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion, finding them unlikely to succeed on the merits. ORR defends the data-sharing change as a child-welfare measure, with its acting director saying some children released to unvetted sponsors under the prior policy 'were sexually assaulted, others deceased, and some committing heinous crimes'; an ORR spokesperson told Mother Jones the agency is being 'careful, not slow, because children's lives are at stake,' a DHS spokesperson said 'ICE does not separate families,' and an HHS spokesperson told the Guardian 'ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process.' The legal-aid cut was not reversed: after a court ordered the funding restored in April 2025, HHS withheld payments from about November 2025 and let the Acacia contract lapse on July 31, 2026. The $65 million figure is Acacia's; the court ordered $65 million paid in August 2026. Acacia said in July 2026 that its network had provided counsel to more than 20,000 children; that figure is not directly comparable to the roughly 26,000 cited in 2025. The almost-200,000 removal-order figure is an advocacy group's analysis of Justice Department data, counts orders rather than completed deportations, and covers all children in immigration court, not only the unaccompanied children in ORR care that the rest of this entry describes; the Guardian's article also once describes the total as more than 200,000. The Guardian's account of Stephen Miller's role rests on unnamed sources. Mother Jones' 20% interior-referral share and 3,500-referral total come from an unnamed source familiar with the data, the 3-5% historical baseline from a former ORR official, and the 'about half' share from attorneys' estimates; no outlet has independently confirmed these figures, and ORR does not systematically track children of arrested parents labeled unaccompanied.

section_summaries.what_changed: ORR shares sponsor data with ICE and tightened vetting; ICE sends hundreds of interior children to ORR; legal aid lapsed and HHS created its own lawyers' division for the children.
section_summaries.confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the policy changes, corroborated by the NYT, Reuters, and Migration Policy Institute.
section_summaries.human_toll: 460,000+ ORR leads to ICE, 12,000+ arrests; custody up from 30 to 194 days; 500-700+ children re-referred; ~200,000 child removal orders; legal aid lapsed, children reportedly in court unrepresented.

what_changed.base: Beginning in February 2025, ORR reimposed strict fingerprint-based background-check requirements for every adult in a household sponsoring an unaccompanied migrant child -- a policy first introduced in 2018 and later rolled back after it was found to cause mass detention overcrowding and discourage otherwise-qualified sponsors, many of whom are themselves undocumented, from coming forward for fear of their own deportation. In March 2025, the administration went further, issuing an interim final rule, effective March 25, 2025, that struck a provision of ORR's April 2024 Foundational Rule (45 CFR 410.1201(b)) that had kept sponsors' immigration status information from being shared with immigration enforcement specifically so status alone would not deter family reunification; ORR began providing ICE with sponsor and household immigration-status data on request, and no longer barred denying a child's release based on a sponsor's immigration status. Separately, on March 21, 2025, HHS's Office of Refugee Resettlement terminated its contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, worth more than $200 million a year, which funds legal representation for unaccompanied children in immigration court -- U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin (N.D. Cal.) issued a temporary restraining order on April 1, 2025 blocking the termination, and on April 29, 2025 granted a preliminary injunction ordering the funding restored; NBC News reported in mid-April 2025, citing a filing by the plaintiffs' attorneys, that the administration had not complied with the restraining order. Reuters reported on July 28, 2026, citing internal government data it reviewed exclusively, that ORR had shared more than 460,000 'leads' with ICE about unaccompanied children, sponsors, and other household members since January 2025, that more than 12,000 people had been arrested following ORR tips during Trump's second term, and that **the additional vetting requirements had driven the average time a child spends in ORR custody from about 30 days in fiscal year 2024 to 194 days by June 2026, according to ORR figures.**

updates.label: Added
updates.text: Added 2026-08-17: At a June 11, 2026 news conference, Acting ORR Director Angie Salazar defended the data-sharing change, saying some children released to unvetted sponsors under the prior policy 'were sexually assaulted, others deceased, and some committing heinous crimes,' and framing the change as closing a child-welfare gap rather than an enforcement expansion: 'when the government lacks reliable contact information or an effective means of tracking children, that is a child welfare failure.' Former Biden-era ORR deputy director Jen Smyers countered that 'the claim that children were released to unvetted sponsors is factually inaccurate.'

updates.label: Added
updates.text: Added 2026-08-30: Separately from the Acacia Center for Justice legal-aid contract case, a second lawsuit -- N. v. HHS (also captioned Diego N. v. HHS), 1:26-cv-00577 (D.D.C., Judge Carl J. Nichols), filed February 23, 2026 -- directly challenges the re-vetting practice at this entry's core: four unaccompanied minors alleged they were 'suddenly uprooted' from living with previously-approved sponsors and held in federal custody without individualized justification after ORR began forcing sponsors to reapply, raising Fifth Amendment due-process and Administrative Procedure Act claims. The court denied plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion on April 30, 2026, finding them unlikely to succeed on the merits; defendants filed a motion to dismiss May 4, 2026, arguing the case was moot after ORR released three of the four named plaintiffs to a parent; plaintiffs filed an interlocutory appeal to the D.C. Circuit May 8, 2026; and the case was stayed pending settlement negotiations as of May 15, 2026.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-01: the district court's May 15 stay order required the parties to file a joint status report within 90 days; in that report, filed Aug. 6, 2026, the parties said settlement talks had ended without a resolution and asked the court to keep the case stayed pending the plaintiffs' D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 26-5157), which was fully briefed, with the plaintiffs' reply brief filed July 31, 2026, and set for argument on Sept. 15, 2026. Separately, the plaintiffs' own complaint alleges that, 'upon information and belief' and as of January 2026, more than 300 children had been separated from previously-approved sponsors and re-referred to ORR under the challenged re-vetting policy -- a scale figure beyond the four named plaintiffs, but sourced only to the plaintiffs' own pleading (not independently corroborated by a government count or a second source) and not independently adjudicated.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-26: ORR's contract with the Acacia Center for Justice lapsed on July 31, 2026, ending funding for a network of nearly 100 legal service providers that Acacia said had served more than 20,000 unaccompanied children; Acacia said HHS had withheld more than $65 million, with payments stopping around November 2025, and PBS NewsHour, reporting the same day, said Acacia claims the administration stopped making the payments late the previous year. On Aug. 6, 2026, Judge Martinez-Olguin ordered HHS to pay the withheld funds, and CBS News reported the next day that payments were being processed. ORR announced on Aug. 6, 2026 that it intended to award a single-source cooperative agreement of up to $150 million to Burke Law Group, a Houston law firm, to represent children in its care; the firm withdrew from consideration on Aug. 11, and ORR published a withdrawal of the notice on Aug. 17. NPR reported on Aug. 12, 2026 that ORR had awarded a no-bid $158 million contract, running Aug. 7, 2026 to Feb. 6, 2027, to Our Rescue, formerly Operation Underground Railroad, and that ORR had been using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to represent children in its care since Aug. 5. The D.C. Circuit (Judges Millett, Pillard and Childs) heard argument in the N. v. HHS appeal on Sept. 15, 2026.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-03: The Guardian reported on Sept. 19, 2026, citing several unnamed sources briefed on the initiatives, that White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller is directing an effort across at least five cabinet-level departments -- HHS, the Department of Homeland Security (including ICE and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services), and the Justice Department, which houses the immigration courts, with the State Department and the Pentagon in more subsidiary roles -- to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children. Sources told the Guardian that ICE officers are present at new in-person appointments in the sponsorship process, that prospective sponsors have been detained shortly before or after a child's scheduled release, that ORR appears to be working with USCIS to rush children's asylum interviews, and that ICE now has access to children's confidential ORR files; sources also said ORR was pushed to adopt tactics meant to increase deportations of children and their family members; these are allegations from unnamed sources, not official findings. The Guardian reported that more than 1,800 children were stuck in ORR custody. Citing an analysis of Justice Department immigration-court data by the advocacy group Mobile Pathways, it reported that **immigration judges have ordered almost 200,000 children removed from the U.S. since January 2025, about 70% of them under the age of 13**, with monthly removal orders for children rising from 7,366 in January 2025 to a peak of 16,750 in July 2026 before easing to 14,744 in August; that count covers all children in immigration court, whether they arrived alone or with family, not only unaccompanied children in ORR care. The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort but said it was not new; spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the agencies were 'working to locate and rescue these children' and reunite them with their families in their home countries, and an HHS spokesperson said 'ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process.' HHS also told the Guardian it had considered detailing military lawyers to represent children in its care but was no longer pursuing that option.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-06: On Oct. 1, 2026, ORR released a memo that identifies six types of fraud in the Biden-era unaccompanied children program -- false or fraudulent identity documents, manipulated photographs, misrepresented or unverifiable addresses, fingerprint-related fraud, failure to disclose household members, and children misrepresenting their age. HHS's announcement says the report concludes that intentional document fraud by some sponsors put children at risk and in some instances released them into dangerous or harmful situations. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the prior administration 'weakened safeguards and prioritized speed over scrutiny' and that HHS is 'restoring rigorous oversight, verifying who takes custody of these children.' These are HHS's own findings, not an independent review.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-11: Mother Jones reported in October 2026 that federal agents have picked up hundreds of immigrant children in the interior of the country and sent them to ORR, which it called 'a vast departure from prior administrations, when interior referrals to the agency were rare.' According to sources familiar with the cases, anywhere from 500 to more than 700 of these children had previously crossed the border alone and spent time in ORR custody, but were living with their sponsors when ICE returned them to the agency -- the 're-referrals' the N. v. HHS lawsuit challenges. Mother Jones also described a second group: children who were never unaccompanied but whom ICE labeled 'unaccompanied' and sent to ORR, such as an 11-year-old Venezuelan boy taken into custody with his father, who had brought him to the U.S. and lived with him, and placed in foster care after the father's arrest. ORR does not systematically track how many such children there are, and DHS did not answer the magazine's questions about them, but a source with knowledge of federal immigration data said they now make up a 'huge chunk' of ORR's caseload. Citing a source familiar with the data, Mother Jones reported that ORR received just 3,500 referrals from July 2025 through May 2026 and that interior referrals were about 20 percent of the total in that period; Jonathan White, who managed ORR's unaccompanied children program in 2017, said interior referrals were between 3 and 5 percent of the total under the Obama administration and the first Trump administration, and many attorneys the magazine interviewed believe they now make up about half of all new ORR cases. Mother Jones compared the practice to the 2018 zero-tolerance family separations at the border. A DHS spokesperson said 'ICE does not separate families,' and an ORR spokesperson said its vetting changes are meant to ensure children are not placed with criminals and that ORR is being 'careful, not slow, because children's lives are at stake.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-13: On Sept. 29, 2026, HHS published a Federal Register notice, signed by Secretary Kennedy, that creates an Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division in its Office of the General Counsel. Its attorneys are to 'provide direct legal advice and counsel' to unaccompanied children and 'represent individual UAC as counsel in immigration proceedings, including by entering appearances on behalf of UAC before immigration courts,' and the notice says the division works 'independently of' ORR and the Administration for Children and Families. HHS told the AP the division would give the department 'an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support,' but did not say whether it would keep contracting with nongovernmental groups or when the division would be fully operational, and it did not tell Mother Jones when the lawyers would begin work. Under the plan, the children's lawyers, the immigration judges (Justice Department) and the attorneys seeking the children's deportation (DHS) would all be federal employees. Acacia executive director Shaina Aber told the AP that placing children's representation 'inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,' and Kids in Need of Defense president Wendy Young called the new team 'part of a pattern of attacks' on children's representation. Mother Jones wrote that the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act and other federal regulations require that unaccompanied children be assigned independent lawyers; the statute's counsel provision directs HHS to ensure children have counsel 'to the greatest extent practicable' and does not itself use the word 'independent.' Advocates told the AP that children have lately been going to their court hearings without lawyers. Acacia's leaders have said HHS withheld the earlier payments because the network's attorneys refused to hand over sensitive case data on the children, such as medical records and the kinds of legal relief they were seeking; ORR did not respond to States Newsroom's request for comment for that article. The AP reported that the Our Rescue contract has a potential value of up to $244 million; NOTUS, citing the federal contracting database, reported that just over $158 million had been allocated toward it, the figure NPR reported as the contract's value. Mother Jones reported that the Our Rescue award was put on hold after Acacia filed a bid protest, and the AP that the transition has led to short-term arrangements, including a temporary contract with the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants; immigration advocates said in recent court filings, according to Mother Jones, that USCRI was not representing children in court and that its lawyers often sat silently as judges considered the children's cases.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-10-19: Law360 reported on Sept. 24, 2026 that the Government Accountability Office, in a Sept. 18 decision, denied Acacia's protest of the terms of a new ORR solicitation for children's legal services, finding that ORR had justified requiring invoices to be submitted at the completion of a representation or an identified phase of it, which ORR said ties payments to services actually delivered. Law360 also reported that at a Sept. 8, 2026 evidentiary hearing on whether the administration had violated Judge Martinez-Olguin's order to maintain funding for the children's legal services, ORR acquisitions chief Richard B. Debany acknowledged the government could not quickly secure a long-term replacement after the Acacia contract expired, said he could not specify how many children were unrepresented, and testified that competing bidders' GAO protests had slowed a replacement.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence on the fingerprinting reimposition and the ICE data-sharing policy change, corroborated by the New York Times, Reuters, and the Migration Policy Institute. HIGH confidence on the March 2025 legal-aid contract termination and its judicial blocking, corroborated by AP, NBC News, and Fox News's contemporaneous coverage, and on the contract's July 31, 2026 lapse, reported by PBS NewsHour and the Acacia Center for Justice. MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the cumulative 460,000-lead/12,000-arrest/194-day figures, which come from Reuters' July 28, 2026 report citing government data rather than an official ORR/ICE public report -- worth rechecking against any official accounting if one is published. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to the underlying policy or figures since last verification; added ORR's own on-record defense (Acting Director Salazar, June 11, 2026) and an outside critic's on-record rebuttal (Smyers) for balance, since the original entry omitted the agency's stated rationale entirely -- these quotes predate this entry's write date and are backfilled context, not a new development.

title: ICE Detained a Harvard Cancer Researcher for Months Over Undeclared Frog Embryos, Disrupting Her Lab's Research
status: Out of custody since June 12, 2025. Three-count criminal case pending in D. Mass.; government objections to a vindictive-prosecution discovery order undecided as of Sept. 24, 2026. A court voided CBP's visa cancellation (Apr. 2026); her removal case was still open as of July 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02-16 (detained at Boston Logan Airport) through 2025-06-12 (released from federal custody after ~4 months); indicted 2025-06-25
what_changed: On February 16, 2025, Kseniia Petrova, a Russian-born researcher at Harvard Medical School's Kirschner Lab (cell and developmental biology, including cancer research), was stopped at Boston's Logan International Airport on returning from France after she did not declare frog embryo samples she was carrying for her lab. A U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer canceled her J-1 visa and declared her inadmissible; she was not permitted to return to France but was instead arrested, detained, and placed in removal proceedings. She was held by ICE in Vermont and then, from the day after she filed a habeas petition in Vermont federal court on February 23, in Louisiana, and the government moved to deport her; her attorneys said she fled Russia over her anti-war protests and faced imprisonment if returned. In April 2025 her attorney said an immigration judge in Louisiana had found the government's initial charging document in the deportation case legally deficient. On May 2, 2025, after the Vermont court had scheduled a May 14 hearing, Homeland Security Investigations headquarters referred her for a criminal investigation, according to a later magistrate judge's order. Prosecutors filed a sealed smuggling complaint in Boston on May 12 and, USA Today reported, unsealed it on May 14 just hours after Petrova first appeared in Vermont federal court on her lawsuit; **the single smuggling count carries up to 20 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.** She was moved into U.S. Marshals custody, and the government argued that the criminal arrest made her habeas petition moot; she was later transferred from Louisiana to Massachusetts. On May 28, U.S. District Judge Christina Reiss ordered her released on bail from immigration custody, but she stayed in criminal custody until June 12, 2025, when prosecutors withdrew their request to detain her and a magistrate judge in Boston released her on conditions after roughly four months in federal custody. Petrova says prosecutors offered to defer the case if she dropped her immigration claims and left the country, and that she declined. On June 25, 2025, a grand jury indicted her on the smuggling count plus one count of concealment of a material fact and one count of false statement. A colleague told NBC News in April 2025 that she had written the scripts to analyze the 100,000 images from the lab's one-of-a-kind microscope, and that without her its research potential could not be realized. On February 20, 2026, the Boston Immigration Court ruled that she could not be admitted because her visa had been canceled. On April 1, 2026, Magistrate Judge Judith Dein ordered the government to produce discovery on Petrova's claims that her prosecution is vindictive and selective, finding enough evidence to warrant it; the government objected, and as of a September 24, 2026 filing its objections were still pending before District Judge Leo Sorokin, with no trial date set. On April 7, 2026, Judge Reiss ruled that CBP had unlawfully canceled Petrova's visa, over the frog embryo samples and for no other reason, and set the cancellation aside; final judgment for Petrova followed on July 30, 2026. On April 24, 2026, U.S. District Judge William Young in Boston ordered the immigration court to act on her renewed request for admission, barred her re-detention for immigration purposes until further court order, and barred her removal while her criminal case is pending; the immigration judge denied the request that day, finding no authority to admit her, and the government appealed Young's order to the First Circuit. She remains in the United States on release conditions set in the criminal case.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the timeline, charges, and rulings, drawn from the CourtListener dockets and court orders plus NBC News, AP, CBS News, GBH, USA Today, The Hill, and PBS. The retaliation claim is Petrova's: a magistrate judge found enough evidence to order discovery on it, which is not a finding that the prosecution was vindictive, and the government's objection is pending. The April 2025 immigration-judge finding is her attorney's account. A federal court did rule the visa cancellation unlawful. DHS says she lied to officers about the samples; Petrova says the written statement CBP had her sign misreported her words, and that question is untried. Petrova is named because she has spoken publicly and is a party in her own court cases; the CBP officer who canceled her visa is not named in any source. Re-verified 2026-10-18: the criminal and mandamus dockets show no new rulings since the government's Sept. 24, 2026 status report.
pull_quote: Prosecutors unsealed the smuggling charge hours after Petrova first appeared in Vermont federal court on her lawsuit; a magistrate judge later ordered discovery on her claim that the prosecution is vindictive.

narrative_override.headline: Senate confirmed Rodney Scott as CBP chief despite unresolved 2010 cover-up allegations.

what_changed: On May 28, 2010, CBP agents detained Anastasio Hernández Rojas, a Mexican father of five who had lived in San Diego for 25 years, as he crossed the border; according to his family's filings before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, agents hit, kicked, tased and smothered him while he lay handcuffed at the San Ysidro Port of Entry, and his death was ruled a homicide. Rodney Scott, later Chief of the U.S. Border Patrol, was then Acting Deputy Chief Patrol Agent in Border Patrol's San Diego Sector, per Sen. Ron Wyden's letter (Wyden and 10News describe him as leading the sector). Wyden's April 23, 2025 letter to DHS, citing those filings, says CBP handled the death through its own Critical Incident Team instead of referring it to outside investigators, delayed handing video to San Diego police and let its recording be taped over, and that Scott signed an administrative subpoena for Hernández Rojas's medical records, which CBP then refused to release to police. CBP's then-head of Internal Affairs called the subpoena "illegal and potentially obstruction of justice" and former Internal Affairs official James Wong called it "improper if not criminal"; Wong later accused Scott of overseeing a "cover-up." At Scott's confirmation hearing to lead CBP, Wyden said CBP officers "taped over the only video copy" of the death and tampered with physical evidence, "according to court documents." Scott denied interfering and called the subpoena standard procedure. The Senate confirmed him as CBP Commissioner on June 18, 2025 by a 51-46 party-line vote.
legal_status: Scott has not been charged; the subpoena and cover-up allegations against him are alleged, and Sen. Wyden requested DHS's unreleased Inspector General report and CBP's Critical Incident Team report on April 23, 2025. No agent was charged in Hernández Rojas's death; DOJ closed the case in 2015, and his family settled with the government for a million dollars. In 2025 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights found the United States responsible, finding agents tortured him, used excessive force and conducted an incomplete and biased investigation, and called for the criminal investigation to be reopened.

human_toll.summary: Anastasio Hernández Rojas died after CBP agents beat and repeatedly tased him while he was handcuffed during his removal at the San Ysidro Port of Entry, leaving a wife and five children. His family spent 15 years seeking accountability; the allegations here are that the investigation into his death was steered to protect the agency.

glance.who: An ICE HSI agent on South Padre Island
glance.what: Shot dead U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez at a traffic scene; DHS did not disclose its role for 11 months

what_changed: Backstory: late on the night before the March 15, 2025 shooting, a crash with several injuries closed a busy intersection on Padre Boulevard in South Padre Island, Texas, and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents from a maritime border enforcement task force, normally focused on transnational criminal organizations at seaports, helped local police and Texas game wardens redirect traffic, per ICE's internal incident report. Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, a U.S. citizen from San Antonio celebrating his birthday, drove up with his friend Joshua Orta as passenger; body-camera footage shows a game warden spotting an open bottle of liquor, an official telling him to pull over, and then someone saying "keep going." **After officers yelled for him to stop and the car halted and then began a slow left turn, HSI Special Agent Jack Stevens fired three shots through the open driver's-side window, according to state records; Martinez was pronounced dead at a Brownsville hospital at 1:27 a.m. on March 15, 2025.** ICE's report says the car "accelerated forward" and struck a second HSI agent, who "wound up on the hood" and was treated for a knee injury and released; neither federal agent wore a body camera. Orta was held in a police car for more than four hours and then interviewed by the Texas Rangers, who led the investigation. Local media reported an officer-involved shooting at the time, but no agency publicly disclosed that an HSI agent fired. In late July 2025, an insurer handling Martinez's life insurance through his employer, Amazon, told his mother, Rachel Reyes, that he would have been charged with a felony had he survived, limiting her claim. In September 2025, Orta gave the family's lawyers a statement, never signed, saying Martinez "did not strike anyone" and that an agent fired without warning. In February 2026, the watchdog American Oversight obtained the ICE incident report through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit, and the Associated Press and Newsweek reported that an ICE agent had killed Martinez. On February 20, 2026, DHS confirmed the shooting and said Martinez "intentionally ran over" an HSI agent, leading another agent to fire "defensive shots"; it did not say why it had made no disclosure for 11 months. On February 21, Orta died in a high-speed crash in San Antonio. On February 25, Cameron County District Attorney Luis V. Saenz presented the case and a grand jury returned a no-bill, declining to indict; an ICE spokesperson said the grand jury "unanimously found no criminality." On March 6, the Texas Department of Public Safety released more than 100 records, including body-camera footage; the New York Times found some footage from key moments missing or grainy, and the family's lawyers said it showed the car "barely moving" and braking when Martinez was shot. On March 24, Reps. Robert Garcia and Greg Casar of the House Oversight Committee asked the DHS Inspector General to investigate the shooting and "any subsequent action taken by HSI and other DHS officials to conceal the facts," requesting a briefing by April 6; no public response was found. In a May 4, 2026 Texas Tribune report, then-Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said in an email that the shooting "was investigated from every possible angle by an independent body, and it cleared our officer." On July 22, 2026, NPR reported that Reyes was still seeking accountability and that her attorney was "exploring all legal options"; no lawsuit by the family has been found. The broader weakening of ICE oversight in which this case figures is covered in TAP's entry on ICE cutting training and vetting while limiting oversight visits.
legal_status: No charges. On February 25, 2026, a Cameron County grand jury declined to indict the HSI agent who fired, returning a no-bill; KSAT reported it found the shooting a justifiable homicide, which is not a court ruling. Reps. Garcia and Casar asked the DHS Inspector General on March 24, 2026 to investigate the shooting and alleged concealment; no OIG investigation has been publicly confirmed. No civil lawsuit by the family has been found; in February 2026 a draft affidavit indicated the family was preparing a wrongful-death suit, and in July its attorney said it was exploring all legal options.

human_toll.summary: Ruben Ray Martinez, a 23-year-old U.S. citizen with no criminal record per his family's lawyers, was shot three times through his car window and died hours later. His mother learned only about a year later that an ICE agent fired, and an insurer cited an alleged felony to limit her life-insurance claim. His friend Joshua Orta, the passenger and only known civilian witness, died in a car crash eleven months later; his family believes learning of ICE's role may have contributed.

human_toll.caveat: The shooting sequence comes from ICE's redacted incident report, state body-camera footage and records, and witness statements, and they conflict. DHS says Martinez "intentionally ran over" an HSI agent and that the other agent fired "defensive shots to protect himself, his fellow agents, and the general public"; the struck agent was treated for a knee injury. The footage does not settle it: the New York Times found key moments missing or grainy, and NPR said it is unclear whether the car struck an agent. Orta told the Rangers he saw an officer "on the hood" but that Martinez "didn't hit him" and "caught his feet." Toxicology showed a blood alcohol level of 0.124, above Texas's 0.08 limit, plus THC and alprazolam; the family's lawyers note he was not stopped for suspected intoxication. The 23-person count comes from House Oversight Democrats.

The agent who fired is named by two independent outlets from official records: Newsweek from a South Padre Island police report and KSAT from Texas DPS records and video; the Texas Tribune names him as one of the two agents from their statements to the Texas Rangers; DHS asked Newsweek not to publish the name, citing threats against agents. The Inspector General request has no public outcome, and no lawsuit was found as of October 19, 2026.

pull_quote: DHS's own contracting officer and lawyers found the agency's contacts with Salus 'created an appearance of impropriety' -- then DHS waived the conflict rules and, two days later, gave the first-time contractor a deal worth up to $915 million.

glance.what: DHS gave a Noem-linked donor's firm a $915M self-deportation deal its lawyers flagged as appearing improper

what_changed: Salus Worldwide Solutions, founded in 2023 by former State Department official William Walters, had never held a federal contract when it sent DHS an unsolicited proposal in early 2025 to run what became the administration's 'self-deportation' program, Project Homecoming, which pays immigrants' plane fares and a stipend to leave the country. According to a May 2026 Court of Federal Claims opinion, DHS employees met and emailed with Salus about the requirement from February through April 2025, and DHS's contracting officer and Office of General Counsel found that those contacts raised potential organizational conflicts of interest and **'created an appearance of impropriety'**; DHS's head of contracting waived the conflict rules, citing the program's urgency. DHS then ran a limited competition under the 'unusual and compelling urgency' exception: it met six vendors it had selected on May 13, 2025, issued the request for proposals on May 15, took proposals on May 19, and on **May 20, 2025 awarded Salus a contract with an expected maximum value of $915 million**, overriding a rival's protest stay the same day. Federal spending records show $748 million obligated on the main delivery order and an end date of November 21, 2026; The New York Times has described the contract as worth nearly $700 million. Walters gave $10,000 in October 2024 to a political committee tied to Noem, and his other company, Daedalus Aviation, later sold DHS aircraft under a separate no-bid contract. In March 2026, NBC News reported, citing one person familiar with the discussions, that in September 2025 a Salus representative told a marketing firm it would have to hire a consultant tied to Corey Lewandowski, then a top adviser to Noem, to work on a planned $20 million contract for a DHS agency, saying 'we need to make sure we are properly thanking the person who gave it to us' (NBC said that contract was not ultimately awarded to Salus); Salus called the account 'entirely false' and Lewandowski called it 'patently false.' Senators and House Oversight Democrats then demanded Salus's records on Lewandowski. In May 2026 the court dismissed the rival's challenge for lack of standing; in denying a request to notice congressional inquiries, it said that despite concerns it raised at oral argument about how DHS ran the procurement, the record showed no evidence of bad faith or unfair dealings and DHS had acted properly. DHS, now under Secretary Markwayne Mullin, gave Salus a $200 million six-month extension that month; Rep. Bennie Thompson demanded in July that the contract be canceled, saying Salus is part of the inspector general's review of Lewandowski. In late September 2026, DHS awarded the follow-on contract, worth up to $2.062 billion over three years, to another company, Response AI Solutions; Salus protested the award, with a decision due by January 11, 2027.
legal_status: Sued: rival CSI Aviation's bid protest (CSI Aviation v. United States, Court of Federal Claims No. 25-1338C) was dismissed in May 2026 for lack of standing; in denying a judicial-notice request the court said the record showed no evidence of bad faith or unfair dealings. Salus has protested DHS's September 2026 award of the follow-on contract to Response AI Solutions, with a decision due Jan. 11, 2027. The payment request involving a Lewandowski-linked consultant is alleged, denied and unadjudicated; senators said it would, if true, violate federal bribery and procurement-integrity laws. Per Rep. Bennie Thompson, Salus is part of a DHS inspector general review of whether Lewandowski accepted kickbacks (under investigation; no finding reported). No charges have been reported.

human_toll.summary: Two groups bear the cost. Taxpayers funded a first-time contractor's deal with a $915 million ceiling, $748 million obligated and a $200 million extension, while a sworn Salus filing showed 17,406 completed stipends as of Dec. 1, 2025, against company projections of 276,000 removals in the first year. Detained immigrants are the people the contract targets: Salus's two-person enrollment teams sign people up to self-deport inside ICE detention, having entered at least 50 facilities by early July 2026, and attorneys for detainees say the choice offered in detention can be coercive.

human_toll.caveat: The award figures come from the court record and USAspending.gov and are firm; outlets differ on size because some use the $915 million ceiling and The New York Times says nearly $700 million. Performance numbers conflict: the sworn December filing shows 17,406 completed stipends, while Salus says it has helped over 130,000 people leave (137,000 by Aug. 3, 2026) and saved taxpayers over $2.2 billion, figures it has not documented publicly. None of the numbers show what happened to people after they left or how many signed while detained. The coercion concern rests on detainees' attorneys; a DHS spokesperson called it 'categorically false [that] we would pressure someone to self-deport,' and Salus calls its program a more humane alternative to prolonged detention. DHS's and Salus's stated case on the award: the President's May 2025 Project Homecoming proclamation created a real urgency that justified a limited competition; the contracting officer who flagged the appearance issue also concluded the Salus contacts 'were not irregular or improper' and the conflict rules were waived with mitigation steps; Salus was rated the only 'high confidence' technical offer at the lowest evaluated price; DHS's general counsel's office told The Washington Post it reviewed Salus's interactions and found no legal violations; and a federal judge found no evidence of bad faith and said DHS's pivot to a competition seemed to mitigate even the appearance of impropriety. On the Lewandowski account, Salus's lawyer says every marketing firm it contacted confirmed no such discussion took place; a Daedalus spokesman said Walters was unaware the committee he gave to was tied to Noem; and Walters blames the criticism on rival detention and charter contractors.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on how the contract was awarded: the limited competition, the timetable, the $915 million expected maximum value and DHS's internal appearance-of-impropriety finding come from a federal court opinion based on the agency record, and obligations come from USAspending.gov. Outlets describe the size differently: up to $915 million (MS NOW, using the ceiling) and nearly $700 million (The New York Times); federal records show $748 million obligated. Several outlets and senators call it 'no-bid,' but the court record shows a days-long limited competition with four offers, not a sole-source award. LOW-to-MODERATE confidence on the Lewandowski link: it rests on one anonymous source in NBC News's reporting, is denied by Salus and Lewandowski, and is unadjudicated. The $200 million extension and performance figures come from PunchUp/Daily Beast reporting. No source shows Noem personally approved the award, and no criminal or inspector general finding has been reported. The favoritism reading is contested: the court's no-bad-faith remarks came in denying a judicial-notice request after it dismissed the case on standing, not in a ruling on the award's merits, while DHS, Salus and DHS's general counsel's office say the award was proper. Salus's self-deportation totals are its own unverified claims, and the coercion concern comes from detainees' attorneys and is denied by DHS.

what_changed:
On June 11, 2025, Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate, head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, issued a memo making denaturalization one of the division's top five enforcement priorities: "The Civil Division shall prioritize and maximally pursue denaturalization proceedings in all cases permitted by law and supported by the evidence." The memo listed priority categories but said "These categories do not limit the Civil Division from pursuing any particular case." In April 2026, the New York Times reported that DOJ had singled out 384 naturalized citizens for possible denaturalization and, citing an official familiar with an internal briefing, that attorneys in 39 regional offices would soon be assigned to bring the cases; why those 384 were chosen was unclear. DOJ said it was pursuing "the highest volume of denaturalization referrals in history, thanks to close partnerships with DHS and USCIS," and Axios reported that USCIS lawyers were temporarily moved to U.S. attorneys' offices to work on the cases. A DOJ spokesperson later told Bloomberg Law the administration had a goal of filing at least 250 cases by October.

The filings then sped up. DOJ announced on August 3, 2026 that it had filed 25 complaints between July 20 and August 3, and 123 civil denaturalization complaints since January 20, 2025, "the most in recorded history"; Shumate called it "the largest denaturalization surge in recorded history." On October 5, DOJ announced that it had filed **denaturalization actions against 40 more people between August 21 and October 2, which it called the largest such filing in a single period under the Trump administration.** Attorney General Todd Blanche said "Today's announcement marks the largest denaturalization effort in modern history," and Shumate said "Every single one of these individuals lied their way into U.S. citizenship." According to the department's list, the defendants are 26 to 76 years old and come from 21 countries, including nine from Mexico and four from Pakistan, and the suits were filed in 19 federal districts. Some cases involve people convicted of espionage, voluntary manslaughter or sexual offenses against minors, such as former Navy sailor Jinchao Wei, sentenced to 200 months for espionage-related crimes. Others rest mainly on alleged immigration or naturalization fraud, such as false identities, concealed deportation orders or fraudulent marriages. One defendant, Walid Osman, denies the allegations; his lawyer told USA TODAY the filing contained errors and speculation.

DOJ itself says the claims are allegations only and that no liability has been determined. The government must prove in federal court that citizenship was illegally procured or obtained by concealing a material fact or by willful misrepresentation; in Maslenjak v. United States (2017), the Supreme Court held that an illegal act in the naturalization process must have played a role in obtaining citizenship. The DOJ office that handles these cases has lost roughly a third of its attorneys since January 2025, Bloomberg Law reported. According to the Brennan Center, the government filed about 11 denaturalization cases a year from 1990 to 2017. In June 2026, an NPR review of 34 publicly announced cases found that in many of them the defendant had no lawyer, and some ended in revocation with minimal or no court appearance by the defendant. Law professor Cassandra Robertson told NPR that "The denaturalization efforts are an attempt to suppress the political speech of naturalized citizens"; Boston College's Daniel Kanstroom said protections for people facing denaturalization "are pretty robust."
legal_status: No court has ruled on any of the 40 suits DOJ filed August 21 to October 2, 2026; each is a civil complaint that DOJ says states "allegations only." Defendant Walid Osman denies the allegations, and his lawyer told USA TODAY he will contest the case. Earlier suits in the drive have ended in revocation in some cases: NPR counted 11 revocations among 34 cases it reviewed in spring 2026. TAP found no reported lawsuit challenging the June 2025 memo or the filing goal itself.

human_toll.summary: Naturalized U.S. citizens sued by the Justice Department to revoke their citizenship: 40 in the six weeks to October 2, 2026, aged 26 to 76 and from 21 countries, and more than 200 to date by a DOJ spokesperson's count. A lost case means losing citizenship. NPR found that in many earlier cases the defendant had no lawyer, and some citizenships were revoked with little or no court appearance by the defendant. A former DOJ attorney told NPR that lawyers were pressed to generate cases quickly, even over minor paperwork errors, and critics warn the threat chills the speech of the estimated 24 million naturalized citizens.

what_changed: On January 13, 2026, in a speech at the Detroit Economic Club, **Trump said: 'We're also going to revoke the citizenship of any naturalized immigrant from Somalia or anywhere else who is convicted of defrauding our citizens,' Reuters reported.** Two weeks earlier, on December 31, 2025, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on Fox & Friends that the Department of Homeland Security and the State Department were 'looking at' revoking the citizenship of people of Somali descent if they are convicted in the federal fraud probe in Minnesota (The Hill, Al Jazeera); The National News Desk reported she described a joint State Department-DHS effort to determine the steps needed and said the administration is 'not afraid to use denaturalization.' The same morning Trump wrote on Truth Social that 'much of Minnesota Fraud, up to 90%, is caused by people that came into our Country, illegally, from Somalia' -- though, per The National News Desk, the vast majority of the Somali-descent defendants are U.S. citizens. In a New York Times interview reported by Newsweek, Trump said of Somali-Americans, 'I would do it in a heartbeat if they were dishonest,' and 'I think that many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country,' while saying the effort would not be limited to Somalis. The fraud at issue includes the Feeding Our Future child-nutrition case, in which, the U.S. Attorney's Office for Minnesota said, defendants falsely claimed to have served 91 million meals and fraudulently received nearly $250 million in federal funds. Of the 98 people DOJ had charged in its Minnesota fraud probe dating to 2022, 85 are of Somali descent (The Hill; Attorney General Pam Bondi gave the same figures, per Al Jazeera); the scheme's convicted ringleader is white, The Hill noted. The threat rests on an existing, nationality-neutral DOJ policy: a June 11, 2025 Civil Division memo from Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate stating that the division 'shall prioritize and maximally pursue denaturalization proceedings in all cases permitted by law and supported by the evidence,' with priorities that include fraud against individuals or the government, such as PPP loan or Medicaid fraud (NPR). Newsweek reported that mid-December 2025 guidance asked USCIS field offices to supply DOJ with 100-200 denaturalization cases a month in fiscal 2026. Experts cited by Newsweek say focusing denaturalization on a single nationality would likely face legal challenges, and a former USCIS official told Newsweek it would raise due-process and equal-protection problems; legal experts quoted by The National News Desk expect 'significant' court challenges to denaturalization efforts generally. No denaturalization case citing the Minnesota fraud or the announcement has been reported. On June 3, 2026, DOJ sued in federal court in Minnesota to revoke the citizenship of Abdikadir Ali Kadiye, who pleaded guilty in 2023 to wire fraud in the Feeding Our Future case; the complaint alleges he applied for immigration benefits under two identities in the late 1990s and 'illegally procured his naturalization,' and, per MPR News, neither it nor DOJ's news release mentions his fraud conviction. DOJ listed USCIS and ICE as assisting in that round of cases. MPR News reported Kadiye is at least the second Minnesotan targeted: in May, DOJ began proceedings against Salah Osman Ahmed, who pleaded guilty in 2009 to providing material support to al-Shabab. Separately, DHS announced plans to end Temporary Protected Status for Somalis in the U.S., a related action affecting non-citizens (Straight Arrow News).
legal_status: No court has ruled on, and no lawsuit has been reported against, the announced review of Somali-Americans' citizenship. DOJ sued on June 3, 2026 (D. Minn., No. 0:26-cv-02832) to revoke Feeding Our Future defendant Abdikadir Ali Kadiye's naturalization on alleged identity-fraud grounds; those allegations are unproven and no ruling has been reported. Legal experts say a nationality-focused effort would face due-process and equal-protection challenges; that is an argument, not a finding.

human_toll.summary: Somali-American naturalized citizens, many of them in Minnesota, were publicly named by the President and his press secretary as a group whose citizenship the administration was reviewing, on top of DHS's announced end of TPS for Somali non-citizens. One Feeding Our Future defendant, Abdikadir Ali Kadiye, now faces a denaturalization suit, though on immigration identity-fraud grounds rather than his fraud conviction. No one is reported to have lost citizenship under the announced fraud-conviction basis.

pull_quote: "[T]his payment used funding from the Migration and Refugee Assistance account making this the first ever government-to-government transfer of such funds, which are intended to respond to global refugee and humanitarian crises." -- Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the $7.5 million payment to Equatorial Guinea, Nov. 10, 2025

glance.what: Pledged $410M+ for deportation deals, paying some governments from its refugee-aid account

what_changed:
The State Department's Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration (PRM) had been, in the words of its top official Andrew Veprek, a "humanitarian assistance" office with a budget of about $4 billion a year that "focused on bringing people to the United States." Under the second Trump administration, money from the bureau's Migration and Refugee Assistance (MRA) account was redirected toward deportation. On May 7, 2025, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau signed a determination under the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962 that assistance to migrants "without legal basis to remain in the United States to voluntarily return to their country of origin or country of legal status will contribute to the foreign policy interests of the United States" (published in the Federal Register on May 30). On June 4, 2025, a State Department spokesperson told Reuters that the department had moved $250 million to the Department of Homeland Security "to provide a free flight home and an exit bonus to encourage and assist illegal aliens to voluntarily depart the United States" under DHS's Project Homecoming; Reuters reported that the money came from the MRA account. Elizabeth Campbell, a former deputy assistant secretary of state, said those funds had historically been used "to provide protection to vulnerable people" overseas and to resettle refugees in the U.S.

In 2025 the department also created an Office of Remigration, a division of about 15 employees inside PRM led by Christian Ehrhardt, a career Diplomatic Security officer, to negotiate and fund agreements under which other countries accept people deported from the United States who are not their citizens. After the July 2025 State Department layoffs, staff of PRM's office for humanitarian programs in the Caribbean and Latin America were reassigned to it, The Washington Post reported. One of the office's first assignments, in October 2025, was a $7.5 million deal for Equatorial Guinea to accept up to 250 third-country nationals. Federal spending records show a $7.5 million award to Equatorial Guinea dated October 29, 2025, described as for the country's "humanitarian and migration-related needs to be used for 'assistance to or on behalf of refugees,'" and listed under PRM's Overseas Refugee Assistance Programs for Africa. An identically worded $7.5 million award to Palau, dated December 29, 2025, is charged to the Migration and Refugee Assistance account. In a November 10, 2025 letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote that the Equatorial Guinea payment "used funding from the Migration and Refugee Assistance account making this the first ever government-to-government transfer of such funds, which are intended to respond to global refugee and humanitarian crises." She asked how it was a permissible use of an account "meant to assist refugees overseas."

On September 21, 2026, The Washington Post, reporting as part of a consortium of 26 media organizations organized by the Paris-based nonprofit Forbidden Stories, said internal State Department records showed the administration had authorized or pledged at least $410 million to facilitate third-country deportation agreements with 31 countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America, as of the end of June 2026. That total comprised about $81 million in direct payments to 13 foreign governments, $179 million in grants to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), $124 million to the U.N. Refugee Agency (UNHCR), and about $27 million to other organizations. According to the Post, officials determined they could speed up the payments by invoking a provision of the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act that lets the executive branch bypass statutory foreign-aid restrictions to fund crucial programs for refugees; former State Department staffers called this a perversion of Congress's intent to ensure urgent, life-saving humanitarian assistance. One former official said "the whole point was to circumvent [congressional] notification that money was being sent to a government known to be corrupt." The grants to IOM and UNHCR were negotiated by foreign governments in connection with their deportation deals and have largely replaced the voluntary contributions the U.S. traditionally made to the two agencies, the Post reported; a current U.S. official called them "sweeteners." The Central African Republic deal, for example, included $85 million for IOM, $60 million of it for "community stabilization" such as road building. The administration had already cut its regular contributions to IOM and to U.N. refugee programs in its 2025 foreign-aid review, which the Post said left them with budget shortfalls of 30 percent and 24 percent, respectively. "We're not giving funding to UNHCR and IOM as we were in the past ... We're only giving funding for the most part linked to the agreements," a current U.S. official told the Post, Forbidden Stories reported.

Most of the deportation slots the deals pay for remained unfilled, according to the records: only three people had been sent to Palau under its $7.5 million agreement to accept up to 75. **Deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea under the first deal the office processed have alleged, through their lawyers, that they were beaten by armed guards, denied food and given inadequate medical care while held in a decommissioned hotel in Malabo.** Equatorial Guinea's government denied the abuse allegations, and PRM officials who visited wrote that claims of refoulement were "hard to substantiate."

The State Department did not answer the Post's detailed questions, saying in a statement that the U.S. would use "all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country," and said the Post had mischaracterized the work of Veprek, Ehrhardt and PRM official Spencer Chretien. Administration officials say third-country deportations are the only way to remove some migrants whose home countries refuse to take them back or who are protected by law from being returned there. The Post reported that the agreements were secured under the orders of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, and that Miller and Veprek are the key drivers of the policy; former officials said Veprek effectively directed PRM from the State Department counselor's office before formally leading it. Deputy Secretary Landau, not Secretary Rubio, has been involved in negotiating the agreements and traveled to Palau for talks on a deal, current and former officials told the Post. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has struggled to find migrants who fit the deals' requirements, and deportation flights are often sparsely populated, people with knowledge of the situation told the Post. "We have changed the orientation of the bureau completely," Veprek said at an April event at the Center for Immigration Studies; "Now, we are focused on implementing the president's immigration agenda." Veprek has since been promoted to oversee all U.S. foreign assistance and humanitarian affairs. On September 28, 2026, President Trump nominated Ehrhardt to be ambassador to Cameroon, which the State Department records list as an operational deportation partner with $30 million pledged to organizations.

These figures differ in scope from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democratic staff's estimate of at least $32.3 million paid to five governments through January 2026: the Post's $81 million covers direct payments to 13 governments as of June 2026, and its $410 million total also counts grants to international organizations.
legal_status: No lawsuit, court ruling or inspector-general review of the use of refugee-assistance funds for the deals was identified; Sen. Shaheen questioned the Equatorial Guinea payment in a Nov. 10, 2025 letter to Secretary Rubio. The third-country removals the deals enable are the subject of D.V.D. v. DHS, a class action in which a federal appeals court on Sept. 18, 2026 largely upheld a ruling that the practice is unlawful; on Sept. 29, 2026 the Supreme Court stayed the district court's judgment and agreed to hear the case, with argument set for Dec. 9, 2026. Lawyers for deportees held in Equatorial Guinea filed a complaint with the African Union's main human rights body in June 2026, alleging refoulement, and human rights lawyers have sued Eswatini's government over its deal.

human_toll.summary: Money Congress appropriated to help refugees and people displaced by war and disaster has gone to deportation: $250 million of Migration and Refugee Assistance funds went to DHS for voluntary-departure flights and exit payments, and $7.5 million payments each to Equatorial Guinea and Palau for accepting deportees were drawn from refugee-assistance funds. Those payments are part of at least $410 million the State Department authorized or pledged for third-country deportation deals as of June 2026; the Post reported that officials determined they could speed payments by invoking a refugee-assistance law provision, but no source says how much of the $410 million came from the refugee account. U.S. grants to IOM and the U.N. Refugee Agency, which have largely replaced the regular contributions the U.S. once made to them, are now tied to those deals, according to current and former officials and people familiar with the deals; earlier, broader U.S. aid cuts had left IOM and U.N. refugee programs with shortfalls of 30% and 24%. No source counts how many refugees lost assistance as a result. Deportees sent under the first deal allege beatings and denial of food in detention in Equatorial Guinea, which its government denies.

what_changed:
A Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democratic staff report said the total cost of the Trump administration's third-country deportations -- sending migrants to nations other than their own, where they typically have no prior connection, rather than to their countries of origin -- was unknown but likely upward of $40 million through January 2026, as immigration officials expanded the practice over the prior year. That total comprised at least $32.3 million paid directly to five governments, at least $7.2 million on flights to at least ten third countries, and $307,000 to house deportees on a U.S. military base in Djibouti. The report identified payments ranging from $4.7 million to $7.5 million made to the five countries (Equatorial Guinea, Rwanda, El Salvador, Eswatini, and Palau) in exchange for accepting deportees, which together had received roughly 300 people as of January 2026: El Salvador about 250 Venezuelan nationals, and the other four far fewer (29 to Equatorial Guinea, 15 to Eswatini, 7 to Rwanda, and none to Palau). The report estimated the cost per migrant (payment plus flights) at about $1.1 million for Rwanda ($7.5 million plus an estimated $601,864 in flights, for seven people), $413,333 for Eswatini, $282,126 for Equatorial Guinea and $20,755 for El Salvador, and said the administration 'has paid at least one country more than $1 million per third country national received.' DHS itself had said in a May 5, 2025 release that 'the average cost to arrest, detain, and remove an illegal alien is $17,121.' The report also said that 'in many cases, migrants could have been returned directly to their home countries, avoiding costly third country deportations': as of January 2026, more than 80 percent of the migrants sent to the paid countries had returned to their country of origin or were in the process of doing so, and in some cases the U.S. paid to fly migrants to a third country and later paid again to fly them home. It said the money went to foreign governments 'including those with records of corruption, human rights abuses and human trafficking'; the State Department's own 2023 human rights reports on Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea and Eswatini each cite credible reports of arbitrary or unlawful killings, including extrajudicial killings, and of political prisoners or detainees. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the committee's top Democrat, characterized the practice as the 'epitome' of 'fraud, waste and abuse.' State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott did not comment directly on the report's figures, saying it 'only underlines much of the unprecedented work that the Trump administration has done to enforce our immigration laws,' ABC News reported.

Eswatini was itself an early, closely watched test case of the practice: **on July 16, 2025, five men (of Vietnamese, Laotian, Yemeni, Cuban, and Jamaican nationality, all convicted of crimes in the U.S.) were flown to Eswatini's capital Mbabane on a U.S. military plane and held in solitary confinement for an undetermined time, under a secretive deal the U.S. and Eswatini governments did not publicly disclose in advance.** The lack of transparency prompted about 150 women, organized by the Eswatini Women's Movement, to protest outside the U.S. embassy, and a coalition of seven women's groups delivered a petition demanding the deportees' return and questioning the deal's legality; Eswatini's largest opposition party, the People's United Democratic Movement (Pudemo), separately called it 'human trafficking disguised as a deportation deal,' The Guardian reported. A later court hearing in Eswatini over four of the men was delayed when the presiding judge failed to appear.

On February 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) ruled in D.V.D. v. DHS that the administration's expedited third-country removal practice is unlawful, violating due-process guarantees and the Convention Against Torture's non-refoulement principle, because it gave migrants no meaningful opportunity to contest removal to a country where they feared persecution or torture. The Supreme Court had twice stayed an earlier, broader version of Murphy's injunction in 2025 without ruling on the merits. The Trump administration (DOJ) appealed Murphy's February ruling to the First Circuit, which stayed the district court's decision on March 16, 2026, allowing third-country deportations to continue while the appeal on the merits proceeded.

Separately, on April 7, 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, Rep. Delia Ramirez, and Rep. Troy Carter sent a letter demanding that the DHS and State Department inspectors general investigate the deportation program; DHS's Office of Inspector General responded that a government shutdown at the time prevented it from opening new reviews. The April 7 letter said the administration had entered agreements with 27 countries to receive non-nationals deported from the United States; that as of early March 2026, ICE had over 500 people in its custody slated for third-country deportations; and that DHS had signaled it had its sights on deporting over 8,000 people to third countries. It also cited the Senate report's figure of over $32 million paid to the five countries (El Salvador, Rwanda, Eswatini, Equatorial Guinea, and Palau) -- the direct-payments part of the report's roughly $40 million total, not a separate estimate. Sen. Warren publicized the letter on April 8, 2026, and Rep. Ramirez issued her own press release on the same letter on April 16, 2026.

No further Inspector General action was identified on the Warren/Van Hollen/Ramirez/Carter April 7, 2026 request for a DHS/State Inspector General investigation beyond DHS OIG's shutdown-related response. The DHS-specific government shutdown that IG cited ended April 30, 2026; as of late August 2026, roughly four months later, no third-country-removal review appeared among DHS OIG's listed audits, inspections, or evaluations, nor was any State OIG review of the same subject identified -- the stated blocker has lapsed with no confirmed follow-through.

Merits briefing on the appeal was completed on April 20, 2026, and the First Circuit held oral argument on the merits appeal (case 26-1212) on May 13, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. in the En Banc Courtroom of the Moakley U.S. Courthouse in Boston. On September 18, 2026, a First Circuit panel (Judges Montecalvo, Howard and Aframe, in an opinion by Judge Aframe) largely affirmed Murphy's judgment: the government must give class members effective notice of a planned third-country removal and a meaningful opportunity to contest it on the ground that they reasonably fear persecution or torture there. The panel vacated only, for lack of standing, the declarations that DHS must first try to remove people to countries they designated or of which they are citizens. On September 23, after the plaintiffs told the court that DHS planned to deport class members to Burundi, Rwanda and the Central African Republic the next day, the First Circuit dissolved its March 16 stay, putting Murphy's ruling back into effect. The government asked the Supreme Court for a stay the next day, telling the justices it had already canceled a flight carrying 70 people to three countries. On September 29, 2026, the Supreme Court, in an unsigned order, stayed Murphy's February 25, 2026 order and judgment until it decides the case, treated the government's application as a petition for review and granted it, and set argument for its December 2026 session on whether the district court had jurisdiction, whether it could grant classwide relief, and whether the government's third-country removal guidance is lawful under the removal statute, the Due Process Clause and the law implementing the Convention Against Torture. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have denied the stay. The Court then set argument for December 9, 2026, with the government's opening brief due October 23 and the challengers' brief due November 16. The order lets third-country removals proceed without the notice and fear screening the lower courts required; it does not decide the legality question, which remains unresolved rather than settled in the administration's favor, and a decision would likely come by summer 2027, CBS News reported. **The challengers told the Supreme Court that removed class members have faced indefinite detention by foreign governments, onward removal to countries they had fled, disappearance, and beatings and sexual assault in detention**, and, citing a Washington Post estimate, that DHS had deported more than 25,000 people to at least 28 third countries in 2025 and 2026; a tracker run by Refugees International and Human Rights First likewise counts more than 25,000 people sent to at least 29 countries. Those counts cover every third-country removal, far beyond the roughly 300 sent to the five paid countries: the Migration Policy Institute, as reported by NBC News, put 2025 third-country deportations at about 15,000, with Mexico receiving the majority. DHS's own data, obtained by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA and analysed by Al Jazeera in October 2026, includes more than 16,000 third-country deportation cases from January 2025 through August 2026, a count Al Jazeera said is likely an undercount.

human_toll.summary: The practice sends migrants to countries where they typically have no prior connection -- five men deported to Eswatini on July 16, 2025, all convicted of crimes in the U.S., were held in solitary confinement for an undetermined time -- and a federal judge ruled the expedited practice unlawful because it gave migrants no meaningful opportunity to contest removal to a country where they feared persecution or torture, a ruling the First Circuit largely affirmed in September 2026 but the Supreme Court stayed on September 29, 2026 pending December argument, so deportations continue. The challengers, citing a Washington Post estimate, said DHS had deported more than 25,000 people to at least 28 third countries in 2025 and 2026 (most of them to Mexico, per other counts), and that removed class members have faced indefinite detention and abuse in custody abroad; DHS's own data, analysed by Al Jazeera, shows more than 16,000 such cases from January 2025 through August 2026, likely an undercount. An April 7, 2026 congressional letter said that as of early March 2026 ICE held more than 500 people in custody slated for third-country removal and DHS had signaled intent to deport more than 8,000 people to third countries. On cost, a Senate Democratic staff report put the total through January 2026 at likely upward of $40 million, including more than $32 million paid directly to five countries that had received roughly 300 migrants (the payments figure the April letter cites). The report estimated the cost per migrant at about $1.1 million for Rwanda, $413,333 for Eswatini and $282,126 for Equatorial Guinea, and $20,755 for El Salvador, which took about 250 of the ~300. DHS separately put its own average cost to arrest, detain and remove a person at $17,121 (May 2025), close to the El Salvador figure. The report argued that in many cases migrants 'could have been returned directly to their home countries, avoiding costly third country deportations': more than 80% of those sent to the paid countries had returned or were returning home by January 2026. The payments also went to governments -- Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea and Eswatini among them -- for which the State Department's own 2023 human rights reports cite credible reports of extrajudicial killings.

human_toll.caveat: The cost figures come from a Democratic-staff Senate Foreign Relations Committee report, not a GAO or IG audit; its payment figures come from federal spending data and the agreements themselves, and its flight costs are staff estimates from flight-tracking data and published charter rates; the 'fraud, waste and abuse' characterization is the minority's own. A State Department spokesman did not dispute the dollar figures directly. The report calls the total unknown but likely upward of $40 million, including flights to at least ten countries, while ~300 counts only those sent to the five paid countries; DHS's $17,121 average (arrest, detention and removal) is a rough benchmark, not like-for-like. The 8,000+ figure is DHS's signaled intent, not completed removals. The 25,000+ count is an outside estimate and the 16,000+ count is DHS's own data, which Al Jazeera calls likely incomplete; both cover all third-country removals, including to Mexico, and are not comparable to the ~300 sent to the five paid countries. The harms to removed class members are the challengers' allegations. The administration says these deals are needed because home countries refuse to take their nationals back (the Senate report says evidence contradicts this), and DHS's Tricia McLaughlin, saying the five men sent to Eswatini had been convicted of crimes including child rape and murder, called them 'so uniquely barbaric that their home countries refused to take them back.' Murphy's February 25, 2026 unlawfulness ruling was largely affirmed by the First Circuit but stayed by the Supreme Court on September 29, 2026 pending its own review, so the legality question remains unresolved.
