title: DHS Ended CHNV Parole and TPS for Hundreds of Thousands, Costing Nursing Homes Their Immigrant Caregivers
status: CHNV parole ended after a May 2025 Supreme Court order; Haiti TPS ended in early Aug. 2026 after the Court's Mullin v. Doe ruling; the Venezuela TPS case went back to the Ninth Circuit Oct. 5, 2026. Providers report continued staff losses; a House-passed Haiti TPS extension is stalled in the Senate.
date_of_action: 2025-03-25 (DHS terminates CHNV parole programs) through 2026-10-05 (Supreme Court sends the Venezuela TPS case back to the Ninth Circuit)
what_changed:
On March 25, 2025, DHS under then-Secretary Kristi Noem terminated the parole programs for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans (CHNV), acting "consistent with" President Trump's Executive Order 14165, which directed DHS to end categorical parole programs including CHNV. About 532,000 people had been paroled in under the programs; the notice ended, as of April 24, 2025, the parole of those whose parole had not already expired, and DHS said it intended to revoke their parole-based work permits (Federal Register). After the Supreme Court let the termination proceed on May 30, 2025, employers began identifying and terminating CHNV parolees, and a retirement community in Florida was among those that had already started letting workers go (U.S. Chamber of Commerce; Refugees International). DHS also moved to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designations: the Supreme Court allowed the termination of Venezuela's 2023 designation to proceed in an October 3, 2025 order, and on November 28, 2025, Noem announced the termination of Haiti's TPS, effective February 3, 2026, saying conditions there no longer met the criteria (Latin Times; Congressional Research Service). A federal judge stayed the Haiti termination in February 2026, but on June 25, 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing non-constitutional challenges to a termination; Haitian TPS work permits ran through July 27, 2026, and the termination took effect in early August, after the D.C. Circuit's August 4 mandate and Judge Ana Reyes's order lifting her stay, affecting over 300,000 Haitians (CRS; Gothamist; Jackson Lewis; National Immigration Forum).

Long-term-care providers, which lean heavily on immigrant labor, reported the effects as each program ended. More than a quarter of an estimated 4 million U.S. direct-care workers are foreign born, according to PHI (AP, July 2025). **One Boca Raton, Florida senior community lost 10 workers whose humanitarian parole ended, with less than 24 hours' notice, and was slated to lose 30 more with the end of TPS for Haitians;** its CEO raised salaries and referral bonuses but said "Americans are not drawn to applying" for the open jobs. A.G. Rhodes, which runs three Atlanta-area nursing homes, expected eight workers to be forced out after their TPS was revoked, and its CEO said "We feel completely beat up right now" (AP, July 2025; the same AP story ran in Fortune and The Haitian Times). In April 2026 he said one A.G. Rhodes housekeeping department was almost entirely made up of workers affected by the November 2025 removal of Haitian TPS, forcing the operator to hire and train replacements quickly, and LeadingAge said providers "are forced to fill gaps overnight" when legally authorized workers lose status (Skilled Nursing News). After the Haiti termination took effect, Cabrini nursing home in Westchester, New York laid off seven full-time Haitian caregivers (Gothamist, August 2026), and Hebrew SeniorLife in the Boston area prepared to terminate 40 Haitian workers whose work permits were expiring (The New York Times, July 2026).

Update 2026-10-19 (Venezuela TPS litigation): Most Venezuelan TPS holders had already lost protection; work authorization for a narrow remaining group ran to October 2, 2026 (Latin Times). On October 5, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated a Ninth Circuit ruling that had found DHS unlawfully ended TPS for certain Venezuelan and Haitian nationals and sent the case back for reconsideration in light of Mullin v. Doe (Envoy Global).
legal_status: CHNV parole: sued (Doe v. Noem, D. Mass.); the Supreme Court on May 30, 2025 let DHS proceed with the termination and work-permit revocations, and on Sept. 12, 2025 the First Circuit vacated the district court's order blocking the terminations and remanded the case. Haiti and Syria TPS: sued (Miot v. Trump, D.D.C.; Doe v. Noem, S.D.N.Y.); district courts stayed the terminations, then the Supreme Court in Mullin v. Doe (June 25, 2026, 6-3) held the TPS statute bars review of non-constitutional claims and that the Haitian plaintiffs' equal-protection claim will likely fail. The D.D.C. stay was lifted Aug. 5, 2026; the equal-protection case remains pending there. Venezuela TPS: the Supreme Court let the termination proceed in October 2025 and on Oct. 5, 2026 vacated and remanded a Ninth Circuit ruling against DHS (Mullin v. National TPS Alliance). Congress: the House passed a Haiti TPS extension earlier in 2026; a Senate unanimous-consent request was blocked June 22, 2026.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the government actions and court rulings, which rest on the Federal Register notice, the Congressional Research Service and contemporaneous legal and news reporting. HIGH confidence that the terminations caused documented staff losses at specific long-term-care facilities: AP (July 2025, repeated verbatim by Fortune and The Haitian Times, so one outlet's reporting), Skilled Nursing News (April 2026), Gothamist (August 2026) and The New York Times (July 2026) each name affected facilities from their own sourcing. These are facility-level accounts; no national count of caregivers who lost work authorization through TPS or parole terminations has been identified, and some reported losses at the same facilities stem from other policies (DACA renewal delays, visa backlogs, the refugee halt), which the entry does not count here. No health or mortality figure tied to the staffing losses has been identified. Earlier versions cited state direct-care workforce losses (New York ~45%, Massachusetts ~38%, Texas ~22%) credited to AP; they come from a 2025 Economic Policy Institute projection of a 4-million-deportation scenario, not of TPS or parole terminations, so they were removed, as was a $129,575 national median private-room cost, which is market context rather than an effect of these terminations.
pull_quote: "When legally authorized workers lose status or face sudden changes in eligibility, providers are forced to fill gaps overnight." -- Amanda Mead, LeadingAge, April 2026

human_toll.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people who had lived and worked legally under CHNV parole or TPS lost their status and work permits, many with little notice, leaving them unable to keep their jobs and exposed to removal. Nursing homes and senior communities, drawing on a national direct-care workforce that is more than a quarter foreign born, lost aides, housekeepers, kitchen staff and nurses in waves as each program ended, and providers warned that older and disabled residents lose the continuity of care that long-time caregivers provide.

human_toll.caveat: The program-wide counts come from DHS's own Federal Register notice and from researchers and advocacy groups quoted by news outlets; the facility counts are what operators told reporters and are examples, not a national tally of caregivers who lost work. Workforce shares come from PHI and KFF. No measured change in resident health or care quality has been tied to these losses. DHS's stated rationale: the CHNV notice said the programs had not delivered the border-security and migration benefits claimed for them and that the government's interest in ending them outweighed reliance interests, including those of employers, who were given 30 days' notice; Noem said conditions in Haiti no longer met TPS criteria; and the administration has said TPS was abused and has become a de facto permanent immigration program. The Supreme Court found the Haitian plaintiffs unlikely to show that race motivated the Haiti termination; the three dissenting justices disagreed.

title: Trump repeatedly proposed deporting convicted U.S. citizens to a Salvadoran prison; none is known to have been sent

officials.name: Donald Trump
officials.role: President; repeatedly proposed deporting convicted U.S. citizens to El Salvador (Feb. 4, April 14 and July 1, 2025)

officials.name: Marco Rubio
officials.role: Secretary of State; announced Bukele's offer to jail "dangerous American criminals," including U.S. citizens, and called it "an act of extraordinary friendship"

officials.name: Pam Bondi
officials.role: then-Attorney General (until April 2, 2026); Trump said in April 2025 she was studying whether convicted U.S. citizens could legally be sent to El Salvador

people.unnamed_affected: No U.S. citizen is known to have been deported under the proposal. Its stated targets are U.S. citizens convicted of violent crimes, whom Trump called 'homegrown criminals.'

status: Unresolved -- remains a repeated public proposal, backed by El Salvador's standing offer to receive such transfers for a fee, but no confirmed executed deportation of a U.S. citizen under it as of the reporting reviewed for this entry.
date_of_action: 2025-02-04 (Trump backs Bukele's offer to jail US citizens) through 2025-07-01 (Trump repeats proposal at Alligator Alcatraz)
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a policy-level accountability question about a stated intent to remove constitutional protections from U.S. citizens, rather than a confirmed completed legal violation. The March 2025 Alien Enemies Act removals, which came between Trump's first endorsement of the idea in February and his April repetition of it, are covered in the entry on the Alien Enemies Act removals.
pull_quote: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly endorsed Bukele's original offer to house convicted U.S. citizens in Salvadoran prisons as “an act of extraordinary friendship.”

glance.what: Repeatedly proposed deporting convicted U.S. citizens to a Salvadoran prison; none is known to have been sent

what_changed: On February 3, 2025, after meeting Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Bukele had offered to house deportees in El Salvador's jails -- including, Rubio said, 'dangerous American criminals in custody in our country, including those of U.S. citizens and legal residents' -- and called the offer 'an act of extraordinary friendship.' The next day, February 4, Trump told reporters at the White House the idea would be 'a lot less expensive' than U.S. prisons, adding: 'We'll have to find that out legally. I'm just saying if we had the legal right to do it, I would do it in a heartbeat.' In a February post on X, Bukele said El Salvador would take convicted criminals, including convicted U.S. citizens, into its CECOT mega-prison for a fee. Trump repeated and escalated the proposal in April 2025. Meeting Bukele in the Oval Office on April 14, he could be heard telling him, 'The homegrowns are next, the homegrowns. You've got to build about five more places,' and he told reporters he would like to include 'homegrown criminals' -- U.S. citizens -- adding that Attorney General Pam Bondi was studying whether it could legally be done. That followed the March 2025 deportation of 238 alleged Venezuelan gang members and 23 alleged MS-13 members to El Salvador's maximum-security prison, 137 of the Venezuelans under the 1798 Alien Enemies Act, according to the White House as reported by Human Rights Watch (a separate, separately litigated episode tracked elsewhere in this database as the Alien Enemies Act removals entry). Constitutional and legal experts across multiple outlets characterized deporting U.S. citizens as unconstitutional, since citizens cannot be denationalized or removed from the country against their will absent a specific, narrow legal process that this proposal does not follow. **Trump raised the idea again on July 1, 2025, touring Florida's newly opened 'Alligator Alcatraz' migrant detention facility: speaking of violent criminals who are 'old to our country,' he said, 'Many of them were born in our country. I think we ought to get them the hell out of here too,' and 'maybe that will be the next job.'** As of the reporting reviewed for this entry, no confirmed instance of an actual U.S. citizen being deported to El Salvador under this proposal had occurred -- it remained a repeatedly and publicly stated intention, paired with the Salvadoran government's standing offer to accept such transfers for a fee.
legal_status: None: no lawsuit, charge or ruling, because no U.S. citizen is known to have been deported under the proposal. Legal experts quoted by ABC News, NPR, NBC News and Al Jazeera called it unconstitutional or illegal; ABC News reported in July 2025 that the issue had not come before the courts.

human_toll.summary: No U.S. citizen is known to have been deported or imprisoned abroad under the proposal, so its harm is projected, not documented. Its targets would be U.S. citizens convicted of crimes, sent to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison, which Al Jazeera reported is notorious for mistreating inmates and bars visits, education and recreation, per multiple reports including Human Rights Watch's. Legal experts told NPR the idea would effectively strip U.S. citizens of constitutional and legal protections.
human_toll.caveat: There is no count of people affected because the proposal has not been carried out. The White House presents it as conditional and narrow: press secretary Karoline Leavitt called it "an idea he has simply floated and has discussed" on April 8, 2025, and said on April 15 that Trump would consider it only "if legal, for Americans who are the most violent, egregious, repeat offenders of crime." Trump said, "We'll have to find that out legally," and Rubio, the day after announcing the offer, said, "There are obviously legalities involved. We have a Constitution." None of the reporting reviewed describes an executive order or agency directive implementing it. Critics such as the Cato Institute's David Bier told NPR the real risk is the administration deporting citizens before courts can review it, as it did with non-citizens sent to El Salvador.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence that the proposal was made, repeated, and publicly endorsed by both Trump and Rubio -- reported by ABC News, NPR, NBC News, and Al Jazeera, with the July 2025 remarks also in the official transcript. The administration describes it as an idea conditional on legality rather than binding policy, and no case of an actual U.S. citizen deported this way has been found, so there is no public figure for people affected; this entry does not establish that any citizen has been sent to a foreign prison. Investigated and ruled out two adjacent-but-distinct cases that could be mistaken for this: Walter Josue Huete Alvarado, a U.S. citizen imprisoned in El Salvador since May 2023 after being arrested by Salvadoran (not U.S.) police at a party during the Biden administration, per The Intercept, unrelated to this proposal; and Kilmar Abrego Garcia, deported to CECOT in March 2025 despite a 2019 immigration-court order shielding him from removal there and returned to the U.S. in June 2025 per the AP, who is a Salvadoran citizen, not a U.S. citizen. Overall deportations to El Salvador roughly doubled in early 2026 (5,033 Salvadorans January-March 2026 vs. 2,547 the same period in 2025, per El Salvador migration figures reported by the AP), but that growth is in non-citizen removals and doesn't bear on this entry's citizen-specific claim. Trump raised the idea a third time on July 1, 2025 at the 'Alligator Alcatraz' facility, per ABC News and the transcript in the Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents -- HIGH confidence. His admission that he did not know whether it was legal ('We'll have to find that out legally ... I would do it in a heartbeat') dates from February 4, 2025, not July 1; ABC's July 1 story repeats that quote without dating it, and it does not appear in that July 1 transcript. Re-verified 2026-10-19: no later statement, directive, lawsuit or deportation of a citizen under the proposal found.

what_changed: Backstory: the government does not count how often immigration agents hold U.S. citizens. ProPublica reported in March 2025 that the GAO had found Customs and Border Protection and ICE "are not even required to track how often they hold citizens on immigration charges." **Early 2025.** Starting the week of January 22, 2025, at least 15 Indigenous people in Arizona and New Mexico reported being stopped at home or work, questioned or detained by federal agents and asked to prove their citizenship, according to Navajo Nation officials; an Arizona state senator said many reported that agents "didn't acknowledge" tribal documents as valid proof, and Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren said citizens had "traumatizing" experiences. In a Philadelphia car-wash raid that January, agents held a 21-year-old citizen at gunpoint and handcuffed him. On February 4, Reps. Jamie Raskin and Pramila Jayapal wrote to acting ICE Director Caleb Vitello and Secretary Kristi Noem about "troubling reports that U.S. citizens have been detained"; ICE called one Milwaukee report "completely false." The same day, after a Border Patrol checkpoint stop in Texas, immigration authorities removed a 10-year-old citizen recovering from brain cancer and four siblings to Mexico with their undocumented parents, who had been rushing her to an emergency checkup in Houston; CBP called the reports "inaccurate," saying people who disregard expedited removal orders "will face the consequences." In early March, ICE agents looking for someone else stopped and handcuffed Jensy Machado, a naturalized citizen, near his Virginia home and released him after he showed his license. **April 2025.** Jose Hermosillo, a 19-year-old citizen from Albuquerque, was held for 10 days at Florence Correctional Center in Arizona after approaching a Border Patrol officer in Tucson for help; DHS said he identified himself as a Mexican citizen who entered illegally, while he said he cannot read and signed the statement because the officer told him to "sign everything." He was released April 17 after his family gave a court his birth certificate. That day, Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, a 20-year-old born in the U.S., was held in Florida at ICE's request after a state immigration charge, though a county judge called his birth certificate "indeed an authentic document". DHS departure emails also reached citizens, including a Pennsylvania-born doctor told "It is time for you to leave the United States"; CBP said notices "may have been sent to unintended recipients." By mid-April, ProPublica found at least a dozen members of Congress had written to the administration about detained citizens without a response. On April 22 and 24, the New Orleans ICE field office detained two mothers and their children at check-ins, held them "incommunicado" according to the ACLU, and deported them to Honduras early on April 25 with three citizen children aged 2, 4 and 7; the 4-year-old, being treated for a rare metastatic cancer, went without his medication. Judge Terry Doughty set a hearing "in the interest of dispelling our strong suspicion that the Government just deported a U.S. citizen with no meaningful process," and DHS's Tricia McLaughlin said the 2-year-old's parents "made the decision" to take her. On April 27, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the children "were not deported" and "The parents make that choice," and border czar Tom Homan said "No U.S. citizen child was deported. Deported means ordered by an immigration judge"; the families' lawyers said the mothers were given no choice. **Mid-2025.** George Retes, a disabled veteran, was held three days without charges after a July 10 raid at the California farm where he worked, per Rep. Jayapal's office; asked about such cases on July 16, Rep. Ralph Norman said, "No, I'm not concerned about that." On July 31, the two Honduran mothers and their children sued ICE, DHS, Noem, acting ICE Director Todd Lyons and others in federal court in Louisiana under pseudonyms, alleging the removals broke ICE's own directive on detained parents and violated the Constitution, and asking that the families be returned. **Fall 2025.** On October 2, masked agents told Frank Miranda, a citizen born in California, he was "on an overstay," handcuffed him outside his Portland workplace and held him for hours at the city's ICE building, his attorney said. That month Noem said "there's no American citizens that have been arrested or detained," according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal's office, and ProPublica counted more than 170 citizens held by immigration agents in the administration's first nine months; McLaughlin told ProPublica, "We don't arrest US citizens for immigration enforcement." On October 21, Raskin and Jayapal renewed their demand, calling the administration's response "flippant and unserious." In the Louisiana suit, the court heard the families' motion to have them returned on November 11. **December 2025.** On December 4, masked agents chased Jacelynn Guzman, 23, to her home in Marrero, Louisiana, as she told them she was born in the U.S.; DHS said she was "a female matching the description of the target" and that agents left once they saw she was not. Asked about that case and a Florida health care worker's detention on CNN on December 7, Homan said "as soon as that questioning's over, if they're a U.S. citizen, they'd be released." On December 9, Senate Democrats on the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations released a minority staff report on 22 citizens detained by federal immigration agents, seven of them held more than 24 hours. Around the end of December, Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino told Fox News that "many of those citizens assaulted federal officers." **2026.** In January, ICE agents in Minneapolis arrested four Oglala Sioux Tribe members at a homeless encampment and moved three to the Fort Snelling ICE facility; Tribal President Frank Star Comes Out said DHS gave only first names and would release more only if the tribe "entered into an immigration agreement with ICE." On February 3, people including U.S. citizens described aggressive encounters with DHS agents at a Capitol Hill forum held by Democratic lawmakers. By mid-February, Star Comes Out still had no information, and DHS told TIME it could not verify that ICE had arrested any tribe members. In March, ProPublica reported that Democratic investigators had compiled 128 cases of children, citizens and noncitizens, injured, left unattended or put at risk in DHS operations; a DHS spokesperson said ICE "does NOT deport United States citizens or separate families." Noem's March 2026 testimony on citizen detentions is part of a perjury referral covered in the Noem perjury referral entry. On April 3, a Texas trooper stopped a pickup near Fredericksburg carrying Brian José Morales García, whose birth certificate shows he was born in Denver; ICE asked officers to hold him, Border Patrol took custody, and he was removed to Mexico on April 7. DHS said agents "did NOT arrest a U.S. citizen" and that he admitted entering the country illegally; he said he was pressured into saying so, and sued in federal court in Austin. ProPublica reported in October that he had been allowed back into the country using his birth certificate. On May 6, ICE agents in the Bronx tackled and handcuffed Jeury Concepcion, leaving him visibly injured; DHS said he matched their target's description and "became combative," and disputed that he was held by mistake; Rep. Ritchie Torres asked the DHS inspector general on May 8 to investigate his "unjust detainment" based on mistaken identity. On May 12, a bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced the Respect Tribal IDs Act to require DHS training on tribal identification; DHS said ICE agents already recognize tribal ID cards as proof of citizenship. Also in May, ICE took the deported 2-year-old's father into custody and removed him to Honduras, where the family was reunited, according to a court filing. On September 20, ICE agents in Evanston, Illinois, detained a citizen they mistook for their target, leaving him with injuries to his head, neck and teeth; DHS said he "was not cooperative and refused to identify himself." On September 21, Judge Brian A. Jackson denied the reunited family's request to be returned after they withdrew it, and paused the other family's while asking for briefing on the boy treated for cancer, who has no access to the care he needs in Honduras and travels to New Orleans for treatment without his mother, the families' lawyers told the court. **On October 6, 2026, ProPublica published an expanded count of 506 U.S. citizens held by immigration agents from January 2025 through September 2026, including more than 100 held after agents questioned their citizenship (nearly all people of color), at least 70 children and teens, 36 held at least a day without being able to reach a lawyer or family, and roughly a dozen deported, mostly children.** DHS told ProPublica, "DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted. We do our due diligence." A brief was filed in the Louisiana suit on October 13. On October 17, ICE agents targeting someone else in Long Beach, California, detained Ricardo Gonzalez, a former city employee who says he is a citizen, and police found him handcuffed and bleeding, and he was taken to a hospital; his daughter said he was struck by an unmarked vehicle while on an e-bike and tased, witnesses said agents broke his arm, while ICE said it "did NOT hit an individual on a bike" and that he "smashed the mirror of a government vehicle."
legal_status: Sued: two Honduran mothers and their U.S.-citizen children sued ICE, DHS, Noem, Lyons and others in July 2025 (M.D. La., 3:25-cv-00669), alleging unlawful seizure, due process violations and breach of ICE's directive on detained parents; on Sept. 21, 2026 the court denied one family's request to be returned after they withdrew it and stayed the other family's pending supplemental briefing; a brief was filed Oct. 13, 2026, and no return has been ordered. In April 2025 Judge Doughty said he had a "strong suspicion" a 2-year-old citizen was deported with no meaningful process; her family's lawyers said on May 13, 2025 that they were dropping that case, before the hearing. A DHS inspector general investigation of one Bronx detention was requested in May 2026; no opening was found. No court has ruled the pattern unlawful.

human_toll.summary: U.S. citizens were stopped, handcuffed, held at gunpoint, injured or detained for hours to days, some without access to a lawyer or family; nearly all of those held after agents questioned their citizenship were people of color. About a dozen, mostly children, were removed from the country, most with deported parents. Indigenous people had tribal IDs rejected and now carry papers to prove they belong. Children recovering from or being treated for cancer were cut off from their care.

human_toll.caveat: No government count exists, so the figures come from ProPublica's own tally, built from social media, court records and local news with at least two sources per case; ProPublica calls it an undercount and counts anyone held against their will for any time, including brief stops, so "detained" is not the same as arrested or jailed. The Senate report is a Democratic minority staff document, not a committee finding, and many individual accounts are the citizens' own or their lawyers'. DHS's position is that it is "NOT arresting U.S. citizens by mistake," that its operations are "highly targeted," that agents may briefly question people they reasonably suspect are in the country illegally and release citizens once confirmed, that some citizens were held for allegedly assaulting or obstructing officers, and that the deported children left with parents who chose to take them, which the families' lawyers dispute.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence that immigration agents detained U.S. citizens and that three citizen children were removed to Honduras with their mothers: the individual cases are documented by NBC News, AP, the Washington Post, NPR, Popular Information (republished by Mother Jones), CNN and ProPublica, and the Louisiana removals by a federal judge's order and the families' court filings. The overall count rests on ProPublica's independent tally rather than government data, so the exact figure is MODERATE confidence and likely low. DHS disputes both the pattern and individual accounts (Hermosillo, Guzman, Concepcion, the Evanston man, Gonzalez, Morales García and the Louisiana mothers' consent); those accounts are reported as each side gives them. Noem's October 2025 quote comes from Sen. Blumenthal's press release. The date of Bovino's Fox News interview is given as The New Republic reported it, a Tuesday around the end of December 2025. Gonzalez's citizenship rests on his and his family's statements, which CNN said it was working to verify, and the claim that agents struck him with a vehicle is his daughter's and a witness's: the Long Beach Post found no video of it or first-hand witness, and ICE denies it. Named citizens either went public or were named by their attorneys or in major reporting; the deported children sued under pseudonyms and are not named here. No rank-and-file agents are named.

status: A rule giving refugees 10 days, not 30, to contest termination took effect Oct. 14, 2026; comments close Nov. 13; no court challenge reported. A nationwide stay on detaining refugees for lacking green cards stands, and the Tenth Circuit held Oct. 5 that courts can review termination findings.
date_of_action: 2025-11-21 (USCIS memo orders review and re-interview of refugees admitted under Biden) through 2026-10-15 (challengers file final summary-judgment brief in Jean A. v. Noem)
what_changed:
Backstory: People admitted through the U.S. refugee program are screened and approved abroad before they arrive, and must apply for a green card after a year here. By law, DHS can terminate refugee status only if it finds the person was not a refugee when admitted. USCIS first sends a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT); until October 2026 the person had 30 days to respond, and there is no administrative appeal of a termination (Federal Register; National Immigration Forum). Terminations had historically been "exceedingly rare" (National Immigration Forum), and DHS said it could not analyze past NOIT outcomes "because USCIS terminated so few cases" (Federal Register). A 2010 ICE policy held that a refugee's failure to apply for a green card was not a proper basis for detention (Jean A. v. Noem docket).

On November 21, 2025, USCIS Director Joseph Edlow signed a memo ordering a comprehensive review and "re-interview of all refugees admitted from January 20, 2021, to February 20, 2025," and immediately suspending green card approvals for them; it said a person found not to have qualified "has no right to appeal" USCIS's decision, though they could plead their case in immigration court (AP, via News4JAX). The Biden administration had admitted 185,640 refugees from October 2021 through September 2024 (AP). On December 18, 2025, an ICE memo began rescinding the 2010 detention policy (Jean A. v. Noem docket).

On January 9, 2026, DHS announced Operation PARRIS (Post-Admission Refugee Reverification and Integrity Strengthening), a "sweeping initiative" to reexamine refugee cases through new background checks and reinterviews, starting with about 5,600 refugees in Minnesota who had not yet received green cards (Federal Register; Reuters, via Yahoo; KSTP). It came as thousands of federal immigration agents were deployed to Minneapolis and St. Paul (Reuters, via Yahoo). **ICE agents then arrested refugees at their homes and elsewhere and flew many to detention centers in Texas.** A class-action lawsuit said more than 100 refugees with no criminal background were arrested (NPR); USCIS records later released under the Freedom of Information Act count 72 unadjusted Minnesota refugees arrested and detained (IRAP). Some were released in Texas with "no money, no documents, no way to get home," the head of a Minnesota resettlement agency told NPR. On January 28, U.S. District Judge John Tunheim in Minneapolis issued a temporary restraining order in U.H.A. v. Bondi barring the arrest or detention of Minnesota refugees on the basis that they had not adjusted to permanent residence, and ordering detained class members released and returned to Minnesota (CourtListener; FOX 9; Reuters, via Yahoo). On February 9 he refused to dissolve the order (CourtListener; KSTP).

On February 18, Edlow and Todd Lyons, the senior official performing the duties of ICE director, issued a joint memo taking the position that DHS may arrest and detain refugees who have lived in the U.S. for a year without obtaining a green card (Federal Register; IRAP). Tunheim granted a preliminary injunction in part on February 27, and the government appealed (CourtListener). On March 23, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Massachusetts, in Jean A. v. Noem, stayed the December and February memos nationwide for the duration of the case, finding the challengers likely to succeed; the government had not opposed the stay (CourtListener). In April the Minnesota plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their suit because the Massachusetts stay already covered Minnesota refugees, Sahan Journal reported, and on a joint stipulation the Eighth Circuit dismissed the government's appeal and vacated the Minnesota injunction (CourtListener; Sahan Journal).

Re-vetting interviews continued in Minnesota, peaking in February and March, often on no more than 48 hours' notice and lasting up to eight hours; USCIS then began sending NOITs from an office in Georgia that conducts computer-based reviews of refugee cases, attorneys told Sahan Journal. They said many notices were left at landlord offices or never reached the refugees, and that terminations rested on credibility findings, small differences between old and new interviews, and social media posts (Sahan Journal). One Ethiopian refugee admitted in 2022, identified by Sahan Journal only under a pseudonym, missed an interview notice, had his refugee status terminated in June 2026, and was placed in removal proceedings at Fort Snelling Immigration Court (Sahan Journal). IRAP sued USCIS, ICE and DHS in the Southern District of New York on May 14 over unanswered records requests about PARRIS; on August 24 USCIS produced 249 pages and data, including records describing Operation PARRIS as "a model for additional vetting operations" and counting 185,539 unadjusted refugees nationwide as of October 2025 (IRAP).

On October 5, the Tenth Circuit ruled 2-1 in Mukantagara v. Mullin that federal courts can review USCIS's finding that a person did not meet the refugee definition when admitted, the mandatory first step of a termination, and sent the case back to the district court; Judge Tymkovich dissented (Tenth Circuit opinion). The lead plaintiff, Agnes Mukantagara, a refugee from Rwanda admitted in 2005, had her status terminated in 2016 when USCIS found the persecutor bar applied to her, which she denies; an immigration judge later found her credible and granted her asylum, and granted it again after a Board of Immigration Appeals remand, with the government's appeal of that grant on hold pending this case. Her son, who had aged out, was ordered removed (Tenth Circuit opinion; IRAP). The same panel had ruled for her in January 2026, then vacated that decision in July to consider a new Supreme Court ruling (Tenth Circuit order).

**On October 14, 2026, an interim final rule signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin cut the time to respond to a NOIT from 30 days to 10, effective immediately and without prior public comment** (Federal Register). Termination ends the person's work authorization at once, and USCIS then processes them for removal (Federal Register). DHS said about 186,000 refugees who arrived in fiscal years 2015 through 2025 have not adjusted status, the maximum population the rule could reach, and that USCIS and ICE are identifying subsets for vetting (Federal Register). Three days are added for mailed notices, but the period runs from the mailing date, not receipt (National Immigration Forum). Comments are due November 13, 2026 (Federal Register). The separate cuts to refugee admissions and resettlement funding are not covered here.
legal_status: Minnesota arrests: sued (U.H.A. v. Bondi, D. Minn., Judge John Tunheim). Temporary restraining order Jan. 28, 2026; motion to dissolve denied Feb. 9; preliminary injunction granted in part Feb. 27; the government appealed, the plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed in April, and the Eighth Circuit dismissed the appeal and vacated the injunction on a joint stipulation Apr. 21. National detention policy: sued (Jean A. v. Noem, D. Mass., Judge Richard Stearns); the December 2025 and February 2026 memos stayed Mar. 23, 2026 for the duration of the case; cross-motions for summary judgment pending, with the government's final brief due Nov. 5, 2026. Judicial review: the Tenth Circuit held Oct. 5, 2026 in Mukantagara v. Mullin that USCIS's finding that a person was not a refugee at admission is reviewable in federal court (2-1; remanded). Records: IRAP sued for PARRIS records (S.D.N.Y., May 14, 2026); USCIS produced documents Aug. 24. The Oct. 14, 2026 rule: no lawsuit reported; comment period open to Nov. 13.

human_toll.summary: Refugees who were screened abroad and admitted lawfully face reinterviews, notices that USCIS intends to end their status, loss of work authorization and removal proceedings. In Minnesota, dozens to more than 100 were arrested in early 2026, many flown to Texas, before courts ordered them released. Under the new rule they have 10 days from service (13 if mailed, counted from the mailing date) to contest a termination, with no administrative appeal.

human_toll.caveat: The 186,000 figure is DHS's own ceiling, everyone admitted in fiscal years 2015-2025 who has not adjusted, not a projection of notices or terminations; the 185,539 count and the 72 arrests come from USCIS records as summarized by IRAP, an advocacy group and litigant, and differ from the more than 100 arrests the class action alleged. No official count of NOITs, terminations or removals has been published: a Minnesota legal aid attorney said hundreds there are potentially affected, and IRAP said it had not yet seen large numbers of notices outside Minnesota (Sahan Journal). DHS's stated rationale: Biden-era processing put admission numbers ahead of screening, a preliminary review of Minnesota cases found the evidence insufficient in most, and a longer notice period "could provide opportunities for aliens to evade enforcement or engage in harmful activities" (Federal Register). A USCIS spokesman said the administration is "ensuring that refugee status is reserved only for those who were eligible under the law" (AP), and DHS called Minnesota "ground zero for the war on fraud" (KSTP). Resettlement groups dispute the claim of lax vetting.

what_changed:
Backstory: on June 6, 2025, federal agents began what administration officials called "the largest Mass Deportation Operation in History" in Los Angeles, with roving patrols stopping people at bus stops, car washes, Home Depot lots, tow yards and farms (the operation itself is covered in the entry on DHS's Los Angeles raid campaign). On June 20, 2025, detained workers including Pedro Vasquez Perdomo filed a habeas petition in the Central District of California; on July 2 the ACLU of Southern California, Public Counsel and other groups turned it into a class action, joined by the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, United Farm Workers, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and Immigrant Defenders Law Center. The suit alleged that masked agents, often without visible badges, stopped people based on race, ethnicity, accent, or presence at day-laborer sites, bus stops, car washes or farms, and denied detainees lawyers in the B-18 basement of the downtown federal building. DHS spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin called claims of targeting by skin color "disgusting and categorically FALSE." On July 7, the City and County of Los Angeles and seven cities moved to intervene in support of the plaintiffs.

**On July 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong issued a temporary restraining order barring stops without reasonable suspicion and barring agents from relying "solely, alone or in combination" on four factors: apparent race or ethnicity, speaking Spanish or accented English, presence at places like bus stops or car washes, and type of work.** She wrote that the government would have the court believe, "in the face of a mountain of evidence," that "none of this is actually happening." A second order required lawyer access at B-18 seven days a week. On August 1, the Ninth Circuit refused to stay the order, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed, though it found one clause too vague. On August 8, 13 more cities joined the intervenors. **On September 8, 2025, the Supreme Court stayed the order pending appeal, without a majority opinion, letting roving patrols resume.** Justice Brett Kavanaugh, concurring, wrote that "apparent ethnicity alone cannot furnish reasonable suspicion" but can be a "relevant factor" with others. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, dissented, describing U.S. citizen Jason Gavidia being pushed against a fence after agents repeatedly asked if he was American, and U.S. citizen Jorge Hernandez Viramontes being driven to a warehouse for questioning. On November 13, 2025, Frimpong granted a preliminary injunction on lawyer access at B-18.

On January 16, 2026, Magistrate Judge Sheri Pym ordered the government to forensically image every phone used by an agent present at 15 identified operations. On February 19, Frimpong let the Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims proceed, writing that the Supreme Court "has not issued any decisions saying that what the Government did in Los Angeles" was lawful and that "What the Government is saying about the Supreme Court decision is false." By May 26, 2026, the government said 885 of 1,253 CBP agents who answered a questionnaire used personal phones for work and 88 consented to imaging; as of June 29 it had imaged no personal phones. On July 27, plaintiffs sought a new injunction against stops based on Latino ethnicity; CalMatters reported the filing cited agents' texts and body-camera footage using the slurs "wet" and "tonks" to pick people to stop, and a May 2025 ICE headquarters directive to "turn the creativity knob up to 11" and arrest more "collaterals." **On July 28, 2026, Frimpong held the government in civil contempt for failing to image the phones, finding the violation by "clear and convincing evidence" and ordering it to pay $500 a day to the court until it complies.** DHS responded that "Our agents are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage."

On September 2, 2026, Frimpong separately enjoined warrantless civil immigration arrests in the district without an individualized finding that the person is likely to escape, barred reliance on a January 2026 memo by then-acting ICE director Todd Lyons to the extent it treats unlawful status alone as enough, and certified a class of people arrested that way since June 6, 2025. On September 21, the magistrate judge rejected the government's request for relief from imaging agents' personal phones; the government objected and asked for a stay, arguing it has no legal power to seize privately owned devices. On October 13, the Justice Department reported its latest weekly payment of $3,500 under the contempt order, said it had complied, and pointed to its pending motion to pause the payments. On October 16, it appealed the September 2 injunction and class certification to the Ninth Circuit.
legal_status: Sued: Vasquez Perdomo v. Noem, No. 2:25-cv-05605 (C.D. Cal.), filed June 20, 2025, renamed Vasquez Perdomo v. Mullin in July 2026. A July 11, 2025 temporary restraining order on stops was stayed by the Supreme Court on September 8, 2025 pending appeal; that order did not rule on whether the stops were lawful. A November 13, 2025 preliminary injunction requires lawyer access at B-18; the government's appeal of it (No. 26-209) is pending. Motions to dismiss were largely denied on February 19 and August 11, 2026. The government was held in civil contempt on July 28, 2026 ($500 a day until it complies with the phone-imaging order) and ordered to pay plaintiffs' fees; it disputes that it can be made to image agents' personal phones. A September 2, 2026 preliminary injunction on warrantless arrests, with a certified class, is on appeal to the Ninth Circuit (filed October 16, 2026). Whether agents' stops violated the Fourth Amendment has not been finally decided, and no agent has been charged or disciplined in any source reviewed.

human_toll.summary: Latino workers, street vendors and U.S. citizens across the Los Angeles region were stopped, handcuffed or detained at bus stops, car washes, tow yards and Home Depot lots, some held in the B-18 basement without lawyers; plaintiffs say people, including citizens, were stopped more than once. Local officials described residents afraid to leave home and canceled community events. The Supreme Court dissent counted nearly 2,800 arrests in the operation's first month; the number of people stopped is not public.

human_toll.caveat: The stop accounts come from plaintiffs' declarations and news interviews, and the phone and arrest-file figures from court records, mostly the government's own reporting to the court; no one has published a count of people stopped. The court's findings so far are preliminary or procedural (a TRO, preliminary injunctions, contempt over discovery), not a final ruling. DHS denies racial profiling: McLaughlin said "DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted" and agents ask questions to determine status, and government lawyers told the court agents weigh appearance only within the "totality of the circumstances," sometimes with "targeted, individualized packages." The Justice Department says it has no legal right to seize agents' personal phones, that imaging hundreds of devices is "enormously burdensome," and that it has now complied. The Supreme Court majority's stay, and Kavanaugh's view that ethnicity can be one factor, favored the government; the slur messages are cited in plaintiffs' filing and not yet tested by the court.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the court record: the TRO, Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court rulings, the contempt order, the September 2026 injunction and the government's October filings were read in the orders and filings themselves (Supreme Court and CourtListener copies), with the case history cross-checked against the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse summary; the Ninth Circuit's August 1 reasoning and the February 19 quotes are taken from that summary. MODERATE confidence on the stop accounts, which are plaintiffs' declarations as described in the Supreme Court dissent and in news reports, and are contested by DHS. The slur texts and the ICE "creativity knob" directive are as CalMatters described plaintiffs' July 2026 filing; the filing itself was not read. Named affected people are plaintiffs named in court filings. Whether the contempt fine has stopped is unresolved: the government says it has complied, while it is still contesting the personal-phone imaging requirement.

section_summaries.what_changed: A judge barred LA stops based on race, language, place or job; the Supreme Court let them resume; in 2026 she held DHS in contempt over agents' phones.
section_summaries.human_toll: Latino workers and U.S. citizens were stopped and detained across the region; of about 1,460 agents tied to the operation, only 88 agreed to phone imaging.
